This paper develops a theoretical account of formative assessment and argues that existing definitions and practice lists are insufficient without a unifying rationale. Black and Wiliam frame formative assessment as classroom practice in which evidence about student achievement is elicited, interpreted, and used by teachers, learners, or peers to make better-founded decisions about next instructional steps.

The paper synthesizes prior literature on formative assessment, self-regulated learning, classroom discourse, cognitive acceleration, and dynamic assessment. Rather than reporting a new empirical study, it proposes a framework of five formative assessment strategies: clarifying learning intentions, engineering effective discussions and tasks, providing feedback that moves learners forward, activating students as instructional resources, and activating students as owners of their learning.

The authors discuss how teachers interpret student responses, how feedback should be strategically and tactically shaped, and how formative assessment relates to broader pedagogies such as cognitive acceleration and dynamic assessment. The main conclusion is that formative assessment is best understood as contingent, interactive regulation of learning, and that improving teacher practice requires stronger models of learner thinking, classroom discourse, and the purposes of instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment can strengthen metacognition, self-assessment, and learner autonomy, but it does not report new outcome data. Its claims are grounded in prior research and conceptual synthesis rather than direct measurement in this article.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-assessment, learner autonomy, and regulation of learning (conceptual outcomes discussed via prior literature)

finding.finding_summary: The authors contend that formative practices can support motivation, persistence, and students’ willingness to maintain learning intentions, especially through self-regulation and volitional strategies. However, this paper does not present original empirical estimates for these outcomes.
finding.measure: Motivation, persistence, volitional strategies, and well-being versus growth orientation

paper_profiles.title: Formative assessment in the English as a foreign language classroom in secondary schools in Poland. Report on a mixed-method study
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Education Culture and Society
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether formative assessment (FA) is actually used in Polish secondary-school English as a foreign language (EFL) classrooms, and if so, how often it is used relative to summative assessment. The study is motivated by the strong educational case for FA and by the fact that formative assessment has been promoted in Poland for years, yet there is little evidence about its everyday classroom use.

The author uses a retrospective mixed-method questionnaire study with 106 first-year university students who had recently graduated from a range of Polish high schools. Students reported, on an 8-point scale, how often they experienced summative assessment and formative feedback for different language skills and subskills (grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation, speaking, writing, reading, listening), as well as which tasks were used for each type of assessment. Open-ended questions asked whether feedback was sufficient, which skills were neglected, and whether assessment patterns affected English learning and relationships with teachers.

The findings suggest that formative assessment was neglected in the participants' EFL schooling, especially for pronunciation and oral skills. Many students reported rarely or never receiving feedback without a credit, and pronunciation was the most commonly identified neglected area. Students also reported negative consequences for learning and motivation, and many linked assessment practices to weaker rapport with teachers. The paper concludes that Polish EFL teachers need more training in formative assessment, especially in pronunciation teaching and assessment, and that assessment practices should be emphasized in both pre-service and in-service teacher education.

finding.finding_summary: Assessment and feedback for writing and reading were reported as relatively infrequent, especially for formative assessment. For formative assessment, 22% to 27% of students said they never received feedback on writing/reading-related skills, and 4% to 12% reported never receiving summative assessment on these skills depending on form; students also specifically named writing as a neglected area (5% in one open-ended item).
finding.measure: Student-reported frequency of summative and formative assessment for writing and reading skills; open-ended reports of neglected skills

finding.finding_summary: The strongest negative finding concerned speaking, listening, and pronunciation. For formative assessment, 20% to 27% of students reported never receiving feedback for speaking/listening, and pronunciation was especially neglected: 25% to 28% reported never receiving formative feedback on pronunciation subskills, while 34% to 36% reported never receiving summative assessment on pronunciation in some forms. In open responses, pronunciation (92% too rarely assessed; 75% too little feedback) and speaking (51% too rarely assessed; 19% too little feedback) were the most frequently identified gaps.
finding.measure: Student-reported frequency of summative and formative assessment for speaking, listening, and pronunciation; open-ended reports

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that sparse formative feedback and assessment practices harmed motivation, confidence, and engagement. In the open-ended responses, 79% believed there were serious negative consequences from receiving so little feedback on progress, and 58% said assessment frequency/manner and choice of skills affected their success in learning English. The paper reports that lack of feedback reduced awareness of weaknesses, encouraged neglect of unassessed skills, and contributed to harder-to-change errors and poorer communication confidence.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of effects on learning success, attitudes, and consequences of limited feedback

finding.finding_summary: The study found limited support for metacognitive development through formative assessment, because feedback that would promote self-assessment, self-monitoring, and reflection was often absent. Students explicitly noted that they were not shown strengths/weaknesses or how to work on problems, and the article concludes that inadequate formative assessment likely weakened autonomous learning habits and self-regulation, especially in pronunciation and speaking.
finding.measure: Student-reported feedback that included strategies, strengths/weaknesses, and self-assessment support; open-ended reflections on learning habits

finding.finding_summary: At the institutional level, the study indicates that formative assessment was not being implemented regularly despite policy support in Poland. Across multiple schools and regions, students reported that FA was often rare or absent, suggesting a gap between national expectations and classroom practice; the author concludes that pre-service and in-service teacher training should devote more time to formative and summative assessment, with particular emphasis on pronunciation.
finding.measure: Survey-based reports of assessment practices across schools and student comments about classroom assessment culture

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not reported (position paper spanning primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional development contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper asks how large language models, especially ChatGPT, might be used beneficially in education and what risks and constraints must be addressed before broad adoption. Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the authors synthesize early research and provide a conceptual overview of opportunities for students and teachers, along with challenges related to bias, privacy, copyright, overreliance, integrity, and unequal access.

The paper discusses potential educational uses across primary, secondary, university, and professional learning contexts, including personalized practice, feedback, lesson planning, assessment support, tutoring, and content generation. It also surveys emerging applications of large language models in education, such as quiz generation, pedagogical agents, code explanation, adaptive feedback, and automated assessment, while emphasizing that most evidence is early-stage and that human oversight remains essential.

The main conclusion is that large language models are promising but should be integrated cautiously, ethically, and with strong pedagogical design. The authors argue for continued research on best practices, transparent governance, and hybrid human-AI workflows that preserve critical thinking, fairness, and educational integrity rather than replacing teachers or authoritative sources.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models can reduce teacher workload by automating or semi-automating tasks such as quiz generation, feedback generation, lesson planning, and grading. For example, it cites work where grading effort was reduced by up to 85% using NLP-based feedback systems, and describes GPT-3-based tools for generating questions, answers, and instructional materials.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, and time spent creating instructional materials

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that large language models may support critical thinking, problem-solving, and reflective learning by providing explanations, prompts, and scaffolds rather than just answers. However, it also warns that overreliance on model-generated output could weaken students' independent thinking if the tools are used as replacements rather than supports.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, and evidence-based use of information

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes positive uses of large language models for reading and writing support, including grammar correction, summaries, outlines, reading comprehension questions, and writing assistance. It cites examples such as GPT-3-generated reading comprehension quizzes and text supports intended to improve literacy-related learning tasks.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension and writing support tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that conversational agents and LLM-based tools can improve engagement, curiosity, participation, and willingness to communicate, especially in language learning and group/remote learning settings. It cites examples where GPT-3 was used to stimulate children's question-asking and where chatbots supported learners with language anxiety.
finding.measure: Engagement, curiosity, participation, and language-learning anxiety/willingness to communicate

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is institutional readiness, governance, and policy implications of adopting large language models in education. The authors argue that successful implementation requires privacy and security protections, bias monitoring, copyright compliance, sustainable infrastructure, fair access, and clear human oversight; they also note risks such as cheating bans and inequitable access.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy/security, fairness, sustainability, and institutional adoption conditions

paper_profiles.title: High-Leverage Instructional Practices for Students with Autism and Mild Disabilities in Traditional and Remote Learning Settings
paper_profiles.venue: Global Journal of Intellectual & Developmental Disabilities
paper_profiles.population: K-12 students with autism and mild disabilities
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article addresses how teachers can implement high-leverage instructional practices (HLPs) for students with autism and mild disabilities in both traditional in-person and remote learning settings, especially during the COVID-19 era. The paper is organized around three teaching principles: plan with a purpose, teach for success, and actively engage learners. It emphasizes that instruction should be individualized, purposeful, data-driven, and aligned with student needs, goals, and curriculum demands.

The article synthesizes practitioner guidance and research-backed strategies for 12 instructional HLPs, including goal setting, systematic lesson design, curriculum adaptation, scaffolding, explicit and intensive instruction, flexible grouping, student self-regulation, generalization/maintenance, active engagement, assistive and instructional technology, and constructive feedback. It discusses how these practices can be adapted for remote learning, such as chunking assignments, using digital tools, monitoring understanding, and providing timely feedback and reteaching.

The population focus is K-12 students with autism and mild disabilities, with particular attention to inclusive general education and special education contexts. Rather than testing an intervention experimentally, the article offers a conceptual and practical review of how these instructional practices may improve academic and social-behavioral outcomes. The main conclusion is that evidence-based, well-planned, and data-informed instruction—delivered with scaffolding, feedback, and technology supports—can help students with disabilities succeed across settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that active student engagement, motivation, and self-regulation can be improved through high-leverage instructional practices, but it does not report original effect estimates. It cites prior research and practitioner guidance that timely feedback, purposeful goal setting, and engaging instruction support student participation and motivation in K-12 settings.
finding.measure: student engagement, motivation, self-regulation

finding.finding_summary: A central focus is teaching cognitive and metacognitive strategies, flexible grouping, and helping students maintain and generalize learning across settings. The article states that these practices support organization, problem-solving, collaboration, and transfer of skills over time, but it does not present new empirical effect sizes.
finding.measure: metacognitive strategy use, collaboration, maintenance/generalization of skills

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes that systematic planning, data-driven progress monitoring, chunking instruction, and the use of assistive/instructional technologies can maximize instructional time and improve the efficiency of teaching and learning. No original quantitative data are reported; the claims are based on synthesized practice recommendations.
finding.measure: instructional efficiency, maximizing instructional time, progress monitoring

paper_profiles.title: Adaptive learning systems for English literature classrooms: A review of AI-integrated education platforms
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Scientific Interdisciplinary Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews how adaptive learning systems integrated with AI are being used in English Literature classrooms and what outcomes they are associated with. Following PRISMA guidelines, the authors synthesize evidence from 94 peer-reviewed papers across native-English, EFL/ESL, bilingual, and resource-constrained settings.

The review focuses on how adaptive platforms tailor text difficulty, sequencing, scaffolds, feedback, and assessment to individual learners. It highlights common technological mechanisms such as natural language processing, learner modeling, recommendation engines, dashboards, and automated writing analytics, alongside pedagogical mechanisms such as scaffolding, formative feedback, mastery learning, and adaptive grouping.

Across the reviewed literature, the strongest and most consistent findings are positive effects on reading comprehension, interpretive accuracy, literary analysis, and writing quality, especially thesis clarity and evidence integration. The review also reports benefits for metacognition, self-regulated learning, engagement, and equity, with adaptive supports helping lower-proficiency, bilingual, and underserved learners access demanding literary texts. Teachers are positioned as facilitators who use dashboard data to reteach, form groups, and lead richer discussions rather than as routine evaluators. Overall, the paper argues that AI-enabled adaptive systems can transform literature instruction when aligned with curricular goals, teacher agency, and accessibility needs.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies (n=94 papers), adaptive learning systems consistently improved reading comprehension, recognition of literary devices, interpretive accuracy, and writing outcomes in English literature contexts. The review reports gains in comprehension of complex texts, thesis clarity, evidence integration, and iterative revision, but it does not provide a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension, literary device recognition, interpretive accuracy, writing quality/thesis clarity/evidence integration

finding.finding_summary: The reviewed literature indicates that adaptive platforms increased engagement, time on task, enjoyment of literature, and motivation by providing individualized feedback and appropriately challenging tasks. The paper describes these effects consistently across settings, but does not report a single quantitative effect size.
finding.measure: Engagement, time on task, enjoyment, motivation

finding.finding_summary: Adaptive systems were reported to strengthen metacognitive development and self-regulated learning through dashboards, progress monitoring, reflective prompts, and iterative feedback. The review also notes improved critical interpretation and collaborative discussion, but the most central durable-skill outcomes are metacognition and self-regulation.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-regulated learning, critical interpretation, collaboration

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests adaptive tools reduced teacher time spent on repetitive explanations and enabled more targeted instruction by surfacing class-wide patterns of difficulty. Teachers used dashboards and analytics to form groups, reteach shared weaknesses, and focus classroom time on higher-order discussion rather than routine correction.
finding.measure: Teacher time on repetitive explanations, instructional targeting, grouping/retargeting of instruction

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that adaptive learning systems can improve equity and accessibility across native-English, EFL/ESL, bilingual, and resource-constrained settings by reducing performance gaps and supporting offline/mobile access, disability-inclusive features, and culturally relevant text selection. These claims are synthesized from the literature rather than estimated with a single quantitative effect size.
finding.measure: Equity/accessibility, performance gaps, access in low-resource contexts

paper_profiles.title: Effect of Differentiated Instruction on Reading Comprehension of Third Graders
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines whether differentiated instruction improves third-grade students’ reading comprehension, addressing a persistent literacy problem in New Mexico and the broader United States. The author frames the study around weak reading achievement, the fourth-grade slump, and the need for elementary teachers to use research-based instruction to support students who are reading below grade level and have limited academic vocabulary.

The study compares differentiated instruction with nondifferentiated instruction using archived PARCC reading comprehension scores from three school years. In this cross-sectional, quasi-experimental causal-comparative design, 128 third-grade students from rural eastern New Mexico school districts were split evenly between an experimental group (differentiated instruction) and a comparison group (nondifferentiated instruction). The intervention lasted the full school year. The analysis used independent-samples t tests and found that differentiated instruction significantly improved PARCC reading scores in all three years examined.

The dissertation argues that differentiated instruction may help teachers meet diverse learning needs through customized lessons, flexible grouping, collaboration, formative assessment, and responsive reteaching. The author emphasizes that teacher training and implementation fidelity matter, and suggests that the findings support professional development and evidence-based literacy instruction in PK-3 classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: Differentiated instruction significantly improved third graders’ reading comprehension as measured by PARCC reading scores across all three school years analyzed. The study included N=128 students (n=64 differentiated instruction, n=64 nondifferentiated instruction) and found statistically significant gains favoring the differentiated group, though the dissertation text provided no exact effect sizes, confidence intervals, or standard deviations.
finding.measure: PARCC reading comprehension scores

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ perceptions of their self-regulated learning practices in elementary school classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study investigates how K–5 teachers implement self-regulated learning (SRL) in their classrooms, how they perceive their own confidence in teaching SRL, and whether their practices differ by school type (public vs. private). The authors frame SRL as an important but often under-taught set of metacognitive, motivational, and behavioral strategies that can support student learning and lifelong thinking skills.

The study used semi-structured interviews with 12 in-service elementary teachers from one public charter school and one private school in Southern California. Interview questions were organized around Zimmerman and Moylan’s cyclical SRL model (forethought, performance, self-reflection) and focused on goal setting, time management, monitoring, help-seeking, and reflection. Teachers reported using SRL mostly implicitly rather than explicitly, often via goal setting based on student needs, monitoring progress, adapting instruction, and reflecting on lessons; they also described high confidence in planning and adjusting instruction.

Across interviews, teachers emphasized structured goals, frequent monitoring of student progress, immediate feedback, and lesson adaptation as central practices. They also described using reflection to improve instruction and attributed success to classroom climate, student relationships, planning, and teaching strategies. Public school teachers reported more summative tracking and time management, whereas private school teachers described greater flexibility and autonomy. The paper concludes that teachers value SRL but typically implement it in implicit ways, suggesting a need for more explicit teacher training and support for SRL instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that SRL-related practices were strongly tied to student engagement, motivation, confidence, and self-efficacy. In the interview data (n=12 teachers), participants described setting socioemotional goals, using feedback to support students, and valuing students' pride and excitement as indicators of success, suggesting SRL is used to promote student motivation and engagement rather than only academic outcomes.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview responses about student engagement, motivation, confidence, and self-efficacy

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on SRL as a durable skill, including metacognition, goal setting, monitoring, time management, help-seeking, self-reflection, and adaptive instruction. In interviews with 12 K–5 teachers, these practices were frequently reported as part of instruction, but usually in implicit rather than explicit form; teachers also said they used reflection and monitoring to adapt lessons and improve instruction.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview responses coded for SRL practices (goal setting, monitoring, time management, help-seeking, reflection, adaptive teaching)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described SRL practices as supporting instructional organization and classroom management, including structured schedules, timers, flexibility, and constant monitoring of student progress. The study does not test productivity outcomes quantitatively, but the interview findings indicate that teachers use SRL to manage time, track goals, and adjust instruction more efficiently in practice.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview responses about time management, goal tracking, assessment, and adaptation of instruction

paper_profiles.title: Secondary Teachers' Perceptions of the Implementation of Response to Intervention
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines why secondary teachers at one urban high school were struggling to implement Response to Intervention (RTI) with fidelity. The study is framed by the Concerns-Based Adoption Model and asks what teachers perceive about RTI implementation, what procedural concerns they have, and what supports or resources they need to implement the model effectively.

Using a qualitative case study design, the author gathered data from a purposeful sample of 12 Grades 9-12 teachers through semistructured interviews and two classroom observations per teacher. The study found recurring themes of limited and ineffective professional development, inadequate knowledge of differentiated instruction, inconsistent implementation procedures, and a strong need for additional professional development. The main conclusion is that teachers need clearer guidance, more consistent implementation expectations, and stronger training/support to deliver RTI as intended; the project that emerged from the study was a 3-day professional development plan aimed at improving fidelity of RTI implementation and, ultimately, student academic outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that RTI implementation at the school was undermined by inconsistent procedures, limited and ineffective professional development, and insufficient support/resources. Based on interviews and classroom observations with a purposeful sample of 12 secondary teachers, the study concluded that a 3-day PD intervention was needed to improve fidelity of implementation and support the school’s RTI system.
finding.measure: Semistructured teacher interviews; classroom observations; thematic analysis of RTI implementation perceptions and fidelity-related concerns

paper_profiles.title: How Secondary English Teachers Employ Formative Assessment and Feedback to Scaffold Students’ Odyssey in English Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative case study examines how secondary English teachers in rural Nepal use formative assessment and feedback to support students’ English learning. The authors focus on a gap in the literature: while formative assessment is widely advocated, less is known about how teachers actually enact it in everyday EFL classrooms, especially how assessment results are used for scaffolding and immediate feedback.

Using semi-structured interviews and classroom observations, the study involved eight English teachers and eight students from eight community secondary schools in five districts of Nepal. The analysis, guided by sociocultural theory, the zone of proximal development, and Lajoie’s adaptive scaffolding framework, found that teachers mainly used oral questioning, classwork, homework, class tests, and repeated reteaching to check understanding and provide support. However, feedback was often delayed, limited, and mostly verbal, frequently delivered in Nepali rather than English, and none of the teachers used ICT for feedback.

The study concludes that teachers did use some formative assessment and scaffolding practices, and students valued collaborative/group learning and peer support, but implementation was constrained by limited teacher training, heavy workload, large classes, and examination-oriented teaching. The authors argue that more targeted professional development in formative assessment and feedback is needed so teachers can better connect evidence of learning with instructional responses that improve English language development.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers’ use of formative assessment, especially oral questioning, classwork, homework, class tests, and reteaching, was reported to support students’ English learning, particularly in written activities. However, the study is qualitative and reports no effect sizes; the main evidence is that these practices were perceived as helpful for identifying misunderstandings and supporting progress (n=16 participants: 8 teachers, 8 students).
finding.measure: Teachers’ and students’ reports/observations of English learning support through formative assessment; classroom work and written exercises

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests formative assessment and immediate feedback could support English language learning more broadly, but teachers focused more on written work than oral communication, and their feedback was often insufficient to develop communicative competence. Students valued oral interaction and group work, yet the observed practice did not strongly support speaking/listening development.
finding.measure: Classroom observations of oral questioning, feedback, and group interaction; participant perceptions of English learning

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers reported that collaborative activities and peer support improved engagement with English learning, and students preferred group work to individual work. The study does not measure motivation or self-regulation directly, but it indicates that collaborative formative practices were perceived to encourage participation and shared problem-solving.
finding.measure: Reports of student preference for group work, peer feedback, and collaborative classroom participation

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly links formative assessment and feedback to scaffolding, peer collaboration, and support for problem-solving in English learning. Teachers’ group tasks and peer assistance were described as helping students share ideas and solve learning problems, although these practices were inconsistently implemented and not strongly individualized.
finding.measure: Interview and observation evidence of collaborative learning, peer assistance, and scaffolding practices

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that large class sizes, heavy workloads, and limited time made it difficult to check work and provide timely feedback. The study shows formative feedback practices were constrained by staffing and scheduling realities, reducing the efficiency and consistency of implementation.
finding.measure: Teacher reports about workload, class size, time constraints, and ability to provide timely feedback

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that school and system-level conditions in Nepal shape formative assessment use: teachers reported limited training on assessment and feedback, examination-oriented practices, and weak administrative monitoring. The paper argues that teacher professional development and institutional support are needed to improve implementation, but it does not evaluate policy effects directly.
finding.measure: Teacher accounts of training, administrative support, and examination-oriented assessment practices

paper_profiles.title: Informal Professional Development for Enhancing a High School Mathematics Teacher’s Blended Learning Data Practices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines a practitioner-researcher’s use of informal professional development to improve blended learning data practices in a high school mathematics classroom. The central problem is that many in-service teachers are expected to implement blended learning without targeted training, especially on pedagogical uses of digital formative assessment, data-informed grouping, and differentiated instruction.

The study used mixed methods action research in an Algebra 2 Honors classroom with 29 students during the 2024–2025 school year. The intervention consisted of three iterative action research cycles using digital warm-ups and exit tickets, self-efficacy surveys, practitioner journal reflections, critical friend field notes, and student feedback/reflections. The author used these data to adjust instruction, strengthen mastery-level grouping, and refine scaffolds and pedagogical alignment.

The dissertation concludes that data-driven decision-making improved instructional responsiveness and that data-informed grouping supported differentiated learning. It also reports that scaffolding, student-centered design, and peer modeling were associated with improved academic performance and stronger student confidence/engagement. Overall, the study argues that iterative action research can function as an effective form of informal professional development for teachers who lack formal blended-learning training.

finding.finding_summary: The dissertation reports improved academic performance in an Algebra 2 Honors classroom after the teacher implemented digital formative assessments, data-driven instructional adjustments, and differentiated instruction across three action research cycles. The study involved 29 students; however, no standardized achievement effect size or confidence interval is reported in the text provided.
finding.measure: Algebra 2 academic performance / content mastery

finding.finding_summary: Students reported greater confidence and engagement after the blended learning data practices were implemented. The dissertation describes increased self-efficacy, with peer modeling, mastery-oriented practice, and a supportive classroom environment cited as contributing factors; descriptive statistics are referenced for pre- and post-intervention self-efficacy, but no effect size is provided in the excerpt.
finding.measure: Student self-efficacy surveys; engagement reflections

finding.finding_summary: The study indicates that students benefited from scaffolding, mastery-oriented practice, and peer modeling, suggesting gains in self-regulation and related learning behaviors within the blended learning environment. These outcomes were discussed as part of the classroom changes associated with the intervention, but the excerpt does not report a separate durable-skills effect size or inferential test.
finding.measure: Student reflections and classroom observations related to self-regulation and learning behaviors

paper_profiles.title: Data-Driven Instruction Use for Residency II Candidates After Clinical Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This doctoral study examined a local problem in teacher preparation: Residency II teacher candidates were reportedly scoring adequately on formal assessments of instructional decision-making, yet mentor teachers and candidates themselves indicated weaker real-world ability to use assessment data to modify instruction. The study asked how scores on the edTPA Task 3 Rubric 15, TEAM evaluations, mentor perceptions, and candidates’ self-reports compared, with a focus on whether teacher candidates could collect, interpret, and act on student assessment data during field experience.

Using a qualitative case-study design, the author reviewed preexisting institutional data for Residency II candidates at a southeastern public state university, including edTPA Rubric 15 scores, TEAM rubric scores from master clinicians and university supervisors, mentor teacher surveys, and a candidate survey. The population was Residency II teacher candidates in a K-6 elementary licensure context, with references to samples such as 27 candidates in the qualitative study and related institutional cohorts from prior years. The study also informed a 3-day professional development workshop project intended to strengthen data-driven instruction skills.

The main conclusion was that candidates were generally meeting expectations on edTPA and TEAM measures, but survey data suggested dissatisfaction with their training in using assessment data and a lack of qualitative feedback to support instructional modification. The dissertation argues that teacher preparation programs should provide more structured, practice-based training in data use, feedback, and instructional adjustment, rather than relying mainly on performance measures that do not capture whether candidates can actually implement data-driven instruction in classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that Residency II candidates met expectations on formal evaluation measures related to using assessment data, but the evidence suggested gaps in practical training and feedback for actually modifying instruction. The abstract reports n=27 candidates in the qualitative case study, and institutional data showed low satisfaction with data training; however, no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: edTPA Task 3 Rubric 15, TEAM rubric, mentor teacher survey, candidate qualitative survey

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies an institutional mismatch between teacher-preparation assessments and actual candidate readiness to use data for instruction. Candidates’ survey responses indicated insufficient satisfaction with data training, suggesting the program may need redesigned professional development; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Alignment among edTPA, TEAM, mentor evaluations, and candidate survey results

finding.finding_summary: The dissertation centers on candidates’ ability to analyze assessment data, make instructional decisions, and modify teaching based on evidence—skills closely tied to data literacy and reflective decision-making. Findings indicated that candidates were meeting rubric expectations yet still reported insufficient preparation and support for these skills; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Assessment-data analysis and instructional modification competency

paper_profiles.title: A Critical Review of Research on Student Self-Assessment
paper_profiles.population: K-20 students (elementary through postsecondary; studies largely K-16/K-20 contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper critically reviews research on student self-assessment, with a particular emphasis on work published from 2013 to 2018. The author revisits what self-assessment is, arguing that it is most useful when treated as a formative feedback process rather than a summative judgment of ability. She proposes a taxonomy organized by what is assessed (competence, process, or product), why it is assessed (formative vs. summative), and how it is done (e.g., rubrics, checklists, self-monitoring, self-testing).

The review synthesizes 76 empirical studies across K-20 settings, including elementary, secondary, and postsecondary contexts. It examines four major research areas: consistency between student self-assessments and external judgments, links between self-assessment and achievement, student perceptions of self-assessment, and the relationship between self-assessment and self-regulated learning. The paper argues that formative, criteria-based self-assessment is more likely than summative self-assessment to support learning and performance, especially when students are given explicit standards, feedback, and chances to revise their work.

Across the reviewed studies, the most consistent pattern is that formative self-assessment is associated with improved learning outcomes and stronger self-regulated learning, while summative self-assessment often shows poor alignment with external grades or ratings. The author concludes that future work should move away from merely measuring accuracy and instead investigate the cognitive and affective mechanisms through which self-assessment influences learning, as well as the pedagogical conditions under which it is most effective.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that formative self-assessment is consistently associated with improved writing quality and other literacy outcomes. A meta-analysis of 10 studies found an average weighted effect size of 0.62 on writing quality, and multiple quasi-experimental/experimental studies found treatment groups outperformed comparison groups on writing tasks when self-assessment was scaffolded with rubrics, criteria, and revision opportunities.
finding.measure: Writing quality / written assignment scores
finding.study_size: n=10 studies in one meta-analysis; additional studies across K-20, not_reported total participants

finding.finding_summary: The review includes evidence that formative self-assessment supports speaking and English language performance, though this is based on a smaller set of studies than writing. The author notes experimental/quasi-experimental findings showing treatment groups outperformed comparison groups on speaking English outcomes and that students using formative self-assessment generally improved their performance.
finding.measure: Speaking English / language performance outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review cites studies in math-related contexts indicating that self-assessment can improve numeracy-related performance, including work on math word problems and task-specific self-evaluation. However, the paper does not pool a math-specific effect size; the evidence is summarized narratively as positive when self-assessment is formative and criteria-based.
finding.measure: Math word problem performance / mathematical task performance

finding.finding_summary: The review includes science-oriented studies and reports positive associations between self-assessment and science-related learning outcomes, particularly when students use formative self-evaluation to improve reports or understand scientific concepts. The paper emphasizes that such effects are strongest when self-assessment is linked to clear criteria and revision.
finding.measure: Science reports / science learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Across non-literacy academic tasks, the review reports that formative self-assessment generally improves performance in diverse subjects and contexts, including exams, map-making, dart-throwing, and vocational tasks. The paper concludes that the strongest pattern across the 25 achievement studies is a positive association between formative self-assessment and learning, though specific pooled effects are only reported for writing and self-grading.
finding.measure: General academic achievement across varied subject tasks
finding.study_size: 25 achievement studies reviewed; not_reported total participants
finding.effect_size: g=0.34 (self-grading meta-analysis); additional task-specific studies not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that self-assessment is associated with stronger self-regulated learning, motivation, self-efficacy, self-satisfaction, and related motivational beliefs, especially in formative contexts. For example, studies of task-based self-evaluation reported gains in self-efficacy and motivation, and the review describes consistent positive perceptions and self-regulatory benefits when students actively revise based on self-assessment.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning questionnaires; motivational beliefs; self-efficacy; self-satisfaction
finding.effect_size: eta^2=0.06–0.42 in some studies; other effects not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that self-assessment supports metacognition and other durable skills, especially when students use rubrics, checklists, self-monitoring, and self-testing to judge their own work. Studies summarized in the review found small-to-moderate, statistically significant gains in self-regulation and metacognitive processes, with one study showing associations across forethought, performance, and reflection phases of SRL.
finding.measure: Metacognition / self-regulation measures; think-aloud protocols; self-report questionnaires
finding.study_size: 12 SRL studies; additional process studies not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review discusses task selection and study efficiency as downstream effects of self-assessment, but evidence is limited and mostly indirect. One cited study of 15 students found inaccurate self-assessment was linked to poor task selection, while the broader conclusion is that self-assessment may help learners make more appropriate next-step decisions when it is formative and criteria-based.
finding.measure: Task selection / study behavior after self-assessment
finding.study_size: n=15 in one exploratory study; broader evidence not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Online Instruction in Higher Education: Promising, Research-based, and Evidence-based Practices
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Education and e-Learning Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews recent empirical literature on online learning in higher education to identify instructional practices associated with effective learning, engagement, satisfaction, and persistence. The authors deliberately narrowed the corpus to studies published from 2013 to 2019 and focused on undergraduate and graduate learners because earlier online-learning research was considered outdated due to rapid changes in pedagogy and technology.

Using a systematic review approach, the authors screened 516 studies and retained 104 empirical studies that met criteria for methodological detail and verifiability. The review organized findings into five themes: course design factors, student support, faculty pedagogy, student engagement, and student success factors. Across these studies, the authors found that many common online-course features—such as multiple pedagogies, strong instructor presence, clear feedback, socialization, and academic support—were associated with better satisfaction or outcomes, but results were often mixed and few studies supported strong causal claims.

A central conclusion is that there is limited evidence for any single research-based intervention in online higher education beyond faculty feedback, which the authors identify as the only clearly evidence-based practice in their corpus. Many other approaches show promise, especially timely and useful instructor feedback, orientation to online learning, and support structures that increase engagement and persistence, but the review emphasizes the need for more rigorous experimental and meta-analytic work before stronger causal conclusions can be made.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, engagement, satisfaction, motivation, self-efficacy, persistence, and sense of community were often associated with stronger outcomes in online higher education, but findings were inconsistent across measures and contexts. Examples reported in the review include significant links between feedback/presence and motivation, engagement and course grades, and student support and retention, but several studies also found no effects for some interaction or support variables.
finding.measure: Engagement surveys, satisfaction surveys, motivation scales, self-efficacy measures, persistence/retention indicators, course grades, and course completion/withdrawal rates
finding.study_size: n=104 studies (review corpus); individual study sizes varied

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies several durable-skill-related practices associated with learning in online courses, especially collaboration, self-regulation, metacognition, and help-seeking. Reported findings include positive associations between group trust and knowledge building, metacognitive support and higher self-regulation scores, and feedback use and improved performance on similar tasks, although not all studies found consistent benefits.
finding.measure: Knowledge-building outcomes, self-regulation/metacognition scales, collaboration indicators, and performance on related tasks
finding.study_size: n=104 studies (review corpus); individual study sizes varied

finding.finding_summary: The review covers a wide range of non-literacy academic outcomes in higher education, including course achievement, exam scores, concept understanding, writing, and problem-solving. Overall, online, blended, and face-to-face modalities often showed no significant differences in course achievement, though some specific interventions such as instructor feedback, learning-partner recommendations, metacognitive supports, and certain support structures improved performance in particular studies.
finding.measure: Course grades, end-of-term tests, exam scores, writing scores, problem-solving task completion, and concept understanding measures
finding.study_size: n=104 studies (review corpus); individual study sizes varied

finding.finding_summary: The review includes a smaller set of findings relevant to operational efficiency, especially the use of clickstream data, clickers, and instructional feedback to modify teaching and improve student learning activities. Some studies reported better learning outcomes and engagement when instructors used student learning data responsively, but the paper does not provide a consistent effect estimate across studies.
finding.measure: Learning analytics indicators, clickstream data use, engagement during instructional activities, and instructional adjustment outcomes
finding.study_size: n=104 studies (review corpus); individual study sizes varied

paper_profiles.title: Incorporating fantasy into gamification promotes student learning and quality of online interaction
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether adding a fantasy/narrative element to an existing gamification design model improves online learning outcomes in a postgraduate e-learning course. The authors were motivated by evidence that the original goal-access-feedback-challenge-collaboration (GAFCC) gamification model produced early engagement but that students’ interest declined over time, suggesting a novelty effect.

Using a design-based research approach, the study compared two implementations of the same fully online postgraduate course across two consecutive semesters. Study 1 implemented the original GAFCC model with 26 postgraduate students; Study 2 refined the design by adding a narrative fantasy layer (GAFCC-F, “Save Princess Joanne”) and included 23 postgraduate students. The course was delivered synchronously online via Zoom and used Moodle, with the same instructors, content, rubrics, and assignments across both iterations.

The paper combines quantitative evidence from pre-, mid-, and post-tests, forum participation logs, content coding of discussion posts, and social network analysis, with qualitative evidence from student and teacher interviews. The main conclusion is that the fantasy-enhanced gamification model produced better learning performance and richer online interaction than the original gamified design, while also being positively perceived by most students and teachers. The authors argue that fantasy helped sustain motivation, create a sense of narrative progression, and reduce the decline in engagement seen in the original gamified version.

finding.finding_summary: Compared with the original GAFCC model, the GAFCC-F model produced significantly higher learning performance on the mid-term test (M=69.13, SD=14.29 vs. M=42.50, SD=21.56; t(47)=-5.02, p<0.001) and post-test (M=83.52, SD=7.35 vs. M=77.82, SD=9.89; t(47)=-2.26, p=0.028). Prior knowledge did not differ at pre-test (t(46)=-0.54, p=0.595).
finding.measure: Pre-test, mid-term test, and post-intervention test of learning performance in an e-learning design course
finding.std_deviation: Pre-test SD=11.11 vs 10.77; mid-term SD=14.29 vs 21.56; post-test SD=7.35 vs 9.89

finding.finding_summary: The fantasy-enhanced model improved engagement and motivation-related outcomes. Students in the GAFCC-F group participated more in discussion forums over time, showed higher forum post quality, and reported greater interest and enjoyment of the online learning experience than students in the original GAFCC group. The paper reports strong qualitative evidence of reduced novelty effects and sustained involvement in the narrative-based condition.
finding.measure: Forum participation logs, student reflections/interviews, and perceptions of engagement in fully online learning
finding.study_size: Study 1 n=26; Study 2 n=23; interviews with 15 students and 2 teachers

finding.finding_summary: The GAFCC-F group showed stronger peer interaction and higher-level online discourse than the GAFCC group. Social network analysis indicated higher density (0.289 vs. 0.223), lower centralization (0.269 vs. 0.309), and higher out-degree/in-degree centrality (0.601/0.4112 vs. 0.509/0.342), suggesting more distributed interaction. Content analysis also found more elaborating/giving examples (46 vs. 35) and reflecting/evaluating posts (68 vs. 42), along with higher knowledge quality in discussion forums.
finding.measure: Discussion forum post quality, coded interaction themes, and social network indicators (density, centralization, out-/in-degree centrality)
finding.std_deviation: Knowledge quality SDs reported per forum; density/centrality are network measures, not SD-based

finding.finding_summary: The fantasy-enhanced model was associated with more sustained task completion and discussion participation over the semester, countering the drop-off observed in the original GAFCC condition. The paper frames this as improved engagement efficiency in the online course, with more students continuing to complete tasks and interact across the 10-week implementation.
finding.measure: Counts of forum posts and quiz attempts over time; participation patterns in the gamified course

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper examines the role of formative assessment in improving student learning and describes how it could be implemented through the BlackBoard Learning System at Swinburne University of Technology’s Sarawak campus. The paper frames formative assessment as a diagnostic process that provides frequent feedback during instruction, contrasting it with summative assessment and arguing that regular, low-stakes testing can support learning more effectively than end-of-semester exams alone.

The implementation described involves weekly or fortnightly online tests delivered through Blackboard, with question formats such as multiple choice, true/false, matching, and essay items. The system was designed to provide immediate score reporting and detailed feedback after each attempt, and the paper argues that this would help students identify mistakes quickly, keep up with course content, and prepare better for semester-end assessments.

Empirically, the study relies on a student questionnaire about perceptions of continuous assessment and Blackboard-based testing, supplemented by descriptive and inferential analyses of attitudes across Business, Engineering, and IT streams. Students generally supported frequent internal assessments and preferred the Blackboard option because of immediate feedback, flexibility, and the ability to study content in smaller chunks. The paper concludes that formative assessment, especially when paired with timely feedback and e-learning tools, is viewed favorably by students and may help improve learning and summative performance, though the paper does not report direct achievement outcome data.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported favorable attitudes toward frequent internal assessments and Blackboard-based formative testing because they believed the approach supported learning in steps, provided constant feedback, and helped them stay on track. Open-ended responses also suggested that immediate feedback reduced delay in correcting mistakes, although some students worried that too many tests could create stress and pressure.
finding.measure: Student perceptions/attitudes survey about continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and Blackboard online tests

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on formative assessment’s role in metacognition and self-monitoring, arguing that frequent assessment with feedback helps students reflect on their performance, identify strengths and weaknesses, and understand how to improve. Students said the approach helped them check whether they were on track and learn topics progressively, but these are perception data rather than direct performance measures.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of self-monitoring, reflection, and checking understanding through feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Blackboard-based formative assessment would help students learn course content progressively and better prepare for semester examinations. However, no direct achievement scores or pre/post test results are reported; the evidence is limited to student perceptions that the method would improve learning and future exam performance.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of learning progress and preparedness for summative semester examinations

paper_profiles.title: On ℓ2-performance of weakly-hard real-time control systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies control systems in which the feedback/control input can be lost because of communication failures or deadline misses, modeled using weakly-hard real-time (WHRT) constraints. The central question is how to analyze and synthesize controllers not just for stability, but for ℓ2-performance, i.e., worst-case disturbance amplification from an input signal to an output signal.

The authors formulate WHRT control systems as constrained switched systems whose switching sequences are generated by a graph representation of the allowable packet-loss patterns. They derive sufficient linear matrix inequality (LMI) conditions for ℓ2-performance analysis and then introduce a lifting method that 'discretizes' the system at successful control attempts, producing a smaller graph and enabling controller synthesis. The lifting also removes the need for an auxiliary state in the hold strategy and keeps the ℓ2-gain unchanged.

The paper is mathematical and control-theoretic, with a numerical example illustrating the approach on a 2-state discrete-time plant. No K-12 or postsecondary learners, classrooms, or educational interventions are studied. The main conclusions are that the proposed lifted formulation reduces computational complexity relative to the non-lifted graph, and that LMI-based synthesis can produce controllers with improved guaranteed ℓ2-performance compared with a previously proposed stabilizing controller.

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review and practical guide arguing that generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment when used in pedagogically informed ways. The authors frame formative assessment around three core questions: where learners are going, where learners currently are, and how to move them forward. They then map LLM uses onto these functions, including rewriting learning objectives in student-friendly language, generating prompts for co-constructing success criteria, producing sample work for critique, creating questions to diagnose current understanding, and drafting process-level feedback.

The paper is not an empirical test of an intervention. Instead, it synthesizes existing research and illustrates likely classroom uses through examples, prompt templates, and screenshots, including examples drawn from high school biology and undergraduate functional MRI teaching contexts. The authors repeatedly stress that LLMs should augment, not replace, teacher expertise, and that outputs must be checked for accuracy, appropriateness, and alignment with pedagogical goals.

The main conclusion is that accessible LLMs may help scale formative assessment tasks that are often time-consuming for educators, especially in large classes or resource-constrained settings. However, the paper also emphasizes important limitations: current evaluation benchmarks often miss formative qualities of feedback, LLM outputs can vary unpredictably, and educators need stronger prompt design knowledge and domain expertise to use these tools well. The paper ultimately calls for future research on robust metrics, culturally responsive applications, and AI-aware assessment strategies that build transferable skills while reducing overreliance on AI-generated responses.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or streamlining formative assessment tasks such as rewriting objectives, generating sample work, drafting questions, and producing feedback. No empirical study is reported, so the claim is conceptual rather than measured; the paper presents illustrative examples showing how these tools may save time in large or resource-constrained classrooms.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review specifically links LLM-supported formative assessment to durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, and self-regulation. It argues that generating exemplars, co-constructing success criteria, and providing process-level feedback can help students reflect on quality, monitor their own learning, and avoid passive reliance on AI, but no direct outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper gives multiple literacy-focused examples, especially rewriting formal learning objectives into student-friendly language and generating sample methods sections or essays for critique. These are presented as plausible supports for reading and writing instruction, but the paper does not report experimental effects or learner outcome data.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Scientific-reasoning applications are illustrated through biology and fMRI examples, including generating simplified biology objectives and sample scientific methods text. The paper suggests these uses can clarify scientific concepts and method-writing expectations, but it provides no empirical evidence of improved scientific reasoning outcomes.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Data-Driven Control of Nonlinear Systems: Beyond Polynomial Dynamics
paper_profiles.venue: Proc. IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a control-theoretic problem rather than an education problem: how to design stabilizing controllers for unknown continuous-time nonlinear systems using only measured input-state data. The authors focus on systems with rational dynamics and, more broadly, nonlinear systems that can be expressed using non-polynomial basis functions.

The proposed approach reformulates the unknown system dynamics into a linearly parameterized polynomial equation and uses a quadratic noise-bound assumption to characterize all systems consistent with the data. With this parametrization, the paper derives sum-of-squares (SOS) conditions for robust state-feedback controller design, including a performance extension that can enforce quadratic performance such as an L2-gain bound. The paper demonstrates the method on numerical examples, including a rational two-state system, a drug-distribution model, and an undamped pendulum.

The contribution is methodological and computational: it shows that robust stabilization and performance guarantees can be obtained from noisy data without an explicit model, and that the approach extends to systems linear in non-polynomial basis functions via polynomialization. No K-12 or postsecondary learning intervention is studied, and there are no student learning outcomes in the paper.

paper_profiles.title: Geometric Programming-Based Control for Nonlinear, DAE-Constrained Water Distribution Networks
paper_profiles.population: Not education population; urban water distribution networks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of controlling water distribution networks (WDNs) under nonlinear hydraulic constraints. The authors focus on the operational challenge of selecting pump and valve schedules that satisfy mass and energy balance while minimizing costs and maintaining safe tank levels, despite the nonconvexity introduced by pipe head-loss and pump head-gain equations.

The proposed approach is a geometric programming (GP)-based model predictive control (MPC) method. The key idea is to transform the original nonlinear difference-algebraic equation (DAE) control problem into a sequence of convex GP problems by exponentiating variables and iteratively approximating nonlinear pipe and pump relationships with monomial constraints. Unlike prior methods, the formulation does not require known flow directions and does not restrict the network topology to trees.

The paper presents a simulation case study on an 8-node benchmark water network from the EPANET manual, using varying water demand over a 24-hour horizon. Results show that the GP-MPC controller maintains tank water levels near a safety setpoint and adapts pump speed to changing demand, while the iterative GP procedure converges over successive optimization windows. This is a control-systems paper about infrastructure operations rather than an education study, so it does not provide evidence relevant to student learning outcomes or formative assessment.

paper_profiles.title: Analysis and design of model predictive control frameworks for dynamic operation: An overview
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an overview of model predictive control (MPC) frameworks for dynamic operation in nonlinear constrained systems. It addresses a control-theoretic problem: how to design MPC schemes when the desired operating point is not stationary, can change online in unpredictable ways, or is not directly expressible as a feasible setpoint or trajectory.

The article synthesizes several strands of MPC research, including stabilizing terminal ingredients for tracking, time-varying reference tracking, artificial-reference MPC, periodic tracking, partially decoupled tracking and planning, and economic MPC. It explains the theoretical conditions needed for recursive feasibility, constraint satisfaction, stability, and performance, and contrasts design choices such as terminal equality constraints, parametrized terminal costs/sets, and online optimization of artificial references.

The paper is methodological and mathematical, focused on nonlinear control applications such as robotics, aerospace, autonomous driving, HVAC, water and power systems. It does not study an educational population or educational intervention, and it reports no K-12 or postsecondary learning outcomes. Its main contribution is a unified exposition of existing MPC methods, their guarantees, limitations, and open problems for dynamic operation.

paper_profiles.title: On Controller Design for Systems on Manifolds in Euclidean Space
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a control-theoretic method for designing controllers for dynamical systems whose state evolves on a manifold rather than in Euclidean space. The central idea is to embed the manifold in a higher-dimensional Euclidean space, extend the system to the ambient space, and then modify the dynamics off the manifold to add transversal stability while preserving the original on-manifold dynamics.

The author then uses ordinary linearization in the ambient Euclidean space to construct tracking controllers, avoiding the need for local charts or more specialized differential-geometric linearization methods. The paper provides theoretical results guaranteeing exponential convergence to the manifold under the transversal-stabilization construction and derives several tracking controllers for two benchmark mechanical systems: a fully actuated rigid body and a quadcopter.

The paper is methodological and control-theoretic rather than educational: it does not study students, schools, or instructional interventions. Its evidence consists of mathematical proofs and simulations demonstrating tracking performance and robustness to disturbance in the two engineering examples. As a result, it does not provide empirical findings relevant to K-12 or postsecondary learning outcomes or formative assessment.

paper_profiles.title: Kernel-based error bounds of bilinear Koopman surrogate models for nonlinear data-driven control
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a control-theoretic problem: how to obtain rigorous, deterministic error bounds for data-driven surrogate models of unknown nonlinear dynamical systems. The authors focus on Koopman-operator-based modeling, specifically kernel extended dynamic mode decomposition (kEDMD), and seek to overcome limitations of prior approaches that either rely on probabilistic guarantees or on restrictive assumptions about dictionary invariance.

The proposed method constructs a bilinear surrogate model for a sampled nonlinear continuous-time system using a Wendland-kernel reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) lifting. The paper derives pointwise, state- and input-dependent approximation error bounds for the surrogate, showing how the residual scales with sampling period, fill distance, and system properties. These bounds are then linked to robust controller design, yielding end-to-end closed-loop guarantees for the original nonlinear system.

The paper is methodological and purely in the control/systems domain, with no human participants or educational setting. A numerical example on a nonlinear building temperature control process illustrates the surrogate model and compares it to a SafEDMD-based baseline, showing that the proposed kEDMD surrogate can support guaranteed controller design and favorable prediction performance. The main conclusion is that kernel-based Koopman surrogates can provide rigorous control guarantees while avoiding some of the theoretical weaknesses of earlier data-driven approaches.

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CHI-like workshop paper / ACM venue)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers can co-design AI-integrated curriculum for use in regular classrooms, with the broader goal of making AI education more accessible beyond computer science courses. The authors argue that AI education is often designed as standalone computing content, which can limit access for students and teachers in non-CS settings.

To address this, the authors ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators from a range of subject areas (e.g., ELA, science, history, ESL, computer science, STEM, library science). Teachers received introductory presentations on AI, explored AI tools, completed pre-work, and then worked in small groups with researchers to design lesson plans integrating AI into core subjects. The paper reports on teachers’ values and design considerations during the process, emphasizing evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration as major concerns.

The workshop produced three example integrated curricula: a social studies lesson on data and government policy, an ESL lesson using AI for pronunciation practice, and a literacy lesson for students with learning disabilities. The authors conclude that teachers were enthusiastic about integrating AI into core subjects and particularly valued scaffolding for ethics, reflection, and student engagement. The paper is primarily descriptive and design-oriented rather than an intervention study of student learning outcomes, but it suggests that integrated AI curriculum could broaden access to AI learning for non-CS and non-technical students.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified collaboration, reflection, and engagement as central design goals in integrated AI curricula, and the co-designed lessons explicitly incorporated group work, student reflection, and discussion. The paper reports that these features were viewed as important for supporting learning and participation, but it does not measure student outcomes, so the finding is based on teacher-design evidence rather than learner performance data.
finding.measure: Teacher workshop discussions, co-designed lesson plans, and thematic coding of workshop audio/transcripts

finding.finding_summary: Teachers repeatedly emphasized student engagement as a key consideration, proposing anchors such as real-world issues, student-driven topics, competition, and gamification to motivate learners. The paper reports that participants viewed these approaches as effective for increasing interest and participation in AI-integrated lessons, but it does not include direct measures of student motivation or engagement.
finding.measure: Teacher workshop discussions and curriculum drafts

finding.finding_summary: One of the three curriculum drafts focused on ESL and integrated AI into pronunciation practice using an AI-powered application. The paper describes how students would record correct and incorrect pronunciations to train a classifier and use the app to support pronunciation learning, but it reports no student outcome data or effect estimates.
finding.measure: Co-designed ESL curriculum concept focused on pronunciation practice
finding.study_size: n=15 teachers (design study); student sample not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The workshop produced a literacy curriculum for students with learning disabilities in which vocabulary words, images, and classification tasks were used to integrate AI concepts with literacy learning. The paper indicates this design was intended to support vocabulary development and literacy engagement, but it does not report direct literacy achievement outcomes.
finding.measure: Co-designed literacy curriculum for vocabulary/image classification activities
finding.study_size: n=15 teachers (design study); student sample not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that co-design with teachers can improve the accessibility and likely classroom adoption of AI curriculum by aligning it with teachers’ needs, subject contexts, and practical constraints. Evidence is qualitative and based on participants’ feedback that the workshop increased familiarity with AI and confidence in integrating it into their curriculum; no institutional implementation outcomes are measured.
finding.measure: Teacher self-ratings of familiarity/confidence and thematic analysis of workshop discussions

paper_profiles.title: Online Diagnostic Assessment in Support of Personalized Teaching and Learning: The eDia System
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual analysis paper introduces the eDia online diagnostic assessment system and argues for its role in supporting personalized teaching and learning through regular formative feedback. The paper is motivated by a central problem in education: teachers need timely, objective information about what students already know in order to differentiate instruction in heterogeneous classrooms, but traditional paper-based assessments are too slow and resource-intensive to provide this at scale.

The authors describe the theoretical basis of eDia, including three-dimensional assessment frameworks in reading, mathematics, and science that distinguish disciplinary knowledge, application, and psychological/cognitive dimensions. They explain how the system combines item banking, automated scoring, adaptive test construction, immediate feedback, and data analytics to make frequent diagnostic assessment feasible in schools. The platform was designed primarily for Grades 1–6 in Hungary, though the paper also notes use in preschool, higher education, and international research contexts.

Rather than testing a single intervention in an experiment, the paper synthesizes development work, pilot studies, and examples of eDia-based applications. Its main conclusion is that technology-based diagnostic assessment can improve the practicality and richness of formative assessment, especially by enabling frequent feedback, better measurement of harder-to-observe constructs, and support for differentiated instruction. The paper also emphasizes that assessment alone does not improve learning; its value depends on how teachers use the feedback, and it argues for teacher training and instructional models that can act on the assessment information.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that eDia improves assessment efficiency by automating item delivery, scoring, data processing, scaling, and feedback generation. It reports that the system can handle regular diagnostic testing for a large population (up to about 600,000 Grade 1–6 students) and has operated in experimental mode in more than 1,000 schools with over 25,000 items, but no effect size is reported because this is a conceptual/system description rather than an outcomes trial.
finding.measure: Assessment system functionality, scalability, automated scoring, and feedback turnaround

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents eDia as an infrastructure for school- and system-level diagnostic assessment, including centralized assessments, teacher-initiated assessments, and use in longitudinal national research. It reports deployment in over 1,000 Hungarian primary schools and use in the Hungarian Educational Longitudinal Program, suggesting institutional adoption and scalability, but it does not report causal policy effects or impact estimates.
finding.measure: Institutional adoption, implementation scale, and use in longitudinal/national assessment programs

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes reading assessment frameworks and item banks for Grades 1–6 and argues that diagnostic feedback can support personalized instruction in reading. It summarizes validation work showing that the three-dimensional reading framework is usable in the eDia system, but it provides no learning-outcome effect sizes for reading achievement.
finding.measure: Reading diagnostic assessment within eDia (framework-based reading tasks and feedback)

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes mathematics assessment frameworks, adaptive testing options, and diagnostic use in Grades 1–6. It emphasizes that the system can provide formative information on mathematical development and application, but it does not report experimental effects on math achievement or provide any quantitative effect size.
finding.measure: Mathematics diagnostic assessment within eDia (framework-based math tasks and feedback)

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents science assessment frameworks and notes that eDia has been used for assessing scientific reasoning and scientific inquiry skills in Hungary and in international studies.
