The paper argues that these assessments would better reflect scientific reasoning, but it does not report empirical outcomes.
finding.measure: Structured scientific investigations, science inquiry tasks, science portfolios

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses broader academic areas beyond literacy, math, and science, including social studies/history, arts, world language, career/technical education, and interdisciplinary projects. These are presented as part of the proposed accountability and portfolio system, with no empirical outcome estimates reported.
finding.measure: History/social studies inquiry, arts performance, world language demonstrations, CTE competencies

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines formative assessment as a way to improve learning and student performance, with emphasis on how an online learning management system (BlackBoard) can support frequent low-stakes assessment and immediate feedback. The authors frame formative assessment as a diagnostic process that should help students identify weaknesses, reflect on feedback, and improve before summative semester-end exams.

The implementation described is a Blackboard-based online testing approach at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus). The proposed format involved weekly or fortnightly online tests with detailed immediate feedback, and a survey of university students was used to gauge attitudes toward continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and the Blackboard test option. Students generally supported the approach because it broke work into smaller topic-based assessments, provided immediate feedback, and helped them track their understanding; some also worried that too many tests could increase stress and overemphasize learning over grades.

The paper does not report an experimental comparison of learning outcomes, but instead combines a conceptual review of formative assessment literature with descriptive survey findings about student perceptions. It concludes that formative assessment can support learning, especially when feedback is timely, specific, and criterion-referenced, and argues that the Blackboard system is a practical tool for implementing such assessment in higher education. The paper also suggests, drawing on prior literature, that formative assessment may be particularly helpful for low achievers, though that claim is not directly tested in this study.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent Blackboard-based formative assessments were helpful because they provided immediate feedback, helped them monitor strengths and weaknesses, and kept them engaged with the subject throughout the semester. However, some students also reported stress and pressure from too many tests, indicating a mixed affective response rather than uniformly positive engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Student perception survey on continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and Blackboard test implementation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment supports metacognition because students are given time to reflect on feedback and their own performance, and then work with the teacher to improve. In the student survey, respondents said the approach helped them understand where they stood and learn topics progressively, but no direct performance measure of metacognitive skill was reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of metacognition plus student perceptions of feedback usefulness

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students supported splitting course work into multiple small-topic assessments, particularly because it helped them study in manageable steps and receive immediate feedback. A statistically significant difference by stream was found for views on continuous assessment as open-book assessments (Cramer’s V=0.206, p<0.05) and on rating the Blackboard test option (Cramer’s V=0.236, p<0.05), with engineering students favoring the option more strongly than business and IT students.
finding.measure: Survey of attitudes toward frequent internal assessments, open-book assessment, and Blackboard test option

finding.finding_summary: At the institutional level, the paper argues that Blackboard can make formative assessment more workable in university teaching by enabling weekly or fortnightly online tests with detailed feedback. The evidence is descriptive and implementation-focused rather than outcome-based, but the authors conclude that this approach could support continuous assessment practices and potentially improve semester grades.
finding.measure: Implementation feasibility and student perception of Blackboard-supported continuous assessment

paper_profiles.title: Embedded Formative Assessment in the Undergraduate Engineering Classroom
paper_profiles.venue: American Society for Engineering Education (ASEE) Conference & Exposition
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an overview of embedded formative assessment in undergraduate engineering education, with a particular focus on how technology has made in-class feedback collection easier and more common. The authors argue that formative assessment helps students think actively, improves metacognition, and gives instructors timely information about student misunderstandings, but they also note that its benefits depend on how instructors use the feedback.

The paper describes classroom uses of clickers, cell-phone polling, and especially open-format responses collected in real time, including examples from an undergraduate electromagnetics course for third-year engineering physics majors. The examples illustrate how open-ended questions can reveal student misconceptions, gaps in mathematical fluency, and shortcuts in reasoning, and how instructor interpretation of those responses can guide subsequent instruction.

Overall, the article is primarily a conceptual and practitioner-oriented discussion rather than an empirical evaluation. It concludes that technology-facilitated formative assessment can support active learning and metacognition in undergraduate engineering classrooms, but that its learning impact is limited if instructors do not respond to the feedback or if questions fail to expose student thinking.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that embedded formative assessment increases student metacognition by making learners more aware of what they know and do not know, and by prompting them to refine their understanding. The claim is illustrated through an undergraduate electromagnetics example (n=60) in which open-format responses revealed misconceptions and incomplete reasoning, but no formal effect size or controlled comparison is reported.
finding.measure: Metacognition and revealed student thinking in open-format classroom responses
finding.study_size: n=60 (illustrative classroom example); not_reported for overall evidence base

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that formative assessment actively engages every student with learning and can increase confidence by helping students realize what they know and what they do not know. It also suggests that confronting cognitive dissonance can prompt further interest in learning, but these points are presented as theoretical/practitioner claims rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Student engagement, confidence, and interest in learning

finding.finding_summary: In the undergraduate electromagnetics example, students’ open-format responses showed difficulties with calculus-related skills such as expressing infinitesimal charge, setting integral limits, and evaluating dot products. The paper uses these responses to argue that formative assessment can surface gaps in mathematical fluency and support immediate instructional response, but it does not report a quantified treatment effect.
finding.measure: Calculus fluency and problem-solving in electromagnetics derivations
finding.study_size: n=60 (illustrative classroom example); not_reported for overall evidence base

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on using embedded formative assessment to improve understanding in STEM/engineering contexts, especially through questions that probe conceptual understanding, derivations, and graphical reasoning in electromagnetics. In the example with n=60 students, responses revealed misconceptions about Gauss’s law and the electric field of a nonuniformly charged sphere, showing how open-format prompts can expose scientific reasoning processes, though no numerical effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual understanding and reasoning in undergraduate electromagnetics
finding.study_size: n=60 (illustrative classroom example); not_reported for overall evidence base

finding.finding_summary: A major argument of the paper is that technology-facilitated formative assessment reduces clerical burden for instructors by streamlining collection and analysis of student responses through clickers, mobile polling, and tools such as InkSurvey. The paper presents this as a practical improvement in classroom workflow rather than a measured productivity outcome, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Instructor clerical burden / efficiency of collecting and analyzing responses

paper_profiles.title: Student’s Video Production as Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.venue: ICPE 2013 – International Conference on Physics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether student-produced videos can serve as a useful formative assessment tool in high school physics. The authors argue that videos may reveal not only whether students understand physics content, but also how they reason, plan, collaborate, and communicate in ways that traditional tests may miss.

The approach was implemented in a Brazilian federal high school (Colégio Pedro II) with first-, second-, and third-year students in physics. After formal instruction, students worked in self-selected groups of up to five to create short videos on course topics; they also submitted a brief written explanation. The teacher reviewed and discussed the videos, then analyzed them for content accuracy, clarity, coherence, technical format, and evidence of understanding.

The paper reports descriptive findings from 55 videos produced by 232 students in 2011. The authors found that many videos were only partially correct in physics content, but that video production still exposed misconceptions and learning difficulties that were not always visible in standard assessments. They also report a strong correlation between technical quality and content quality, and conclude that student video production can function as a reliable formative assessment tool in high school physics, while also supporting collaboration and metacognitive reflection.

finding.finding_summary: The videos revealed mixed evidence of physics understanding: 35% (19/55) were judged correct, 45% (25/55) partially correct, and 15% (8/55) incorrect. The paper also reports that the physical ideas were clear in 47% (26/55) of videos and that the content was logically sequenced in 87% (48/55), suggesting that student-produced videos can expose both accurate and inaccurate scientific reasoning.
finding.measure: Teacher analysis of physics content accuracy, clarity, logical sequence, and connection between proposal and product in student-produced physics videos

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that video production elicited metacognitive and collaborative processes because students had to plan, replan, coordinate group work, and choose communication forms. While not quantified with a formal effect size, the author’s qualitative analysis suggests that the activity supported planning, self-monitoring, and collaboration as part of completing the project.
finding.measure: Qualitative observation of planning/replanning, collaboration, and project completion during video production

finding.finding_summary: The videos were described as engaging and motivating for students, with the authors noting that students spent time preparing them and that the activity fostered interaction and socialization. The paper presents this as evidence that video production can support engagement and persistence in learning physics, though no formal engagement measure was reported.
finding.measure: Observational evidence of student engagement, motivation, and participation during the video project and class discussion

paper_profiles.title: Foundations for AI-Assisted Formative Assessment Feedback for Short-Answer Tasks in Large-Enrollment Classes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether natural language processing can support formative assessment of short-answer responses in large-enrollment introductory statistics courses. The motivation is that write-to-learn tasks can promote learning in science and mathematics, but scoring open-ended responses is too time-consuming for instructors in large classes.

Using de-identified responses from 1,935 postsecondary students across 29 class sections at 15 institutions, the authors compare agreement among human raters and between human raters and an automated scoring model (SFRN), then pilot clustering of response texts to support scalable feedback. The paper does not test student learning outcomes directly; instead, it establishes that detailed rubrics and NLP-based scoring can achieve substantial reliability, with pairwise QWK values generally above 0.74, Fleiss’ kappa around 0.68-0.70, and automated scoring accuracy of 83% versus 72% for an LSTM baseline.

The main conclusion is that human-machine collaboration appears feasible for scalable formative assessment in large statistics courses. The study emphasizes operational feasibility and scoring reliability rather than effects on achievement or other learner outcomes, and it suggests future research on feedback, revision, and learning gains enabled by automated scoring.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that NLP-assisted scoring can support scalable formative assessment with high inter-rater agreement and strong algorithm-human agreement. Across 1,935 students and 7,258 unique task responses, human raters showed substantial agreement (pairwise QWKs = 0.71-0.83; Fleiss’ kappa = 0.68-0.70), and the SFRN algorithm reached 83% classification accuracy, suggesting reduced instructor burden for grading short-answer tasks.
finding.measure: Inter-rater reliability, algorithm classification accuracy, and clustering consistency for short-answer scoring

paper_profiles.title: Teacher Learning of Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how science and mathematics teachers learn to implement Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment (TEFA), a pedagogy that combines classroom response system technology with question-driven instruction, dialogical discourse, formative assessment, and meta-level communication. Rather than testing student outcomes directly, the project asks how teachers change over time, what tensions they encounter, and what professional development supports their learning.

The study is a five-year, longitudinal, staggered-site professional development project involving approximately 39 teachers across four sites in western Massachusetts. The participants are mostly middle school and high school math/science teachers, and the paper uses a mixed-methods design with interviews, journals, surveys, classroom video, logs, and observations. Four teacher cases (high school chemistry, high school math, middle school science, middle school math) are presented to illustrate different learning trajectories.

The main conclusion is that TEFA is challenging but learnable, and that teachers can meaningfully change their classroom practice within a year of sustained professional development. Across cases, teachers became more comfortable with the technology, improved their question design and classroom discourse, and increasingly used formative assessment information to adjust instruction. The paper also argues that teacher learning follows an evolving trajectory: early struggles are often centered on technology, then question design, then classroom discussion, while deeper adaptation of TEFA depends on integrating the pedagogy with teachers’ contexts, constraints, and students’ needs.

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes one high school math teacher and one middle school math teacher, but it does not report student achievement effects on mathematical numeracy. The evidence is mainly that TEFA was used in mathematics classrooms to support review, diagnose student understanding, and improve discussion quality; no quantitative mathematics outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: teacher-reported classroom implementation and use of TEFA in mathematics lessons; no direct student math achievement measure reported

finding.finding_summary: Science teachers used TEFA to elicit students’ thinking about concepts and to promote discussion and reasoning in chemistry and middle school science classes. The paper reports that teachers gained more information about how students were thinking about concepts and changed lessons accordingly, but it does not provide student-level effect sizes or standardized science outcomes.
finding.measure: classroom discussion quality, formative assessment use, and teacher reports/video evidence of students’ thinking in science lessons
finding.study_size: approximately n=39 teachers total; 2 focal science cases plus other participating teachers

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that TEFA increased student participation, engagement, and willingness to discuss ideas, though this varied by class and teacher approach. Examples include increased voluntary participation in whole-class discussion, more student-student interaction, and better engagement after implementation changes; no formal engagement scale or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: student participation, engagement, and classroom interaction patterns observed in video, logs, and teacher reports
finding.study_size: approximately n=39 teachers; student survey administered once per semester to every student in participating classes

finding.finding_summary: This is a central focus of the paper: TEFA is explicitly designed to develop metacognitive skills, self-regulation, and collaborative/discursive habits through question-driven instruction and meta-level communication. The paper reports qualitative evidence that teachers believed TEFA helped students reflect on their thinking, participate in dialogue, and self-monitor confidence, but it does not report student effect sizes.
finding.measure: metacognitive prompting, self-regulation, discussion/collaboration, and student thinking made visible during TEFA cycles
finding.study_size: approximately n=39 teachers across middle and high school settings

finding.finding_summary: A major finding is that TEFA has clear implementation costs for teachers: it requires substantial preparation time, classroom time, and sustained professional development, and teachers often struggled with question design and managing class time. At the same time, teachers reported becoming more efficient with practice, gaining more actionable information about students, and using TEFA as a classroom-management and instructional tool.
finding.measure: teacher time spent on preparation and discussion, implementation logs, PD reflections, and reported instructional agility
finding.study_size: approximately n=39 teachers; four focal case studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that TEFA was adapted across math and science classes and used for content review, conceptual discussion, and exam preparation, but it does not report direct outcomes for other academic subjects. Its academic contribution is mainly about how teachers use formative assessment to support subject-specific instruction rather than measured gains in a non-math/science content area.
finding.measure: content-specific lesson use and teacher-reported instructional adaptation

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Curiosity Using Interactive Simulations Combined with Real-Time Formative Assessment Facilitated by Open-Format Questions on Tablet Computers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether real-time formative assessment, coupled with interactive simulations and open-format questions, can be used to reveal and stimulate student curiosity in a lecture-based STEM course. The authors argue that curiosity is often hidden in traditional settings because only a small subset of students ask questions, and they propose a technology-mediated approach to collect student-generated questions as learners explore simulations.

The intervention used InkSurvey on tablet computers to let junior-level engineering physics undergraduates submit open-ended responses while interacting with four online physics simulations. Student questions were categorized into six curiosity types (incongruous, congruous, modifying, generalizing/analogy, causal/creative, informational), and the distribution of categories was analyzed across activities. Across simulations, most questions were congruous, with smaller proportions reflecting incongruity, modification, analogy, and creativity, suggesting that students were actively engaged and that the method surfaced forms of curiosity not usually visible in class.

The study concludes that students were more curious than they appeared in lecture and that the approach can support metacognition, critical thinking, and richer class discussion even without extrinsic incentives. The authors suggest the method could be adapted broadly in science and engineering courses, but the evidence comes from a single undergraduate physics class and is primarily descriptive rather than causal.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that interactive simulations paired with open-format formative assessment elicited extensive science-relevant questioning from engineering physics undergraduates, indicating engagement with scientific models and mechanisms. Across four simulations, 32-68 student questions per activity were categorized mostly as congruous scientific questions, with additional incongruous, modifying, and analogy-based questions that reflected model-based reasoning and critique.
finding.measure: Student-generated open-ended questions about interactive physics simulations, categorized by curiosity type

finding.finding_summary: The central claim is that the formative assessment approach increased or revealed student curiosity and participation without extrinsic motivation. The authors report that students were willing to submit multiple questions in real time, that curiosity appeared higher than visible in lecture, and that the activity supported motivation to engage with the material.
finding.measure: Frequency and content of student questions; observed participation/engagement during simulation activities

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly argues that the activity fostered metacognition, critical thinking, and question generation skills. Students used open-format prompts to reflect on what they observed, what the simulation illustrated, and what they were curious about, and the resulting questions were used to discuss model limitations and connections across phenomena.
finding.measure: Student question categories; instructor interpretation of metacognitive and critical-thinking behaviors

finding.finding_summary: The intervention supported physics content learning and mathematical application by motivating students to ask how to calculate the consequences of the models shown in simulation. The authors note that several responses reflected interest in computation, geometry, inductance, and model limitations, which were used as springboards for introducing course content and misconceptions.
finding.measure: Student comments/questions about calculation, geometry, and model application in physics contexts

paper_profiles.title: A Chain-of-Thought Prompting Approach with LLMs for Evaluating Students’ Formative Assessment Responses in Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can be used to score and explain short-answer formative assessment responses in K-12 science, with a particular focus on middle school Earth science. The authors argue that open-ended science assessment is difficult and time-consuming for teachers to score, especially when responses involve both conceptual understanding and scientific reasoning, and that automated scoring systems should also provide explanations that are useful for feedback.

The proposed approach combines GPT-4 with few-shot in-context examples, chain-of-thought prompting, and a human-in-the-loop active learning workflow. The system is evaluated on 270 students’ responses from two Vanderbilt SPICE studies in a middle school Earth science curriculum about water runoff. The assessment items asked students to interpret and critique a conceptual model, and the model was tested on scoring subscores for conceptual knowledge and scientific reasoning, comparing zero-shot, few-shot, few-shot plus chain-of-thought, and chain-of-thought plus active learning variants.

Results show that GPT-4 often aligned well with human scorers, with some subscores reaching strong or near-perfect agreement depending on the prompting strategy. However, performance varied by item type: chain-of-thought and active learning sometimes improved performance, but they also sometimes caused overfitting and reduced accuracy on more ambiguous sub-scores. The paper’s main contribution is methodological rather than instructional: it demonstrates a viable approach for automated formative assessment in middle school science and identifies where prompt-based scoring is fragile, especially for open-ended items that require nuanced reasoning or rubric refinement.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates automated scoring of middle school science formative assessment responses that included scientific reasoning subscores. Across the three questions, GPT-4 with chain-of-thought prompting and active learning often improved agreement with human scorers; for example, Q3 scientific reasoning achieved QWK=0.94 with CoT+AL for Runoff Direction reasoning and QWK=1.00 for Arrow Size reasoning in the few-shot and CoT+AL settings, while Q2 reasoning subscores were more difficult and sometimes declined with added CoT/AL due to ambiguity and overfitting.
finding.measure: Agreement between GPT-4 and human scores on science reasoning subscores; Macro F1 and Cohen’s Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK)

finding.finding_summary: A central aim of the paper is to reduce teacher workload by automating scoring and generating explanations for open-ended formative assessment responses. The authors report that the system could score responses and provide rubric-linked explanations, suggesting potential efficiency gains for teachers in middle school science, although the study did not directly measure time saved, workload reduction, or implementation cost.
finding.measure: Automated short-answer scoring and explanation generation for formative assessment responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses formative assessment as supporting students’ self-evaluation and learning from feedback, and its system is intended to generate explanations that can help students understand why responses were scored a certain way. However, metacognition/self-regulation are not directly measured as student outcomes; the evidence is indirect and mainly tied to the system’s explanatory capacity rather than student behavioral change.
finding.measure: Explanation quality and rubric-linked feedback generation intended to support self-evaluation

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment II. Indications of Effectiveness in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether InkSurvey, a free web-based tool for real-time formative assessment using open-format responses on pen-enabled mobile devices, can support learning across diverse educational settings. The authors argue that instructors need an efficient way to gather timely evidence of student thinking so they can adjust instruction before misconceptions become entrenched.

The paper presents a set of seven vignettes from physics, mathematics, chemical engineering, food science, and biology courses spanning K-12, community college, undergraduate, graduate, and university settings in the United States and Mexico. Students used tablet PCs, iPads, and Android tablets/smartphones to submit sketches, graphs, calculations, and written responses. Across the cases, instructors report that InkSurvey made student thinking more visible and allowed immediate feedback, re-teaching, and enrichment.

The reported evidence is mostly descriptive, combining instructor observations, student comments, and some pre/post or comparison data. The paper reports reduced persistence of a calculus misconception (1 of 87 students vs 12 of 103 in a comparison section), improved Algebra I mastery in a high school class, higher quiz performance in redesigned undergraduate and graduate food chemistry courses, steady growth in problem-solving skill in an upper-level engineering physics course, and increased conceptual understanding in chemical engineering simulations. It also reports that students felt more engaged, more aware of their understanding, and more reflective about their learning, suggesting potential benefits for metacognition and classroom participation. Overall, the paper concludes that InkSurvey is a promising formative assessment approach, but the evidence is heterogeneous and largely based on case studies rather than controlled experimental designs.

finding.finding_summary: A calculus III vignette reported that after an InkSurvey-guided lesson on triple integrals over general regions, only 1 of 87 students still showed the targeted misconception on a summative assessment two weeks later. In a comparison lecture section without InkSurvey, 12 of 103 students made the same mistake on the corresponding exam questions, indicating substantially better conceptual retention and problem performance for the InkSurvey section.
finding.measure: Summative exam questions on triple integrals over general regions; persistence of a specific misconception

finding.finding_summary: In chemical engineering courses using interactive simulations plus InkSurvey, student understanding across six targeted concepts increased from about 1.8 to about 3.1 on a 4-point competence scale after scaffolded instructor questioning and feedback. The paper interprets this as stronger conceptual understanding when real-time formative assessment was used to diagnose misconceptions and guide exploration.
finding.measure: Conceptual understanding/competence ratings on six chemical engineering concepts

finding.finding_summary: In undergraduate and graduate food chemistry courses redesigned with InkSurvey and related pedagogy, students showed improved performance on summative quizzes compared with the same courses four years earlier. Mean quiz scores improved by 0.6 points in the undergraduate course and 0.5 points in the graduate course out of 10 possible points.
finding.measure: Summative quiz scores in food chemistry courses

finding.finding_summary: Student survey and focus-group evidence suggests InkSurvey increased engagement, motivation, and active participation. In one survey of 63 junior-level physics students, 54 (86%) said InkSurvey gave the instructor a better understanding of what they did and did not understand, and 48 (76%) said creating responses helped them better understand the material or realize what they did not understand.
finding.measure: Student attitude survey; focus-group comments about engagement and motivation

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports evidence that InkSurvey supported metacognition and self-assessment. In the junior-level undergraduate physics survey (n=63), 48 students (76%) reported that constructing InkSurvey responses helped them better understand the class content or recognize what they did and did not understand, and instructors noted that students could analyze their own and classmates’ thinking. The authors also describe gains in problem-solving skill in an upper-level engineering physics course, with steady improvement across the semester.
finding.measure: Self-reported metacognition/self-assessment; problem-solving skill ratings
finding.study_size: n=63 for survey evidence; course study size not_reported for problem-solving vignette

finding.finding_summary: Instructors report that InkSurvey made it easier to identify common difficulties quickly and provide immediate feedback, reducing the delay between misconception diagnosis and instructional response. The paper describes this as improving classroom instruction and allowing teachers to tailor lessons in real time, though no formal workload or time-efficiency metric is reported.
finding.measure: Instructor-reported ability to identify difficulties and deliver immediate feedback

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment I. Applications in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.population: Mixed (K-12, Community College, Undergraduate, Graduate School)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a set of seven instructional vignettes showing how InkSurvey, a free web-based tool for real-time formative assessment, can be used with pen-enabled mobile devices (tablet PCs, iPads, and Android devices) across a range of educational settings. The central problem addressed is how instructors can gather richer evidence of student thinking during class, respond immediately to misconceptions, and make formative assessment more practical than traditional methods such as clickers or delayed written work.

The approach relies on open-format questions that students answer using digital ink to draw, sketch, graph, or write responses. Instructors then review the responses in real time and use them to guide discussion, scaffold understanding, and adjust instruction. The vignettes span mathematics, physics, biology, food chemistry, and chemical engineering in K-12, community college, public university, private university, and graduate settings in the United States and Mexico.

The paper is primarily descriptive and does not report a controlled evaluation of learning outcomes in this article itself; instead, it argues that InkSurvey is broadly applicable and can support active learning, reveal misconceptions, and promote metacognition and engagement. The authors note that a companion paper provides data and conclusions on effectiveness. Overall, the paper concludes that real-time, open-ended formative assessment with mobile devices is feasible across diverse contexts and may help instructors repair misunderstandings more quickly than with conventional classroom response systems.

finding.finding_summary: In the mathematics vignette, 87 first-term college students in university honors Calculus III used InkSurvey to answer open-ended questions about setting up triple integrals over a tetrahedral region. The instructor reported that 32 of 83 responses initially showed a misconception about constant bounds, but after real-time discussion and a revised question, all students responded and none gave all-constant bounds, suggesting improved understanding of integral setup within the lesson.
finding.measure: Student responses to open-ended calculus questions about defining integration bounds for triple integrals
finding.study_size: n=87 (83 responses on the initial question)

finding.finding_summary: Across physics, biology, food chemistry, and chemical engineering vignettes, InkSurvey was used to probe student reasoning about concepts such as force and motion, pH and enzyme activity, and conceptual models in STEM simulations. The paper reports that open-ended responses revealed misconceptions that instructors could address immediately, supporting conceptual refinement and more accurate scientific understanding, but it does not provide comparative effect sizes.
finding.measure: Open-ended conceptual responses in physics, biology, chemistry, and engineering classes

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly describes increased engagement and participation when students submitted real-time responses and discussed them in class. In the community college biology vignette, students were described as motivated to participate and engaged in the learning process, while in the creativity-in-physics vignette the anonymity of responses was said to reduce evaluation apprehension and encourage participation.
finding.measure: Class participation, engagement, and evaluation apprehension described in instructor vignettes

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes metacognition and related durable skills as key benefits of InkSurvey. Instructors reported that asking students to justify answers, write questions, and compare alternative solutions helped students reveal what they did and did not understand, think more carefully, and repair misconceptions; the creativity vignette explicitly states that the request for questions enhances metacognition.
finding.measure: Metacognitive reflection, justification of answers, and generation of questions/ideas

finding.finding_summary: The tool is presented as improving instructional efficiency by allowing instructors to scan all student responses quickly and respond immediately, rather than waiting for a few students to present work or for delayed homework. In the high school Algebra vignette and the calculus and physics examples, the instructor could review the whole class's work in real time and correct misconceptions before students left class, reducing the need to proceed blindly.
finding.measure: Instructor ability to review and respond to student work in real time

paper_profiles.title: AI-driven formative assessment and adaptive learning in data-science education: Evaluating an LLM-powered virtual teaching assistant
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes VITA (Virtual Teaching Assistants), an adaptive distributed learning platform for data-science education that embeds an LLM-powered chatbot (BotCaptain) into Moodle. The authors aim to address the need for scalable personalized support, timely formative feedback, and integrity-aware assessment in online and hybrid courses, especially where instructors must manage large numbers of learners with diverse backgrounds.

The intervention combines contextual prompt engineering, Socratic dialogue, xAPI logging, learning-record-store dashboards, and adaptive pathways that route students toward progression, reinforcement, or remediation content based on formative assessment data. The paper compares BotCaptain conceptually with other AI tutoring systems and proposes assessment designs intended to make ChatGPT-style misuse harder in assignments. The context is postsecondary data-science and related STEM education, with examples centered on undergraduate course workflows rather than K-12 classrooms.

The paper is primarily a design/implementation and benchmarking article rather than an empirical outcomes study. It argues that conversational AI can improve engagement, provide immediate feedback, support reflective reasoning and metacognition, and reduce instructor workload through automated analytics and formative assessment. However, it does not report controlled learner-outcome data, effect sizes, or subgroup analyses for multilingual learners, students with disabilities, or lower-achieving students.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that VITA/BotCaptain can improve instructional efficiency by automating formative assessment, feedback delivery, and learning-analytics monitoring. It describes dashboard-based identification of outliers and automated xAPI logging, but reports no controlled evaluation, sample-size-based workload measure, or effect size.
finding.measure: Instructor productivity, automated assessment/analytics workflow, dashboard monitoring of learner activity

finding.finding_summary: The system is explicitly designed to support critical thinking, reflection, and metacognitive engagement through Socratic dialogue, elaborative scaffolding, and contextual prompting. The paper provides design examples and qualitative claims about personalized questioning, but no quantitative measure of metacognition or critical-thinking gains is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognitive engagement, reflective dialogue quality

finding.finding_summary: The authors claim the chatbot can increase engagement, timely help-seeking, and self-paced learning by providing always-available support and personalized responses. These claims are descriptive and not tied to a formal outcome evaluation, so no effect size or validated engagement measure is reported.
finding.measure: Engagement, help-seeking, self-paced learning support

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on data-science education content, including ethics, privacy, statistics, and data visualization/mining tasks. It claims the AI tutor supports comprehension of course concepts through contextual explanations and formative feedback, but it does not report test-score outcomes or other quantitative achievement results.
finding.measure: Course concept understanding in data science, ethics, and statistics-related tasks

finding.finding_summary: The platform is presented as an institutional infrastructure for scalable AI-supported instruction, including LMS integration, xAPI interoperability, LRS dashboards, and future multi-course deployment. The paper emphasizes scalability and interoperability, but it does not report institutional-level outcome data, adoption metrics, or policy effects.
finding.measure: LMS/LRS interoperability and scalable deployment architecture

paper_profiles.title: The Effect of Student Learning Styles on the Learning Gains Achieved When Interactive Simulations Are Coupled with Real-Time Formative Assessment via Pen-Enabled Mobile Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether learning gains from a pedagogical model that combines interactive computer simulations with real-time formative assessment differ by students’ learning styles. The authors focus on whether the Coupled Model is especially effective for certain learners in an undergraduate STEM setting, using the Index of Learning Styles (ILS) to test for relationships between style preferences and gain.

The intervention/context is an undergraduate engineering physics laboratory course in which students used interactive simulations together with InkSurvey on pen-enabled mobile devices to submit open-format responses in real time. The study examined five simulation activities (including circuits, Fourier analysis, diffraction, standard deviation, and least squares) across two course sections with a total of 41 students, and learning was measured with pre-tests and summative assessments scored by rubric.

Results showed significant learning gains on all five simulations, with class-average normalized gains ranging from 60% to 75% and all paired tests reported as p < 0.001. Correlations between learning gains and learning-style dimensions were near zero and not statistically significant, leading the authors to conclude that the Coupled Model improved learning broadly across learning styles rather than favoring any particular style. The paper therefore provides evidence that this approach can support learning in undergraduate STEM classrooms without detectable dependence on ILS-defined learner preferences.

finding.finding_summary: Students in an undergraduate engineering physics laboratory showed large, statistically significant gains when interactive simulations were coupled with real-time formative assessment. Across five simulation activities, class-average normalized learning gains ranged from 60% to 75%, with paired tests reported as p < 0.001 for each activity; no meaningful differences were found by learning-style category.
finding.measure: Pre-test to summative assessment scores on simulation-based physics/science concepts and problem explanations
finding.std_deviation: 0.12 (inter-rater reliability estimate SD for nine reliability estimates; not a learning outcome SD)

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly argues that the Coupled Model increased student metacognition by prompting open-format explanations, scaffolding, and immediate feedback during simulation use. However, this was not analyzed as a separate outcome with a dedicated quantitative measure; the evidence is indirect and based on the instructional design and qualitative discussion rather than a direct metacognition assessment.
finding.measure: Open-format InkSurvey responses and instructor-guided scaffolding during simulations

paper_profiles.title: EvoGrader: an online formative assessment tool for automatically evaluating written evolutionary explanations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents EvoGrader, a free online formative assessment system that automatically scores students’ written explanations of evolutionary change. The authors address a practical problem in undergraduate biology: instructors need scalable ways to evaluate open-ended explanations of natural selection, but human scoring is time-consuming and expensive.

EvoGrader uses supervised machine learning (LightSIDE) trained on a large human-scored corpus of 10,270 evolutionary explanations to detect six scientific concepts, three naïve ideas, and four holistic reasoning models. The paper describes the system architecture and then tests its scoring performance against trained human raters using 2,200 new responses: 1,100 ACORNS responses from introductory biology students at one public Midwestern university and 1,100 ACORNS-like responses from undergraduates at 59 institutions.

Results show strong agreement between EvoGrader and human scoring for ACORNS items, with kappa values above 0.81 for all six scientific concepts and strong agreement for reasoning models; performance was somewhat lower on ACORNS-like prompts, especially for some naïve ideas, but still generally acceptable. The authors conclude that EvoGrader is a valid, efficient tool for formative assessment in undergraduate biology and may reduce teacher workload while supporting diagnostic assessment, homework, and pre/post course measurement. They also suggest the architecture could be adapted to other science domains.

finding.finding_summary: EvoGrader closely matched trained human raters on written evolutionary explanation scoring, indicating that it can reliably assess scientific reasoning about natural selection. For ACORNS items (n=1100), kappa values for the six scientific concepts ranged from 0.855 to 0.984, and total key-concept scores correlated with human scores at Spearman's rho=0.927; reasoning-model agreement was also strong (kappa=0.821, agreement=88.4%).
finding.measure: Scoring of written evolutionary explanations for scientific concepts and holistic reasoning models; inter-rater agreement with human scores
finding.study_size: n=1100 ACORNS responses; total n=2200 including ACORNS-like responses

finding.finding_summary: The system substantially reduced scoring time relative to trained human raters. The authors report that EvoGrader scoring took 99% less time than human scoring, while also being free and able to process large batches of written responses online.
finding.measure: Time required to score written explanations
finding.study_size: n=2200 total written explanations in validation samples; training corpus n=10,270

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that EvoGrader could support broader institutional use of formative assessment in biology education and could be adapted to other domains. While this is not tested as an institutional outcome study, the system is positioned as a scalable infrastructure tool for instructors and potentially for other educational settings.
finding.measure: Potential applicability and scalability of the online assessment infrastructure

paper_profiles.title: Towards a Success Model for Automated Programming Assessment Systems Used as a Formative Assessment Tool
paper_profiles.venue: ITiCSE 2023 (Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education V. 1)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates what drives student satisfaction with automated programming assessment systems (APASs) when they are used as formative assessment tools in introductory university programming courses. The authors position APASs as a response to increasing student heterogeneity, limited tutor availability, and the need for timely, objective feedback in programming education.

To study APAS success, the paper develops a structural success model grounded in DeLone and McLean’s information systems success framework and a blended learning success model. The model includes motivation, information quality, system quality, and service quality as exogenous factors, with learning climate, blended learning flexibility, and task-technology fit as mediators leading to student satisfaction. The model is tested with survey data from 414 students enrolled in introductory programming courses at a university setting, using the ArTeMis APAS; after cleaning, 368 responses were analyzed with PLS-SEM.

The findings show that motivation, information quality, and system quality each have significant indirect effects on satisfaction through the mediators, while service quality does not significantly affect satisfaction directly or indirectly. Learning climate, blended learning flexibility, and task-technology fit are all positively associated with satisfaction, indicating that students value enjoyable use, self-paced learning support, and fit between APAS services and learning needs. The paper concludes that APAS success depends less on support services and more on the quality of feedback, platform functionality, and the extent to which the system fits student learning goals.

The study is limited to computer-science-related undergraduate learners in introductory programming during a blended-learning pandemic context, so generalizability to other APASs, disciplines, and grade bands is uncertain.

finding.finding_summary: The APAS was associated with higher student satisfaction through enjoyment/pleasure and motivation-related constructs. Motivation significantly influenced learning climate, blended learning flexibility, and task-technology fit, and these mediators in turn significantly predicted satisfaction; however, no direct effect size for satisfaction was reported.
finding.measure: Student satisfaction, motivation, learning climate, blended learning flexibility, task-technology fit (Likert-scale survey constructs)

finding.finding_summary: The system was linked to task-technology fit and learning flexibility, which are durability-related learning supports, but the paper does not directly measure metacognition or collaboration. The central finding is that better perceived fit between APAS services and learning needs predicted higher satisfaction, via significant indirect effects from information quality and system quality.
finding.measure: Task-technology fit, blended learning flexibility, learning needs fit (Likert-scale survey constructs)

finding.finding_summary: The APAS was studied as a tool to support efficient formative assessment in large programming courses, with the authors arguing it helps lecturers manage many students and provide timely feedback. Empirically, students rated the system’s information quality and system quality positively, and these constructs significantly predicted satisfaction indirectly; no efficiency effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived information quality, system quality, service quality, and student satisfaction with the APAS

finding.finding_summary: In introductory university programming, the APAS was positively associated with perceived success in the course context through better feedback, system quality, and task support. The paper does not report programming achievement scores or test performance outcomes, but it does show that the platform’s information quality and system quality significantly improved satisfaction via mediation pathways.
finding.measure: Perceived quality of programming assignment feedback, system quality, and student satisfaction

paper_profiles.title: Explainable Action Form Assessment by Exploiting Multimodal Chain-of-Thoughts Reasoning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces a new computer vision task called Human Action Form Assessment (AFA), which goes beyond action recognition to judge whether a human movement is performed in a standard or non-standard form and to generate explanatory feedback. The authors argue that existing action-quality datasets are limited because they rely on subjective scores or lack detailed, step-by-step explanations, and they propose AFA as a more objective assessment paradigm for workout actions.

To support the task, the paper presents CoT-AFA, a new dataset of 3,392 workout videos spanning 141 action categories across martial arts and fitness. The dataset includes standard/non-standard labels, multi-view annotations, and Chain-of-Thought style textual explanations that describe the error, its consequence, and a corrective suggestion. A corresponding model, Explainable Fitness Assessor (EFA), combines visual features with standard technical steps using dual branch multimodal fusion and a dynamic gating layer to jointly predict action class, quality label, and explanatory text.

Experiments are conducted on the CoT-AFA dataset using classification and text-generation metrics. The proposed model outperforms baselines on explanation generation and achieves 77.2% top-1 action-class accuracy and 81.8% quality-assessment accuracy. The paper concludes that structured textual guidance and bidirectional multimodal alignment help models produce more accurate assessments and richer explanations for action form evaluation. The work is primarily a computer vision and multimodal reasoning study, not an education intervention study, though it has potential relevance for coaching and training contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies performance on a new action-form assessment task rather than academic learning. On the CoT-AFA dataset (n=3,392 videos), the proposed EFA model improved action-class prediction to 77.2% top-1 accuracy and action-quality assessment to 81.8% accuracy, indicating better structured assessment of workout actions. The model also improved explanation generation, with CIDEr increasing by 16.0% over prior methods.
finding.measure: Action-class accuracy, action-quality accuracy, and text-generation metrics for explanatory feedback (BLEU, METEOR, CIDEr, ROUGE-L)

paper_profiles.title: Physics teaching assistants’ views of different types of introductory problems: Challenge of perceiving the instructional benefits of context-rich and multiple-choice problems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how physics graduate teaching assistants (TAs) enrolled in a semester-long professional development course perceive different formats for introductory physics problems, with special attention to multiple-choice and context-rich problems. The study asks whether TAs see these formats as instructionally beneficial, how challenging they think they are for students, and when they would choose to use them if they had full control of the course.

The intervention/approach was not a student learning treatment, but rather a TA professional development activity in which 97 physics graduate TAs at a large research university reviewed example problem formats, listed pros and cons, ranked them by instructional benefit, challenge, likeability, and intended use, and later 12 participants were interviewed to probe their reasoning. The context included introductory physics recitations/labs and large-enrollment undergraduate instruction.

The main finding is that TAs generally viewed multiple-choice and context-rich problems as the least instructionally beneficial of the formats presented. Multiple-choice problems were seen mainly as summative assessment tools or as efficient grading tools, while context-rich problems were viewed as unclear, overly time-consuming, and excessively challenging. The interviews confirmed that these views were broad and not limited to the specific example items. The authors conclude that physics TAs often fail to recognize the formative-assessment value of well-designed multiple-choice questions and the problem-solving benefits of context-rich tasks, suggesting an important target for TA professional development.

finding.finding_summary: TAs commonly viewed multiple-choice problems as making grading faster and easier, and as saving time for students in some cases. For multiple-choice items, the most common pro was efficient grading (9% mentioned this explicitly), while 14% mentioned time savings for students; however, these were described as logistical benefits rather than instructional gains.
finding.measure: TA rankings and open-ended pros/cons about grading and time efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly reports TAs’ perceptions of whether problem types support problem-solving, reasoning, and metacognitive engagement. TAs largely failed to recognize these benefits, especially for multiple-choice formative use and context-rich problem solving, and instead emphasized confusion, lack of clarity, or time cost. The study does not measure student skill gains, but it substantively analyzes beliefs about the development of these durable skills in introductory physics.
finding.measure: TA rankings, written pros/cons, and interview responses about problem-solving, reasoning, and metacognition

paper_profiles.title: Video-based Formative and Summative Assessment of Surgical Tasks using Deep Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of objective, scalable assessment of surgical skill from video. The authors note that traditional video-based assessment is time-intensive, subjective, and limited by inter-rater reliability, particularly for both low-stakes formative feedback and high-stakes summative scoring.

To address this, they develop VBA-Net, a deep-learning pipeline that combines Mask R-CNN tool tracking with a denoising autoencoder and classifier. The system uses complete surgical videos from Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery (pattern cutting) tasks and benchmark kinematics from the JIGSAWS dataset to predict summative skill scores (FLS, OSATS, GRS) and pass/fail or novice/intermediate/expert classes, while also producing formative feedback through class activation maps (CAMs).

The study uses two pattern-cutting datasets from medical students and the public JIGSAWS dataset from surgeons. Results show strong predictive performance and generalization across unseen subjects and tasks, with high correlations for score prediction and high classification accuracy, including perfect accuracy for some expert classifications. The CAM validation analysis suggests the highlighted regions are meaningful for skill assessment, supporting the potential of the approach for automated formative feedback as well as efficient summative evaluation. The paper is focused on surgical training rather than K-12 education, so it does not provide evidence on multilingual learners, students with disabilities, or school-grade-band differences.

finding.finding_summary: VBA-Net substantially improved the automation and speed potential of video-based surgical assessment by replacing manual post-hoc review with an object-detection plus deep-learning pipeline. On the primary pattern-cutting dataset (n=2,055 videos from 21 students), it achieved strong predictive performance for FLS scores (Spearman ρ=0.915±0.002), accuracy=0.955±0.002, sensitivity=0.958±0.003, specificity=0.922±0.010, and AUC=0.989±0.001. The authors argue this reduces reviewer workload and can support time-efficient formative and summative assessment.
finding.measure: Model performance for automated video-based surgical skill assessment; downstream assessment efficiency/workload implications
finding.study_size: n=2,055 videos (primary dataset); n=307 videos (additional validation dataset); n=8 surgeons in JIGSAWS benchmark

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes formative feedback via class activation maps intended to make salient the motions associated with better or worse performance, which is closest to a durable-skill mechanism of self-monitoring/metacognitive guidance. CAM validation showed that masking inputs by CAM and retraining improved classification performance from accuracy=0.951±0.019 to 0.997±0.004, sensitivity from 0.954±0.019 to 0.998±0.004, and specificity from 0.925±0.056 to 0.990±0.019 (10-fold CV), suggesting the highlighted regions correspond to diagnostically useful features. However, the study does not directly measure learner metacognition or self-regulation, only the quality of the feedback signal.
finding.measure: CAM-based formative feedback validity; classification performance before vs after CAM masking
finding.study_size: 10-fold CV on the primary PC dataset
finding.std_deviation: 0.019 (accuracy before), 0.004 (accuracy after); 0.019/0.056 and 0.004/0.019 for sensitivity/specificity as reported

finding.finding_summary: The authors position the method as useful for certification, credentialing, and proctoring, and report strong generalizability on unseen subjects and tasks relevant to surgical training programs. On the additional pattern-cutting dataset (n=307 videos from 12 students), the model achieved ρ=0.937 with accuracy=0.876±0.002 and AUC=0.955±0.002; on JIGSAWS it achieved mean classification accuracy=0.946 (LOUO) and 0.975 (LOSO), with high OSATS/GRS correlations, indicating potential institutional utility for standardized assessment. These are technical validation results rather than direct policy or organizational outcomes.
finding.measure: Generalization to unseen subjects/tasks; certification-relevant classification and score prediction performance
finding.study_size: n=307 videos; n=8 surgeons in JIGSAWS

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure engagement, motivation, persistence, or self-regulation, but it motivates formative assessment as a way to provide timely feedback and reduce uncertainty for trainees. The strongest directly reported evidence is improved predictive reliability on surgical performance, which the authors argue could support learners during practice; however, no learner-reported social-emotional outcomes were collected.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Improving Students’ Understanding of Quantum Mechanics by Using Peer Instruction Tools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping students develop conceptual understanding in quantum mechanics, a topic the authors characterize as especially difficult even for advanced undergraduates and graduate students. The central question is whether research-based concept tests used within a peer instruction format can improve students’ grasp of core quantum mechanics ideas compared with traditional lecture-based instruction.

The intervention consists of multiple-choice concept test questions integrated into junior-senior level quantum mechanics courses at 10–15 minute intervals or at the start of lecture. Students answer individually, discuss with peers, and then receive instructor feedback; the authors iteratively refine the questions based on student responses and instructor suggestions. The paper describes the development of about 500 concept-test items and provides examples focused on bound vs. scattering states, wavefunctions, and potential wells, often using multiple representations (verbal, graphical, mathematical) and sequences from easier to harder items.

The evidence comes from several undergraduate quantum mechanics classes over three consecutive years (2008–2010) plus a comparison class receiving traditional instruction only. Students in the peer-instruction classes performed substantially better on a quiz about the 1D infinite square well, with mean scores of 5.5, 7.0, and 7.6 across the three experimental cohorts versus 1.8 for the comparison group (10-point quiz), and the difference was reported as statistically significant (p<0.0001). The paper concludes that peer-instruction concept tests are effective for improving conceptual understanding in quantum mechanics and that iterative refinement of the concept tests further improves student performance.

finding.finding_summary: Peer instruction concept tests improved students’ conceptual understanding of quantum mechanics relative to traditional lecture. On a 10-point quiz about the 1D infinite square well, experimental groups scored 5.5 (n=25), 7.0 (n=13), and 7.6 (n=20) across 2008–2010, compared with 1.8 for the traditional-instruction comparison group (n=18), with p<0.0001. The authors also report that performance improved further over time as the concept tests were refined.
finding.measure: Quiz on basic quantum-mechanical concepts for the 1D infinite square well (7 multiple-choice and 3 open-ended items)
finding.study_size: n=76 total across experimental groups; n=18 comparison group

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that peer instruction keeps students actively engaged, encourages discussion with peers, and helps students monitor their own learning. This is supported primarily by descriptive observations rather than a dedicated engagement measure, so the evidence is indirect.
finding.measure: Classroom participation/engagement observed during peer discussion; self-monitoring of learning described qualitatively

finding.finding_summary: The authors claim the approach helps students organize, extend, and repair their knowledge, and that articulating answers with peers requires attention to logic and organization of thought. These outcomes are conceptualized as metacognition and collaboration benefits, but they are not measured with a dedicated instrument.
finding.measure: Qualitative classroom discourse and authors’ interpretation of students’ reasoning/collaboration during peer instruction

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a benchmark dataset for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German-language tasks grounded in middle school curricula. The authors argue that existing VLM benchmarks are often English-only, heavily multiple-choice, and too decontextualized, so they created a dataset of 2,038 open-ended questions over 486 images across nine school subjects, including math, biology, history, physics, arts, music, religion, geography, and sports.

The study does not test an educational intervention; instead, it evaluates the performance of 13 open-weight VLMs on these tasks using LLM-as-a-judge and a panel-of-LLMs scoring approach. The benchmark emphasizes real curricular images, some questions embedded in images, and additional adversarial items that are intentionally unanswerable from the image to test whether models can refuse appropriately.

Results show that the strongest models achieved under 45% overall accuracy, with particularly weak performance in math, music, and adversarial items. Performance varied substantially by subject, and the authors conclude that middle school-level visual-reasoning tasks are challenging for current VLMs, especially in German, and that public benchmark rankings do not necessarily transfer to this more realistic setting. The paper also suggests that smaller or medium-sized models can outperform larger ones on this benchmark, and that models remain poor at saying “no” when a question is not answerable from the image.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark included 308 math questions, and the best model reached only 34.09% on math (Qwen2.5VL 32B), with several models far lower (e.g. Ovis2 4B at 9.09%). The authors note that models were better at calculation than at counting, but still struggled with basic geometry, reading coordinate values, and identifying figures correctly, leading to many incorrect answers.
finding.measure: Open-ended math question accuracy on middle school curriculum items

finding.finding_summary: Scientific subject performance was weak, especially in biology and physics where models had trouble matching terms to diagram parts, interpreting circuit and astronomy explanations, and reading information from visuals. In physics, the best score reported was 47.65% for Qwen2.5VL 32B, but many explanation-based items were answered incorrectly; in biology, performance varied but remained error-prone on terms and label identification.
finding.measure: Open-ended biology and physics question accuracy; explanation and diagram interpretation
finding.study_size: n=169 biology questions; n=234 physics questions

finding.finding_summary: Across the non-STEM school subjects, performance varied by domain rather than showing a uniform effect. History and religion were among the strongest areas overall (best scores around 54% in discussion; 54.36% history and 52.92% religion in the table), while music was especially difficult (best around 31.03%). The paper also reports subject-specific confusions in arts, geography, sports, and religion, indicating substantial domain sensitivity.
finding.measure: Open-ended accuracy on arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports questions
finding.study_size: n=286 arts; n=251 geography; n=264 history; n=166 music; n=206 religion; n=154 sports

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the benchmark requires visual reasoning, background knowledge, and sometimes explanation-based inference, and reports persistent failures on questions needing multi-step reasoning, reverse lookup, and interpretation of diagrams or maps. Although this is not a direct measure of metacognition or collaboration, the results substantively reflect models’ performance on reasoning-intensive tasks that resemble durable skills demands.
finding.measure: Open-ended reasoning accuracy across multi-step visual-question items

paper_profiles.title: Quantum Computing as a High School Module
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a one-week instructional module on quantum computing designed for motivated high school students ages 15–18. The module is organized around core quantum concepts such as superposition, measurement, qubits, beam splitters, Stern-Gerlach measurements, quantum cryptography, quantum gates, entanglement, teleportation, and a simple quantum algorithm (Deutsch-Jozsa). It includes problem sets, simulation-based labs, and worked examples intended to bridge popular science explanations and advanced undergraduate treatments.

The paper is primarily a curriculum/lesson-design manuscript rather than an empirical evaluation study. It explains the pedagogical sequence, prerequisites, learning objectives, and example activities, and it emphasizes multiple representations (coin analogies, matrices, bra-ket notation, simulation tools, and interferometer models) to support understanding. The authors argue that the content can be used after AP exams, in extracurricular settings, or independently, but they do not report outcome data from learners, comparisons across groups, or measured effects on achievement or engagement.

Because the manuscript is descriptive and instructional, it does not provide evidence about differential effects for multilingual learners, students with disabilities, lower-achieving students, or specific grade-band comparisons beyond its intended high-school audience. It also does not report experimental or correlational findings for academic, social-emotional, or durable-skill outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: The Illusion of Understanding: How Middle-Schoolers Fail to Regulate Inquiry with ChatGPT in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle school students regulate inquiry when using ChatGPT in science investigation tasks. The authors ask whether students can discriminate between efficient and inefficient prompts, evaluate AI answers accurately, regulate their question-asking through follow-up prompts, and ultimately produce conceptual explanations of the science content.

The study was conducted with French middle school students (final n=63, ages 14–15) during six science tasks completed in school. Students judged prompt suggestions as efficient or inefficient, interacted with ChatGPT 3.5 freely, rated each AI response for usefulness, and then wrote short answers in their own words. The paper also measured AI attitudes, prior domain confidence, and metacognitive skills to see how these individual differences related to interaction quality and learning outcomes.

Results show that students generally performed at chance in distinguishing prompt quality (mean d′=0.19) and in judging AI answer quality (mean d′=0.07), and very few asked follow-up questions (14 students total; 22 follow-up questions across six tasks). Students often accepted low-level AI answers as useful, indicating an illusion of understanding, and higher self-reported prior knowledge did not protect them from this effect. Better metacognitive regulation predicted stronger prompt discrimination, while more positive AI attitudes and higher prior confidence were associated with worse evaluation. Final task success was moderate (M=0.51), and was predicted by receiving more high-level AI answers, better answer-sensitivity, and more follow-up questioning.

finding.finding_summary: Middle school students struggled to use ChatGPT for science inquiry in a way that supported conceptual understanding. Final task success averaged M=0.51 (SD=0.25) across six science problems (n=63), and performance was only moderate despite unrestricted access to ChatGPT; better outcomes were predicted by receiving high-level AI answers, being more sensitive to answer quality, and asking follow-up questions.
finding.measure: Science task success based on written explanations of scientific concepts

finding.finding_summary: Students showed weak metacognitive regulation and poor question-asking quality in the GenAI setting. Prompt discrimination was near chance (mean d′=0.19, SD=0.8; t=1.77, p=0.08), answer-evaluation sensitivity was near zero (mean d′=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65), and only 14 of 63 students asked any follow-up question (22 total across six tasks). Higher metacognitive regulation predicted better prompt discrimination, but overall regulation with ChatGPT was poor.
finding.measure: Prompt discrimination sensitivity, answer evaluation sensitivity, follow-up question frequency, metacognitive regulation
finding.effect_size: d′=0.19; d′=0.07; β=.30 (metacognitive regulation to prompt sensitivity)

finding.finding_summary: The study found low persistence and limited engagement in QA cycles with ChatGPT. Students frequently terminated inquiry prematurely, and only 14 of 63 students asked follow-up questions, suggesting weak regulatory engagement even after receiving unsatisfactory answers. Final success was modest (M=0.51), consistent with shallow engagement rather than sustained inquiry.
finding.measure: Follow-up-question behavior and premature termination of QA cycles

paper_profiles.title: Surveying Turkish high school and university students’ attitudes and approaches to physics problem solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines Turkish students’ attitudes and approaches toward physics problem solving using a Turkish translation of the Attitudes and Approaches to Problem Solving (AAPS) survey. The authors ask whether problem-solving attitudes differ by grade level, school type, and gender, and whether Turkish university students differ from comparable U.S. students in algebra-based introductory physics. The study is motivated by prior work showing that expert-like problem-solving attitudes are associated with better learning and performance in physics.

The AAPS survey was translated into Turkish and validated through expert review and one-on-one interviews with high school students. It was then administered to 528 students in Turkey: 10th- and 11th-grade students from regular, science, and vocational high schools, plus first-year university science-education majors taking introductory algebra-based physics. Responses were analyzed descriptively and with chi-square tests; an exploratory factor analysis was also conducted to examine item groupings.

Overall, there were no statistically significant differences in total survey means by gender or between 10th and 11th grade, but item-level differences appeared across many questions. University students were generally more expert-like than vocational high school students on average, though in some items university students were less favorable than high school students. Turkish university students scored more expert-like than U.S. university students on a few items about applying principles across contexts and reflecting on solutions, but U.S. students were more expert-like on most items. The factor analysis suggested the survey reliably captured dimensions such as metacognition and novice-like problem-solving approaches.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly measured attitudes and approaches to physics problem solving, including metacognitive behaviors such as checking answers, tracing errors, and applying principles across contexts. Overall survey means did not differ significantly by gender or by 10th vs. 11th grade, but item-level differences were common; for example, university students were more expert-like on several metacognitive items (e.g., item 22: 89.7% favorable vs. 5.1% unfavorable, item 29: 92.5% favorable vs. 2.5% unfavorable) while less expert-like on others. The exploratory factor analysis found a factor explicitly related to metacognition.
finding.measure: AAPS survey items on problem-solving attitudes and metacognition; item-level favorable/unfavorable response frequencies; exploratory factor analysis

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines physics problem-solving attitudes in introductory physics, including use of physics principles, equations, and conceptual reasoning. University students were more expert-like than vocational high school students overall (average favorable responses 50% vs. 42%), and Turkish university students differed from U.S. introductory physics students on more than half of the items (18 items), with U.S. students more expert-like on most of those items. No standardized achievement test or learning outcome was reported; the evidence is based on survey responses about scientific problem-solving epistemology.
finding.measure: AAPS survey responses about physics problem solving, use of principles/equations, and conceptual versus quantitative reasoning
finding.study_size: n=528 in Turkey; comparison subgroup n=43 Turkish university students and n=397 U.S. university students

paper_profiles.title: Development of a test in German language to assess middle school students’ physics proficiency
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
