This paper addresses the lack of accessible, subject-specific German-language achievement tests for middle school physics. The authors developed a 20-item multiple-choice test by translating and adapting released TIMSS science items into German, aiming to create a test that is efficient, objective, and psychometrically sound for assessing students’ physics proficiency.

The test was administered to 177 eighth-grade students in Hamburg, Germany. The authors used Rasch modeling to evaluate item fit, remove misfitting items, assess reliability, and examine correlations with external variables such as interest in science, self-concept in science, physics grades, and cultural/economic capital. The final 20-item form showed adequate Rasch fit, person-separation reliability of 0.78, item-separation reliability of 0.97, and expected positive correlations with science interest and self-concept; however, the paper is primarily a test-development and validation study, not an intervention study.

The main conclusion is that the resulting German-language TIMSS-based instrument provides a valid and efficient measure of middle-school students’ physics proficiency for research use. The authors note important limitations: the evidence is based only on eighth graders from Hamburg, so generalization to other grades or education systems is not yet supported, and the test underrepresents electrics and does not yet cover the full extremes of ability well.

finding.finding_summary: The study did not test an instructional treatment or report gains in scientific reasoning; instead, it developed and validated a physics proficiency test. The final instrument is intended to measure middle-school physics content and procedural knowledge, but the paper does not report causal effects on scientific reasoning outcomes.
finding.measure: German-language multiple-choice physics proficiency test based on adapted TIMSS science items; Rasch item/person fit and reliability

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on assessment development rather than instructional impact. It reports that 20 translated/adapted items remained after Rasch-based item screening and that the resulting test adequately covered middle-school physics content areas such as mechanics, optics, thermodynamics, electrics, magnetism, and acoustics.
finding.measure: Physics proficiency/achievement test performance; item fit and difficulty parameters

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that converting released TIMSS open-ended items into multiple-choice single-select format improves test economy and objectivity. The final instrument is designed to take about 20 minutes, making administration and scoring more efficient than open-ended item formats, though no direct workload or time comparison experiment was reported.
finding.measure: Test administration format and estimated completion time

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 (Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle school students think about and design an AI peer for collaborative mathematical problem solving (CPS). The authors ask what students perceive as helpful or unhelpful when AI is framed not as a tutor, but as a teammate inside small-group math work.

The study used a five-day participatory design summer camp with 24 rising grades 6–8 students. Students completed human-only CPS tasks and AI-involved CPS tasks using a custom text-based technology probe with two AI peers, then reflected on the experience, co-designed ideal AI peer features, and completed preference surveys. The mathematics tasks were aligned to middle-school standards and focused on ratio/proportional reasoning, expressions and equations, and early functions/geometry.

The main finding is that students preferred an AI peer that acts as a scaffold-first collaborator: it should give hints, checks, concept refreshers, and emotional encouragement before direct answers. Students disliked AI behavior that felt teachery, repetitive, overly controlling, or emotionally unresponsive, and they wanted explicit control over when the AI speaks and how much help it gives. Quantitatively, compared with human-only CPS, AI-peer CPS reduced perceived temporal demand (M=5.67 vs. 9.62, d=1.15) but increased physical demand (M=8.48 vs. 4.90, d=1.14) and lowered social cohesion/coordination (ATGS M=5.21 vs. 6.50, d=0.94; GIT p=0.047, d=0.81). Overall, the paper contributes design guidance for AI peers in middle-school mathematics collaboration rather than evidence of learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on middle-school mathematics CPS tasks, but it does not report achievement gains from the AI peer. Students worked on grade-aligned ratio/proportional reasoning, expressions/equations, and early functions/geometry problems, and they perceived the AI peer as helpful for procedural scaffolding and faster task completion. However, the study evaluates design preferences and interaction experience rather than math learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Grade-aligned middle-school mathematics collaborative problem-solving tasks; student perceptions of help with math problem solving

finding.finding_summary: Students reported lower affective/social engagement with AI peers than with human-only CPS. On the GEQ, Attractions to Group-Social (ATGS) was lower in the AI condition (M=5.21, SD=1.81) than in pure human CPS (M=6.50, SD=2.05), d=0.94, and students repeatedly described frustration, reduced trust, and the need for emotional scaffolding and encouragement. At the same time, AI peers reduced temporal demand on NASA-TLX, suggesting a mixed experience that was faster but less socially warm.
finding.measure: GEQ (ATGS) and interview/reflection reports of frustration, trust, encouragement, and emotional support
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired survey comparisons; n=18 interviews

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies collaboration/co-agency and student expectations for joint problem solving, which are durable skills. Students wanted the AI to work with them, ask what they thought, and support shared reasoning rather than take over; they disliked rigid, repetitive, or overly directive behavior that broke co-agency. On the GEQ, Group Integration-Task (GIT) was lower with AI peers than with human-only CPS (p=0.047, d=0.81), indicating weaker perceived coordination, even though AI peers helped maintain momentum.
finding.measure: GEQ Group Integration-Task (GIT); qualitative reflections/interviews about collaboration, co-agency, and turn-taking
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired survey comparisons; n=18 interviews

finding.finding_summary: AI peers reduced perceived time pressure during collaborative math work. On NASA-TLX, temporal demand was significantly lower in the AI-peer condition (M=5.67, SD=4.38) than in human-only CPS (M=9.62, SD=4.13), with a large effect (d=1.15, p=0.002). Students also described the AI as helping them move through tasks more quickly, although this efficiency came with higher physical/interactional workload from typing and navigating the text-based interface.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand; qualitative comments about task speed and interface overhead
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired survey comparisons; n=18 interviews

finding.finding_summary: The study also directly concerns metacognitive support, such as checking work, negotiating methods, and asking students to justify answers. Students preferred hints, error detection, concept refreshers, and double-check prompts, but they rejected AI behavior that merely repeated itself or provided divergent answers without clarification. The evidence is qualitative rather than outcome-based, so the paper shows design preferences for supporting metacognition rather than measured gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative reflections, interviews, and design artifacts about hints, checks, justification, and method negotiation

finding.finding_summary: Students often perceived AI behavior as rude, mean, or not listening when the agents repeated themselves or failed to acknowledge their contributions. These reports suggest that the AI peer’s conversational style could undermine students’ sense of belonging and emotional safety in group work. The study does not measure these constructs directly with a validated scale beyond GEQ, but the qualitative evidence is central to the paper.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview and reflection themes about listening, respect, trust, and emotional attunement

paper_profiles.title: Democratizing Signal Processing and Machine Learning: Math Learning Equity for Elementary and Middle School Students
paper_profiles.venue: Submitted to IEEE Signal Processing Magazine
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article argues that strong early mathematics preparation is foundational for later success in signal processing, machine learning, and other STEM fields. The authors frame math learning gaps as cumulative and equity-relevant, especially for students affected by systemic barriers such as under-resourced schooling, language barriers, and low expectations. The paper is not an empirical evaluation of a single intervention; rather, it is a perspective/practice article that explains why early math support matters and how schools and universities can help.

The paper describes three out-of-school math support programs run with university or foundation involvement: CyMath at Iowa State, Algebra by 7th Grade (Ab7G) at Purdue, and Math Motivators from the Actuarial Foundation. These programs provide tutoring/mentoring, adaptive practice via ALEKS, parent communication, and STEM enrichment for students in roughly grades 3-12, with emphasis on students from underrepresented, disadvantaged, and under-served backgrounds. The authors also discuss practical lessons learned, such as the value of strong school partnerships, parent awareness, regular practice, access to technology, and mentor continuity.

Evidence in the article is mostly descriptive and anecdotal, but it includes a few reported program outcomes. The strongest concrete result mentioned is from Ab7G, where students who completed a full grade level in ALEKS each year showed significant gains in mathematics proficiency (n=20) and those gains correlated with proficiency-or-higher on Indiana’s ILEARN assessment. For CyMath, the authors report percentile increases on standardized tests for a small set of students, but note that percentile changes are noisy and only large, consistent changes should be interpreted cautiously. Overall, the paper concludes that early supplemental math support may help close learning gaps, but it does not provide rigorous causal evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports descriptive evidence that university-run tutoring/mentoring programs may improve mathematics proficiency for elementary and middle school students. The clearest result cited is from Ab7G: students who completed a full grade level in ALEKS each year showed significant growth in mathematics proficiency, and this growth was associated with proficiency-or-higher performance on Indiana’s ILEARN assessment (n=20). CyMath also reports individual percentile gains on MAP/iReady, but the authors caution that these are noisy and anecdotal rather than rigorous evidence.
finding.measure: Mathematics proficiency; standardized math tests (ALEKS progress, Indiana ILEARN, MAP, iReady percentile scores)
finding.study_size: n=20 for the cited Ab7G result; additional CyMath student counts reported descriptively (e.g., 14, 35, about 25)

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes program structures intended to support student self-efficacy, motivation, and engagement, such as recognition for reaching goals, parent encouragement, and fun-lab activities paired with tutoring. However, these outcomes are discussed as part of program design and lessons learned rather than measured with formal instruments, so the evidence is descriptive rather than causal.
finding.measure: Student self-efficacy, motivation, engagement, and persistence as described through program design and participation practices

finding.finding_summary: The article emphasizes durable-skill development through mentoring, collaboration, and learning routines such as consistent practice, goal setting, and working with tutors. It specifically notes that mentor-student connection, parental engagement, and regular practice schedules help keep students on track, but it does not report formal quantitative measures of metacognition or collaboration outcomes.
finding.measure: Metacognitive and self-management supports implied by goal setting, routine practice, and mentor-guided learning

paper_profiles.title: Brazilian National High School Examination: assessing student’s learning in Physics
paper_profiles.venue: Revista Brasileira de Ensino de Física
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what the Brazilian National High School Examination (Enem) can reveal about learning in high school Physics. Using microdata from the Natural Sciences section of Enem from 2009–2014, the authors combine item response theory (3PL IRT), classical test theory, and qualitative content analysis of Physics items to characterize item difficulty, discrimination, distractor patterns, and student performance.

The study is not an intervention study; it is a large-scale observational analysis of an existing high-stakes assessment used for university admissions. The sample focuses on students concluding high school who took the exam and had valid responses, with analyses at the item level and subgroup comparisons by gender and school type (federal, state, city, private). The paper also examines whether the exam behaves consistently with IRT assumptions and whether item content aligns with the construct being measured.

Main findings are that students’ performance in Physics is low overall, with roughly one-third of items answered correctly on average, and that items requiring disciplinary knowledge, quantitative reasoning, problem solving, graphical interpretation, or practical/laboratory understanding are especially difficult. The authors report clear subgroup differences: male students score higher than female students, and students from federal and private schools score higher than those from state schools. The paper concludes that Enem reveals important inequities and suggests a gap between the intended construct of the exam and actual Physics learning in Brazilian high school.

finding.finding_summary: Across Enem Natural Sciences items from 2009–2014, Physics questions were often answered correctly by only about one-third of students, and items requiring disciplinary Physics knowledge, quantitative reasoning, problem solving, graph/figure interpretation, or laboratory/practical understanding were especially difficult. For example, on one Physics item (Enem 2012 Q47), 43.9% chose the correct answer, while on another (Enem 2011 Q70) only 34.7% answered correctly; the authors characterize several items as having low discrimination or poor fit to the 3PL model, suggesting construct/measurement concerns as well as weak learning.
finding.measure: Natural Sciences/Physics item performance; item characteristic curves; correct-answer percentages; IRT difficulty/discrimination
finding.study_size: n=864,827 to n=1,374,821 high-school-concluding participants per year (2009–2014); item-level analyses across 45-item tests

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students performed worse on Physics items requiring basic mathematical reasoning and quantitative problem solving than on items relying mainly on textual interpretation. The authors explicitly note that some quantitative reasoning items had percentages of correct answers well below the exam average, indicating weak numeracy-related performance within the Physics section.
finding.measure: Correct-response rates on Physics items requiring arithmetic/algebraic reasoning and quantitative interpretation
finding.study_size: n=864,827 to n=1,374,821 high-school-concluding participants per year (2009–2014); item-level analyses

finding.finding_summary: This paper is not primarily about engagement or self-regulation, but it does report that some multi-step Physics items elicited patterns consistent with test-taking heuristics rather than deep understanding (e.g., elimination of distractors and near-random selection among similar options). The evidence is indirect and descriptive, so it does not support a clear estimate of motivation or engagement effects.
finding.measure: Distractor-choice patterns on Physics items
finding.study_size: n=864,827 to n=1,374,821 high-school-concluding participants per year; item-level analyses

finding.finding_summary: Enem is presented as a high-stakes assessment that shapes access to public universities and scholarships/loans, so the paper uses score patterns to diagnose inequities in the Brazilian secondary system. The authors find substantial subgroup disparities by gender and school type: female students score lower than male students, and state-school students—who make up about three-quarters of candidates—score lower than federal and private-school students, indicating structural inequality and possible fairness concerns in the assessment system.
finding.measure: IRT group scores by gender and school type; participation distributions; Enem score patterns used for university access
finding.study_size: n=864,827 to n=1,374,821 high-school-concluding participants per year; subgroup comparisons across 2009–2014
finding.std_deviation: reported in subgroup tables (e.g., female 488.2±94.6 vs male 521.5±100.9 in 2009; state 475.6±83.4 vs federal 600.5±92.4 in 2009)

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how elementary school students and teachers perceive a generative-AI-supported activity for creative mathematical writing. The paper is motivated by the challenge that some young learners struggle to engage in creative math writing and by the question of whether GenAI can scaffold the process in a way that supports learning rather than replacing it.

The researchers implemented a classroom-based GenAI system built around a three-step workflow: Ask, Represent, and Transform. Students first analyzed math story prompts, then visually represented their thinking, and finally collaborated with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 to draft and revise culturally relevant math stories. The study involved 79 fifth-grade students across six classrooms in two U.S. elementary schools, with 10 students interviewed in focus groups and all six teachers interviewed individually; open-ended survey responses and observation notes were used to triangulate the qualitative data.

Findings indicate that students and teachers perceived several benefits: the activity fostered creativity in math, supported mathematical understanding, promoted AI literacy, and improved affective outcomes such as interest, curiosity, and ownership of learning. At the same time, participants identified important challenges, including weak critical evaluation of AI output, difficulty generating coherent stories, the AI being perceived as "too perfect," insufficient pedagogical feedback, reduced autonomy, weak social connection, and limited accessibility features such as speech-to-text. Overall, the paper argues that GenAI can enrich elementary math writing and understanding, but only when carefully designed to balance support, imperfection, feedback, collaboration, and accessibility.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived that GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing helped students understand math problems, represent mathematical knowledge, and uncover misconceptions. The study is qualitative and reports no effect size; it is based on interviews, open-ended surveys, and observations from 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers in two U.S. elementary schools.
finding.measure: Perceptions of mathematical understanding, problem representation, and misconception detection during creative math writing activities

finding.finding_summary: Participants described the GenAI-supported activity as making math more interesting and enjoyable, sparking curiosity, and increasing ownership of learning. These outcomes were reported through interviews, survey responses, and classroom observations rather than quantitative outcome measures; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership in learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students used prompt engineering strategies, refined their inputs through trial and error, and learned to evaluate AI strengths and weaknesses, which the authors frame as AI literacy and flexible reasoning. Because the study is qualitative, no effect size or interval is reported; evidence comes from participant perceptions in a 79-student elementary classroom implementation.
finding.measure: Perceived prompt engineering use, evaluation of AI strengths/weaknesses, and flexible/divergent/convergent thinking during story creation

finding.finding_summary: Although the activity was math-focused, the paper substantively examines creative writing as the core task and reports that GenAI helped students draft, revise, and expand their stories. Participants also noted that the tool supported original story creation and richer narrative development, but the evidence is qualitative and does not include quantitative writing scores.
finding.measure: Perceptions of creative mathematical writing, story drafting, revision, and narrative development

paper_profiles.title: The mathematics in middle-aged Arab caliphate and it application to contemporary teaching in high schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a descriptive historical overview of major mathematical contributions made by scholars in the Arab caliphate during the Middle Ages. Its purpose is to highlight the development of algebra, number theory, arithmetic, and related mathematical ideas, and to connect those historical contributions to contemporary high school teaching.

The paper does not evaluate a pedagogical intervention or report a study with measured student outcomes. Instead, it presents a series of historical examples, puzzles, and theorem summaries involving mathematicians such as al-Khwarizmi, Thabit ibn Qurra, al-Haytham, al-Karaji, and others. These are framed as content that teachers might incorporate into high school mathematics lessons to stimulate interest and cultural understanding.

Because the article is essentially a narrative/historical exposition rather than an empirical education study, it provides no direct evidence about learning gains, achievement, retention, transfer, metacognition, self-regulation, or engagement for any learner group. Its relevance to education is limited to suggested classroom use in high school mathematics, especially algebra and number theory topics.

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses mathematical content and historical theorems that could be used in high school teaching, but it does not test any instructional approach or report student outcomes. No quantitative evidence is provided for achievement, conceptual understanding, retention, transfer, or related mathematics learning measures.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Исследовательские задачи и Московская математическая конференция школьников
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a reflective, practice-oriented account of the Moscow Mathematical Conference for School Students (MMKSh). Its central purpose is to explain how the conference is organized so that school students can engage in authentic mathematical research: formulating clear statements, writing complete proofs, revising work based on peer review, and gradually moving from exploratory problem solving toward research-like work that can be judged as reliable and publishable.

The authors describe the conference’s nomination structure, the review and consultation process, and the criteria used to distinguish between educationally valuable work and work that claims scientific novelty. A major emphasis is placed on the role of thorough, transparent peer review, including written referee reports, iterative revision, and the public posting of submitted works and reviews. The paper argues that requiring completed proofs, honest labeling of conjectures and sketches, and explicit checking of novelty helps students learn mathematical rigor and develop realistic expectations about research.

The context is a Russian high-school mathematical culture centered on circles, olympiads, and student research conferences, with examples drawn from several years of MMKSh submissions and outcomes. The paper is not an empirical intervention study with measured student outcomes; rather, it is a descriptive and normative discussion supported by examples of student works that were revised, accepted, and sometimes later published. Its main conclusion is that a well-structured conference with strong editorial/review practices can support the transition from school mathematics to genuine research while protecting students from overstating results or presenting incomplete work as finished science.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that participating in the conference helps students learn to solve mathematical problems, formulate precise statements, and produce completed proofs. No quantitative effect size is reported; the evidence is illustrative and based on examples such as student works that took 1-2 years to mature into finished proofs and eventually received awards or publication.
finding.measure: Mathematical problem solving, proof writing, and completion of research-style mathematical texts

finding.finding_summary: A central claim is that the conference develops research habits such as self-directed inquiry, formulation of hypotheses, attention to precision, and the ability to revise work in response to critique. The paper does not report a numeric effect size; instead it presents a conceptual and procedural account of how students’ intuition, independence, and mathematical communication improve through repeated consultation and re-writing.
finding.measure: Self-directed inquiry, precision in formulation, revision after review, research-oriented thinking

finding.finding_summary: The authors claim that the conference process increases students’ motivation and engagement by making work feel like a meaningful public event and by giving feedback, recognition, and opportunities for revision. No quantitative estimates are provided; evidence is based on conference practice and examples showing that consultation and acceptance can sustain students’ effort over long periods.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, persistence in long-term mathematical work

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes a review-and-consultation workflow intended to improve the efficiency and quality of student submissions: short initial versions are reviewed, feedback is provided quickly, and students iterate before final acceptance. This is presented as a procedural improvement to the conference’s handling of student work, but no numerical workload or time-savings data are reported.
finding.measure: Turnaround and efficiency of reviewing, revising, and accepting student research texts

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s primary empirical content is institutional: it documents a conference system built around transparent peer review, public posting of submissions and reviews, nomination-based distinctions, and openness in governance. The claimed effect is improved fairness, accountability, and protection against unsupported novelty claims, but the paper does not quantify institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Conference governance, transparent peer review, nomination and acceptance procedures

paper_profiles.title: A mathematical model for the bullying dynamics in schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a mathematical compartmental model to study bullying dynamics in schools. The model is motivated by the idea that bullying can spread through social interaction in ways analogous to contagion, and it introduces four states: susceptible individuals, bullies, exposed/victimized individuals, and violent individuals. The author also incorporates spontaneous transitions meant to represent recovery, anti-bullying school programs, parental intervention, and escalation to violence.

The analysis is entirely theoretical and simulation-based, using ordinary differential equations for a homogeneous-mixing population and agent-based simulations on a two-dimensional grid. The model derives a basic reproduction number, R0 = α/γ, and shows two equilibrium regimes: a bullying-free equilibrium when α < γ and an endemic bullying equilibrium when α > γ. Stability analysis indicates that stronger anti-bullying control (higher γ) reduces bullying persistence, while stronger contagion (higher α) increases it.

The paper does not study a real intervention or empirical student sample; instead, it uses mathematical and agent-based simulation to explore conditions under which bullying can persist or be eliminated. Results from grid simulations qualitatively match the mean-field analysis, showing that higher contagion leads to sustained bullying, exposure, and violence, whereas sufficiently strong school and family interventions can drive the system toward a bullying-free state. Because the work is a theoretical model rather than a study of measured educational outcomes, it provides no direct evidence about achievement, engagement, or other student learning outcomes by grade band or learner subgroup.

finding.finding_summary: The model suggests that robust anti-bullying school programs and parental actions can control or eradicate bullying in schools. In the theoretical equilibrium analysis, bullying disappears when the bullying-contagion rate α is lower than the recovery/control rate γ, and the endemic bullying state is stable when α > γ (R0 = α/γ).
finding.measure: Mathematical equilibrium/stability of bullying dynamics under varying control parameters (α, γ, δ, λ, ǫ)

paper_profiles.title: Identification of Books That are Suitable for Middle School Students Using Artificial Neural Networks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of identifying books that are suitable for middle school students. The authors argue that book selection for school use is time-consuming and subjective, and propose an automated screening method to help educators and Ministry of Education officials determine appropriateness more quickly and more consistently.

The approach combines natural language processing and an artificial neural network. The authors built a custom dataset of 416 books labeled as suitable or unsuitable, using books approved by the Turkish Ministry of National Education, Oxford and Cambridge University Libraries, the Gutenberg Project, Amazon age ratings, and books with R-level content as negative examples. They extracted structural and semantic features from the texts, including sentence/word sentiment counts and ratios, words per sentence, and vocabulary-complexity indicators such as middle-school and high-school word ratios, then trained an ANN to classify suitability.

The paper is not an evaluation of formative assessment or student learning outcomes; instead, it is a content-classification system for children’s books. On a held-out test set of 83 books, the model reportedly achieved 90.06% consistency, with 91.2% accuracy for appropriate books and 80.7% for inappropriate books. The authors conclude that the method may serve as a screening tool for schools, teachers, parents, and the Ministry of Education, though they note limitations in handling academically complex texts and recommend a much larger dataset for future work.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed ANN-based screening system improved the efficiency of book selection by automating suitability classification for middle school texts. Using a custom dataset of 416 books, the model achieved 90.06% overall consistency on 83 test books, suggesting it could save time for schools and education officials compared with manual review.
finding.measure: Book-suitability classification accuracy / consistency of an ANN screening model
finding.study_size: n=416 training books; n=83 test books

finding.finding_summary: The system is framed as a tool for the Ministry of Education and schools to support curriculum book selection and age-appropriate screening. The authors argue that the model could provide a preliminary reference source and speed up institutional decisions about which books are appropriate for middle school curricula.
finding.measure: Proposed institutional use for curriculum/book-selection screening

paper_profiles.title: Introducing Computer Science to High School Students through Logic Programming
paper_profiles.venue: Theory and Practice of Logic Programming
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how an introductory computer science course for high school students, taught through Answer Set Programming (ASP) in the SPARC language, affects students’ understanding of computer science and computing. The authors frame the work as a response to the lack of research on logic programming as an introductory paradigm for K-12 CS, especially compared with the more common procedural and visual programming approaches.

The intervention was a summer enrichment course (TexPREP) for 16 high school students in Texas (mostly 10th grade, with some 11th and 12th graders). Students learned to model problems in English first and then translate those models into SPARC code, using an explicit methodology centered on identifying objects, relations, and knowledge before coding. Activities included family relations, map coloring, battleship-like problems, recursion, and Sudoku, supported by labs, surveys, and clinical interviews.

The study is qualitative and combines survey responses, interview transcripts, and programming assignment scores. The main conclusion is that students were able to engage in abstraction, representation, reasoning, and revision within the LP/ASP environment, and that the structured methodology helped them think more deeply about problems and broaden their view of computer science beyond simple programming. The paper does not report experimental causal effects, but it argues that ASP is a viable paradigm for high school novices because it supports problem solving, knowledge representation, and debugging while reducing some barriers of traditional programming languages.

finding.finding_summary: The course aimed at introductory computer science learning, and the qualitative evidence suggests students gained understanding of CS concepts, especially problem solving, abstraction, and knowledge representation through SPARC/ASP. Post-survey responses indicate a shift from viewing CS mainly as programming to viewing it more holistically as problem solving and technology use; lab averages were high (overall 90%, with abstraction 92% and correctness 83%), but no causal effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Post-survey definitions of computer science; clinical interview evidence; programming lab rubric scores (completion, abstraction, correctness, style, documentation)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly analyzes abstraction, reasoning, and representation as central learning processes. Interview coding showed frequent instances of abstraction, reasoning, and representation across participants, and the authors conclude that the explicit modeling methodology helped students think more generally, translate ideas into code, and reason through problems more carefully. No standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Clinical interview coding categories (abstraction, representation, reasoning, revision, procedures); qualitative utterances

finding.finding_summary: Students generally reported enjoying the course and finding the ASP activities interesting, with comments suggesting increased engagement and willingness to continue using the language. Some students noted that the approach made them look at code differently and that the methodology made the tasks easier to understand, but the evidence is descriptive and not based on a formal engagement scale.
finding.measure: Post-survey feedback on course enjoyment, interest, and perceived ease of use
finding.study_size: n=13 respondents to feedback items (out of 16)

paper_profiles.title: Logic Programming for an Introductory Computer Science Course for High School Students
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of a conference paper (venue not specified in provided text)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how high school students approach an introductory computer science course taught in the Answer Set Programming (ASP) / Logic Programming (LP) paradigm. The authors ask whether adopting ASP helps students understand computer science and computing, especially through abstraction, representation, reasoning, and debugging processes that are central to introductory programming.

The study was conducted in a summer enrichment setting (TexPREP at Texas Tech University) with 16 selective high school students in grades 10–12, most of whom had prior experience with Scratch and Alice but no experience with LP or declarative programming. Data came from pre/post open-ended surveys and one-on-one clinical interviews while students solved SPARC programming tasks involving family relationships. The analysis is qualitative and grounded-theory based, producing categories such as abstraction, representation, reasoning, revision, and procedural understanding.

Findings suggest that students were able to learn and apply the explicit problem-solving methodology of ASP, including translating English descriptions into rules, reasoning about relationships, and revising programs via queries. Students’ definitions of computer science broadened from simply “programming” to more problem-solving oriented conceptions by the end of the course. The authors conclude that LP/ASP is a viable option for introductory CS courses, though students may still struggle to see its real-world applications beyond the assignments.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported learning to reevaluate their thinking, translate goals/rules/knowledge from English into SPARC code, and approach problems from a different perspective. In the interviews, abstraction, representation, reasoning, and iterative revision were central processes used to solve programming tasks, suggesting gains in metacognitive problem solving and critical thinking rather than just syntax knowledge.
finding.measure: Pre/post open-ended surveys and clinical interview coding of abstraction, representation, reasoning, and revision during SPARC programming tasks

finding.finding_summary: The course increased students’ understanding of introductory computer science concepts in the context of logic programming. By the end of the course, students described CS less as mere programming and more as problem solving and the study of how computers work, indicating improved conceptual understanding of course content.
finding.measure: Open-ended pre/post survey responses about what computer science is and what was learned in the course

finding.finding_summary: Students generally reported understanding the course topics and being able to complete the tasks, though a few noted time pressure, repetition, or uncertainty about real-world applicability. The paper does not report a formal engagement or motivation metric, but qualitative responses suggest mostly positive task engagement and confidence during the course.
finding.measure: Post-survey self-reports of understanding and task comfort; interview observations of task completion

paper_profiles.title: Analysis of Brownian Motion by Elementary School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports a remote, hands-on science workshop for motivated Japanese elementary school students designed to introduce Brownian motion and the basic logic of scientific inquiry. The workshop used two complementary activities: students tracked Brownian motion in video microscopy using the open-source program Tracker, and they performed a dice-based 2D random-walk experiment to model the mechanism of Brownian motion.

The study’s broader aim was not only to teach a science topic, but also to help young students experience a simplified research process: asking a question, analyzing data quantitatively, proposing a hypothesis, and testing it with a model. The authors emphasize that elementary students, despite limited prior knowledge of physics and mathematics, were able to complete the activities with support and found them interesting even when difficult.

The context was a distance-education workshop held twice during the Japanese academic year of 2020 because of COVID-19. Participants were 27 motivated 4th- to 6th-grade students recruited from public elementary schools; 26 completed the post-workshop survey. Results are based on questionnaire responses and descriptive analysis of student work rather than a controlled comparison. The paper concludes that carefully scaffolded, challenging-but-interesting workshops can stimulate curiosity and introduce foundational scientific reasoning in early science education.

finding.finding_summary: The workshop was designed to teach students the scientific process by having them analyze Brownian motion data, propose a mechanism, and test it with a dice-based random-walk model. The authors report that students were able to complete the analysis and experiment, and that the workshop helped them engage with core practices such as setting a question, doing quantitative analysis, building a hypothesis, and verifying it with a simple model (n=27; post-survey n=26).
finding.measure: Video analysis of Brownian motion; dice-based 2D random-walk experiment; post-workshop questionnaire on understandability and interest

finding.finding_summary: Students’ survey responses suggest that the workshop successfully conveyed scientific inquiry as an activity that is difficult but interesting: 14/26 rated the workshop difficult or very difficult, yet all 26 rated it interesting or very interesting. This indicates engagement with scientific reasoning activities even when the conceptual content was challenging.
finding.measure: Post-workshop 5-point ratings of difficulty and interest
finding.std_deviation: difficulty mean/SD not_reported; interest mean=4.69, SD=0.64; difficulty mean=3.27, SD=1.09

finding.finding_summary: The workshop produced strong positive student reactions, with all respondents rating it interesting or very interesting and more than half rating the activities easy or very easy to perform. The authors interpret this as evidence that the workshop was effective at stimulating curiosity and motivation among these motivated elementary students.
finding.measure: Post-workshop interest ratings and ease-of-use ratings

finding.finding_summary: The activity required students to carry out guided data collection, share data in a spreadsheet, and work through a sequence of analysis steps with support from parents and teaching assistants. The paper frames these processes as practice in quantitative analysis and hypothesis testing, but it does not report a direct measure of durable skills such as metacognition or collaboration.
finding.measure: Observed completion of tracking, data sharing, and group-supported experiment tasks

paper_profiles.title: The Use of Fractional Blocks to Improve Mathematics for Second Grade Elementary School Students at South Bangka Indonesia
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This classroom action research examined whether using fractional blocks could improve second-grade students’ mathematics learning, specifically fraction concepts. The paper starts from the problem that students at SD 9 Simpang Rimba were performing poorly on fractions, with instruction relying heavily on teacher explanation and two-dimensional images that did not match young learners’ concrete-operational development.

The intervention was the use of three-dimensional wooden fractional blocks, implemented through a cycle of planning, action, observation, and reflection. Twenty-three second-grade students (11 girls, 12 boys) participated, and the teacher observed student motivation while documenting test performance before and after the intervention. The study reports that learning motivation rose from a low pre-action mean of 2.52 to 3.91 after the second cycle, while average achievement increased from 65.0 to 80.2 and mastery reached 100%.

The authors conclude that fractional blocks helped make abstract fraction ideas more concrete, increased student participation and interest, and improved mathematics outcomes. The study is limited to a small single-classroom setting in an Indonesian elementary school and focuses on fractions rather than broader math content or differential effects across learner subgroups.

finding.finding_summary: Using fractional blocks was associated with improved fraction achievement in a second-grade classroom action study with n=23. The average math score increased from 65.0 before the action to 73.7 after the first cycle and 80.2 after the second cycle, with reported learning completeness rising from 39% to 100%.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning outcomes in fractions (achievement test / documented scores)

finding.finding_summary: Student learning motivation improved substantially after the fractional-block intervention. The mean motivation score increased from 2.52 before the action (low) to 3.43 after cycle 1 and 3.91 after cycle 2 (high), with an N-gain of 46.49% reported for motivation.
finding.measure: Student learning motivation / activeness ratings (Likert-based observation)

paper_profiles.title: Competency-Based Education in Three Pilot Programs: Examining Implementation and Outcomes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This RAND report evaluates the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation’s Project Mastery initiative, which funded three competency-based education pilot efforts across five U.S. secondary-school settings. The central question is how these programs were implemented, how students experienced them, and what student outcomes were associated with exposure to the new competency-based materials and systems.

The pilots differed in emphasis but all used technology-rich tools intended to support personalized, competency-based learning. Adams 50 focused on mathematics games, teacher-made videos, and an upgraded competency-based learning management system; Asia Society worked with four partner schools to develop performance outcomes, rubrics, curriculum modules, and an LMS; and Philadelphia piloted a ninth-grade English curriculum, a new LMS, and an optional afterschool digital-filmmaking badge program. The report relies on mixed methods: site visits, interviews, student surveys, and nonexperimental outcome analyses tailored to each site’s data and comparison possibilities.

Overall, the report finds that implementation was uneven and shaped by tensions around crediting out-of-school learning, defining proficiency, sustainability, and equity. Student survey results suggested generally positive experiences of value, engagement, choice, and flexibility, though patterns varied by site and subgroup. Outcome findings were mixed: Adams 50 saw a decline in mathematics performance relative to prior trends; Newfound showed a small, nonsignificant increase in reading; some Asia Society schools outperformed comparable peers while others were similar; and Philadelphia showed no clear achievement advantage but modest gains in attendance, with stronger attendance and promotion outcomes for students participating in the optional badge program.

finding.finding_summary: Philadelphia’s Project Mastery students performed below comparison students on the fall language arts assessment after about three months of exposure, were about the same on the winter assessment after five months, and showed no clear advantage on promotion outcomes for the year. The report also notes a modest positive reading association for Newfound Regional High School of about 0.1 standard deviation, but this estimate was not statistically significant and was based on a low-power synthetic comparison analysis.
finding.measure: Language arts assessment scores; reading test scores; promotion to 10th grade
finding.effect_size: about -0.22 SD on fall language arts for Philadelphia; about +0.10 SD reading for Newfound

finding.finding_summary: In Adams 50, the move to a competency-based model was associated with lower mathematics performance on the state accountability test in the five years after the transition. The report summarizes the decline as about 0.22 of a student standard deviation in 2013, with statistical significance at the 10-percent level.
finding.measure: State accountability mathematics test scores

finding.finding_summary: The report includes outcomes for non-math/non-literacy measures such as school completion-related promotion outcomes and performance in the Asia Society schools’ state accountability results, but these were not the primary focus of the report. In Philadelphia, Project Mastery students were about the same as comparison students on promotion to 10th grade, while the optional filmmaking badge program was associated with higher promotion rates (3.0 percentage points) and attendance (6.6 percentage points) for regular participants.
finding.measure: Promotion to 10th grade; school attendance; state accountability outcomes in Asia Society schools
finding.effect_size: +3.0 percentage points promotion and +6.6 percentage points attendance for badge participants

finding.finding_summary: Student survey evidence suggests generally positive experiences of engagement, enjoyment, perceived value of school, and perceptions of flexible pacing and choice across the sites, with DCIS standing out as the most positive on these dimensions. The report also notes modest racial/ethnic differences in survey responses, indicating variation in how students experienced the competency-based tools and approaches.
finding.measure: Student surveys on school value, engagement/enjoyment, choice, flexible pacing, and technology use
finding.study_size: 65.3% overall survey response rate; exact n not reported

finding.finding_summary: The report discusses student choice, self-directed projects, and flexible pacing as core features of the competency-based models, but durable-skills outcomes were not measured directly with a dedicated instrument. Evidence is therefore indirect, drawn mainly from survey responses and descriptions of the learning models rather than from separate tests of collaboration, metacognition, or critical thinking.
finding.measure: Student surveys and implementation descriptions of project-based/choice-based learning

finding.finding_summary: The report documents substantial implementation and institutional challenges, including tensions around awarding credit for out-of-school learning, defining and authorizing proficiency, sustainability of the LMS and hardware infrastructure, and equity concerns. It also reports that the programs were continuing in modified form after the pilot period, suggesting some institutional uptake despite uneven implementation.
finding.measure: Implementation findings from site visits, interviews, and document review; continuation/use of materials after the pilot

paper_profiles.title: Interventions to improve mathematical achievement in primary school-aged children
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report is a systematic review of classroom-based mathematics interventions for primary school-aged children who were not selected because of diagnosed or suspected mathematical disability. The review asks what kinds of interventions have been studied, how effective they are, and what features characterize more promising approaches, with an emphasis on mainstream classroom practice rather than home- or parent-delivered programs.

The authors searched multiple databases and grey-literature sources and included 80 studies published from 2000 to 2017: 45 randomized controlled trials and 35 quasi-experimental studies, covering 14,198 children ages 4–11. The interventions spanned conceptual understanding, magnitudes, basic number skills, fluency practice, strategy use, manipulatives, feedback, technology-based engagement, and varied delivery contexts. Across the review, many studies reported positive effects on at least one mathematics outcome, but the evidence was highly heterogeneous in content, measures, and quality, which prevented meta-analysis.

The main conclusion is that a range of classroom interventions may improve mathematical learning, especially those that focus on key topic areas, support conceptual understanding, use manipulatives appropriately, provide timely feedback, and vary how content is delivered. However, the report stresses caution because many studies used author-generated measures, had diverse intervention intensities, and varied in rigor. The evidence base is promising but not yet strong enough to support simple one-size-fits-all guidance for practice or policy.

finding.finding_summary: Across the 80 included studies, 72 reported a positive impact on at least one academic mathematics outcome, but effects varied widely by intervention type and outcome. The review did not report a single pooled effect size; rather, it narratively summarized positive, mixed, and null findings across conceptual understanding, magnitudes, basic skills, fluency, strategy use, manipulatives, feedback, and technology-based interventions (n=14,198 total across studies).
finding.measure: Curriculum-based assessments, standardized mathematics tests, and cognitive experimental measures of mathematics skills

finding.finding_summary: The review included studies that measured mathematics-related attitudes, anxiety, confidence, enjoyment, and engagement, and several interventions produced positive secondary effects. For example, the executive summary reports 12 studies with benefits for secondary outcomes such as attitudes or anxiety related to mathematics, while some technology-based interventions also improved self-monitoring or engagement-related outcomes.
finding.measure: Mathematics anxiety, attitudes, self-efficacy/confidence, enjoyment, and self-monitoring/engagement measures

finding.finding_summary: Several included interventions explicitly targeted metacognitive and strategy-related skills, including reflection on strategy use, problem solving, and self-monitoring. The review reports that interventions such as strategy training, metacognitive reflection, and web-based problem-solving approaches often improved strategy efficiency and self-monitoring compared with controls, indicating gains in durable skills beyond narrow computation.
finding.measure: Strategy efficiency, problem solving, metacognitive reflection, and self-monitoring tasks

paper_profiles.title: Feedback: Unveiling Its Impact and Enhancing Its Effectiveness in Education
paper_profiles.venue: Revista de Pedagogie / Journal of Pedagogy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article reviews the educational literature on feedback, focusing on what feedback is, why it matters, and how it can be made more effective in teaching and learning. Rather than testing a new classroom intervention, it synthesizes prior research and theory on written, oral, online, and peer feedback, drawing on classic assessment and learning frameworks such as Bloom, Black & Wiliam, Hattie & Timperley, Vygotsky, and feedback intervention theory.

The paper argues that feedback is a central mechanism for improving student learning, motivation, self-regulation, and growth mindset, but that its effectiveness depends on how it is delivered: it should be timely, specific, constructive, comprehensible, and aligned with learner needs. The article also emphasizes that poorly designed or overly negative feedback can undermine confidence and motivation. It concludes with a proposed feedback model that encourages effort recognition, self-reflection, goal-setting, and periodic assessment to support continuous improvement.

Because this is a narrative/systematic literature review with no original sample or controlled comparison, it does not provide experimental evidence about a specific instructional program or control condition. Its contribution is conceptual: it summarizes how feedback is used across educational settings and identifies features associated with more effective practice, especially in higher education and general classroom assessment contexts.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, constructive and timely feedback is described as supporting student motivation, self-esteem, engagement, and persistence, while poorly delivered negative feedback can reduce confidence and discourage continued interest. The paper does not report a single pooled effect size; instead it synthesizes prior studies and theory to argue that feedback influences learners’ emotional and motivational responses.
finding.measure: Student motivation, engagement, self-esteem, confidence, and persistence as reported in prior studies and theoretical sources

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that effective feedback can foster self-regulation, metacognitive awareness, self-evaluation, and goal-setting. It repeatedly emphasizes that feedback helps students monitor their learning, reflect on errors, and make adjustments, but it does not quantify these effects in the article itself.
finding.measure: Self-regulation, metacognition, self-evaluation, and goal-setting discussed in the reviewed literature

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that feedback improves overall academic performance and learning outcomes across educational contexts, particularly when it is written, oral, online, or peer-based and when it is specific, prompt, and actionable. No original dataset or effect size is reported in this review; the claim is based on synthesis of earlier studies cited throughout the paper.
finding.measure: General academic performance and learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that feedback can improve instructional efficiency by helping teachers identify curriculum gaps and by making teaching and learning more responsive to student needs. However, this is a conceptual argument derived from reviewed literature rather than a measured effect in the present article.
finding.measure: Teaching/learning process efficiency and identification of curriculum gaps

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative/practical guide that examines how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback in education. It is framed around established formative-assessment theory and focuses on the core questions of where learners are going, where they are now, and how they can move forward.

The authors do not report an empirical intervention study; instead, they synthesize prior work and provide illustrative prompting examples for educators. They show how LLMs can be used to rewrite learning objectives in student-friendly language, co-construct success criteria, generate sample work, create quiz questions and other short-cycle checks for understanding, and produce feedback at task, process, and self-regulatory levels.

The paper’s main conclusion is that LLMs may help scale formative assessment by reducing teacher workload and making feedback and questioning more accessible, but only when used with strong pedagogical judgment. The authors emphasize that LLM outputs must be checked for accuracy, appropriateness, and alignment with learning goals, and they caution that LLMs should augment, not replace, expert teaching practices.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce educator time and effort in creating formative assessment materials, such as rewriting objectives, generating exemplars, and producing quiz items and feedback. This is presented as a scalability and workload benefit rather than as an empirically tested effect; no sample size, effect size, or statistical estimate is reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload / time required to create formative assessment materials

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that LLM-supported formative assessment can promote metacognition, critical thinking, and self-regulation by helping students understand goals, monitor progress, and reflect on sample work. This claim is conceptual and supported by cited prior literature rather than original data; no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: metacognition, self-regulation, critical thinking, reflection

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides examples of LLM use in writing-related formative tasks, including simplifying learning objectives, generating sample essays/method sections, and drafting student-friendly prompts. These examples are meant to support academic writing and understanding across subjects, but the paper does not report an empirical writing outcome, effect size, or sample size.
finding.measure: writing tasks / learning-objective clarity / exemplar generation

finding.finding_summary: Scientific and STEM examples are used throughout the paper, especially biology and fMRI methods, to illustrate how LLMs can support formative assessment in science learning. The paper argues that LLMs can help clarify scientific goals and generate questions or exemplars, but it does not present a direct empirical test of scientific reasoning outcomes.
finding.measure: science-oriented formative assessment tasks and scientific writing/method understanding

paper_profiles.title: Globally Networked Learning in a University Classroom: A Pilot Program
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes and evaluates a pilot Collaborative Online International Learning (COIL) program implemented in a Texas A&M University College of Liberal Arts course context. The authors argue that COIL can provide an international, high-impact learning experience for students who may not study abroad, while also supporting intercultural competence and retention among first-generation students.

The intervention paired Texas A&M classes with classes in Australia and Italy for several weeks of asynchronous and synchronous online collaboration. Students completed shared projects, email negotiations, peer review, reflection journals, and presentations using tools such as Skype, email, Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter. Faculty in both institutions coordinated the work, and students were assessed by their home instructors. The paper also reports related institutional efforts to extend COIL to a first-year retention initiative for Regents Scholars. The main conclusions are that the collaborative online format was feasible, produced strong student work, and was viewed by instructors as meeting learning objectives, with promising implications for intercultural learning and retention, though the evidence is descriptive and based on small pilot experiences rather than a controlled outcome study.

finding.finding_summary: The pilot COIL courses were reported to strengthen collaboration, reflection, and critical thinking through sustained cross-national teamwork. In the Australia/Texas A&M and Italy/Texas A&M collaborations, instructors reported that students took the projects seriously, worked extensively with peers abroad, and produced high-quality papers and final presentations, but no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student project quality, reflection journals, email threads, and instructor judgment of collaboration/critical thinking

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the COIL experience was intended to and appeared to foster intercultural awareness, engagement, and student persistence/retention, especially for first-generation students. The authors cite retention increases in related COIL initiatives (e.g., students retained at 90-95% versus typical institutional rates around 70%), but those figures are presented as contextual evidence rather than a direct estimate from this pilot.
finding.measure: Retention rates, student participation, and instructor/student reports of engagement and intercultural awareness

finding.finding_summary: At the institutional level, the paper argues that COIL provides a low-cost alternative to study abroad and can be scaled to support first-generation student retention and internationalization goals. The authors describe renewed COIL programming and planned expansion into Regents Scholars and other first-year initiatives, but do not provide causal evidence of institutional impact from the pilot itself.
finding.measure: Program implementation, renewal of COIL offerings, and reported retention figures in related initiatives

finding.finding_summary: Students completed disciplinary academic work through international collaboration, including legal conflict-management case studies and classics research papers. The paper reports that the collaborative projects met course objectives and produced very high-quality outputs, including papers later collected into a published volume, but it does not report standardized academic test scores or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Course projects, research papers, PowerPoint presentations, and instructor evaluation of course objectives

paper_profiles.title: Analyzing the assessment of lesson planning in medical teacher training program
paper_profiles.venue: Annals of the University of Craiova, Series: Psychology-Pedagogy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how the criteria used to assess lesson plans influence the scores obtained by teacher-training students in a medical specialization program. The authors compare two non-equivalent samples of lesson plans from Level I of a postgraduate teacher-training program, one from 2020–2021 and one from 2022–2023, to see whether more detailed, subsequent assessment criteria produce different scoring outcomes than more general criteria.

The intervention is not a classroom teaching intervention but an assessment design comparison. Across 94 lesson plans (47 in each sample), the paper contrasts a rubric with mostly general criteria against a rubric with more fine-grained, subsequent criteria, particularly for objectives and strategy. The study finds that adding subsequent criteria lowers final scores, suggesting that detailed rubrics capture more deficiencies in lesson planning, especially in how objectives are formulated and aligned with competences, methods, materials, feedback, and assessment grids.

The context is teacher education for medical specialization at the West University of Timișoara, Romania. The paper concludes that lesson-plan assessment should use clearly specified criteria because these help reveal weaknesses in planning and can guide improvement in future lesson design. It argues that more detailed criteria provide a stronger framework for developing lesson-planning competence in pre-service medical teachers.

finding.finding_summary: Using more detailed, subsequent assessment criteria led to lower final lesson-plan scores than using only general criteria. In 94 lesson plans (n=47 per sample), the rubric with more specific criteria appears to have identified more shortcomings in planning, especially in objectives and strategy alignment.
finding.measure: Lesson plan assessment scores based on rubric criteria

finding.finding_summary: The more detailed rubric revealed weaknesses in students' ability to formulate objectives, align them with competencies, and connect them to methods, materials, and assessment. These are planning and metacognitive design skills central to lesson preparation rather than direct student learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Quality of lesson-plan objective formulation and alignment across rubric criteria

paper_profiles.title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
paper_profiles.population: Not reported (the paper is a literature review of self-regulated learning models, not a study of a single participant population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of six major self-regulated learning (SRL) models: Zimmerman, Boekaerts, Winne and Hadwin, Pintrich, Efklides, and Hadwin/Järvelä/Miller. Its central purpose is to compare the models’ theoretical structures, empirical support, and measurement approaches, and to draw implications for future SRL research and educational practice.

The article does not test a new intervention. Instead, it synthesizes prior empirical and meta-analytic work on SRL, highlighting how the models differ in their treatment of metacognition, motivation, emotion, context, and collaborative learning. It also notes that available meta-analytic evidence suggests differential effects of SRL models depending on students’ developmental stage or educational level.

Because this is a conceptual and review paper, the relevant evidence comes from previously published studies discussed within the review rather than from a new sample in this paper. The paper’s main conclusion is that SRL models provide an integrative framework for understanding and teaching strategic learning, but that researchers and teachers should pay closer attention to developmental and contextual differences when applying SRL theory. It further argues that future work should better examine how learner characteristics, contexts, and collaborative settings shape SRL processes and outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: This review argues that self-regulated learning models are broadly useful for explaining and improving metacognition, strategic learning, and self-regulation, but that their effects vary by developmental stage and educational level. The paper synthesizes prior evidence rather than reporting a new effect size; it concludes that differential effects exist and should be applied in instruction, but it does not provide a pooled estimate for learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning processes, metacognition, and strategic learning as reported across prior studies and meta-analyses

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes that SRL includes motivational and emotional components, and that prior studies show emotions, motivation, and self-regulation interact in important ways. However, the paper does not estimate a single overall effect; it summarizes heterogeneous evidence suggesting SRL can support motivation and persistence, with effects depending on context and learner level.
finding.measure: Motivation, emotion regulation, and self-regulation constructs reported in SRL studies

paper_profiles.title: The effects of self-monitoring and self-reflection in A1 adult learners in an English blended learning environment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This master’s thesis examines whether self-monitoring and self-reflection strategies influence the learning experience of A1 adult learners in an English blended-learning course. The study is framed as a learner-centered response to traditional assessment practices that emphasized grades over feedback, with the goal of promoting formative self-assessment, autonomy, and greater learner involvement.

The intervention was implemented in a blended English course for adult distance tutors at Universidad Nacional Abierta y a Distancia (UNAD) in Bucaramanga, Colombia. Data sources included checklists, surveys, and student journals, and the analysis focused on how participants perceived and responded to self-assessment practices embedded in face-to-face and online sessions.

The findings indicate generally positive effects: participants became more aware of the language-learning process, identified areas for improvement, monitored their progress, and set learning goals. The study also reports positive responses to scaffolded instruction and to the blended modality itself. Because this is a qualitative action-research thesis with no reported inferential effect sizes, the evidence is best interpreted as descriptive and context-specific rather than causal or generalizable.

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported improved awareness of their English learning process and increased engagement with language practice in the blended course. The study does not report standardized fluency test scores, but it describes positive perceived effects on language learning progress among the A1 adult learners (n=not_reported).
finding.measure: Self-reported perceptions of English learning process and progress; journals, surveys, and checklists

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was associated with more active involvement in learning, greater motivation to monitor progress, and positive reactions to self-assessment and scaffolded instruction. Participants identified strengths and weaknesses, followed their progress, and set learning goals, suggesting gains in self-regulation and engagement (n=not_reported).
finding.measure: Student journals, surveys, and checklists capturing engagement, involvement, and self-regulation

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally examines metacognitive and self-regulatory processes, especially self-monitoring, self-reflection, planning, and goal setting. Findings indicate that participants developed awareness of their strengths and weaknesses, monitored learning and progress, and planned learning goals; no quantitative effect size is reported (n=not_reported).
finding.measure: Metacognitive/self-regulation evidence from journals, surveys, and checklists

paper_profiles.title: Scaffolding in Teacher–Student Interaction: A Decade of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines a decade of research on scaffolding in teacher–student interaction, focusing on how scaffolding has been defined, how it appears in classroom practice, and whether it is effective. The authors argue that scaffolding is commonly used too loosely in the literature and propose three core characteristics that should define it: contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility.

The review synthesizes theoretical, descriptive, and a small number of effectiveness studies from primary and secondary education contexts across literacy, mathematics, science, and other classroom domains. It finds that most research is descriptive and that scaffolding is most often studied in literacy, with many studies also in math and science. The review concludes that the limited effectiveness evidence generally suggests positive effects of scaffolding on students’ metacognitive/cognitive activity and, to a lesser extent, affect, but emphasizes that stronger measurement and more rigorous studies are needed.

The paper also offers a framework distinguishing scaffolding means (e.g., questioning, modeling, feedback) from intentions (e.g., metacognitive, cognitive, affective support) to help analyze future classroom interactions. Overall, the article is primarily a synthesis of the scaffolding literature rather than a single empirical test, and its main contribution is conceptual clarification and methodological guidance.

finding.finding_summary: In the reviewed effectiveness studies, scaffolding generally improved students’ mathematics learning. In Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998), fourth- and fifth-grade students who received fully contingent support solved significantly more long-division problems than peers in other conditions at immediate and delayed posttest (n=40 across five groups; 8 per condition). In Murphy and Messer (2000), 5- to 7-year-olds in a one-to-one scaffolding condition advanced more in representation level on a balance-scale task than children working collaboratively or alone, although only the comparison with the small-group condition was significant (n=122).
finding.measure: Math problem solving (long division) and balance-scale representation/transfer tasks

finding.finding_summary: Several effectiveness studies in science-related contexts found benefits of scaffolding for conceptual understanding and transfer. Azevedo et al. (2005) reported that seventh- and 10th-grade students receiving adaptive human scaffolding showed more shifts in mental models and greater gains on circulatory-system knowledge than students receiving fixed or no scaffolding (N=38, 34, 37). Chiu et al. (2002) found that 10th-grade students in a cognitive apprenticeship/scaffolding condition constructed better mental models of chemical equilibrium than a control group (N=20 vs. N=10).
finding.measure: Mental model change, conceptual understanding, and science knowledge/transfer

finding.finding_summary: The review reports positive effects of scaffolding on engagement, involvement, and enjoyment in some studies, but the evidence is mixed. Turner et al. (1998) found that whole-class scaffolding strategies intended to support motivation and emotion were more common in higher-involvement fifth and sixth grade mathematics classes (N=42 across 34 lessons). In Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998), students in the no-support condition reported significantly lower enjoyment than students in the scaffolded conditions, although the scaffolded conditions did not differ from one another.
finding.measure: Student involvement/enjoyment questionnaires and coded classroom discourse

finding.finding_summary: The strongest recurring evidence in the review concerns metacognition, self-regulation, and collaborative reasoning. Mercer et al. (2004) found that students in the Thinking Together condition were better able to use talk for reasoning and made greater gains on nonverbal reasoning than controls (N=109 vs. N=121). Azevedo et al. (2005) found that adaptive human scaffolding was associated with more self-regulating behavior and greater knowledge gains than fixed or no scaffolding, and Chi et al. (2001) reported higher transfer-question performance and greater learner responsibility under more interactive, contingent tutoring.
finding.measure: Reasoning talk, self-regulated learning behaviors, transfer questions, and constructive learning activity

finding.finding_summary: The review states that scaffolding is most fully developed in literacy and describes numerous descriptive studies of literacy instruction, but it does not present a single pooled effect estimate for literacy outcomes. It does note that literacy scaffolding studies commonly examined comprehension, strategy use, and text discussion, and that several studies reported effective scaffolding in these contexts. Because the evidence summarized here is largely descriptive rather than comparative, the finding is best characterized as generally positive but not quantified.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension, literacy strategy use, and text discussion

paper_profiles.title: Beyond feedback: Developing student capability in complex appraisal
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
