This paper addresses a theoretical and practice-oriented problem in higher education assessment: why detailed feedback often fails to improve student work, even when instructors invest substantial time in providing it. Sadler argues that the common model of feedback-as-telling is limited because students frequently lack the conceptual and tacit knowledge needed to interpret, connect, and act on feedback comments.

Rather than proposing another feedback format, the article develops an alternative pedagogical model centered on purposeful peer assessment. The approach is designed to help students build capability in complex appraisal by learning three core concepts: task compliance, quality, and criteria. Through repeated evaluative practice on peers’ work, students are expected to develop the judgment, vocabulary, and tacit knowledge needed to understand quality, explain evaluations, and self-monitor their own work.

The paper is set in higher education and is mainly conceptual, drawing on prior literature and the author’s earlier work rather than reporting a new empirical study. Its main conclusion is that improving learning in complex tasks likely requires moving beyond teacher-generated feedback toward structured appraisal experiences that induct students into the practices of expert assessors. The paper does not present subgroup analyses, grade-band comparisons, or quantitative effects for different learner populations.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative feedback alone often has limited effect on students’ ability to judge quality, but that purposeful peer appraisal can develop evaluative judgment, critical thinking, and self-monitoring. No new empirical effect sizes are reported; the claim is conceptual and based on prior literature and examples from higher education assessment practice.
finding.measure: Evaluative judgment, critical thinking, self-monitoring, complex appraisal capability

finding.finding_summary: The article contends that effective formative assessment should support students’ engagement and self-regulation, but notes that teacher feedback often does not produce measurable improvement because students cannot decode or use it well. The paper does not provide direct empirical measurement of motivation or engagement in a new study.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning, engagement with assessment processes

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses the labor-intensive nature of individualized written feedback and suggests that structured peer assessment may reduce reliance on teacher feedback while also supporting learning. This is an argumentative claim rather than a reported empirical comparison, so no quantitative impact estimate is provided.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, feedback production effort

paper_profiles.title: A Critical Review of Research on Student Self-Assessment
paper_profiles.population: K-20 students (elementary through undergraduate; mixed settings)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper critically reviews research on student self-assessment, primarily studies published between 2013 and 2018, to clarify what self-assessment is, how it should be operationalized, and what kinds of outcomes it influences. Andrade argues that self-assessment is most useful when treated as formative feedback: students judge their own work or learning processes against criteria, then use that information to revise, regulate learning, or improve performance.

The review synthesizes 76 empirical studies, including quasi-experimental, experimental, correlational, and qualitative work, plus two meta-analyses. It covers summative versus formative self-assessment, the consistency of students’ judgments with external evaluations, student perceptions, achievement outcomes, and links to self-regulated learning. Across the reviewed evidence, formative self-assessment is generally associated with better achievement and stronger self-regulated learning, while summative self-assessment is often inconsistent with external judgments and can encourage grade inflation.

The paper also highlights subgroup and developmental patterns noted in the literature: older and more academically competent learners tend to be more consistent in self-assessment, and some studies report differences by gender. Andrade concludes that future research should move away from asking whether self-assessment is accurate in the abstract and instead examine how formative self-assessment works, for whom it works best, and how cognitive and affective mechanisms translate self-assessment into learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: Across 20 formative self-assessment studies plus two meta-analyses, the review reports a positive association with literacy outcomes, especially writing quality. The Graham et al. meta-analysis (10 studies) found an average weighted effect size of 0.62 on writing quality, and all non-meta-analytic formative studies in this set showed positive learning effects.
finding.measure: Writing quality / written assignment scores

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that formative self-assessment is associated with stronger self-regulated learning, including goal setting, self-monitoring, planning, and reflection. Studies using scripts or rubrics reported statistically significant improvements in self-regulation, with small-to-moderate effects (η2 = 0.06–0.42).
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning questionnaires and think-aloud protocols

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes metacognition as a central mechanism and outcome of self-assessment. It reports that rubric- and script-based self-assessment was associated with better metacognitive/self-regulatory behaviors, and one study showed associations across all three SRL phases: forethought, performance, and reflection.
finding.measure: Metacognition / self-regulation measures; think-alouds and questionnaires

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that formative self-assessment improves achievement across a wide range of non-writing academic tasks and disciplines, including exams, dart throwing, map-making, and speaking English. Although most evidence is not summarized with a single pooled estimate, the direction is consistently positive for formative approaches, while one summative study showed no exam-score gain and another did.
finding.measure: Exam scores and varied task-performance outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Learning strategies: a synthesis and conceptual model
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article synthesizes 228 meta-analyses on learning strategies and proposes a conceptual model of learning organized around inputs (skill, will, thrill), success criteria, and three learning phases (surface, deep, transfer), each with acquisition and consolidation stages. The authors ask which strategies are most effective and, more importantly, when they are most effective within the learning cycle.

The paper is not an intervention study itself; it is a meta-synthesis of prior meta-analyses and reviews spanning roughly 18,956 studies and an estimated 11 to 20 million learners. The synthesis emphasizes that strategies are not universally effective: their usefulness depends on whether learners are acquiring surface knowledge, consolidating it, building deep understanding, or transferring learning to new contexts.

Main conclusions are that strategies such as success criteria, feedback, deliberate practice, self-regulation, metacognition, and transfer-oriented instruction show positive average effects, while some environmental factors have small effects and working-memory training shows little evidence of far transfer to academic outcomes. The authors argue that learning strategies should be embedded in subject content and matched to phase and purpose, rather than taught as generic study-skills courses. The paper also notes some moderator evidence by age/grade band and, in one cited subgroup analysis, that help-seeking patterns change in early adolescence.

finding.finding_summary: The synthesis reports positive effects for literacy-related outcomes, especially reading and writing, in the self-regulation literature. In Donker et al.'s meta-analysis summarized here, self-regulation training showed effects of d=0.36 for reading comprehension, and Dignath et al. reported effects of 0.44 for reading/writing outcomes.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension; reading and writing achievement

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports positive effects for mathematics outcomes in self-regulation and strategy training studies. Dignath et al. summarized in the paper found mathematics effects of 0.96 and 1.21 in different analyses, and Donker et al. reported an overall mathematics effect of d=0.66.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement

finding.finding_summary: The synthesis reports positive effects for science achievement in self-regulation training. Donker et al., as summarized in the article, found an overall effect of d=0.73 in science, indicating substantial gains associated with self-regulation interventions.
finding.measure: Science achievement

finding.finding_summary: This paper’s central empirical contribution is a broad synthesis of learning-strategy effects on achievement across many subject areas and criteria. The overall average effect across 301–302 effects is about d=0.53, with strong positive effects for success criteria (d=0.55 overall; specific strategies up to d=1.13), surface learning (d=0.63), deep learning (d=0.57), and transfer (reported effects of 1.32 and 1.14 for similarity/difference and patterns to new situations).
finding.measure: General academic achievement; success criteria; surface/deep learning; transfer outcomes
finding.study_size: 18,956 studies; estimated 11,006,839 reported participants (likely 13–20 million total when prorated)
finding.effect_size: d=0.53 overall; d=0.55 success criteria; d=0.63 surface learning; d=0.57 deep learning; d=1.09 transfer

finding.finding_summary: The synthesis finds generally positive effects for self-efficacy, task value, reducing anxiety, self-concept, and attitude to content. For example, self-efficacy shows d=0.90, task value d=0.46, reducing anxiety d=0.45, and attitude to content d=0.35, suggesting that learning-strategy-related interventions can improve motivational and emotional outcomes tied to engagement and persistence.
finding.measure: Self-efficacy, task value, anxiety, self-concept, attitude to content, motivation

finding.finding_summary: Durable-skill outcomes are a major focus of the paper, especially metacognition, self-regulation, collaboration, help-seeking, and critical thinking. Reported effects are positive for metacognitive strategies (d=0.61), self-regulation (d=0.52), concept mapping (d=0.64), peer tutoring (d=0.54), collaborative/cooperative learning (d=0.38), and critical thinking techniques (d=0.34), with several strategy-specific effects in the 0.7+ range.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-regulation, collaboration, help-seeking, critical thinking, concept mapping
finding.study_size: varies by meta-analysis; not_reported at outcome level
finding.effect_size: d=0.61 metacognitive strategies; d=0.52 self-regulation; d=0.64 concept mapping; d=0.54 peer tutoring; d=0.38 collaborative learning; d=0.34 critical thinking

finding.finding_summary: Several strategies are framed as improving learning efficiency and time use, including time management, reviewing records, practice testing, and deliberate practice. The paper reports positive effects for deliberate practice (d=0.77), time on task (d=0.54), and reviewing records (d=0.49), but also notes that some common efficiency-oriented strategies such as time management have only modest effects (d=0.40) and practice testing is lower (d=0.44).
finding.measure: Time on task, time management, practice routines, reviewing records, deliberate practice
finding.effect_size: d=0.77 deliberate practice; d=0.54 time on task; d=0.49 reviewing records; d=0.40 time management

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that learning strategies should be embedded within subject teaching rather than taught as standalone study-skills courses, implying implications for curriculum design and instructional policy. However, this is mainly a conceptual recommendation drawn from the synthesis rather than a direct institutional-outcome study.
finding.measure: Curricular/instructional design recommendations

paper_profiles.title: The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper revisits the question of how effective feedback is for student learning by conducting a meta-analysis of educational feedback research. The authors explicitly aim to replicate and improve on prior “Visible Learning” syntheses by integrating primary-study effect sizes rather than averaging meta-analytic summaries, and by using random-effects methods, outlier handling, and moderator analyses.

The review includes 435 studies yielding 994 effect sizes and more than 61,000 participants from kindergarten, primary, secondary, college, and university contexts. The paper examines whether feedback effects vary by research design, publication type, outcome type, feedback type, feedback channel, and feedback direction. The main conclusion is that feedback has a medium overall positive effect on learning (d=0.48 after excluding extreme values), but effects are highly heterogeneous and depend strongly on feedback characteristics.

Across outcome types, feedback is more effective for cognitive and physical outcomes than for motivational and behavioral outcomes. The strongest effects are found for high-information feedback, while reinforcement/punishment is much weaker. The authors conclude that feedback should not be treated as a single treatment; instead, its effectiveness depends on the amount of information it provides and on how it is delivered and used in instructional settings.

finding.finding_summary: Across 994 effect sizes from 435 studies (N > 61,000), feedback produced a positive overall effect on student learning, with a random-effects estimate of d=0.48 after removing 35 extreme values (3.5%). The paper treats student learning broadly, including achievement and cognitive test outcomes; the overall summary indicates a medium positive impact on academic outcomes.
finding.measure: Student learning / academic achievement / cognitive outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Feedback had a smaller positive effect on motivational outcomes than on cognitive outcomes, with d=0.33 across 109 effect sizes. The authors note that 21% of motivational effect sizes were negative, especially for uninformative reinforcement/punishment, suggesting that feedback can either help or harm motivation depending on its form.
finding.measure: Intrinsic motivation, locus of control, self-efficacy, persistence

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis found that feedback was more effective for cognitive outcomes than for motivational outcomes, and the discussion links these cognitive outcomes to processes such as understanding, strategy use, and self-regulation. High-information feedback showed the largest effects, indicating benefits for deeper processing and monitoring of learning, though these durable-skill outcomes were not isolated as a separate pooled category.
finding.measure: Cognitive outcomes relevant to strategy use, understanding, and self-regulation

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes behavioral outcomes such as classroom behavior and discipline, but these outcomes show a weak and imprecise pooled effect relative to cognitive outcomes. The summary estimate is d=0.48 across 30 effect sizes, but with a wide confidence interval crossing zero, indicating substantial uncertainty and no clear reliable operational benefit.
finding.measure: Student behavior in classrooms / discipline

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ roles and identities in student-centered classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative case study examines how secondary STEM teachers experience and interpret a shift from traditional teacher-centered instruction to a student-centered, peer-mediated model. The paper is motivated by the need to understand what happens to teachers’ roles, responsibilities, and professional identities when they are asked to implement classrooms in which students work in small groups led by peer instructors and teachers act more as facilitators, assessors, and coaches.

The intervention/context is the Peer Enabled Restructured Classroom (PERC) Program in two urban New York City high schools. Thirteen certified mathematics and science teachers participated; some had easy transitions, some struggled, and one left the program. Data came from interviews, focus groups, observations, and coaching records collected over multiple years. The schools served high-needs student populations, including many multilingual learners and students with special needs, but the paper’s empirical focus is on teacher experiences rather than student outcome comparisons.

Findings show that most teachers reported benefits from the student-centered model, including improved ability to know what students were doing, greater support for individual students, reduced classroom management burden, and a more fulfilling alignment with preferred professional identities. Special education teachers in particular found the model consistent with their student-support orientation. However, teachers whose identities were tightly tied to content delivery or traditional authority roles experienced more difficulty; one teacher resisted the shift and exited the program. Overall, the study concludes that radically changing classroom structure can substantially reshape teacher identity and practice, with implications for professional development and implementation support.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently reported that the PERC model reduced classroom-management burden and made instruction feel more efficient. They described fewer interruptions for basic questions, less time spent repeating instructions, and more time available for higher-level instructional support, but no quantitative effect sizes were reported because the evidence is qualitative.
finding.measure: Teacher interviews, focus groups, and coaching observations regarding classroom management, time on task, and instructional efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The study found that teachers experienced higher professional satisfaction, self-efficacy, and reduced stress when their identities aligned with the student-centered model. These changes were described through interview and focus-group evidence rather than standardized measures; one teacher resisted the change and experienced continuing conflict with the approach.
finding.measure: Teacher self-reports of satisfaction, stress, and self-efficacy in interviews and focus groups

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally examines collaboration, facilitation, and reflective practice as teachers took on new roles in a peer-mediated STEM classroom. Teachers described shifts toward managing groups, assessing peer-led learning, and collaborating with TAS and coaches; the study does not report numeric effect sizes.
finding.measure: Teacher narratives and observations of collaborative, facilitative, and reflective instructional roles

finding.finding_summary: The program was presented as supporting implementation of student-centered pedagogy and improving alignment with teacher evaluation systems, especially the Danielson Framework. Administrators and coaches reported improved observation ratings and stronger program fidelity, but the paper does not provide quantitative institutional outcome estimates.
finding.measure: Administrator, coach, and teacher reports about implementation fidelity and evaluation observations

paper_profiles.title: Investigating the effects of formative assessment on EFL students’ achievement and motivation: a Self-Determination Theory perspective
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This quasi-experimental study examined whether a structured formative assessment (FA) intervention improves middle school EFL students’ English achievement and motivational outcomes, using Self-Determination Theory as the guiding framework. The authors focused on three motivational needs—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—and asked whether FA changes these needs and whether they mediate achievement.

finding.finding_summary: The experimental group receiving formative-assessment-based instruction scored higher on English achievement than the conventional-instruction control group, but the paper’s mediation tests suggest the achievement benefit operated indirectly through motivation rather than as a direct group effect. In the experimental group, the regression model predicting achievement was significant (F(3,128)=4.48, p=0.005, R2=0.095), and autonomy was the strongest predictor (β=0.19, p=0.026).
finding.measure: English achievement test (reading, grammar, writing sections)

finding.finding_summary: Formative assessment had its clearest effect on relatedness, while autonomy and competence increased only modestly and did not reach statistical significance in the main ANCOVA tests. Relatedness at Time 3 differed significantly between groups, F(1,85)=35.65, p<0.001, partial η2=0.298, whereas autonomy and competence were nonsignificant.
finding.measure: SDT-based motivation questionnaire assessing autonomy, relatedness, and competence
finding.effect_size: partial η2=0.298 for relatedness at Time 3; partial η2=0.022 autonomy, 0.014 competence

finding.finding_summary: The study includes a self-regulation-adjacent motivational mechanism through autonomy and reflective assessment practices, but it does not directly measure metacognition or self-regulation outcomes. Evidence is indirect: the authors argue that FA-supported autonomy helps learners monitor and direct their own learning, and autonomy significantly predicted achievement in the experimental group (β=0.19, p=0.026).
finding.measure: Autonomy subscale of SDT-based motivation questionnaire; indirect discussion of reflection and self-monitoring

paper_profiles.title: Classroom assessment and pedagogy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that formative and summative assessment should not be treated as separate domains detached from pedagogy. Drawing on theoretical and scholarly literature, Black and Wiliam propose that classroom assessment is best understood within a broader model of pedagogy that includes aims, planning, dialogue, formative feedback, and summative assessment, all linked through evidentiary reasoning about student learning.

The article is not an empirical intervention study; rather, it synthesizes prior research and conceptual arguments to show how assessment shapes instruction, classroom dialogue, and accountability. The authors emphasize that effective teaching depends on eliciting evidence from students, using that evidence to adapt instruction, and designing assessment so that formative and summative purposes can support one another rather than conflict.

A major theme is the tension between accountability-driven testing and practices that support learning. The paper argues that high-stakes external assessments can distort pedagogy by narrowing what is taught, but it also suggests that teacher-generated assessment can strengthen validity, support richer inferences about learning, and improve classroom decision-making when accompanied by moderation, training, and clear criteria.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative and summative assessment practices can improve the efficiency and usefulness of teachers’ instructional decision-making by providing evidence to adjust teaching and by making moderation and standardisation more rigorous. In the KOSAP discussion, the authors report that moderation and standardisation were described as “incredibly valuable” for ensuring rigour, consistency, and confidence in assessment practice, though no quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher assessment practices, moderation, standardisation, and workload implications

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central claim is that classroom assessment has important systemic implications for accountability, curriculum, and assessment policy. It argues that high-stakes external testing can undermine learning by narrowing instruction, while teacher involvement in summative assessment can improve validity, comparability, and alignment with broader educational aims; however, the paper also notes unresolved tensions and technical challenges.
finding.measure: Assessment policy, accountability systems, validity of assessment use, moderation systems

finding.finding_summary: The paper strongly emphasizes dialogue, collaboration, metacognition, and self-regulation as important aims and mechanisms within formative classroom assessment. These are discussed conceptually rather than with new empirical estimates, with the authors arguing that formative assessment supports learners’ ability to monitor and regulate their own learning and to develop collaborative and critical-thinking habits.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-assessment, peer-assessment, classroom dialogue, collaboration

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Auto-Grading and Feedback System for Constructive Geometry Tasks Using Large Language Models on an Online Math Platform
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a large language model (LLM)-supported auto-grading and feedback system can provide teacher-aligned formative assessment for constructive geometry tasks on the Korean Algeomath platform. The authors focus on a multi-stage set of geometry activities centered on the triangle circumcenter, including closed-ended items, open-ended explanations, and dynamic geometry construction tasks.

The system combines rule-based grading for closed-ended and construction tasks with GPT-4-based few-shot grading for open-ended explanations, plus attempt-aware feedback that becomes more explicit across retries. The field study involved 79 middle-school students in four classes in South Korea and compared machine judgments and feedback quality with teacher judgments. Grading agreement was substantial overall for open-ended items, perfect for rule-based items, and feedback was judged generally serviceable but uneven across items.

The learning evidence is primarily short-term and descriptive. Students often improved after feedback on the same item, with an overall post-feedback conversion rate of 36.7% (260/708), but longer-term transfer effects to later questions were not statistically significant. The paper concludes that LLMs can support scalable formative assessment in mathematics geometry tasks, though terminology precision, avoidance of answer leakage, and stronger scaffolding are needed.

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed and evaluated for constructive geometry tasks in middle-school mathematics. Rule-based grading for closed-ended and dynamic geometry construction tasks achieved 100% agreement with teachers, while LLM grading on open-ended explanations reached 0.866 agreement overall (Cohen’s κ=0.737; n=878 explanatory responses).
finding.measure: Teacher agreement on grading of geometry tasks; open-ended explanation agreement rate and Cohen’s κ

finding.finding_summary: The feedback system appeared to support persistence and short-cycle re-engagement within tasks. Across all questions, 36.7% of initially incorrect responses were converted to correct answers on the next attempt (260/708), and the aggregate learning curve rose from about 0.60 on the first attempt to about 0.73 on the second attempt, suggesting many students benefited from retry opportunities and feedback.
finding.measure: Post-feedback correctness conversion rate; attempt-wise cumulative success curve

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports within-question refinement in explanations, suggesting some metacognitive improvement in precision and conceptual clarity. However, evidence for broader transfer is weak: comparisons on later target questions (Q10, Q11, Q18) showed no statistically significant relationship between prior feedback-driven conversion and later performance (all p>0.05).
finding.measure: Iterative answer refinement; transfer to later target questions; Mann–Whitney U tests and contingency analyses

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper discusses the role of formative assessment in improving student learning and how it can be implemented through an e-learning platform (BlackBoard Learning System). The authors argue that frequent, low-stakes assessments with immediate, detailed feedback can help students monitor progress, identify weaknesses, and prepare better for end-of-semester exams.

The paper is largely conceptual but includes a student perception survey conducted at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus) with undergraduate students from Business, Engineering, and IT streams. Students generally favored weekly or fortnightly online tests over classroom tests because they provided immediate feedback, flexibility, and smaller topic chunks that were easier to study. A statistically significant difference was reported across academic streams in perceived need for the Blackboard test option, with Engineering students showing stronger support than Business and IT students. The paper concludes that formative assessment, especially when delivered online with prompt feedback, may improve learning and summative performance, though the evidence presented here is primarily attitudinal rather than achievement-based.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported positive attitudes toward frequent formative assessments because they provided immediate feedback, reduced the fear of losing many marks on a single test, and helped them stay engaged with the subject throughout the semester. In the survey, a majority supported frequent internal assessments and favored the Blackboard option over classroom testing due to immediacy and flexibility, but the paper does not report an achievement effect size.
finding.measure: Student perception survey items on continuous assessment, feedback, engagement, and perceived usefulness

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes metacognition and self-monitoring as intended benefits of formative assessment: students receive feedback, reflect on errors, and check whether they are on track. However, these are presented as intended mechanisms and student perceptions rather than measured learning outcomes, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Survey responses about feedback, self-checking, and perceived progress monitoring

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment II. Indications of Effectiveness in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.venue: arXiv / WIPTTE 2013 (companion conference paper referenced as WIPTTE 2013)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for an efficient way to implement real-time formative assessment in classrooms and asks whether the web-based InkSurvey tool, used with pen-enabled mobile devices, appears effective across a range of instructional settings. The authors argue that open-format questions answered with digital ink can reveal student thinking, let instructors respond immediately, and support revision of misconceptions before they become entrenched.

The paper is not an experimental test of a single intervention under controlled conditions; instead, it presents seven vignettes from diverse contexts, including K-12 algebra, college physics, engineering physics, chemical engineering, food science, and biology in the United States and Mexico. Evidence reported includes comparison to prior cohorts, within-course improvement over time, survey responses, and qualitative instructor/student observations. Across settings, the authors report learning gains, increased participation, improved metacognition, and stronger instructor insight into student thinking, with some subgroup indications that female students benefited more than males in one high school algebra context and that students with all learning styles showed gains in another study.

finding.finding_summary: In a high school Algebra I context, students receiving regular formative feedback through InkSurvey showed greater mastery of fundamental concepts on standards-based assessments than students not exposed to the intervention. The paper also reports a subgroup pattern in which female students demonstrated much greater learning gains than the control group, but no effect size is provided.
finding.measure: Standards-based Algebra I assessments

finding.finding_summary: Across physics, chemistry/chemical engineering, and engineering physics examples, InkSurvey was associated with improved conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. Reported evidence includes a calculus III misconception dropping from 12/103 students in a comparison section to 1/87 after an InkSurvey-based lesson, a rise in understanding from about 1.8 to 3.1 on a 4-point scale when simulations were coupled with InkSurvey, and steady improvement in upper-level engineering physics problem-solving skills over a semester.
finding.measure: Summative exam questions, concept understanding ratings, problem-solving skill scores
finding.study_size: n=87; n=103; other study sizes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: In food chemistry and related postsecondary courses, students using InkSurvey showed improved performance on summative quizzes compared with earlier cohorts, with mean gains of 0.6 points in an undergraduate course and 0.5 points in a graduate course out of 10. The paper also reports increased participation in class discussions and problem-solving activities in food chemistry settings.
finding.measure: Summative quiz scores; classroom participation/problem-solving activity observations

finding.finding_summary: Student reports were strongly favorable: 54 of 63 students (86%) agreed that InkSurvey helped the instructor understand what they did and did not understand, and 48 of 63 (76%) said it helped them better understand what was being covered or realize what they did and did not understand. Students also reported increased motivation, engagement, and willingness to participate in class.
finding.measure: Anonymous survey responses on understanding, motivation, participation, engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports gains in metacognition and self-assessment, with many students saying that constructing responses in InkSurvey helped them recognize what they understood and what they did not. It also reports improved problem-solving skill development in an upper-level engineering physics course and notes that InkSurvey can foster higher-level thinking by making student reasoning visible and prompting revision.
finding.measure: Survey items on metacognition; problem-solving skill scores; instructor observations
finding.study_size: n=63 for survey; other study sizes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Instructors reported that InkSurvey gave immediate insight into student thinking, allowed rapid identification of common difficulties, and supported timely feedback and instructional adjustment. The paper presents this as improving classroom instruction and reducing the lag between student work and instructor response, though no formal workload metrics are reported.
finding.measure: Instructor observations and qualitative reports of feedback timeliness and instructional adjustment

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative/practical review of how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback in educational settings. It asks how LLMs can be aligned with core formative assessment principles: clarifying learning goals, identifying where learners currently are, and providing feedback that helps learners move forward.

The paper does not report a new empirical study. Instead, it synthesizes prior research and provides classroom-oriented examples of prompting and LLM use for tasks such as rewriting learning objectives into student-friendly language, co-constructing success criteria, generating sample work of varying quality, and creating formative questions and feedback. The examples are illustrated mainly with high-school biology and undergraduate fMRI instruction contexts, but the paper is aimed broadly at educators and researchers across grade levels and subjects.

Its main conclusion is that LLMs can potentially scale and streamline formative assessment practices, but only when used within strong pedagogical design and educator oversight. The authors emphasize limitations of current LLM evaluation metrics, risks of overreliance on AI-generated responses, and the need for better benchmarks that reflect formative assessment quality rather than just linguistic fluency or generic task performance. The paper is essentially a conceptual guide that argues LLMs should augment, not replace, expert teaching.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher time and effort by automating or streamlining tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating sample work, and producing formative questions/feedback. This is presented as a practical benefit rather than a measured effect, and no quantitative workload outcome is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / time needed to create formative assessment materials

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes that LLM-supported formative assessment can foster critical thinking, metacognition, and self-regulation by prompting students to reflect on goals, compare exemplars, and evaluate AI-generated outputs. These claims are theoretical and illustrative, not supported by direct outcome data in the paper.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, self-regulation, and evaluation of exemplars/feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses formative assessment and LLM use as ways to support student engagement and self-regulated learning, especially through clearer goals and immediate feedback. However, the paper does not report original engagement or motivation measurements; the conclusion is conceptual and based on prior literature.
finding.measure: Engagement / self-regulation as discussed in formative assessment literature

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides subject-specific examples in biology and undergraduate fMRI instruction showing how LLMs can generate student-friendly objectives, exemplars, and formative prompts. These examples are intended to improve subject-matter learning processes, but the paper does not test academic achievement outcomes empirically.
finding.measure: Subject-specific formative assessment materials (biology, fMRI/method writing)

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment I. Applications in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes InkSurvey, a free web-based tool for real-time formative assessment using pen-enabled mobile devices. The authors argue that open-format, digital-ink responses can help instructors see student thinking quickly, address misconceptions during class, and make immediate instructional adjustments, compared with more delayed or limited feedback from traditional methods.

The paper is organized as seven vignettes across diverse contexts: university calculus, high school algebra, community college biology, undergraduate and graduate food chemistry, introductory physics, chemical engineering/physics with simulations, and a creativity-in-physics course. In each setting, instructors used InkSurvey to pose open-ended questions and review student responses in real time. The paper is primarily descriptive and illustrative rather than experimental; it concludes that the tool is broadly applicable and useful for engagement, scaffolding, metacognition, and misconception repair, but it does not report a controlled comparison or subgroup analysis of learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: In the university honors calculus vignette, real-time formative assessment with InkSurvey helped reveal and correct misconceptions about setting up triple integrals and inequalities for regions in 3D space. Among 83 student responses to one question, 32 showed the misconception of using all constant bounds; after discussion based on the InkSurvey responses, a follow-up question showed that all students responded and none used all constant bounds, indicating improved understanding during the class session.
finding.measure: Student responses to open-format calculus questions on defining regions of integration and inequalities for triple integrals
finding.study_size: n=87 (first-term college students); specific item analysis n=83 responses

finding.finding_summary: In the introductory physics vignette, InkSurvey was used to replace multiple-choice clicker questions with open-format prompts requiring students to justify answers in writing. The instructor reported that this made faulty reasoning visible even when students arrived at the correct answer, and allowed immediate correction of misconceptions during class; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Written explanations to open-ended conceptual physics questions about momentum and stopping distance

finding.finding_summary: Across several vignettes, the authors report that InkSurvey increased student engagement, motivation to participate, and receptiveness to in-class discussion. In the community college biology class, students were described as being engaged in their learning and motivated to participate in interspersed discussions; in the creativity-in-physics vignette, anonymous submissions were said to reduce evaluation apprehension and encourage participation.
finding.measure: Observed participation, motivation, and engagement during class discussions and formative assessment activities

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly frames InkSurvey as supporting metacognition, self-discovery, and collaborative reasoning. In the creativity-in-physics vignette, requesting questions was said to enhance metacognition by making students write about what they do and do not understand, while the structured idea-generation process supported independent thinking and building on others' ideas; in the biology vignette, a sequence of questions helped students connect prior knowledge and develop relationships among concepts.
finding.measure: Metacognitive prompts, idea generation, collaborative discussion, and conceptual connection-making in class

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that InkSurvey improved the efficiency of formative assessment by letting instructors collect responses instantly, scan them quickly, and adjust instruction in real time. In the algebra vignette, all 25 students could submit work at once rather than only 2-3 students presenting at the board, reducing the time constraint on feedback; similar time-saving claims are made across vignettes.
finding.measure: Instructor ability to collect, review, and respond to student work in real time

paper_profiles.title: Effects of Popular Science Writing Instruction on General Education Student Attitudes Towards Science: A Case Study in Astronomy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether a writing-intensive, popular-science journalism course can improve non-STEM undergraduates’ attitudes toward science and their confidence in engaging with science-related tasks. The authors focus on students in a first-year general-education astronomy/astrobiology seminar that combined popular science writing, journal-style translation exercises, scaffolded article development, reading of scientific and nontechnical sources, and reflection on science communication.

The course was part of a year-long first-year program at a large U.S. public university, with participants drawn from 2021 and 2022 offerings. The data sources were pre/post surveys containing open-ended responses and a small amount of descriptive Likert-scale data, plus interviews with five students. The paper is primarily qualitative, using coding of changes in attitudes across matched pre/post responses and thematic interview analysis; the quantitative results are descriptive and not statistically significant.

Overall, students entered with relatively positive views of science and scientists, but many were initially intimidated by reading research articles and writing about science. After the course, students reported greater comfort with primary literature, more confidence explaining science concepts and writing about discoveries, and a broader view of science that included communication, ethics, and multiple pathways for participation beyond becoming a researcher. The authors conclude that science writing instruction can function as an active-learning bridge between humanities-oriented students and STEM content, improving engagement and perceived ability, though the study does not test causal effects with a control group and does not examine subgroup differences by learner need, language status, or disability.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported clear gains in science-related literacy tasks, especially reading scientific research articles and writing about a new scientific discovery. In the matched pre/post survey coding, 9/15 students reported improved attitudes toward reading scientific articles, and 9 students felt more confident about writing about a new scientific discovery after the course; these shifts were described qualitatively rather than with inferential statistics.
finding.measure: Self-reported comfort/confidence with reading research articles and writing about a scientific discovery; coded open-ended survey responses

finding.finding_summary: The course was intended to deepen students’ ability to understand and communicate science, and students reported improved ability to interpret scientific articles, synthesize evidence, and grasp the scientific process. Interviews emphasized that writing about science forced them to understand content more deeply and to check and research claims, suggesting gains in scientific reasoning and comprehension, though no standardized science achievement test was used.
finding.measure: Self-reported understanding of science/scientific process; interview themes about comprehension and synthesis

finding.finding_summary: Students reported increased engagement, interest, and confidence in science after the writing-intensive course. The paper notes improvements in interest/relevance of science and greater willingness to engage with science beyond the course, including some students considering further science coursework or journalism assignments related to science.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses and descriptive Likert-scale attitudes toward interest/relevance/engagement

finding.finding_summary: The strongest durable-skill gains were in confidence, metacognition, and communication: students increasingly felt able to explain science concepts to others and to write about science for different audiences. Interviewees also described improved critical thinking, synthesis, and a better understanding of audience, style, and structure in science communication.
finding.measure: Self-reported confidence in explaining science and writing for audiences; interview themes on metacognition and communication

finding.finding_summary: Although not a primary language-fluency study, the paper does examine students’ confidence in explaining science concepts and discussing science ideas, which are language-mediated academic tasks. Students shifted from feeling merely comfortable or hesitant to feeling more confident about explaining concepts to others after repeated writing and discussion practice.
finding.measure: Self-reported comfort/confidence with explaining science concepts orally/in writing

paper_profiles.title: Optical images of the Kerr–Sen black hole and thin accretion disk
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies the optical appearance of a Kerr–Sen black hole surrounded by a geometrically thin, optically thin accretion disk. The authors use analytic geodesic calculations and ray-tracing to model photon trajectories, lensing rings, inner shadows, redshift distributions, and emission intensity under different black-hole spin and charge values, viewing inclinations, and observing frequencies (86 GHz and 230 GHz).

The central question is how spin, electric charge, observer inclination, and observing frequency shape the observable image of a Kerr–Sen black hole. The paper is entirely theoretical and does not involve human participants, schools, or educational settings; rather, it evaluates spacetime geometry and radiation transfer in a black-hole environment.

The results indicate that spin has a stronger effect than charge on the distortion of the inner shadow and critical curve. Observer inclination has the largest role in shaping redshift/blueshift distributions, especially near the ISCO, while 86 GHz produces higher peak and total intensity than 230 GHz. The authors conclude that the inner shadow and critical curve remain robust intrinsic signatures of the spacetime, whereas intensity and redshift vary substantially with disk orientation and observation geometry.

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Multimodal Feedback Using Multiple External Representations: Strategy Profiles and Learning in High School Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether elaborated feedback, delivered through multiple external representations (MERs), is associated with better learning in high school physics. The authors focus on a computer-based practice platform that provided standard verification feedback plus optional elaborated feedback in three formats: verbal, graphical/pictorial, and mathematical. They ask whether using elaborated feedback more often predicts higher post-test performance, and whether that association depends on learners’ prior knowledge, confidence, or representational competence.

The study followed 661 German students in grades 10 and 11 across 26 schools and 66 classes over roughly 16–24 weeks. Students completed physics exercises on the KI4SCool platform and could choose whether to open one or more forms of elaborated feedback after each item. The authors used linear mixed-effects models, ANCOVA, and clustering analyses of feedback-use patterns. Across two cohorts, more frequent use of elaborated feedback was associated with slightly higher post-test scores, but the design was observational, so the paper does not establish causality.

The paper also finds that students tended to fall into a few stable MER-use profiles, including a no-feedback group, a group that frequently selected all three representations, a group that favored verbal feedback, and a group with intermediate use. These strategy patterns were not strongly explained by initial representational competence, and mean post-test differences across strategies were mostly small or non-significant after adjustment. One cohort showed a borderline pattern suggesting that more frequent feedback use may matter more for students who alternated among all three representations, but the evidence was not robust enough to support a strong subgroup claim.

finding.finding_summary: In two high-school physics cohorts (Cohort 1 n=351; Cohort 2 n=310), more frequent use of elaborated feedback was associated with higher post-test physics scores. The adjusted standardized association was small but positive in both cohorts (Cohort 1 β=0.13, 95% CI [0.05, 0.22]; Cohort 2 β=0.08, 95% CI [0.00, 0.16], p=.054), after controlling for pre-test score, platform performance, exercises solved, and confidence.
finding.measure: Physics post-test score (percent correct)
finding.study_size: n=661 total; cohort 1 n=351; cohort 2 n=310

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes representational competence and feedback-strategy moderation analyses, but these were used primarily as predictors rather than as primary learning outcomes. Initial verbal, graphical, and mathematical competences did not significantly differ across feedback-strategy clusters in Cohort 1 (Pillai’s trace=0.018, F=0.74, p=.67), suggesting that students’ MER-use profiles were not clearly explained by baseline competence. A later moderation test was reported but the provided excerpt is incomplete, so only limited evidence is available here.
finding.measure: Initial representational competence scores; feedback-strategy cluster membership

paper_profiles.title: Transfer Learning Toolkit: Primers and Benchmarks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces a software toolkit for transfer learning research rather than reporting a study of educational intervention effects. The toolkit bundles 17 representative transfer learning models across feature-based, concept-based, parameter-based, and instance-based categories, with unified Python interfaces intended to make it easier for researchers to run baseline comparisons and reproduce experiments.

The paper explains the design of the toolkit, its dependency on some MATLAB components, and how to invoke the models on a benchmark text classification task. A small case example using the Reuters-21578 dataset demonstrates calling one model (TCA) and reports example accuracy values, but the paper does not evaluate educational populations, formative assessment, or learner outcomes. Its main contribution is infrastructure for machine learning transfer learning experimentation, not empirical evidence about learning effects.

paper_profiles.title: AMACA: Astronomy education with a Multi-sensory, Accessible, and Circular Approach
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Science Education, Part B: Communication and Public Engagement
paper_profiles.population: High School; Primary school; Teachers; Adult public; Undergraduate/Graduate (PhD candidates)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the AMACA project, an astronomy education and public engagement initiative designed to make astronomy more accessible, multi-sensory, and scalable. The authors argue that many existing astronomy outreach resources are single-use, difficult to disseminate, expensive to produce, and not sufficiently co-designed with accessibility expertise or tested with users.

AMACA uses a circular training model: astronomy and education experts train PhD candidates to design hands-on, multi-sensory workshops; the PhD candidates then train high school students; those students deliver the activities at an astronomy festival; and the activities are later reused and adapted by teachers in classrooms. The project integrates disability expertise, Universal Design for Learning principles, and repeated feedback cycles using design canvases, debriefings, questionnaires, and word clouds. Across four years, the project involved more than 10,000 festival visitors, 220 high school students, 45 PhD candidates, and 18 teachers.

The paper reports mainly descriptive and qualitative outcomes, plus questionnaire results showing that high school students and visitors found the activities engaging and useful, and that both groups became more confident that astronomy is accessible for blind and visually impaired people. Teachers also reported satisfaction with the flipped-role, hands-on approach and perceived that it increased student engagement, including among students who were typically disillusioned with school. Overall, the paper concludes that the multi-sensory approach improves engagement, accessibility awareness, and perceived educational value across multiple audiences.

finding.finding_summary: The project emphasizes understanding how astronomy research is done and how multi-wavelength/multi-frequency evidence builds scientific explanations. PhD candidates revised activities to communicate astronomical methods more clearly, and participants in the workshops were reported to gain a more complete understanding of astrophysical sources through multiple sensory representations, but no controlled learning outcome or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Questionnaires, feedback wheel responses, design-canvas revisions, and qualitative observations about understanding of astronomy methods and concepts

finding.finding_summary: High school students reported the project as highly engaging and emotionally meaningful, with the word-cloud analysis showing a shift from knowledge-centered expectations to relationship- and emotion-centered outcomes after participation. In the 2023 questionnaire, 53.8% of HS students rated multisensory astronomy as very engaging (5/5) and 38.5% as engaging (4/5), indicating strong perceived engagement.
finding.measure: Word clouds; self-assessment questionnaire on engagement and usefulness
finding.study_size: n=39 (questionnaire, HS students, 2023); n=200 (word-cloud responses, HS students, 2021-2024)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports growth in communication, collaboration, and problem-solving-related capacities, especially for PhD candidates and high school students. PhD candidates improved their ability to communicate astronomy to non-experts and became more aware of accessibility, while teachers noted that students developed communication and collaboration skills through leading workshops and interacting with the public; no standardized measure or effect size is provided.
finding.measure: Qualitative feedback from focus groups, questionnaires, and observations of workshop delivery

finding.finding_summary: AMACA created a recurring institutional pathway linking universities, schools, disability organizations, and a public festival, with reusable materials uploaded to PlayINAF and teacher training integrated into mandatory professional development. The paper reports adoption across multiple cohorts and settings, but it does not provide quantitative institutional effect estimates.
finding.measure: Program implementation across cohorts; training participation counts; dissemination of reusable resources
finding.study_size: 220 HS students; 45 PhD candidates; 18 teachers; >10,000 festival visitors

finding.finding_summary: For astronomy content specifically, the project increased perceived usefulness of multisensory exploration for understanding astronomy. In 2023, 41.0% of HS students and 55.7% of visitors rated the experience very useful (5/5), and additional qualitative comments indicated learning about astronomy research findings, wavelengths, and accessibility through hands-on activities.
finding.measure: Questionnaire ratings of usefulness for understanding astronomy; qualitative comments about astronomy content learning

paper_profiles.title: Learning and Motivational Impact of Game-Based Learning: Comparing Face-to-Face and Online Formats on Computer Science Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This quasi-experimental study examines whether teacher-authored educational video games are effective for learning and motivation in computer science education, and whether their effects differ when used face-to-face versus online. The authors note a gap in evidence about teacher-authored games and about whether the instructional format changes their effectiveness, especially in engineering and computer science contexts.

The intervention was a teacher-authored educational video game built with the SGAME authoring tool and delivered as a Flappy Bird-style activity that embedded self-grading questions and short learning objects about basic principles of software design. The study involved 321 second-year undergraduate computer science/software engineering students at Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, with 104 students in an online group during the 2019-20 academic year and 217 students in a face-to-face group during 2020-21.

Students completed identical pre-tests and post-tests on software design knowledge and a questionnaire about learning, motivation, usability, and overall perceptions. Results showed significant knowledge gains in both groups (paired t-tests, Cohen’s d=0.71 face-to-face and d=0.79 online), with no significant difference between formats in learning gains (d=0.05). Questionnaire results showed high motivation and positive perceptions in both formats, but some perceptions were significantly more favorable in face-to-face delivery (e.g., overall opinion, perceived learning, fun, future use, and preference for games over traditional materials). The paper concludes that teacher-authored educational video games are effective in both formats, with face-to-face delivery enhancing some subjective aspects of the experience while online delivery remains comparably effective for knowledge acquisition and motivation.

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-authored educational video games produced significant gains in knowledge about basic principles of software design in both delivery formats. Students improved from pre-test to post-test with medium-to-large effects in both groups: face-to-face d=0.71 and online d=0.79, both p<0.001. Between-group differences in post-test scores and learning gains were not statistically significant (learning gains d=0.05).
finding.measure: Pre-test and post-test scores on 10 multiple-choice questions about basic principles of software design
finding.effect_size: Within-group: d=0.71 (face-to-face), d=0.79 (online); between-group learning gains d=0.05
finding.std_deviation: face-to-face pre/post SD=1.77/1.66; online pre/post SD=1.57/1.68

finding.finding_summary: The game-based learning experience was rated as highly motivating and engaging in both formats, with students reporting high agreement that the activity was motivating and fun. Average questionnaire ratings were high in both groups, though several items favored face-to-face delivery: overall opinion (M=4.63 vs 4.37, d=0.36, p<0.01), perceived learning (M=4.59 vs 4.41, d=0.25, p=0.01), fun (M=4.38 vs 4.20, d=0.20, p=0.05), future use (M=4.68 vs 4.47, d=0.29, p<0.01), and preference over traditional materials (M=4.30 vs 3.98, d=0.39, p<0.01). Motivation item differences were not statistically significant (M=4.37 vs 4.23, d=0.16).
finding.measure: Likert-scale questionnaire items on overall opinion, learning help, ease of use, help needed, motivation, fun, integration, future use, and preference over traditional materials
finding.effect_size: d=0.36 overall opinion; d=0.25 perceived learning; d=0.20 fun; d=0.29 future use; d=0.39 preference over traditional materials; motivation d=0.16
finding.std_deviation: varies by item; e.g. overall opinion SD=0.58 face-to-face, 0.94 online; motivation SD=0.82 face-to-face, 0.98 online

paper_profiles.title: Dynamic Models of Learning and Education Measurement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a probabilistic, measurement-based model of learning to explain the behavior of normalized gain in pre/post testing. The central question is why normalized gain often shows little correlation with pretest score in some settings, yet correlates positively with pretest score or other ability measures in others.

The author proposes a dynamic model with three kinds of learning transitions: alpha ( external instruction acting on incorrect knowledge), beta (external instruction acting on correct knowledge), and gamma (associative interaction between correct and incorrect knowledge). Under the common assumption that learning is dominated by the alpha process, normalized gain depends on the instructional effectiveness coefficient and not directly on pretest score; when gamma processes are present, normalized gain can become positively related to pretest score. The paper further argues that observed correlations between normalized gain and measures such as Lawson scientific reasoning, spatial visualization, and SAT scores are consistent with this model.

The empirical examples discussed are drawn mainly from calculus-based introductory physics courses for science and engineering majors, including traditional, interactive-engagement, and honors sections. The paper does not report a new controlled experiment; instead, it synthesizes prior findings and uses the model to interpret subgroup/ability differences, suggesting that higher-ability students tend to show more alpha-like learning while lower-ability groups show more gamma-like patterns.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students' normalized FCI gains are positively correlated with scientific reasoning ability as measured by Lawson's Classroom Test of Scientific Reasoning. The cited study found r=0.51 with N=65, and the author interprets this as evidence that a general reasoning/ability measure is associated with higher learning gains under the proposed alpha-process model.
finding.measure: Lawson Classroom Test of Scientific Reasoning; Force Concept Inventory (FCI) normalized gains

finding.finding_summary: The paper uses force concept learning in introductory mechanics as its main empirical example and reports that normalized FCI gains vary by instructional setting and student group. Across cited studies, interactive engagement courses outperformed traditional instruction by about two standard deviations in average normalized gain, while subgroup analyses showed different gain-pretest patterns for honors/high-ability students versus average university students.
finding.measure: Force Concept Inventory (FCI) pretest, posttest, normalized gain; class-average change scores
finding.study_size: multiple courses; cited totals include N=6542 across 62 courses, and course-level samples such as n~350, n~1500, n~200
finding.effect_size: about 2 SD difference in average normalized gain between interactive engagement and traditional courses; r=0.15-0.33 in some subgroup comparisons
finding.std_deviation: about 2 standard deviations (reported for course-level normalized gain differences)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that normalized gain is positively associated with broader learning ability and reasoning-related skills, especially in settings where gamma-process learning is present. It cites positive correlations between FCI gains and spatial visualization ability (r~0.3, N~60) and with Lawson reasoning scores, suggesting that students with stronger general cognitive/learning abilities tend to achieve larger gains.
finding.measure: Spatial visualization ability; general learning ability proxies linked to normalized gains
finding.study_size: n~60 for the spatial visualization study; other cited samples vary

finding.finding_summary: The paper cites evidence that normalized gains on the Conceptual Survey in Electricity are positively correlated with students' math pretest scores. Reported correlations range from r=0.1 to 0.4 across about three classes (N~150), which the author uses to argue that gain can track general preparation/ability rather than only content-specific prior knowledge.
finding.measure: Math pretest scores; Conceptual Survey in Electricity normalized gains

paper_profiles.title: Creating Experience Value to Build Student Satisfaction in Higher Education
paper_profiles.venue: DINASTI International Journal of Digital Business Management and Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how higher education institutions can build student satisfaction by creating experiential value through co-creation. The authors argue that students are not just passive recipients of educational services; rather, their active participation in campus activities, classroom experiences, and interactions with the institution contributes to the value they derive from higher education.

Using a survey of 357 students from 32 universities in South Sumatra Province, Indonesia, the study applies confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling to test relationships among co-creation, experience value, and student satisfaction. The analysis finds that co-creation strongly predicts experience value (estimate = 0.90, t = 11.43, R² = 0.82), and experience value strongly predicts student satisfaction (estimate = 0.85, t = 8.29, R² = 0.80). The direct path from co-creation to student satisfaction is small and not statistically significant (estimate = 0.05, t = 0.58).

finding.finding_summary: Co-creation was positively associated with student satisfaction indirectly through experience value. In a survey of n=357 students across 32 universities, co-creation strongly predicted experience value (estimate=0.90, t=11.43, R²=0.82), and experience value strongly predicted satisfaction (estimate=0.85, t=8.29, R²=0.80). The direct effect of co-creation on satisfaction was not significant (estimate=0.05, t=0.58).
finding.measure: Student satisfaction survey; experience value scale; co-creation scale

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that institutional practices that increase student participation and co-creation can improve the student experience and, indirectly, satisfaction. The observed structural model suggests substantial institutional leverage via experience value (co-creation -> experience value estimate=0.90; experience value -> satisfaction estimate=0.85), although this is based on correlational survey data rather than an intervention.
finding.measure: Institutional co-creation/participation structures as reported by students; student satisfaction outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Investigating the Efficacy of a Professional Development Program in Formative Classroom Assessment in Middle School English Language Arts and Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates a South Carolina professional development program intended to improve teachers’ formative classroom assessment skills and, in turn, student achievement. The study asks whether teachers who receive the program become more knowledgeable about assessment principles, and whether their students perform better on state English language arts and mathematics tests.

The intervention was a year-long recertification course focused on aligning assessments to standards, creating performance tasks, rubrics, multiple-choice items, portfolios, grading procedures, and interpreting standardized test scores. In Year 1, schools were randomly assigned to treatment or control conditions, with treatment schools receiving support from an assessment coach and control schools receiving no professional development. In Years 2 and 3, the comparison shifted to two treatment levels—coach-led versus relatively untrained facilitator-led implementation—with matched control schools created for student achievement analyses.

Participants were teachers and students in state-identified low-performing middle schools in South Carolina, across grades 6–8. Teacher outcomes were measured with pre/post assessment-knowledge tests; student outcomes were measured with state PACT English language arts and mathematics scores analyzed using multilevel models. The program increased teacher assessment knowledge in all three years, and there was no difference between coach-led and facilitator-led delivery. However, student achievement did not improve; instead, students in treatment schools scored lower than matched controls in Year 1 ELA and in Year 3 ELA and mathematics, leading the authors to conclude that better teacher assessment knowledge alone did not translate into improved student learning and may have coincided with less effective reteaching practices.

finding.finding_summary: Across the three study years, students of teachers who participated in the formative assessment professional development had lower adjusted English language arts PACT scores than matched controls in every year. The adjusted effects were -2.39 points (d=-0.16) in Year 1, -1.15 points (d=-0.08) in Year 2, and -3.46 points (d=-0.26) in Year 3; Year 1 and Year 2 were significant, and Year 3 was strongly significant.
finding.measure: State English language arts PACT scale scores (hierarchical linear models with prior score and student covariates)
finding.study_size: n=2,066 to n=3,203 students per year in ELA; 38-44 schools per year

finding.finding_summary: Student mathematics achievement did not differ in Years 1 or 2, but in Year 3 students in professional-development schools scored lower than matched controls on adjusted PACT mathematics scores. The Year 3 effect was -3.76 points with a standardized effect size of d=-0.33, statistically significant at p=.01.
finding.measure: State mathematics PACT scale scores (hierarchical linear models with prior score and student covariates)
finding.study_size: n=1,297 to n=2,708 students per year in mathematics; 14-44 schools per year

finding.finding_summary: The professional development program improved teacher assessment knowledge regardless of whether it was delivered by a trained coach or a relatively untrained facilitator, suggesting the curriculum itself was effective for teacher learning. However, that systemic improvement in teacher capacity did not produce positive student achievement effects, and the authors argue that the program may have changed assessment practices without improving the use of assessment information to guide instruction.
finding.measure: Teacher assessment-knowledge pretest/posttest scores and implementation of a district/state professional development program
finding.study_size: n=151 teachers in Year 1, n=146 in Year 2, n=71 in Year 3
finding.effect_size: Year 1 ω²=0.11 for time × group on teacher test; Year 2 ω²=0.60 for time; Year 3 ω²=0.56 for time

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and Achievement of Mathematics Students in Community Schools of Nepal
paper_profiles.venue: Social Inquiry: Journal of Social Science Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how formative assessment practices are associated with mathematics achievement among grade 8 students in community schools in Nepal. The author focuses on four classroom formative assessment practices: classwork, homework, project work, and tests, and especially on whether teachers check student work and provide feedback.

Using a survey design and contingency questionnaire, the study sampled 232 grade-8 students from a target population of 547 mathematics students who participated in the District Level Examination. Mathematics achievement was measured using students’ District Level Examination scores. The paper reports that students whose classwork, homework, project work, and tests were checked by teachers generally had higher average mathematics scores than those whose work was unchecked, and that receiving regular feedback was usually associated with better performance.

The strongest association reported was for project work: students who regularly received feedback on project work had notably higher average scores than those receiving feedback only sometimes. The paper concludes that formative assessment, particularly timely teacher feedback and project-based work, is an important strategy for improving mathematics learning in Nepalese community schools, though the design is correlational and does not establish causation.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students exposed to more formative assessment and feedback practices tended to have higher mathematics achievement scores. For example, students whose classwork was checked had a mean score of 38.55 versus 33.00 when unchecked, and students whose project work received regular feedback had a mean score of 43.51 versus 36.31 when feedback was only occasional.
finding.measure: District Level Examination mathematics scores; mean achievement scores by formative assessment status

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment and feedback improve students’ motivation, confidence, and engagement in mathematics. It reports that regular checking and feedback on classwork, homework, project work, and tests were associated with better achievement, and the author interprets this as supporting greater confidence and interest in learning.
finding.measure: Observed teacher feedback/checking patterns and inferred student confidence/motivation from classroom assessment practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper connects project work and other formative tasks with contextualized learning, problem solving, and learning-by-doing. Students who had project work and regular feedback on it showed higher mathematics achievement, which the author links to development of practical understanding, self-regulation, and application of mathematical ideas.
finding.measure: Project work participation and teacher feedback; mathematics achievement scores

paper_profiles.title: Scaffolding in Teacher–Student Interaction: A Decade of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article reviews a decade of research on scaffolding in teacher–student interaction in primary and secondary education. The authors examine how scaffolding has been conceptualized, what forms it takes in classroom practice, and what evidence exists for its effectiveness. A central contribution is a conceptual model that treats contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility as the key defining characteristics of scaffolding, rather than any support strategy alone.

The review synthesizes 66 articles published from 1998 to 2009, including theoretical, descriptive, effectiveness, and one meta-analytic study. The empirical literature is dominated by small descriptive studies, especially in literacy, with fewer studies in mathematics and science. The authors also propose a framework that distinguishes scaffolding means (e.g., modeling, questioning, explaining) from scaffolding intentions (e.g., metacognitive, cognitive, affective support), in order to better analyze classroom interactions.

Across the small set of effectiveness studies, the review finds generally positive evidence that scaffolding improves student learning and, in some contexts, engagement or involvement. However, the paper emphasizes that the field is hampered by measurement problems, inconsistent definitions, and limited use of rigorous experimental designs. The authors conclude that future research should use better instruments, code both teacher and student actions, and attend explicitly to contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that scaffolding is most fully developed and most frequently studied in literacy, with multiple descriptive studies and effectiveness studies indicating beneficial effects on reading and related literacy activities. However, the literacy evidence is largely based on small-scale classroom studies rather than large experimental comparisons, so the conclusion is supportive but not definitive.
finding.measure: Literacy-related classroom interactions, text comprehension activities, and literacy performance/strategies

finding.finding_summary: Several effectiveness studies in mathematics found benefits from contingent scaffolding.
