For example, in Murphy and Messer (2000), children aged 5-7 in one-to-one scaffolding advanced more in representation level on a balance-scale task than children working in small groups or alone, and in Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998), students receiving contingent support solved significantly more long-division problems than students in other support conditions at direct and follow-up testing.
finding.measure: Balance-scale reasoning and long-division problem solving
finding.study_size: n=41, n=40, n=41 in Murphy and Messer; n=8 per condition in Pratt and Savoy-Levine

finding.finding_summary: The review includes science-focused effectiveness studies showing positive effects of scaffolding on conceptual understanding and reasoning. Azevedo et al. (2005) found that adaptive human scaffolding was associated with greater shifts in mental models and greater knowledge gains about the circulatory system than fixed scaffolding or no scaffolding, and Chiu et al. (2002) found that cognitive apprenticeship tutoring improved students’ mental models of chemical equilibrium relative to a non-CA comparison.
finding.measure: Mental model shifts, knowledge gains, and conceptual change in science learning
finding.study_size: n=38, n=34, n=37 in Azevedo et al.; n=20 vs n=10 in Chiu et al.

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies evidence that scaffolding can improve student involvement, enjoyment, and self-regulation-related behaviors. Turner et al. (1998) found that whole-class scaffolding strategies aimed at affect and transfer of responsibility were more common in high-involvement math classes, while Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998) found no overall enjoyment differences across support conditions except that the no-support group reported significantly lower enjoyment than the supported groups.
finding.measure: Student involvement, enjoyment, and self-regulating behaviors
finding.study_size: N=42 students across 34 lessons in Turner et al.; n=8 per condition in Pratt and Savoy-Levine

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the review is scaffolding for metacognitive and cognitive activities such as reasoning, problem solving, strategy use, and transfer of responsibility. Studies summarized in the review generally found that contingent, interactive scaffolding supported more constructive student responses, better transfer performance, and more effective use of reasoning strategies than weaker or absent support.
finding.measure: Metacognitive and cognitive activities including reasoning, strategy use, diagnostic accuracy, transfer questions, and learner responsibility

finding.finding_summary: The review does not study operational efficiency as a primary outcome, but it does discuss scaffolded interaction as a way to make learning more productive and to support performance that students could not yet manage independently. Some included studies suggest improved task efficiency or more effective tutoring interaction, but these are secondary observations rather than a central evaluated outcome.
finding.measure: Tutoring interaction quality and task completion support

paper_profiles.title: Beyond feedback: Developing student capability in complex appraisal
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article argues that the common higher-education practice of providing detailed feedback on assessed work is often insufficient for improving subsequent performance, especially for complex tasks requiring qualitative judgment. Sadler’s central question is not how to make feedback more detailed, but why students frequently cannot use it effectively even when it is well crafted.

The paper develops a theoretical account of what students must know in order to act on feedback: task compliance, quality, criteria, and the tacit knowledge needed to recognize where feedback applies. Rather than proposing feedback alone as the primary instructional mechanism, Sadler advocates structured peer assessment as a pedagogical strategy that gives students repeated appraisal experience similar to that of expert assessors.

The context is higher education, especially undergraduate and postgraduate settings in disciplines where assessment involves extended, open-ended, and qualitatively judged work. The article is conceptual and argumentative rather than an empirical evaluation of a new intervention, and it draws on prior literature and illustrative examples to support its claims. Its main conclusion is that formative improvement depends less on ever-better teacher feedback and more on inducting students into the concepts and practices underlying expert appraisal.

paper_profiles.title: The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education students and teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper revisits the evidence base on feedback in education, responding to the influential Visible Learning syntheses by Hattie and colleagues. The authors ask whether the large claimed effects of feedback hold up when primary studies are re-integrated directly, rather than through a meta-synthesis of prior meta-analyses, and whether the effects vary by important moderators such as feedback type, outcome type, channel, publication type, and research design.

The authors assembled 994 effect sizes from 435 studies (N > 61,000) drawn from 32 prior meta-analyses and primary studies with identifiable educational contexts. They included controlled studies and pre-post designs across kindergarten through university settings, focusing on feedback interventions delivered by teachers, students, or peers. The central comparison is not formative assessment versus another instructional approach in a head-to-head trial, but rather the overall and moderator-specific impact of feedback relative to control or baseline conditions across the literature.

Using a random-effects model, the overall feedback effect on student learning was medium and positive (d = 0.55), and dropped to d = 0.48 after removing extreme outliers. Effects were substantially heterogeneous, with strong evidence that feedback is not a single uniform treatment. More informative feedback types showed larger effects: high-information feedback was strongest (d = 0.99), corrective feedback was moderate (d = 0.46), and reinforcement/punishment was weakest (d = 0.24). Feedback was more effective for cognitive and physical outcomes than for motivational or behavioral outcomes, and teacher-to-student feedback was stronger than student-to-teacher feedback; feedback channel was not a significant moderator. The paper concludes that feedback is generally beneficial, but its impact depends heavily on what information it contains and how it is used.

finding.finding_summary: Across 994 effect sizes from 435 studies (N > 61,000), feedback had a positive overall effect on student learning. The random-effects mean was d = 0.55 (95% CI 0.48 to 0.62), and after removing 35 extreme outliers the pooled effect was d = 0.48 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.51).
finding.measure: Student learning outcomes, including achievement and other academic learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Feedback had a smaller but still positive effect on motivational outcomes such as intrinsic motivation, locus of control, self-efficacy, and persistence. The pooled effect for motivational outcomes was d = 0.33 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.42), with 21% of motivational effect sizes negative; uninformative rewards/punishments accounted for most negative effects.
finding.measure: Motivation-related outcomes (intrinsic motivation, locus of control, self-efficacy, persistence)

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis found stronger effects for cognitive outcomes than for motivational or behavioral ones, indicating benefits for learning-related higher-order performance and processing. For cognitive outcomes the pooled effect was d = 0.51 (95% CI 0.46 to 0.55), suggesting feedback supports understanding, retention, and cognitive test performance.
finding.measure: Cognitive outcomes, including achievement, retention, and cognitive test performance

finding.finding_summary: Some included primary studies measured math-test performance, and the paper reports a positive pooled effect for physical outcomes that is partly based on skill-performance contexts. However, mathematics is not a central separate outcome category in the analysis, so this assignment is modest-confidence and reflects only the paper’s direct inclusion of math-related learning outcomes rather than a dedicated numeracy analysis.
finding.measure: Math test performance and other skill-performance outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review explicitly includes and discusses language-learning feedback studies, especially corrective feedback in second-language learning. While language outcomes are not isolated in the main pooled tables, the paper reports that corrective feedback effects in the broader literature are positive and that feedback is generally more effective when it is informative and task-relevant.
finding.measure: Language-learning outcomes in second-language feedback studies

paper_profiles.title: A Critical Review of Research on Student Self-Assessment
paper_profiles.population: K-20 students (elementary through higher education); review excludes early childhood and professional development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a critical review of research on student self-assessment, focusing largely on studies published between 2013 and 2018. The author argues that self-assessment is best understood as a formative feedback process: students monitor their own work, compare it against criteria or standards, and use the resulting feedback to revise, improve, and regulate learning. The review also proposes a taxonomy of self-assessment based on what is assessed (competence, process, or product), why it is assessed (formative or summative), and how it is done (with or without explicit standards).

The review synthesizes 76 empirical studies and organizes them into major themes: consistency with external judgments, relationship with achievement, student perceptions, and self-regulated learning. It covers work in elementary school, secondary school, and higher education, with many studies involving rubric- or checklist-based self-assessment, self-monitoring, and self-grading. Across the literature, formative self-assessment supported by clear criteria, modeling, feedback, and opportunities to revise generally shows positive associations with achievement and self-regulation, whereas summative self-assessment is more often inconsistent with external judgments.

The central conclusion is that the field should move away from a narrow emphasis on accuracy/consistency and toward understanding the cognitive and affective mechanisms through which formative self-assessment supports learning. The author calls for more research on how students interpret feedback, how they use it to make revisions or choose next steps, and what pedagogical conditions make self-assessment most effective.

finding.finding_summary: Across 20 clearly formative studies and two meta-analyses, self-assessment was associated with improved writing outcomes. The Graham et al. meta-analysis (10 studies) reported an average weighted effect size of 0.62 on writing quality, and the review states that the formative studies consistently showed positive associations with learning and writing improvement.
finding.measure: Writing quality / written assignment scores

finding.finding_summary: Studies on self-assessment and self-regulated learning found that students who used scripts, rubrics, or checklist-based self-assessment were more self-regulated than comparison groups. Reported effect sizes were small to moderate (η2 = 0.06–0.42), and one study found associations with all three SRL phases: forethought, performance, and reflection.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning questionnaires and think-aloud protocols

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that formative self-assessment supports metacognition and self-monitoring, especially when grounded in explicit criteria and opportunities to revise. In the cited studies, rubric-referenced self-assessment was linked to stronger self-regulatory processes and in one study correlated strongly with performance (e.g., r = 0.94 for dart-throwing outcomes and self-evaluation).
finding.measure: Metacognition / self-monitoring / task selection / self-regulation measures

finding.finding_summary: The review summarizes multiple quasi-experimental and experimental studies showing that standards-referenced self-assessment improved performance in non-literacy academic tasks such as vocational stoma care, dart throwing, and mixed disciplinary exams. For example, a quasi-experimental study with n=39 vocational education students found that task-specific criteria outperformed competence-based criteria on task performance.
finding.measure: Task performance / vocational performance / exams / motor-skill outcomes
finding.study_size: n=39 (example study cited); overall review n=76 studies

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ perception of STEM integration and education: a systematic literature review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic literature review examines what empirical research from 2000–2017 reveals about preK-12 teachers’ beliefs, perceptions, barriers, and supports related to STEM education and STEM pedagogy. The paper is not evaluating a specific student intervention; instead, it synthesizes findings from 25 peer-reviewed empirical studies to understand how teachers perceive STEM integration and what factors shape implementation.

Across the included studies, teachers generally viewed STEM positively and believed it could motivate students, support real-world problem solving, and strengthen learning through hands-on, interdisciplinary work. At the same time, teachers reported substantial barriers, including pedagogical shifts away from teacher-led instruction, curriculum integration difficulties, scheduling and structural constraints, lack of assessment tools, insufficient planning time, and gaps in STEM content knowledge—especially around engineering and technology. The review also found that teacher confidence, prior STEM experiences, collaboration, district support, and professional development were repeatedly identified as important supports for implementation.

The authors conclude that successful STEM implementation depends heavily on teacher capacity and school-level support rather than curriculum alone. They recommend high-quality in-service professional development and structured collaboration time, and they argue that school leaders and policymakers should address assessment, scheduling, and resource barriers if they want STEM instruction to be implemented with fidelity and sustainability.

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes evidence that teachers see STEM as supporting students’ problem solving and application of science/engineering concepts, but also report that STEM implementation can weaken direct instruction of science content when pedagogy is poorly aligned. No pooled effect size is reported because this is a qualitative systematic review of teacher perceptions rather than a student-outcome meta-analysis.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of STEM-related scientific/engineering learning, concept integration, and science instruction quality

finding.finding_summary: Teachers repeatedly reported that STEM activities increased student enjoyment, engagement, persistence, and motivation. The review synthesizes findings from multiple studies showing that teachers viewed hands-on STEM challenges and engineering design as motivating and empowering for students, including low-performing students, though no aggregate effect size is available.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student enjoyment, engagement, motivation, persistence, and buy-in during STEM activities

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived STEM pedagogy as supporting durable skills such as collaboration, communication, critical thinking, and problem solving. The review highlights repeated references to teamwork, cross-disciplinary problem solving, and student learning through making mistakes and revising solutions, but it does not report quantitative student skill gains.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of collaboration, communication, problem solving, and critical thinking in STEM lessons

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified workload, planning time, and assessment burden as major barriers to STEM implementation. The review notes concerns about increased planning demands, lack of formative and standardized assessments, and difficulty grading group work; in one included study, more than 40% of teachers reported a lack of STEM assessments.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported workload, planning time, and assessment availability/burden

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on institutional conditions shaping STEM implementation, including district support, scheduling, collaboration time, curriculum alignment, administrative backing, and financial/technology resources. Teachers consistently described these organizational factors as either enabling or impeding STEM adoption; the review provides no causal estimate because it synthesizes qualitative and survey-based studies.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported district, school, and policy-level supports/barriers for STEM implementation

paper_profiles.title: Differentiated Instruction in Secondary Education: A Systematic Review of Research Evidence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what empirical evidence exists for within-class differentiated instruction in secondary education and how different approaches to differentiation are operationalized. The authors define differentiated instruction broadly as planned adaptations in content, process, product, learning environment, or learning time based on student readiness, interest, or other relevant characteristics, and they explicitly exclude mere grouping without instructional adaptation and out-of-class differentiation.

Using a best-evidence systematic review approach, the authors searched major databases for English- and Dutch-language studies published from 2006 to 2016 that examined quantitative effects on academic achievement in mainstream secondary settings. After screening 1,029 papers, 12 unique studies (14 papers) met inclusion criteria. The reviewed interventions included generic adaptive teaching trainings, ability grouping and tiering, individualized reading instruction, collaborative/tiered science instruction, flipped classroom remediation, and mastery-learning-adjacent approaches.

Overall, the review concludes that differentiated instruction shows small-to-moderate positive effects on student achievement in secondary education, but the evidence base is small, heterogeneous, and methodologically uneven. Most included studies reported positive results, yet several effects were small or nonsignificant, and the authors caution that more rigorous research is needed before strong conclusions can be drawn about which differentiated-instruction models work best and under what conditions.

finding.finding_summary: The review found that differentiated instruction in mathematics generally produced positive achievement effects in secondary education, with several studies showing moderate-to-large gains. Reported effects included d=+4.504 for a project-based differentiated math intervention (combined grade 6/7), d=+1.085 for tiered algebra instruction, and d=+0.539 for ability-grouped problem-based learning; however, some math-related subgroup effects were smaller or not significant.
finding.measure: Researcher-made mathematics/algebra achievement tests
finding.study_size: varied across included math studies; e.g., Altintas and Özdemir n=32 control/28 experimental (grade 6) and 42 control/42 experimental (grade 7); Bal n=24 control/33 experimental; Bikić et al. n=77 control/88 experimental
finding.effect_size: mixed across studies; examples d=+4.504, d=+1.085, d=+0.539
finding.confidence_interval: varied by study; examples [3.879 to 5.130], [0.479 to 1.692], [0.228 to 0.851]

finding.finding_summary: In the science-focused studies, differentiated/adaptive instruction was associated with improved science achievement. The collaborative tiered peer-tutoring science intervention reported d=+0.386 overall on a unit test and high-stakes end-of-year science test, while the adaptive teaching competency study reported a small, nonsignificant effect (d=+0.133) on science achievement in the combined sample.
finding.measure: Science achievement tests/unit tests and end-of-year science tests
finding.study_size: e.g., n=213 in the Mastropieri et al. science study; n=623 students in the adaptive teaching competency project (combined primary and secondary sample reported in the paper)
finding.effect_size: mixed across studies; examples d=+0.386 and d=+0.133
finding.confidence_interval: [0.115 to 0.657] for d=+0.386; not_reported for d=+0.133

finding.finding_summary: The individualized reading intervention showed generally positive but small effects on literacy outcomes in secondary education. Across sites, reading comprehension effects were near zero to small positive (e.g., d=+0.030, d=+0.007, d=+0.266, d=+0.135), indicating that the model had modest benefits at best for standardized reading outcomes.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension and fluency tests
finding.study_size: approximately n=832/830 control and n=1179/1198 experimental depending on test/site

finding.finding_summary: The review also included a prevention intervention in which instruction was adapted to students' learning profiles in alcohol/tobacco/other drug prevention lessons. This study reported a large positive effect on the researcher-made prevention survey, suggesting that differentiated presentation and remediation can improve learning in this non-core academic domain.
finding.measure: Alcohol, tobacco and other drug (ATOD) prevention survey
finding.study_size: n=192 control and n=978 experimental students

paper_profiles.title: Students’ perception of Kahoot!’s influence on teaching and learning
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate students experienced the use of Kahoot!, a game-based student response system, in a third-year Information Systems Strategy and Governance course at a research-intensive university in New Zealand. The authors were interested in whether Kahoot! influenced classroom dynamics, students’ engagement, motivation, and learning, especially in relation to traditional lecture-based teaching and formative assessment practices.

The study used a qualitative case-study approach with semi-structured interviews of 14 students from a class of 48. Kahoot! was used across seven lectures in multiple ways: to check prior knowledge before tailoring instruction, to review content after it was taught, to support student-created quizzes, and for occasional off-topic fun activities. Students’ interview responses were thematically analyzed.

Findings suggest that Kahoot! generally improved attention, interaction, engagement, and perceived learning. Students reported that the tool made lectures more lively, encouraged participation through anonymity and competition, and helped them revise and retain material, especially when followed by discussion and feedback. However, the paper also reports mixed effects when competition or fun became distracting, or when quizzes were seen as too off-topic. Overall, the authors conclude that Kahoot! can enrich learning experiences, but its value depends heavily on question design, timing, and post-quiz discussion rather than on the game element alone.

finding.finding_summary: All 14 interviewed students said Kahoot! positively affected engagement, attention, and motivation in the course. Students reported that it helped them stay focused during lectures, made classes more enjoyable, and encouraged participation through anonymity and competition, although a small number noted distraction when competition or off-topic play became excessive.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on attention, engagement, motivation, and enjoyment

finding.finding_summary: Students described Kahoot! as supporting deeper engagement, reflection, and knowledge checking, especially when followed by discussion that helped them understand why answers were right or wrong. At the same time, some students said the competitive and playful aspects could distract from learning, suggesting that the tool’s effect on higher-order learning processes depended on implementation.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on learning, discussion, reflection, and retention

finding.finding_summary: Participants consistently reported that Kahoot! helped them remember lecture content, review for exams, and understand course concepts more deeply. Nine students explicitly described Kahoot! as useful for learning, 12 described it as a revision tool, and students said that post-quiz discussion and feedback improved retention and comprehension.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on learning, revision, and knowledge retention in an Information Systems course

paper_profiles.title: Embedded Formative Assessment in the Undergraduate Engineering Classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2014 ASEE Annual Conference & Exposition?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues for the value of embedding formative assessment into undergraduate engineering instruction, especially in large classrooms where it is difficult for instructors to diagnose student understanding in real time. The paper is framed around the question of how formative assessment can be made more effective and scalable through technology, and why it may still fall short of its potential if instructors do not respond to student feedback or if the questions used do not reveal student thinking.

Rather than reporting a controlled study, the paper synthesizes theory and prior engineering-education examples of technology-facilitated formative assessment using clickers, polling apps, and open-format response tools such as InkSurvey. It emphasizes that real-time, open-ended questions can expose misconceptions, support active learning and metacognition, and help instructors adjust instruction immediately or in the next class. The paper also highlights limitations of multiple-choice-only implementations and argues that open-format responses are better for probing reasoning, creativity, and problem-solving processes in undergraduate engineering contexts.

The paper includes illustrative examples from an intermediate electromagnetics course for third-year engineering physics majors, where 60 students responded to open-format conceptual problems in class. These examples are used to show how instructors can quickly detect gaps in calculus fluency, misuse of symmetry, and disconnects between derivations and subsequent graphing tasks. The main conclusion is that embedded formative assessment is a powerful instructional approach in undergraduate engineering, but its effectiveness depends on the quality of questions, the instructor’s responsiveness, and the use of technology that reduces logistical burden while preserving rich evidence of student thinking.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that embedded formative assessment helps students in undergraduate engineering better reason through scientific/physics problems by making their thinking visible and allowing instructors to target misconceptions. In the illustrative electromagnetics class (n=60), open-format responses revealed problems with applying Gauss’s law, choosing appropriate limits, and using symmetry, suggesting the method can expose and support scientific reasoning, but no comparative effect size or pre/post outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Open-format in-class response quality on electromagnetics conceptual/problem-solving tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly claims that embedded formative assessment increases metacognition and critical thinking by prompting students to reflect on what they know, what they do not know, and how they are reasoning. In the example tasks, student work showed superficial or shortcut reasoning, and the author argues that open-format formative assessment exposes these patterns and supports more deliberate problem solving, but no quantitative effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Metacognition and critical-thinking indicators inferred from student written/graphical responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that formative assessment can actively engage every student, increase confidence by helping students see what they know, and prompt further study when misconceptions are revealed. These claims are supported by theory and anecdotal classroom observations rather than controlled comparisons, so the evidence is descriptive only.
finding.measure: Student engagement, confidence, and willingness to seek assistance/further study

finding.finding_summary: A central claim is that technology-facilitated formative assessment reduces the clerical burden of collecting and reviewing student responses and enables real-time feedback in large classes. The paper describes clickers, mobile polling, and InkSurvey as streamlining response collection and analysis, but it provides no quantitative productivity measure or workload comparison.
finding.measure: Instructor clerical burden / turnaround time for collecting and reviewing formative assessment responses

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how formative assessment might be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically the Blackboard Learning System, in a university context. The authors motivate the study by arguing that frequent assessment with timely feedback can improve learning more effectively than traditional end-of-term summative approaches, especially in a technology-enabled environment.

The paper combines a conceptual review of formative assessment literature with a student survey about continuous assessment and online testing via Blackboard. The proposed implementation involved weekly or fortnightly online tests with immediate detailed feedback, and the authors report that students generally supported the approach because it broke material into smaller topic-based assessments and provided rapid feedback. The survey was administered to university students across Business, Engineering, and IT streams, and students favored Blackboard-based testing over classroom testing mainly for convenience, flexibility, and immediate feedback.

The main conclusion is that formative assessment supported by Blackboard is perceived positively by students and may help them keep up with subject content throughout the semester, identify strengths and weaknesses, and potentially improve summative exam performance. However, the paper does not report direct achievement outcomes from a controlled comparison; its evidence is primarily attitudinal and descriptive, so the claims about improved grades remain speculative rather than demonstrated.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent online formative assessments were helpful because they supported step-by-step learning, provided constant feedback, and reduced anxiety about losing many marks on a single test. In the open-ended responses, students also said the approach helped them stay in touch with the subject throughout the semester, although some feared that too many tests could create stress and pressure.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment, feedback, stress/pressure, and perceived usefulness of frequent BB assessments

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames formative assessment as supporting metacognition and self-regulation by helping students recognize their strengths and weaknesses and check whether they are on track. Students specifically valued immediate feedback and detailed explanations as aids to correcting mistakes and monitoring progress.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of metacognitive support, self-monitoring, and understanding of feedback

finding.finding_summary: Students favored the Blackboard testing option over classroom tests because it offered immediate feedback and greater flexibility/convenience. The paper argues that online formative assessment can deliver detailed feedback efficiently and without delay compared with the traditional classroom-based approach.
finding.measure: Student preferences regarding Blackboard test vs. classroom test and perceived convenience/feedback speed

paper_profiles.title: Inverted Classroom an der Hochschule Karlsruhe - ein nicht quantisierter Flip
paper_profiles.venue: Das Inverted Classroom Model: Begleitband zur ersten deutschen ICM-Konferenz
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter describes the Hochschule Karlsruhe’s SKATING project and its early attempts to introduce the Inverted Classroom Model (ICM) in engineering mathematics and related university teaching contexts. The paper is motivated by problems common in German engineering higher education: high dropout rates, heterogeneous student preparation, limited semester-long study habits, and the need for teaching approaches that better support active learning and individualized pacing.

Rather than reporting a controlled comparison, the chapter is mainly a practice and evaluation report. It outlines several staged variants of inversion, from minimally inverted lecture summaries to partially inverted single topics and a more fully inverted mathematics unit, and describes how videos, a learning platform (ILIAS), discussion forums, online surveys, and classroom observations were used to implement and monitor the approach. The context is an applied sciences university with undergraduate engineering students, where the method was adapted to fit instructors’ preferences, course constraints, and available support from the SKATING project team.

The main conclusion is cautiously positive but explicitly non-quantified: the authors argue that ICM can create more time for in-class application, improve interaction, and potentially support student motivation and study success, but only if it is carefully tailored and evaluated in context. They emphasize that evaluation should include process data, student and instructor perceptions, unintended effects, and later exam results, including comparisons with prior cohorts, but the paper itself does not present a rigorous outcome analysis of comparative effectiveness. It is therefore best read as a methodological and implementation-oriented account rather than direct evidence that ICM outperforms a conventional lecture or formative assessment alternative.

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses most directly on undergraduate higher mathematics, especially an inverted unit on differential equation systems in a third-semester engineering mathematics course (about n=20). However, it reports implementation details and planned evaluation rather than quantitative learning gains; the chapter states that exam results and follow-up measures were planned to assess whether students mastered the topic better, but no outcome statistics are reported.
finding.measure: Mathematics course understanding and exam performance on differential equation systems
finding.study_size: n=20 (pilot course); no analytic sample size reported for outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The chapter reports that the ICM was intended and, in the pilot, perceived as potentially increasing student motivation, curiosity, and satisfaction. Student reactions to the first inverted session were described as mostly positive, though concerns were raised about extra time and reduced ability to ask questions; a follow-up questionnaire on satisfaction was planned, but no quantified effect is reported.
finding.measure: Student motivation, curiosity, satisfaction, and acceptance of the instructional format

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the inverted format should support active problem solving, collaboration, and discussion during class, and it reports that the observed sessions included guided individual and partner work followed by student or instructor presentations. These are described as desirable features and observed process elements rather than measured skill outcomes, so no direct effect size or statistical result is available.
finding.measure: In-class collaboration, active problem solving, and student participation

finding.finding_summary: Operational efficiency is a substantive focus because the chapter repeatedly evaluates preparation, production, and implementation workload for both instructors and support staff. The paper reports that producing a video session required about 1 hour total editing/production time, with roughly 30 minutes of instructor setup and 30 minutes for organization per recording, while the authors argue that later semesters may require less effort; however, they also note that the initial setup is work-intensive and that technical/organizational support is needed.
finding.measure: Instructor and support-staff time required for video production and implementation

finding.finding_summary: The chapter frames ICM as a potential institutional response to engineering-student dropout, heterogeneous entry skills, and the applied-sciences university mission to make study more feasible for broader student populations. Its evidence is programmatic and implementation-based: the SKATING project is presented as a model for piloting, supporting, and disseminating innovative teaching methods across courses, but no institutional outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Institutional implementation of ICM pilot projects and support structures

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: Not a human study; educator-focused narrative review and practical guide
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can be aligned with core principles of formative assessment and feedback. The authors argue that while LLM use in education has grown rapidly, many applications have not been explicitly grounded in formative assessment theory, leading to tools that may be useful but not necessarily pedagogically sound.

The paper is a narrative/practical review rather than an empirical study. It organizes formative assessment around three questions—where learners are going, where learners currently are, and how to move learners forward—and shows how LLMs might support each stage. Examples include rewriting learning objectives in student-friendly language, generating prompts for co-constructing success criteria, creating sample work for critique, designing short-cycle questions, and producing process-level feedback. The discussion repeatedly emphasizes that LLMs should augment, not replace, teacher expertise, and that prompts, context, and pedagogical judgment are critical for useful outputs.

The intended context is K-12 and higher education, with examples drawn from high school biology, undergraduate fMRI instruction, and broader classroom assessment practice. The paper also highlights limitations of current LLM evaluations, such as overreliance on grammatical or surface-level metrics rather than formative utility, and notes risks like overdependence on AI-generated responses. Its main contribution is conceptual and practical: a framework and set of examples for educators and researchers, not comparative evidence of efficacy versus alternative instructional approaches.

paper_profiles.title: The Effect of Student Learning Styles on the Learning Gains Achieved When Interactive Simulations Are Coupled with Real-Time Formative Assessment via Pen-Enabled Mobile Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether the learning gains produced by a pedagogical model that combines interactive computer simulations with real-time formative assessment vary by student learning style. The authors are especially interested in whether the approach is better suited to certain styles, such as visual, sensing, active, or sequential learners, as measured by the Felder-Soloman Index of Learning Styles (ILS).

The intervention is the “Coupled Model”: students work with interactive simulations on pen-enabled mobile devices while instructors collect immediate open-format responses via InkSurvey. The instructor uses these responses to diagnose misconceptions, scaffold thinking, and provide rapid feedback during class. The study was conducted in an undergraduate engineering physics laboratory course (“Advanced Physics Laboratory I”) with two class sections and a total of 41 students, using five simulations spanning circuits, Fourier analysis, diffraction, standard deviation/mean, and least squares.

Learning was measured with pre-tests and end-of-unit summative assessments scored with rubrics, and learning gains were correlated with ILS learning-style scores. The authors found large and statistically significant gains for all five simulation activities, but these gains were not significantly correlated with any learning-style dimension. In short, the Coupled Model appeared broadly effective across a range of student learning styles rather than preferentially helping one type of learner.

finding.finding_summary: Across five simulation-based learning activities, students showed significant gains from pre-test to summative assessment while using the coupled simulation-plus-formative-assessment model. The reported class-average normalized gains were 63% (circuits, n=41), 67% (Fourier, n=41), 60% (diffraction, n=30), 75% (standard deviation/mean, n=40), and 61% (least squares, n=33), with all paired tests reported as p<0.001.
finding.measure: Pre-test and summative assessment scores on simulation-based physics/statistics reasoning tasks scored with rubrics; average normalized gain
finding.study_size: n=41 total across two sections; simulation-specific n ranged from 30 to 41
finding.std_deviation: 0.12 (inter-rater reliability estimate SD for nine reliability estimates)

finding.finding_summary: The study directly tested whether learning-style dimensions moderated the learning gains produced by the coupled model, a question tied to learner fit and metacognitive/learning-process adaptation. Pearson correlations between learning gain and each ILS dimension were near zero across all five simulations (e.g., ACT-REF r=0.02 to 0.25, SEN-INT r=-0.28 to 0.04, VIS-VRB r=-0.06 to 0.14, SEQ-GLO r=-0.15 to 0.06), indicating no statistically significant relationship between learning style and gains.
finding.measure: Pearson correlations between normalized learning gain and Index of Learning Styles dimensions
finding.study_size: n=41 total; simulation-specific n ranged from 30 to 41
finding.confidence_interval: 95% confidence ranges reported for each correlation; see study text (e.g., circuits ACT-REF -0.28 to 0.32)

paper_profiles.title: Student’s Video Production as Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.venue: ICPE 2013 – International Conference on Physics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether student-produced videos can function as a useful formative assessment in high school physics. The authors argue that video production may reveal students’ understanding, misunderstandings, and reasoning in ways that traditional tests and questionnaires often do not, while also capturing broader skills such as collaboration, planning, and persistence.

The approach was implemented in a Brazilian high school context (Colégio Pedro II, Rio de Janeiro) with students aged roughly 14–17 across first, second, and third year high school classes. After a term of traditional instruction in physics, 232 students working in self-selected groups produced 55 short videos on course topics, accompanied by brief written explanations. Teachers reviewed the videos, categorized them by content, format, and general features, and then led whole-class discussion sessions.

The paper reports descriptive and correlational findings rather than a comparison against a control condition. The authors found that many videos contained correct or partially correct physics, most had logical structure, and the connection between the assigned theme and the final product was usually satisfactory. They also report a strong association between technical quality and conceptual accuracy: among technically strong videos, most were conceptually correct. The authors conclude that student video production is a viable and reliable formative assessment tool in physics classes, though the evidence is based on observational analysis of student work rather than an experimental comparison.

finding.finding_summary: Student-produced videos provided evidence of students’ physics understanding and misconceptions, with 19 of 55 videos (35%) judged correct and 25 (45%) partially correct. The authors report that the videos revealed conceptions about elementary dynamics and other topics that were often not visible in traditional tests, and that the videos supported teacher diagnosis during the course.
finding.measure: Qualitative/analytic assessment of physics content accuracy, clarity, and reasoning in student-produced videos

finding.finding_summary: The activity was described as eliciting collaboration, planning, metacognition, and project completion skills in addition to physics content learning. The paper notes that students planned and replanned their productions, worked cooperatively in groups of up to five, and often chose technically elaborate formats that required careful implementation.
finding.measure: Observed features of group video production process and analyst interpretation of collaboration/planning/metacognitive demands

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that the video task engaged students and supported participation in learning, with the classroom discussion and creative format prompting amusement and active involvement. However, the evidence is descriptive and based on observed student behavior rather than a validated motivational measure.
finding.measure: Observed student engagement/participation during video production and discussion

paper_profiles.title: Teacher Learning of Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports on a five-year research project examining how science and mathematics teachers learn to use Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment (TEFA), a pedagogy built around classroom response systems (“clickers”) and structured question cycles. The authors frame the problem as teacher change: how teachers adopt, adapt, and sustain a new pedagogy, and what kinds of professional development are needed to support that process.

The intervention combines clicker technology, the TEFA pedagogy, and an intensive professional development (PD) program. TEFA emphasizes question-driven instruction, dialogical whole-class discourse, formative assessment, and meta-level communication. Teachers at multiple middle and high school sites in western Massachusetts participated in baseline data collection followed by three years of longitudinal support, with data drawn from PD transcripts, journals, implementation logs, surveys, classroom video, and interviews.

The paper is primarily descriptive and qualitative, presenting four detailed teacher case narratives (Tracy, Kim, Renee, and Gina) to illustrate different learning trajectories. Across cases, the authors conclude that teachers can learn TEFA over time, but the process is difficult and idiosyncratic: teachers first become comfortable with the technology, then wrestle with question design and classroom discourse, and later with using formative evidence to adjust instruction. The authors report preliminary cross-case patterns such as increased time in discussion, more student-to-student interaction, reduced IRE patterns, and teachers making instructional changes based on evidence of student thinking. The paper argues that TEFA can become a powerful pedagogical tool, but that effective implementation requires sustained, responsive PD and considerable teacher adaptation.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers generally reported that TEFA and the associated PD were demanding and time-intensive, especially for preparing good questions and managing class time. Several teachers described reduced efficiency pressures over time as they became more comfortable with the pedagogy, but the paper does not report a controlled productivity outcome or quantitative effect size.
finding.measure: Teacher preparation time, class time used for TEFA, implementation logs, journals, and teacher reports of workload

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that TEFA often increased student participation, engagement, and willingness to discuss ideas, and that some teachers used it to improve classroom climate and motivation. Examples include Kim using TEFA to start class and reduce hallway chatter, and multiple teachers reporting stronger participation and more positive student responses over time; no standardized student engagement effect size is provided.
finding.measure: Student survey perceptions, classroom video observations, teacher journals, and implementation logs
finding.study_size: n=approximately 39 teachers; student survey administered to every student in participating classes

finding.finding_summary: TEFA was associated with growth in student-student interaction, classroom dialogue, and teachers’ use of formative evidence to make real-time instructional adjustments, all of which align with collaboration and metacognitive/cognitive flexibility skills. The paper reports more discussion, fewer IRE exchanges, and multiple instances where teachers changed lessons based on what they learned about student thinking, but it does not provide numerical effect sizes.
finding.measure: Classroom discourse patterns in video, teacher reflections, pre/post interviews, and instances of instructional adjustment based on formative assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes middle- and high-school mathematics teachers and describes TEFA being used for reviewing state exam content, probing understanding, and supporting classroom discussion, but it does not report direct student achievement results in mathematics. The authors explicitly state that rigorous controlled evidence on measurable learning impacts is still needed, so the mathematics achievement impact remains preliminary and unmeasured here.
finding.measure: Teacher use of TEFA in math classrooms, student responses in math-related question cycles, and teacher perceptions of usefulness
finding.study_size: n=approximately 39 teachers, including multiple math teachers

finding.finding_summary: In science classrooms, TEFA was used to elicit reasoning, argumentation, and conceptual understanding through question cycles and discussion. The paper reports that teachers gained better information about how students were thinking about concepts and adjusted instruction accordingly, but it does not report direct student science achievement gains or experimental effect sizes.
finding.measure: Science classroom discussion, teacher perceptions of student thinking, classroom video, and lesson adjustments
finding.study_size: n=approximately 39 teachers, including science teachers across middle and high school

paper_profiles.title: WizardLM: Empowering Large Pre-Trained Language Models to Follow Complex Instructions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper introduces Evol-Instruct, a method for automatically generating large volumes of open-domain instruction-following data by iteratively rewriting prompts to increase complexity or breadth. The authors use this synthetic data to fine-tune LLaMA 13B into WizardLM, and then compare WizardLM against several baselines including Alpaca, Vicuna, Baize, CAMEL, Tulu, and ChatGPT-3.5.

The central question is whether AI-generated instruction data can match or exceed human-created instruction data for instruction tuning. The paper reports that WizardLM generally outperforms open-source baselines on a suite of automatic benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, ARC, HumanEval, GSM8k, AlpacaEval, MT-Bench) and on a custom human-evaluated test set, WizardEval. The work is focused on language-model instruction tuning rather than educational interventions, so its relevance to education research is indirect and primarily methodological. It provides evidence that increasing instruction complexity during data generation improves downstream model performance, but it does not study classroom learning, students, or formative assessment.

finding.finding_summary: WizardLM improved math reasoning performance relative to the baselines. On GSM8k, WizardLM-13B scored 37.15 pass@1, compared with 24.34 for Vicuna-13B, 8.35 for Alpaca-13B, 8.95 for Baize-13B, 7.13 for CAMEL-13B, and 36.50 for Tulu-13B; the paper emphasizes this as a substantial gain from Evol-Instruct. The benchmark measures grade-school math word-problem solving, with n=1319 test items.
finding.measure: GSM8k pass@1

finding.finding_summary: Across broad language-model benchmarks, WizardLM-13B outperformed strong open-source baselines. The paper reports an average score of 58.96 for WizardLM-13B versus 54.60 for Vicuna-13B and 43.44 for Alpaca-13B, with gains also on MMLU (52.92), ARC (57.25), HellaSwag (80.88), TruthfulQA (50.55), HumanEval (24.0), AlpacaEval (75.31), MT-Bench (6.35), and WizardEval (89.1). These results indicate improved general instruction following and reasoning on heterogeneous NLP tasks.
finding.measure: Aggregate benchmark scores across MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA, HumanEval, AlpacaEval, MT-Bench, WizardEval

finding.finding_summary: The paper's strongest non-domain-specific claim is that evolving instruction complexity improves reasoning-related capabilities. WizardLM outperformed baselines on benchmarks the authors associate with reasoning and instruction-following quality, including MT-Bench (6.35 vs. 6.21 for Vicuna and 4.78 for Alpaca) and WizardEval human judgments, which explicitly rated relevance, knowledge, reasoning, calculation, and accuracy. The evidence suggests better multi-step reasoning and response quality after instruction tuning with more complex synthetic prompts.
finding.measure: MT-Bench and human pairwise evaluation on WizardEval
finding.study_size: n=218 WizardEval human-evaluated instructions; n=10 annotators

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Evol-Instruct enables large-scale instruction data creation without human annotation, reducing reliance on costly manual data collection. It reports generating 250k instructions using ChatGPT API from 52k seed examples over four evolution rounds, then sampling 70k for fine-tuning, demonstrating a more scalable pipeline for dataset production. This is framed as an efficiency improvement in data generation and model training rather than a measured productivity outcome.
finding.measure: Data generation scale / annotation avoidance

paper_profiles.title: FinGPT: Instruction Tuning Benchmark for Open-Source Large Language Models in Financial Datasets
paper_profiles.venue: Workshop on Instruction Tuning and Instruction Following at NeurIPS 2023
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents FinGPT, a benchmarking and instruction-tuning framework for evaluating open-source large language models (LLMs) on financial natural language processing tasks. The authors ask how different base models respond to task-specific instruction tuning, multi-task instruction tuning, and a zero-shot adaptation setup across several finance-domain datasets.

The approach is not an educational intervention but a model benchmarking study. Six open-source LLMs (Llama2, Falcon, BLOOM, MPT, ChatGLM2, and Qwen) were tuned and compared on sentiment analysis, headline classification, named entity recognition, and relation extraction, using LoRA and standardized prompt templates. The paper also reformulates NER and RE into classification formats for multi-task and zero-shot evaluation, then compares performance across phases to examine transfer and generalization.

The work is situated in financial NLP rather than education and does not study learners, teachers, or classrooms. Its main conclusion is that model performance depends strongly on the task and tuning regime: Llama2 and MPT performed well in task-specific settings, multi-task tuning often helped information extraction more than classification, and ChatGLM2 and Falcon showed the strongest zero-shot generalization. The paper emphasizes openness, reproducibility, and cost-effective benchmarking rather than instructional outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Demystifying Instruction Mixing for Fine-tuning Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how mixing different instruction-tuning datasets affects large language model (LLM) performance. The authors focus on three instruction types: general chat instructions (Alpaca), coding instructions (CodeAlpaca), and reformulated NLP task instructions (P3). They ask whether combining these datasets improves performance uniformly or whether certain mixtures help some capabilities while harming others.

The study fine-tunes LLaMA-2 7B and 13B models on all eight combinations of the three datasets, using balanced 20K subsets and evaluating them on NLP benchmarks, HumanEval code generation, and FLASK-based alignment skill assessments. Results show that each dataset helps most in its own domain: P3 improves NLP benchmark performance, CodeAlpaca improves coding, and Alpaca improves alignment/chat quality. However, mixing all instruction types does not consistently improve all outcomes; in particular, P3 can hurt alignment/chat abilities, while code instructions can also support alignment when combined with general instructions.

The paper further examines mixing ratios and dataset volume, finding that performance on both NLP and code benchmarks peaks at an intermediate ratio of specialized-to-general instructions and tends to plateau beyond about 10K examples per instruction type. Overall, the paper concludes that instruction mixture design should be task- and model-size-aware: larger models can benefit more from diverse mixtures, but some specialized instruction sources can create negative transfer for chatbot alignment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies NLP downstream benchmark performance as a function of instruction-mixture composition. Fine-tuning LLaMA-2 on P3 yielded the best average NLP score among single-dataset runs, while mixtures such as AC, AP, CP, and ACP often improved over the no-fine-tuning baseline but did not uniformly outperform the best specialized model. On LLaMA-2-7B, for example, average NLP scores ranged from 54.6 (None) to 58.2 (P) and 57.1 (ACP); on LLaMA-2-13B, they ranged from 58.8 (None) to 61.9 (CP).
finding.measure: Average zero-shot NLP benchmark score across ARC, Winogrande, PIQA, MMLU, RACE, and HellaSwag

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates code-generation performance using HumanEval pass@1 and pass@10. CodeAlpaca consistently improved coding performance relative to the vanilla model, and mixtures including coding data often helped further; for example, LLaMA-2-13B improved from 15.4 pass@1 without tuning to 18.2 with CP and 20.2 with ACP, while LLaMA-2-7B improved from 13.7 to 17.5 with AC. This indicates a positive effect of coding-focused instruction tuning on task efficiency in code generation.
finding.measure: HumanEval code generation pass rate (pass@1 and pass@10)

finding.finding_summary: The alignment evaluation is a proxy for chat quality and user-facing instruction-following behavior, which the paper treats as a conversational alignment outcome. Alpaca produced the strongest alignment scores, while P3 reduced alignment substantially; for example, average FLASK scores were 58.8 for the 13B vanilla model, 64.0 with Alpaca, but only 47.8 with P3. Mixing P3 with other data lowered alignment by about 2.8 points (7B) and 3.6 points (13B), whereas adding CodeAlpaca to general instructions slightly improved alignment.
finding.measure: FLASK alignment skill scores across logical correctness, factuality, commonsense understanding, comprehension, completeness, insightfulness, readability, and conciseness

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Construction of a Korean Toxic Instruction Dataset for Ethical Tuning of Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of training and evaluating large language models (LLMs) to safely handle toxic, biased, hateful, and criminally oriented user instructions in Korean. The authors argue that existing Korean toxicity datasets are limited in scope and do not adequately reflect the kinds of malicious prompts that generative models receive, especially for instruction tuning. To address this, they introduce KoTox, a 39.2K-item automatically generated dataset of toxic instruction-output pairs spanning political bias, hate, and crime.

The main contribution is a template-and-lexicon-based generation pipeline that combines predicates, Korean politican names, party labels, hate terms, and crime-related terms to create diverse explicit and implicit toxic queries. The dataset is filtered with human-in-the-loop naturalness checks and analyzed for explicitness, targetedness, and toxicity using Perspective API. The paper then evaluates whether fine-tuning a Korean LLM (DaG) on KoTox changes its responses to toxic prompts compared with the unfine-tuned model, as well as compared with ChatGPT and CLOVA X. DaG+KoTox responds more neutrally/ethically than DaG alone on the test prompts, suggesting the dataset is useful for ethical tuning, although the study is limited to a small manually scored test set and does not establish downstream educational effects.

finding.finding_summary: KoTox improved the ethical behavior of a Korean instruction-tuned LLM on toxic-query handling. In the authors' manual evaluation of 10 test prompts per category (political bias, hate, crime) plus unseen prompts, DaG+KoTox produced more neutral/ethical responses than DaG without KoTox, including 80% neutral/ethical responses for politics, 30% for hate, and 60% for crime, versus 10%, 0%, and 0% respectively for the base DaG model.
finding.measure: Human-rated response categories to toxic queries (Neutral/Ethical, Risky/Unethical, Irrelevant/Incorrect)
finding.study_size: n=40 test queries plus unseen test queries; 3 human annotators

paper_profiles.title: Releasing the CRaQAn (Coreference Resolution in Question-Answering): An open-source dataset and dataset creation methodology using instruction-following models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of creating high-quality question-answering datasets that require coreference resolution, especially for evaluating chunking strategies in long-document information retrieval pipelines. The authors argue that existing datasets either focus on coreference resolution or question answering separately, and that available QA datasets do not adequately test cases where answers depend on resolving pronouns or nominal references across sentences.

To address this gap, the paper introduces CRaQAn, an open-source dataset of 261 human-reviewed question-answer pairs derived from Wikipedia articles about modern U.S. laws. The dataset was generated using GPT-4 in an automated pipeline built around a Recursive Criticism and Improvement (RCI) loop, with specialized reviewer prompts and a final human review stage. The method was designed to produce QA pairs that require coreference resolution across two or three sentences while avoiding more complex phenomena such as cataphora and zero anaphora.

The paper is primarily a dataset and methodology contribution rather than an experimental evaluation of learner outcomes. The main conclusions are that instruction-following models can be used to scale dataset generation for complex QA tasks, but that human review, prompt engineering, and generation costs remain important limitations. The authors position CRaQAn as a resource for future NLP research on coreference-aware retrieval and QA, not as a direct educational intervention or assessment study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the automated GPT-4 plus RCI workflow made dataset creation faster than manual generation, with human reviewers needing about 2 minutes on average to evaluate each QA pair. The initial release contained 261 human-reviewed QA samples, and the automated generation yield was approximately 60.2% (348 accepted out of 578 candidate pairs before duplicate removal).
finding.measure: Dataset generation yield; average human review time per QA pair
finding.study_size: n=578 candidate QA pairs; n=261 released QA samples

paper_profiles.title: Ongoing Vaccine and Monoclonal Antibody HIV Prevention Efficacy Trials and Considerations for Sequel Efficacy Trial Designs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses the design of sequel efficacy trials for HIV prevention products in the context of ongoing randomized prevention trials of HIV vaccines and broadly neutralizing monoclonal antibodies. The central problem is how to choose appropriate future trial designs when standard HIV prevention options such as oral PrEP, medical male circumcision, and potentially injectable PrEP are part of the background prevention landscape, and when event rates may become very low.

The article does not test an educational intervention; instead it analyzes trial-design options such as Layer, Compare, and Combine strategies for future vaccine or bnAb efficacy studies. It reviews the ongoing HVTN 702, HVTN 705, HVTN 703/HPTN 081, and HVTN 704/HPTN 085 trials, and then reasons through how different outcomes from those trials would affect the ethics, interpretability, and sample size of sequel trials. A major conclusion is that facilitated access to proven prevention methods is generally appropriate, while placebo-controlled or counterfactual-placebo analyses should usually be secondary rather than primary when better randomized controls are available. The paper also argues that future primary objectives may need to shift if HIV incidence becomes too low, but cautions that alternative endpoints such as additive risk differences or counterfactual-placebo efficacy require strong assumptions and better exposure measurement to be interpretable.

paper_profiles.title: FOUNDATIONS FOR AI-ASSISTED FORMATIVE ASSESSMENT FEEDBACK FOR SHORT-ANSWER TASKS IN LARGE-ENROLLMENT CLASSES
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of making formative assessment feasible in large-enrollment introductory statistics courses. The authors note that short-answer, constructed-response tasks can support learning and reveal misconceptions, but human scoring becomes too time-consuming at scale, especially when instructors want timely feedback.

The study evaluates whether NLP methods can reliably score short-answer responses and support clustering of student answers for later instructor interpretation. Using de-identified responses from 1,935 post-secondary students across 29 class sections at 15 institutions, the authors compare multiple human raters with an automated scoring system (SFRN) and also compare SFRN with an LSTM-based classifier. They find substantial agreement among trained human raters, strong agreement between the algorithm and human raters, and promising but mixed clustering performance depending on representation method.

Overall, the paper is primarily a methodological validation study rather than a direct test of learning effects from formative assessment itself. Its main conclusion is that AI-assisted scoring and clustering may reduce instructor burden and make short-answer formative assessment more scalable in large classes, while preserving reliability comparable to trained human raters. The paper suggests this human-machine collaboration could enable future research on feedback and revision effects, but it does not directly estimate student learning gains from the intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that AI-assisted scoring could substantially improve the feasibility of formative assessment at scale by reducing the workload of scoring short-answer responses in large classes. Human raters showed substantial agreement (pairwise QWKs > 0.74; Fleiss’ kappa = 0.68), and the best algorithm (SFRN) matched human raters closely (pairwise QWK = 0.7403-0.8151; four-way Fleiss’ kappa = 0.678), with classification accuracy of 83% versus 72% for the LSTM baseline.
finding.measure: Scoring reliability and classification accuracy for short-answer response grading

paper_profiles.title: X-Instruction: Aligning Language Model in Low-resource Languages with Self-curated Cross-lingual Instructions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of aligning large language models for low-resource languages, where instruction-following data are scarce and naive translation from English can introduce errors, miss cultural nuance, and produce poor outputs. The authors argue that low-resource-language performance suffers not only from limited pretraining data, but also from a lack of high-quality instruction-tuning examples in those languages.

To address this, they propose X-Instruction, an automatic pipeline that excavates cross-lingual instruction-following samples from multilingual web corpora. The method first generates English instructions for text snippets in other languages, then iteratively refines the resulting instruction-response pairs with a learned evaluator, and finally diversifies the dataset by clustering English instructions. The result is a 320k-sample dataset covering 10 languages (5 medium-resource and 5 low-resource), built largely from unsupervised web text plus a small seed set.

Experiments fine-tuning LLaMA-2-7B and 13B on X-Instruction show improved open-ended generation quality over translation-based and distillation-based baselines, including Bactrian-X and Bactrian-M, and in some settings performance that matches or exceeds ChatGPT as judged by GPT-4 and humans. The paper also finds that models trained with cross-lingual instructions can often follow prompts in the output language without further tuning, suggesting some zero-shot transfer from English-instruction training to multilingual understanding and generation.

finding.finding_summary: Across four open-ended generation benchmarks translated into 10 languages, X-Instruction models outperform translation-based Alpaca-MT and distillation-based Bactrian-X/Bactrian-M baselines. For example, GPT-4 judged X-Instruction13B to have a 67.7% average win rate against ChatGPT across 10 languages, and average GPT-4 score 6.9 vs. 5.6 for Bactrian-M13B on Vicuna/WizardLM comparisons.
finding.measure: GPT-4 pairwise win rates and GPT-4 quality scores on Vicuna, WizardLM, LIMA, and Koala benchmarks

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively evaluates instruction-following ability, language understanding, and response quality on open-ended prompts, which are proxy measures for following complex instructions and generating coherent answers. X-Instruction13B shows consistent gains over baselines across benchmark categories such as commonsense, writing, knowledge, and roleplay, and its zero-shot output-language prompting loses only 5.7% win rate on average relative to standard cross-lingual generation.
finding.measure: Benchmark performance on instruction-following/open-ended generation tasks; category-level win rates and zero-shot comparisons

finding.finding_summary: The main contribution is a scalable data-construction pipeline for multilingual instruction tuning, rather than a learner-level educational intervention. The paper shows that the method can automatically produce a 320k-sample dataset for 10 languages and that iterative refinement improves sample quality and downstream model performance, indicating potential institutional value for multilingual model development workflows.
finding.measure: Dataset construction scale, quality review, and downstream benchmark performance of models trained on the dataset

paper_profiles.title: Socratic Mind: Impact of a Novel GenAI-Powered Assessment Tool on Student Learning and Higher-Order Thinking
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether Socratic Mind, a generative AI-powered formative assessment tool, can improve learning in a large online introductory computing course. The tool uses Socratic questioning to prompt students to explain their reasoning, debug code, and reflect on their understanding rather than simply receiving answers. The authors were motivated by the need for scalable assessment approaches that can support deeper learning and higher-order thinking in higher education, especially in fully online settings.

The study used a mixed-methods quasi-experimental design in a 16-week undergraduate CS1301 course at a U.S. research university. Students completed optional extra-credit AI assignments aligned to unit quiz topics, and the final analytic sample was 171 students (81 in Unit 3, 90 in Unit 4). The researchers analyzed system logs, UX and engagement surveys, open-ended reflections, and course performance data, including quizzes, tests, and final scores.

Results showed high reported engagement and positive UX, with behavioral, affective, and cognitive engagement all averaging near 4 on a 5-point scale. Regression analyses found that stronger engagement was associated with higher perceived learning, and the DiD analysis indicated that students who used the tool experienced a smaller decline in quiz performance over time than comparison peers, with an estimated buffering effect of about 3.3 points. The benefit was stronger for lower-performing students. Qualitative responses suggested perceived gains in problem-solving, critical thinking, and self-reflection, though verbal communication gains were more limited because many students typed rather than spoke.

Overall, the paper concludes that a dialogic GenAI assessment tool can be a scalable formative assessment strategy in online computing education. The authors argue that Socratic AI can complement traditional assessment by promoting reflection, conceptual understanding, and higher-order thinking, but they also note limitations such as quasi-experimental design, single-institution context, and the mismatch between perceived learning and actual assessment performance.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported high engagement with the GenAI tool across affective, behavioral, and cognitive dimensions (means 3.96, 4.07, and 3.96 on a 5-point scale; n=171). Engagement was positively associated with perceived learning, and UX ratings were also high, suggesting the tool supported active and emotionally involved participation.
finding.measure: Engagement survey (affective, behavioral, cognitive engagement) and UX survey
finding.std_deviation: AE SD=0.76; BE SD=0.61; CE SD=0.68

finding.finding_summary: Thematic analysis of 141 open-ended responses indicated perceived gains in higher-order thinking skills, especially problem-solving (69% positive), critical thinking (62% positive), and self-reflection (60% positive). Students credited the Socratic questioning format with helping them reason step-by-step, articulate logic, and evaluate alternatives more carefully.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses about problem-solving, critical thinking, self-reflection, and verbal communication

finding.finding_summary: Using difference-in-differences, the treatment group showed a smaller decline in quiz scores over time than comparison peers. The authors report an average overall drop of about 11.84 points from pre- to post-intervention, but participation in the AI assignment reduced this decline by an estimated 3.30 points (β=0.107, p<.05) in the quiz model (R²=0.303; n=171 for the main sample, 793 observations in the regression table).
finding.measure: Unit quiz scores and course assessment performance over time
finding.study_size: n=171 (analytic sample); regression table uses 793 observations

paper_profiles.title: ConvoLearn: A Dataset of Constructivist Tutor-Student Dialogue
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a pedagogical gap in large language model (LLM) tutoring: current systems often provide answers directly rather than supporting dialogic, constructivist learning. The authors propose a knowledge-building framework for AI tutors and operationalize it across six dimensions: cognitive engagement, formative assessment, accountability, cultural responsiveness, metacognition, and power dynamics.

To support this framework, they create ConvoLearn, a semi-synthetic dataset of 1,250 multi-turn tutor-student dialogues grounded in California middle school Earth Science standards. Human teachers generated dialogues with a simulated student, and the resulting conversations were filtered and annotated for quality and alignment. The dataset was then used for QLoRA fine-tuning of three open-source instruction-tuned LLMs (Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3).

The paper evaluates models both intrinsically with an ordinal classifier and extrinsically with teacher ratings. The fine-tuned Mistral model performed best, and in a human study with 31 teachers it significantly outperformed its base model and Claude Sonnet 4.5 on overall pedagogical effectiveness (M=4.10, SD=1.03 vs. 2.59 and 2.87). The study concludes that training on constructivist dialogue data can meaningfully shift LLM behavior toward more knowledge-building tutoring, although it does not measure downstream student learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies whether fine-tuning on knowledge-building dialogue improves pedagogical performance in middle school Earth Science tutoring. In a human evaluation by 31 teachers (148 rated examples), the fine-tuned Mistral-7B achieved a mean effectiveness rating of 4.10/5 (SD=1.03), significantly outperforming its base model (M=2.59, SD=1.11) and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (M=2.87, SD=1.29) in science tutoring dialogues.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated pedagogical effectiveness of Earth Science tutoring dialogues

paper_profiles.title: Students’ Patterns of Interaction with a Mathematics Intelligent Tutor: Learning Analytics Application
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal on Integrating Technology in Education (IJITE)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students interact with the ALEKS intelligent tutoring system in a foundation mathematics course and whether those interaction patterns predict academic success. The author’s main question is whether the sequence in which students choose topics matters for learning retention, and whether log-derived indicators such as prior knowledge, topics mastered, topics practiced, and the mastered-to-practiced ratio (mtop) can predict final exam performance.

The study used a cross-sectional, observational design with 58 female students in a higher-education institute in the United Arab Emirates.
