Data came from ALEKS system logs and a nine-item student survey; analyses included correlation, regression, clustering, and paired-sample t-tests. The paper found that prior knowledge and mtop together predicted final exam marks (R2=0.42), while mtop alone explained 16% of variance in final exam marks. Students who selected topics sequentially were more likely to retain mastery after the comprehensive assessment, whereas students who chose topics randomly—despite sometimes reporting positive perceptions of ALEKS—showed weaker or significant losses in retained mastery.

Overall, the paper argues that learning analytics from intelligent tutors can help identify students at risk and that topic sequencing is associated with better retention of mathematics learning. It does not test ALEKS against a separate instructional control condition; rather, it uses system-log evidence to describe patterns of use within an ALEKS-supported course and relates those patterns to outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Prior knowledge and the mastered-to-practiced ratio (mtop) jointly predicted final exam performance in foundation mathematics, explaining 42% of variance in final exam marks (R2=0.42). In the stepwise regression, mtop was a significant positive predictor (B=46.008, t=2.518, p=.015), and prior knowledge (IA) was also significant (B=0.649, t=4.855, p<.001).
finding.measure: Final exam marks in foundation mathematics; course assessment scores; comprehensive test (CT) and final exam (FE)
finding.effect_size: R2=0.42; mtop alone explained 16% of variance; prior knowledge alone explained 35% of variance

finding.finding_summary: Survey and cluster results suggest differences in perceptions about ALEKS tutoring/cognitive effects and in study habits. Students with positive perceptions who chose topics sequentially were more likely to retain mastery after the comprehensive test, while students with positive perceptions but random topic choice showed significant loss of retained mastery (paired t=-2.233, p=.036).
finding.measure: Survey ratings of tutoring effect and cognitive effect of ALEKS; topic-selection habit (sequential vs random); paired-sample comparison of mastered topics vs CT performance
finding.effect_size: t=-2.233 for the random-choice/high-perception cluster; t=-1.6 and t=-0.702 for the other clusters

finding.finding_summary: The paper links sequential topic selection with better retention of learning and interprets this as a more effective self-organized study strategy. Students who worked sequentially showed stronger retention patterns than students who selected topics randomly, indicating an association between sequencing behavior and learning persistence/strategy use.
finding.measure: Retention of mastery after the comprehensive assessment; topic-selection sequence from ALEKS logs
finding.effect_size: Correlation between CT and mastered topics in the sequential/high-perception cluster was 0.425 (p=.043); in the random/high-perception cluster it was 0.412 (p=.045)

paper_profiles.title: Learn Like Feynman: Developing and Testing an AI-Driven Feynman Bot
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether an AI-driven conversational study tool based on the Feynman learning technique can improve learning for self-regulated learners who lack peer or instructor support. The authors argue that existing AI study tools help with memorization and question answering, but do not sufficiently promote deeper understanding or higher-order reasoning through discussion.

To address this gap, they developed the Feynman Bot, a large-language-model-based app using retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering to simulate a learning-by-teaching conversation. In the study, 14 working adults enrolled in Harvard’s online Justice course were randomly split into a passive-learning control group and an experimental group that reviewed lecture transcripts with the bot for 25 minutes per session over three days. Both groups completed formative and summative assessments, and the bot group also completed a self-efficacy survey.

The results suggest that the bot group achieved somewhat higher learning gains than the passive-learning group and reported greater comfort with the study material. Participants using the bot also preferred typing over speech for interacting with the system. The authors conclude that the Feynman Bot is a promising tool for self-regulated learning, but they note the small sample size and the need for larger, longer-term studies before drawing stronger claims.

finding.finding_summary: Participants using the Feynman Bot showed higher learning gains than passive learners on the same justice-content material over the same study time. The mean summative score was slightly higher for the bot group (M=6.8, SD=1.3) than the passive group (M=6.5, SD=1.9), and mean learning gain was larger for the bot group (3.83 vs 2.17).
finding.measure: Formative and summative assessment scores on MCQs; open-ended response performance
finding.std_deviation: bot group SD=1.32; passive group SD=1.94

finding.finding_summary: The bot increased learners’ reported comfort and confidence with the study material. All bot users said it increased their comfort enough to discuss the content with peers, over 57% said they felt comfortable enough to teach or converse about it with new learners, and 85.7% viewed it as useful for new topics.
finding.measure: 5-point Likert self-efficacy survey on comfort/confidence with study material and using the bot

finding.finding_summary: The bot appears to support deeper explanation and applied reasoning in open-ended responses. All participants answered the open-ended questions correctly, but bot users more often elaborated with scenario- or case-based explanations, suggesting improved comprehension and ability to articulate concepts.
finding.measure: Open-ended assessment responses analyzed qualitatively/thematically

paper_profiles.title: Learners Teaching Novices: An Uplifting Alternative Assessment
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 55th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education (SIGCSE 2024)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether formative assessment can be redesigned so that students demonstrate understanding by teaching novices, rather than by taking a conventional exam or practice test. The authors propose Assessment via Teaching (AVT), in which CS1 learners tutor novice students for one hour on course topics and are evaluated through the teaching interaction itself.

The study was conducted in a CS1 course at a large R1 university with about 300 enrolled students, alongside a lagged online version of the same course that supplied novice students. Participants were randomly assigned to AVT, a practice-exam control, or no-session controls. AVT learners prepared more, reported greater enjoyment, and showed stronger performance on exam questions aligned with the taught topics than class averages; the paper argues that AVT is both a motivating formative assessment and a useful source of 1:1 support for novices.

The strongest direct comparative result is that AVT performed at least as well as a 1-hour practice exam on the relevant exam questions, while also producing better self-reported experience and motivation. Expert review suggested that novice students generally benefited from the sessions, though some learners needed more guidance to avoid over-explaining or giving away answers. Overall, the paper presents AVT as a promising alternative assessment approach with both learning and service-oriented benefits, while noting implementation challenges around novice access, safety, and scalable measurement of understanding.

finding.finding_summary: In an RCT with CS1 undergraduates (AVT n=15; PracticeExam n=14; Control_C n=244), learners who taught an AVT session scored higher on exam questions aligned to the taught material than the class average. The paper reports gains of about 20-30 percentage points on several relevant questions, with statistically significant improvements on 3 of 5 midterm questions and on the relevant final question (Final Q3, p<0.001).
finding.measure: Midterm and final exam scores on questions aligned to AVT topics (e.g., Q1 midterm; Q3 final)
finding.study_size: n=15 AVT learners (with comparison groups: n=14 PracticeExam, n=244 Control_C)

finding.finding_summary: AVT improved learners’ motivation and enjoyment relative to a traditional practice exam. On the exit survey, AVT participants were about twice as likely to study for more than 1 hour before the session, and they reported higher enjoyment, including an average recommender rating of 4.2/5; the paper also describes an effect size of +0.6 on a 5-point enjoyment scale.
finding.measure: Exit survey measures of preparation time, enjoyment rating, and recommendation rating
finding.study_size: n=15 AVT learners; comparison to n=14 PracticeExam

finding.finding_summary: The teaching intervention appears to strengthen learners’ understanding and reflection while they explain concepts to novices. Expert reviewers and qualitative feedback indicated that AVT helped learners identify weaknesses in their own understanding and prompted deeper conceptual processing; however, the paper does not report a formal effect size for metacognitive outcomes.
finding.measure: Expert review of teaching interactions and qualitative reflections on understanding/metacognition

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames AVT as a scalable assessment format that can provide formative feedback without requiring course staff to continuously create new tests, and that can be retaken repeatedly. These claims are conceptual rather than experimentally benchmarked; the empirical component instead shows that expert instructors could assess novice impact from session recordings, but no quantitative productivity or workload effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of repeatability/scalability and expert review process

paper_profiles.title: Towards a low-cost universal access cloud framework to assess STEM students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of conducting secure, equitable remote assessment for university STEM courses during and after COVID-related disruptions. The authors focus on programming exams, where traditional in-person lab-based testing is difficult to reproduce at home, especially when institutions need to verify identity, restrict cheating, and support students with accessibility needs.

The paper describes a cloud-based assessment architecture built around Kubernetes, JupyterHub, LDAP authentication, and a commercial proctoring tool (Respondus LockDown Browser). The system was used to deliver a remote Introduction to Computer Science exam with a quiz component and a practical coding component, simulating a monitored computer lab while allowing students to use their own devices and home internet connections. The authors also compare this setup with two alternative online assessment arrangements previously used by the university: a video-conferencing surveillance model and a multi-device screen/camera recording workflow.

The main conclusions are that the cloud-based setup was easier for students to use, required fewer instructors for surveillance, reduced IT support burden, and better preserved exam conditions than the alternatives. The paper also argues that the approach is cheaper and more flexible than on-premise equivalents for low-frequency use cases like exams, while being adaptable to formative assessment and collaborative coding tasks. However, the evidence is descriptive and based on a single institutional case rather than a controlled comparison of learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The cloud-based assessment setup reduced staffing and support demands relative to the two alternative online exam configurations. For an exam of about 30 students, setup A required four teachers for surveillance, while the proposed setup C could be administered by a single teacher and required no extra intervention from the IT department; the paper also reports fewer student issues and simpler exam administration.
finding.measure: Teacher surveillance workload; IT support issues; administrative effort during remote exams

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the cloud deployment improves institutional capacity to run secure remote assessments with lower cost and greater flexibility than on-premise equivalents. The authors report that the system was cheaper and more flexible than on-premise installations and could be adapted for exams, collaborative coding, and formative assessment, suggesting broader institutional benefits for access, continuity, and resource management.
finding.measure: Deployment cost, flexibility, and feasibility for institutional assessment infrastructure

paper_profiles.title: RLInspect: An Interactive Visual Approach to Assess Reinforcement Learning Algorithm
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the difficulty of evaluating and interpreting reinforcement learning (RL) training, where reward alone can be misleading and may not reflect true model performance. The authors argue that RL evaluation needs a more comprehensive, interactive approach that examines multiple components of training rather than relying on a single scalar metric.

To address this, they introduce RLInspect, an interactive visual analytics tool for inspecting RL agents during training. RLInspect organizes analysis into modules for state, action, agent architecture, and reward, and generates interactive Plotly-based visualizations from training data. The paper explains how the tool can reveal issues such as under-exploration, shifts in action confidence, policy divergence, vanishing gradients, and reward volatility, using a CartPole/OpenAI Gym example to illustrate the workflow.

The paper is not an empirical study comparing RLInspect against alternative instructional or evaluation approaches in an education context; instead, it is a tool paper focused on RL model diagnostics and debugging. The context is machine learning / reinforcement learning research, with no K-12 population or educational intervention studied. The main conclusion is that interactive, multi-component visual inspection may help users better understand and potentially improve RL training compared with relying on reward alone, but the paper does not report controlled experimental outcomes or quantitative user-study evidence.

paper_profiles.title: SimQFL: A Quantum Federated Learning Simulator with Real-Time Visualization
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (simulation framework paper; no human participants studied)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents SimQFL, a software simulator for quantum federated learning (QFL) that is designed to help researchers prototype, run, and visualize distributed quantum machine learning experiments on classical hardware. The authors argue that existing quantum simulators and FL platforms do not adequately support end-to-end QFL workflows, real-time training visualization, or user-supplied data integration. SimQFL is positioned as a practical environment for experimenting with client-side quantum neural network training, federated aggregation, and real-time monitoring of loss and accuracy.

The system supports configurable numbers of clients, qubits, quantum layers, learning rates, data distributions, and datasets such as MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. The paper describes the simulator architecture, the quantum federated learning workflow, and an illustrative use case that trains a QFL model with a quantum-aware FedAvg procedure. The experiments are not human-subject studies; they compare simulated QFL versus classical FL and explore internal simulator settings such as qubit count, circuit depth, and number of clients. The main conclusion is that SimQFL provides an accessible and interactive platform for experimenting with QFL, and that the simulated quantum model outperforms the classical FL baseline on the reported image-classification benchmarks within this setup.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates a simulated quantum federated learning workflow on image-classification datasets and reports that the quantum model outperforms the classical FL baseline in accuracy and convergence. Specifically, accuracy improvements are reported as about 10.5% on MNIST, 7.3% on Fashion-MNIST, and 23.1% on CIFAR-100, with faster convergence in the QFL setting.
finding.measure: Classification accuracy and loss on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-100

paper_profiles.title: Video2Reward: Generating Reward Function from Videos for Legged Robot Behavior Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of automatically generating reward functions for legged robot behavior learning. The authors argue that prior LLM-based reward-generation methods rely too heavily on textual task descriptions, which are too abstract to precisely specify nuanced locomotion behaviors such as ambling or human-like running. To solve this, they propose Video2Reward, a framework that converts motion in target videos into keypoint trajectories and uses those trajectories, along with auxiliary textual context, to prompt an LLM to generate executable reward code.

The method also includes a video-assisted iterative refinement loop. After training a policy with the generated reward, the robot’s motion is compared with the target video via trajectory similarity, and the resulting feedback is fed back into the LLM to improve the reward function over multiple rounds. The experiments are conducted in the IsaacGym simulator on Anymal (quadruped) and Humanoid (biped) tasks, using video clips of target motions from the internet. The paper reports that the method outperforms Eureka, expert-designed human baselines, and sparse rewards on human-normalized score and trajectory similarity, with the strongest reported gain being a 37.6% improvement over Eureka on Anymal and an 11.1% improvement on Humanoid.

Overall, the paper concludes that video input makes reward generation more controllable and behaviorally precise than text-only prompting. The video-assisted feedback component further improves performance, suggesting that visually grounded iterative refinement helps LLMs produce better reward functions for robot locomotion learning.

paper_profiles.title: Procedural Generation of STEM Quizzes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint addresses the problem of how instructors can create, vary, and maintain large banks of electronic STEM quiz questions more efficiently than with conventional LMS graphical user interfaces. The author argues that form-based quiz authoring in systems like Moodle is slow and poorly suited to reusing structured content, generating randomized variants, or embedding dynamic media such as formulas, plots, images, and 3D interactives.

The paper presents a proof-of-concept Python API for procedural quiz generation. The API supports common question types such as multiple choice, numerical, matching, short answer, and fill-in-the-blanks, plus mechanisms for generating random question variants from lists or key-answer pairs. The context is STEM instruction, where the author assumes many instructors have at least some programming familiarity, and the goal is to let them script question banks that are richer and easier to revise than GUI-authored banks.

The evaluation is a small user study and timing analysis comparing Moodle’s GUI with the script-based approach for creating text-based multiple-choice questions, along with estimated creation times for more complex scripted examples. Five trained users created 20 questions in both systems, and the author fit linear models relating question length to completion time. The main conclusion is that script-based authoring was faster and more scalable for the tested tasks, and that it greatly improved reuse, maintenance, and the ability to produce dynamic content. The paper does not evaluate learning outcomes from formative assessment itself; it mainly evaluates authoring efficiency and question-bank generation.

finding.finding_summary: In a user study with five trained users creating 20 multiple-choice questions, the script-based approach was about 49 seconds faster per question than Moodle’s GUI. The paper reports linear models of question-entry time with strong fit (R² > 0.94) and estimates T = 0.197n + 12.5 s for script-based authoring versus T = 0.19n + 61.3 s for Moodle, showing substantially lower authoring overhead for similar question content.
finding.measure: Question creation time / authoring speed in Moodle GUI versus script-based Python API

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that procedural generation improves question-bank maintenance at the institutional level by making bulk edits, translation, version control, and reuse much easier than in GUI-based LMS workflows. No formal institutional outcome study is reported, but the author claims constant-time maintenance operations for some changes (e.g., renaming terms or changing penalties) that would otherwise require editing each question individually.
finding.measure: Ease and time required for large-scale question-bank maintenance tasks

paper_profiles.title: Theory of neuromorphic computing by waves: machine learning by rogue waves, dispersive shocks, and solitons
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This theoretical paper asks what kinds of computation can be performed by nonlinear wave systems when used as a reservoir layer in a feed-forward machine-learning architecture. The authors study a single wave-layer feed-forward network (SWFN), where an input is encoded into an initial wave state, propagated through a nonlinear medium, and then decoded by linear readout weights from sampled output channels.

The paper focuses on conditions under which the wave reservoir can learn arbitrary functions, finite datasets, and Boolean logic gates. Using the nonlinear Schrödinger equation as the dynamical model, the authors argue that universal learning requires sufficiently strong nonlinearity and adequate output-channel rank; linear or weakly nonlinear propagation is not universal. They illustrate the framework with simulations on a synthetic function, the abalone dataset, and a NAND gate, showing exact or near-exact training when the number of channels matches the number of training points and the transmission matrix reaches full rank.

The context is not an educational intervention or learner population, but rather computational physics and neuromorphic photonics. The main conclusion is that strongly nonlinear wave phenomena such as solitons, rogue waves, and dispersive shocks can support universal approximation and exact dataset interpolation in this model, suggesting possible applications for future photonic or physical machine-learning hardware.

paper_profiles.title: When AI Evaluates Its Own Work: Validating Learner-Initiated, AI-Generated Physics Practice Problems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how to validate on-demand, AI-generated physics practice problems so that a chatbot can decide which generated items are safe and useful to present to students. The authors focus on whether automated checks can match expert judgments on problem quality, and whether those same checks relate to what students actually choose when shown pairs of candidate problems.

The study was conducted in an introductory physics exam-preparation setting at ETH Zurich. Thirty-four undergraduate students used an enhanced chatbot for 1.5 hours and generated 543 candidate problems across topics including mechanical energy, DC circuits, and electric fields. Each problem was expert-rated on many structural and pedagogical quality metrics, then re-rated by commodity LLM judges (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-o3-mini/low) to test agreement, and random-forest models were used to see which metrics predicted student choice.

The main conclusion is that a small set of core checks is enough for practical validation, especially for numerical problems: measures like measurement-unit-is-clearly-stated and includes-solution-strategy were both reliably judged by LLMs and strongly related to student selection. However, several more abstract or multi-category metrics, such as Bloom level and expected difficulty, were weakly recovered by LLMs and were less useful for prediction. Overall, the paper argues that scalable formative assessment does not require exhaustive scoring, but rather a curated subset of structural and learner-visible checks.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central empirical contribution is about the validity of AI-generated physics practice problems for supporting scientific problem solving. In the student-choice analyses, scientific-depth features mattered: for radio-button problems, bloom-level-of-exercise and exercise-difficulty-level were among the strongest predictors of choice (importances 0.138 and 0.137), while for numerical problems includes-solution-strategy was highly influential (importance 0.261). However, automated judgments of higher-order quality were weak for several science-reasoning indicators, with F1 values of 0.397 for bloom-level-of-exercise and 0.231 for exercise-difficulty-level.
finding.measure: Expert ratings of physics problem quality metrics; LLM-as-a-judge agreement; student choice between candidate physics problems; random-forest feature importance

finding.finding_summary: For numerical physics problems, the study found that a small set of quantitative-structure checks strongly predicted which item students selected. The strongest predictors were measurement-unit-is-clearly-stated (importance 0.364) and includes-solution-strategy (0.261), and the numerical-choice model achieved 83.8% test accuracy (5-fold CV accuracy 0.827 ± 0.044; OOB accuracy 84.5%). This suggests that clear numerical framing and solution scaffolding make AI-generated quantitative practice more appealing and practically usable.
finding.measure: Student selection among numerical AI-generated problems; random-forest prediction accuracy and feature importance
finding.study_size: n=34 students; 185 numerical problems total (148 train, 37 test in the model split)

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats learner preference as a proxy for perceived usefulness, appeal, and fit, and the exit survey explicitly asked about usefulness, expectations, trustworthiness, and motivation. The authors report that students’ preferences aligned with problems that felt clearer, more structured, and better scaffolded, and that the chatbot was evaluated in a preparation context meant to support exam readiness and motivation. However, the paper does not report a formal effect on motivation or engagement outcomes, so the evidence here is indirect and based on preference/feedback rather than measured affective gains.
finding.measure: Exit-survey comments and Likert items on usefulness, expectations, motivation, and learning efficiency; student choice data

finding.finding_summary: The study emphasizes metacognitive and problem-solving-related qualities of practice items, especially clarity, completeness, solvability, and strategy hints. These structural features were only moderately recoverable by LLM judges (for example, task-is-solvable F1=0.605, task-is-clear F1=0.588, task-is-specific-and-complete F1=0.575), yet they were among the metrics that mattered for student preference, particularly in the numerical-problem setting where includes-solution-strategy was highly predictive. The findings suggest that AI-generated practice can support self-regulated problem solving when it provides sufficient scaffolding and clear task structure.
finding.measure: Expert quality metrics and student choice among candidate problems

paper_profiles.title: Towards In-Situ Failure Assessment: Deep Learning on DIC Results for Laminated Composites
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of predicting fracture load in notched laminated composite materials from experimentally measured strain fields. The motivation is that composite failure is difficult to predict with conventional analytical or finite-element approaches because failure depends on interacting mechanisms such as delamination, fibre breakage, and matrix cracking, and on factors like layup sequence, fibre orientation, and notch geometry.

The study proposes a deep-learning framework that uses only Digital Image Correlation (DIC) strain-field data from mechanical tests, avoiding finite-element simulations and empirical calibration. Two models are compared: a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that takes selected numerical strain values near the notch, and a convolutional neural network (CNN, DenseNet-121) that takes grayscale strain-field images. The dataset includes 116 quasi-static tests across 31 configurations spanning open-hole and U-notch geometries, multiple laminate layups, and several off-axis/on-axis loading cases.

Results show that both models predict fracture loads well, with MLP achieving R² = 0.86 and CNN achieving R² = 0.82 under the main evaluation setting. The MLP performed slightly better and was more computationally efficient, while the CNN was more sensitive to lower-load/noisier strain fields and benefited from augmentation. Overall, the paper concludes that DIC-based deep learning can provide practical in-situ fracture-load estimation for laminated composites without needing additional simulations.

paper_profiles.title: Adaptive Memory Admission Control for LLM Agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a core systems problem in LLM agents: how to decide which candidate memories should be admitted into long-term memory. The authors argue that existing approaches either rely on hand-crafted heuristics or opaque LLM-driven policies, both of which struggle with hallucinated, redundant, or obsolete content and can be costly to run and difficult to audit.

To address this, they propose Adaptive Memory Admission Control (A-MAC), a hybrid framework that scores each candidate memory using five interpretable signals: future utility, factual confidence, semantic novelty, temporal recency, and content type prior. The approach uses one LLM call for utility and efficient rule-based or embedding-based computation for the other signals, then learns weights and a threshold via cross-validated optimization. The evaluation is conducted on the LoCoMo benchmark with 30 conversational-agent dialogues spanning personal assistant, technical support, and research collaboration contexts, totaling about 1,500 labeled candidate memories.

The main finding is that A-MAC improves memory-admission accuracy and efficiency relative to prior baselines. On the held-out LoCoMo test set, it achieves F1=0.583, outperforming A-mem (F1=0.541), MemoryBank (0.452), MemGPT (0.324), and a random baseline, while also reducing latency by 31% relative to A-mem. Ablation results show that the content type prior is the most influential feature, and cross-domain analysis suggests the learned policy transfers reasonably across personal and professional dialogue domains without retuning. The paper concludes that explicit, interpretable admission control is an effective design principle for scalable and reliable agent memory systems.

finding.finding_summary: A-MAC improved memory admission efficiency and runtime relative to the strongest baseline. On the LoCoMo test set (n=225 candidate memories), it achieved 31% lower latency than A-mem (2644 ms vs 3831 ms per candidate) while also improving F1 from 0.541 to 0.583.
finding.measure: Latency per candidate memory; precision/recall/F1 for admission decisions

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that transparent, interpretable admission control can improve auditability and debugging of LLM-agent memory systems, which is an institutional design implication rather than a direct educational effect. Empirically, the learned policy generalized across personal and professional conversation domains without retuning, with mean F1=0.410 across domain splits (personal F1=0.482; professional F1=0.338).
finding.measure: Cross-domain generalization of learned admission policy; interpretability/auditability claims

paper_profiles.title: Automated Essay Scoring and Feedback Systems for ESL Learners: A Meta-Review of Pedagogical Impact
paper_profiles.population: Secondary, tertiary, and intensive English program ESL learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This meta-review synthesizes empirical research on automated essay scoring (AES) and automated writing evaluation (AWE) systems used with ESL learners. The paper asks whether these systems improve writing outcomes, engagement, and assessment reliability, and it also examines moderators such as learner proficiency, feedback frequency, delivery mode, and tool type. The authors systematically searched major databases and meta-analyzed 54 primary studies published from 2000 to 2024, totaling 7,832 participants.

The review focuses on AES/AWE platforms such as Criterion, Pigai, Grammarly, Write & Improve, and emerging LLM-based systems. Across the included studies, AES/AWE interventions were associated with moderate gains in writing quality, grammar accuracy, and lexical sophistication, with an average effect size of g ≈ 0.60. The paper reports that intermediate learners benefited most, and that more frequent, immediate feedback and higher system-human alignment were linked to stronger outcomes.

The review also concludes that engagement matters: multiple draft cycles, greater uptake of feedback, and shorter feedback latency were associated with better writing development. At the same time, the authors note inconsistent reporting of fairness and bias diagnostics across the literature, arguing that multilingual validation and subgroup analyses are needed. Overall, the paper positions automated feedback as instructionally effective when paired with psychometric rigor, iterative revision, and teacher mediation.

finding.finding_summary: Across 54 primary studies (n=7,832), AES/AWE interventions produced significant improvements in ESL writing quality, grammar accuracy, and lexical sophistication. The review reports an average effect of g ≈ 0.60, indicating a moderate positive impact on writing outcomes.
finding.measure: Writing quality, grammar accuracy, lexical sophistication; holistic and analytic writing scores

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that automated feedback was associated with higher engagement, more draft cycles, higher feedback uptake, and reduced writing anxiety. These affective and behavioral gains were repeatedly linked to better writing performance across the included studies.
finding.measure: Engagement indicators, feedback uptake, writing anxiety/self-efficacy scales, draft counts

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AES/AWE can reduce feedback latency and support scalable, repeatable evaluation, especially in large ESL classes and programs. It emphasizes that these systems can lessen teacher marking burden while providing timely formative feedback, although the meta-review does not pool a single effect size for workload outcomes.
finding.measure: Feedback latency, instructional scalability, teacher workload, repeatable automated scoring

paper_profiles.title: The Role of Large Language Models (LLMs) in Personalized English Language Instruction
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Scientific Interdisciplinary Research
paper_profiles.population: Secondary and tertiary learners (aged 15+), primarily English language learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language models (LLMs) can support personalized English language instruction in authentic classroom settings. The study addresses a practical gap in the literature: there is little quantitative, classroom-anchored evidence showing how LLM-mediated personalization and feedback relate to learner engagement, self-efficacy, and perceived learning outcomes.

Using a quantitative, cross-sectional, case-study design, the author surveyed 312 learners across three enterprise/cloud-supported cases where LLM-mediated tasks had been integrated for 6 to 8 weeks. The survey measured personalization features, feedback quality, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, interaction frequency, engagement, self-efficacy, and perceived learning outcomes, with moderation tests for prior proficiency and AI familiarity. Analyses included descriptive statistics, correlations, hierarchical regressions with case fixed effects, and bootstrapped mediation/moderation tests.

The paper concludes that personalization features and ease of use predict perceived usefulness, feedback quality is the strongest predictor of self-efficacy, and engagement and self-efficacy are the main proximal predictors of outcomes. It also reports conditional effects: lower-proficiency learners show stronger returns, and learners with higher AI familiarity show a steeper usefulness-to-outcome link. Overall, the study argues that LLMs are most effective when they provide actionable feedback, reduce cognitive load, and support frequent, purposeful learner interaction rather than merely generating content.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports positive associations between LLM-enabled personalization and perceived English learning outcomes. In the main quantitative model (n=312), engagement and self-efficacy were the primary proximal predictors of outcomes, while personalization influenced outcomes indirectly through usefulness and engagement; feedback quality influenced outcomes indirectly via self-efficacy. The outcome measure was a self-reported learning outcomes scale (Likert-based), not an external achievement test.
finding.measure: Perceived learning outcomes / self-reported improvement and goal attainment

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies engagement and self-efficacy as central learner mechanisms and finds positive relationships with LLM personalization and feedback quality. In the sample of n=312 learners, feedback quality was reported as the strongest predictor of self-efficacy, and engagement was one of the primary proximal predictors of perceived outcomes. Measures were five-point Likert scales for engagement and self-efficacy.
finding.measure: Engagement and self-efficacy survey scales

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes learner-centered process variables that overlap with durable skills, especially self-regulation and metacognitive/agentic engagement. While these are discussed as mechanisms rather than directly assessed with a dedicated durable-skills instrument, the study finds that personalized LLM use is associated with higher engagement and self-efficacy, which the authors link to self-regulated learning processes. Measures were engagement and self-efficacy Likert scales, with n=312.
finding.measure: Engagement/self-regulation-related survey constructs (engagement, self-efficacy)

finding.finding_summary: The study treats frequency of interaction and ease of use as process variables indicating smoother, more efficient LLM use, and reports that perceived ease of use jointly predicts perceived usefulness. However, operational efficiency is only an indirect focus; there are no direct productivity or workload outcomes. Measures were perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and interaction frequency on five-point Likert scales, with n=312.
finding.measure: Perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, interaction frequency

paper_profiles.title: An Examination of Blended Learning and the Traditional Classroom Using Achievement Scores
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines whether a rotation-model blended learning program improves middle school students’ language arts achievement relative to a traditional classroom model. The study was motivated by a broader gap in K-12 blended learning research, especially the lack of evidence on which models work best for which student subgroups and grade bands.

The author conducted a naturalistic quasi-experiment using historical Georgia CRCT language arts scores from one non-Title 1 public middle school in a metropolitan school district. The sample included sixth, seventh, and eighth graders, and the analysis compared traditional instruction with a rotation model supported by Edgenuity. Moderator variables included prior achievement, teacher effectiveness, learning environment, and student educational label. The main conclusion was that the blended model did not produce a uniform achievement advantage; the dissertation reports no significant difference for special education and regular education students, but gifted students in the blended model performed worse than gifted students in the traditional model. The study suggests that effects of blended learning may differ by subgroup and that implementation decisions should consider potential harms for some students.

finding.finding_summary: The study focused on middle school language arts CRCT scores, comparing a rotation-model blended learning classroom with a traditional classroom. Results were not uniformly positive: the dissertation reports no significant difference for special education or regular education students, but gifted students in the blended model performed at a lower level than gifted students in the traditional model.
finding.measure: Georgia Criterion-Referenced Competency Test (CRCT) language arts scaled scores

paper_profiles.title: Fixations, regressions, and results: eye-tracking metrics as real-time signals of cognitive engagement in flipped-class quizzes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether low-cost eye-tracking measures can provide useful real-time evidence of how undergraduates process formative multiple-choice quiz items in a flipped classroom. The authors focus on two gaze metrics—fixation intensity (total dwell time) and regression rate (backward saccades)—and examine whether these signals relate to item difficulty, correctness, and students’ subjective mental effort after controlling for item text length.

The study was conducted in an English-medium business course with 45 volunteers, of whom 34 provided analyzable data. Students completed 320 item attempts across 55 Bloom-coded quiz items while a 60 Hz tracker recorded gaze; analyses used crossed mixed-effects models with student and item random intercepts and a covariate for total word count. The paper also explored whether gender differences mattered and whether gaze metrics aligned with block-level self-reported effort.

Results showed that once word count was controlled, Bloom level no longer uniquely predicted fixation intensity or regression rate, indicating that apparent higher-order demand effects were largely explained by text length. Fixation intensity was positively associated with correctness and regression rate negatively associated with correctness, though these effects were small and not conventionally significant. Block-level self-reported effort had near-zero correspondence with gaze metrics and accuracy. The authors conclude that gaze can be a useful response-process signal in formative flipped-class quizzes, but only when item length and layout are standardized or modeled statistically; they recommend length-matched item banks and caution against interpreting Bloom-level differences without such controls.

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily studies item-level performance on multiple-choice quiz questions in a flipped business course. Longer fixation intensity was associated with higher odds of answering correctly (OR=1.299 per 1 SD increase in zFI, 95% CI [0.981, 1.72]), while higher regression rate was associated with lower odds of correctness (OR=0.806, 95% CI [0.602, 1.08]) in 320 attempts from 34 undergraduates; however, neither effect reached conventional statistical significance.
finding.measure: Item correctness on Bloom-coded multiple-choice quiz items
finding.effect_size: OR=1.299 for zFI; OR=0.806 for zRR

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines cognitive engagement / mental effort during formative quiz work. Higher fixation intensity and lower regression rate are treated as indicators of engagement, but block-level self-reported mental effort (SR_LOAD) showed near-zero correlations with mean FI, mean RR, and block accuracy, indicating poor convergence between subjective effort and gaze-based engagement signals.
finding.measure: Fixation intensity, regression rate, and block-level self-reported mental effort (SR_LOAD)
finding.study_size: n=320 attempts aggregated to student × block; 34 students
finding.effect_size: Correlation near zero (exact coefficients not reported)
finding.confidence_interval: Fisher 95% CIs exclude even modest associations; exact values not reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames fixation intensity and regression rate as indicators of cognitive engagement and processing effort, which are closely tied to comprehension, monitoring, and self-regulation during task performance. After controlling for word count, Bloom level did not uniquely predict these gaze metrics, but item length did predict fixation intensity; the authors argue that process data can reveal moment-to-moment engagement beyond correctness alone.
finding.measure: Gaze-based processing effort (FI, RR) during item completion
finding.effect_size: β=-0.232 for TotalWC_z predicting zFI; Bloom contrast on zFI β=-0.119 (ns)

finding.finding_summary: A central conclusion is that classroom-friendly eye tracking can provide real-time formative diagnostics that instructors and adaptive systems could use for targeted support. The authors argue that FI and RR can flag potential struggle episodes during pre-class quizzes, enabling just-in-time scaffolds, but only if item length and layout are standardized or statistically modeled.
finding.measure: Feasibility and diagnostic utility of 60 Hz eye-tracking metrics in flipped-class quizzes

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines formative assessment as a strategy for improving learning and whether it can be implemented effectively through an e-learning platform. The authors frame formative assessment as a diagnostic process that provides feedback during instruction, contrasting it with summative assessment, and argue that frequent, low-stakes assessments with timely feedback may improve students’ learning and eventual performance on semester-end exams.

The implementation discussed uses Blackboard Learning System at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus). The paper describes creating weekly or fortnightly online tests with immediate detailed feedback, including a Java-based online test with multiple-choice and true/false items, plus Blackboard features such as discussion forums and virtual classrooms to extend feedback. The context is a university setting with Business, Engineering, and IT students.

Empirically, the paper reports survey results from university students about continuous assessment and the Blackboard test option. Students generally supported frequent internal assessments, immediate feedback, and dividing coursework into smaller topic-based assessments; there were statistically significant differences by stream, with Engineering students more favorable than Business and IT students on some items. The study concludes that formative assessment implemented online is perceived positively and may help students stay engaged with the subject and support summative performance, though concerns about test burden and stress were also noted.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent, small-topic online assessments with immediate teacher feedback were helpful for learning and supported their progress through the semester. Survey responses indicated that the Blackboard formative assessment approach was valued for keeping students on track, measuring strengths and weaknesses, and maintaining engagement, though some students also worried about stress and pressure from too many tests.
finding.measure: Student survey perceptions of continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and Blackboard online test implementation

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes metacognitive and self-monitoring benefits of formative assessment, with students reporting that immediate feedback helped them correct mistakes, understand individual topics progressively, and check whether they were on track. These findings are based on questionnaire responses rather than direct performance measures, so the evidence is perception-based but clearly centers on reflection and self-regulation.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of feedback utility, self-monitoring, and progressive learning

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (practice guide / narrative review of K-12 and higher education contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback in education. The authors frame formative assessment around three core questions: where learners are going, where they currently are, and how to move them forward, and they argue that current LLM use in education often lacks explicit alignment with these pedagogical principles.

Rather than reporting a single empirical intervention study, the paper is a narrative/practical review that synthesizes examples, prompting strategies, and classroom use cases. It discusses how accessible LLMs can help educators rewrite learning objectives in student-friendly language, co-construct success criteria, generate sample work, create formative questions and MCQs, and produce different levels of feedback. The paper also emphasizes limitations, including variability in output quality, the need for educator oversight, and the risk of overreliance on AI-generated responses.

The context spans classroom formative assessment across subjects and grade bands, with illustrative examples drawn from high school biology and undergraduate fMRI/neuroimaging instruction. The main conclusion is that LLMs can augment, but not replace, expert pedagogy: they may reduce teacher workload and scale formative practices, but their use should be grounded in subject expertise, prompt design, and formative-assessment principles. The paper is primarily a conceptual/practice-oriented guide rather than an outcomes study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce educator workload and time spent on tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating sample work, creating formative questions, and drafting feedback. This is a conceptual/practical claim supported by illustrative examples rather than empirical effect estimates; no sample size or quantitative impact is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / task efficiency (conceptual examples of LLM-assisted formative-assessment tasks)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that well-designed LLM-supported formative assessment can promote durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, and self-regulation by encouraging students to reflect on feedback, evaluate exemplars, and avoid passive reliance on AI-generated answers. These claims are presented as pedagogical recommendations and illustrative scenarios rather than measured outcomes, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, self-regulation (conceptual pedagogical outcomes)

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides multiple subject-specific examples showing how LLMs can support learning-objective generation and sample-work creation in disciplines such as biology and undergraduate functional MRI. These uses are presented as ways to improve clarity of goals and task understanding across subjects, but the paper does not report empirical student-learning effects.
finding.measure: Subject-specific formative-assessment materials (learning objectives, exemplars, prompts)

paper_profiles.title: Machine Learning Applications to Diffuse Reflectance Spectroscopy in Optical Diagnosis; A Systematic Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the use of machine learning (ML) for classifying diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (DRS) signals in medical diagnosis. The authors ask what research areas and applications have been studied, what gaps remain, and what methodological considerations should guide future work. They focus on how ML models are used to process broadband DRS spectra, which are difficult to interpret visually but can distinguish biological tissues and disease states.

The review follows PRISMA guidelines and screens studies published after 2004 across multiple databases, ultimately retaining 77 studies. The included work spans several cancer-related and non-cancer applications, with most studies using supervised ML models such as SVM, LDA, neural networks, and KNN on human and animal tissue, often ex-vivo but sometimes in-vivo. Across the reviewed literature, the authors conclude that DRS+ML shows strong promise for tissue differentiation and clinical diagnostics, especially in cancer detection and surgical guidance, but that generalizability is limited by small sample sizes, lack of patient-wise stratification, variable preprocessing, and limited in-vivo validation.

The paper’s main contribution is synthesis rather than new experimental data. It highlights that many studies report high classification accuracy, but also warns that reported performance may be inflated by dataset imbalance, leakage, and insufficient validation. The review recommends larger, more diverse datasets, better reporting of preprocessing, stronger patient/specimen-level stratification, and more explainable and clinically deployable models.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in digital pathology: a diagnostic test accuracy systematic review and meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether artificial intelligence (AI) systems can accurately diagnose disease from whole slide images in digital pathology. The authors conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies, searching PubMed, EMBASE, and CENTRAL through June 2022 and including studies that applied AI to histopathology whole slide images for any disease.

The review included 100 studies in the systematic review and 48 in the meta-analysis, spanning more than 152,000 whole slide images across many disease areas, especially cancers. Across the pooled studies, AI showed high diagnostic accuracy, with mean sensitivity of 96.3% and mean specificity of 93.3%, though the evidence base was highly heterogeneous and nearly all studies had at least one high or unclear risk-of-bias domain. Subgroup analyses suggested particularly strong performance in gastrointestinal and urological pathology, with somewhat lower performance in breast pathology.

The main conclusion is that AI can perform well for disease detection and classification in digital pathology, but current evidence quality is limited by weak reporting, selection bias, unclear data splitting, and sparse external validation. The authors argue that future work needs stronger study design, clearer reporting of raw diagnostic data, and more external validation before routine clinical adoption.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis found high diagnostic accuracy for AI applied to whole slide images across a broad set of pathology tasks. Across 48 studies in the meta-analysis (50 assessments), pooled mean sensitivity was 96.3% (CI 94.1-97.7) and mean specificity was 93.3% (CI 90.5-95.4), indicating strong classification performance for disease detection in histopathology images.
finding.measure: Diagnostic accuracy in whole slide image disease detection/classification (sensitivity, specificity)
finding.study_size: n=48 studies in meta-analysis; 50 assessments; >152,000 WSIs across review

paper_profiles.title: The effect of short-term exposure to the natural environment on depressive mood: A systematic review and meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether brief, direct exposure to natural environments improves depressive mood, and whether any study characteristics help explain differences in effects across studies. The authors conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of peer-reviewed studies published up to March 2018, focusing on short-term exposure to green/natural settings versus built/urban settings and on current depressive mood rather than general well-being.

Across 33 studies involving adult participants, most commonly students but also several clinical and older adult samples, the review found a small overall reduction in depressive mood after exposure to natural environments. The pooled random-effects estimate was g = -0.30 (95% CI [-0.50, -0.10]), but substantial heterogeneity and generally high risk of bias limited confidence in the findings. The authors coded 20 moderators and used MetaForest and meta-regression to explore sources of variation, including sample gender mix, environment type, study region, and baseline measurement, but none were statistically significant in the final meta-regression.

The paper concludes that short-term exposure to natural environments may have a modest beneficial effect on depressive mood, especially in forest, agricultural, or biodiverse settings relative to parks, but that the evidence base is weak, inconsistent, and prone to bias. It recommends better reporting and more rigorous study designs to clarify which environments work best and for whom.

finding.finding_summary: A meta-analysis of 33 adult studies found a small but statistically significant reduction in depressive mood after short-term exposure to natural environments compared with built environments. The pooled random-effects estimate was g = -0.30 (95% CI [-0.50, -0.10]), with substantial residual heterogeneity (Qresid(39)=277.97, p<0.01) and high risk of bias across studies.
finding.measure: Depressive mood / negative affect, primarily measured with POMS depression subscales and related mood instruments (e.g. PANAS, NMS, MACL, ZIPERS, BRUMS, OHS)

paper_profiles.title: Drivers’ attention detection: a systematic literature review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of computational methods for detecting drivers’ attention, with a particular focus on image-based approaches. The authors frame the problem around traffic safety: driver inattention, distraction, fatigue, and drowsiness can lead to severe accidents, so automated attention-detection systems in advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) are needed to detect loss of attention and issue warnings before dangerous situations occur.

The review defines a search protocol, searches IEEE Xplore and ACM Digital Library, and selects primary studies using inclusion/exclusion criteria and a validation step involving three additional researchers. From an initial pool of about 1,000 studies, 50 were selected and 22 remained after validation. The extracted studies cover a wide range of techniques and sensors, including cameras, monocular/RGB-D/infrared cameras, smartphones, eye-tracking glasses, and methods such as PERCLOS, head-pose estimation, decision trees, SVMs, CNNs, fuzzy logic, and Bayesian networks.

The main conclusion is that the literature is highly heterogeneous: many different combinations of attention cues and techniques are used, with head position and eye state being the most common attention elements. The authors argue that there is no single consensus method that solves attention detection robustly across contexts, and they identify gaps in understanding which combinations of cues and methods are most effective. Because the paper is a descriptive SLR rather than an intervention study, it does not estimate causal effects, but instead synthesizes the state of the art and suggests future research directions for building more effective ADAS attention-detection systems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is a systematic review of driver attention-detection methods rather than an evaluation of a single intervention, so it does not report an effect on productivity or workload. Its main contribution is cataloging sensors, cues, and algorithms used in ADAS-style monitoring systems, with head position cited 21 times and eye state 18 times across the reviewed studies.
finding.measure: Characteristics and frequency of attention-detection techniques, sensors, and attention cues in the reviewed literature

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes prior work to inform future research and development of driver-monitoring ADAS, with explicit discussion of how the extracted evidence can support new research projects and prototype design. Its findings are intended to guide system-level development rather than measure a direct institutional outcome, so the impact is conceptual and indirect.
finding.measure: Review synthesis of methods, criteria, and sensors for driver attention detection

paper_profiles.title: Trust and Trustworthiness from Human-Centered Perspective in HRI – A Systematic Literature Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how trust and trustworthiness are conceptualized, measured, and studied in human-robot interaction (HRI), motivated by Industry 5.0’s emphasis on human-centered automation. The authors conduct a systematic literature review to identify common methodologies, trust measures, study foci, and barriers/facilitators for trustworthy HRI.

The review screened literature from 2014–2024 using Web of Science and EBSCO and retained 34 peer-reviewed English-language articles. The paper does not test an intervention; instead, it synthesizes how prior HRI studies operationalize trust, noting that many papers use custom questions, some use validated scales, and nearly 30% do not define trust at all. The review also categorizes trust-related factors into robot-, human-, and environment-related facilitators/barriers, such as transparency, communication, performance, safety, user familiarity, regulation, and ethical design.

The main conclusion is that trust in HRI remains conceptually fragmented and context-dependent, with methodological inconsistency contributing to contradictory findings. The authors argue that domain and application context should guide both trust definitions and measurement choices, and they recommend more tailored, human-centered design approaches that balance trustworthiness, safety, transparency, and user needs. Because the paper is a synthesis of adult HRI studies rather than an evaluation in education settings, it does not provide evidence relevant to formative assessment moderators by subject, grade band, or learner subgroup.

paper_profiles.title: A Review of a Work by Raymond: Sturmian Hamiltonians with a Large Coupling Constant - Periodic Approximations and Gap Labels
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a mathematical review of earlier work by Raymond on Sturmian Hamiltonians, a class of one-dimensional Schrödinger operators used in the spectral theory of quasicrystals. The paper focuses on how periodic approximations of these operators behave when the coupling constant is large, especially the combinatorial structure of spectral bands and how that structure leads to a formula for the integrated density of states and the appearance of all gap labels predicted by the gap-labeling theorem.

The authors rewrite and clarify arguments from the unpublished 1995 work and thesis of Raymond, while also adapting notation to support later work on the complete Dry Ten Martini Problem for Sturmian Hamiltonians. The paper is entirely theoretical and does not involve human participants, learners, schools, or educational interventions. Its conclusions are about spectral approximation, hierarchical band structure, and gap labeling in mathematical physics, not educational outcomes.

Because the paper is a review/expository mathematics article rather than an empirical study, no education-related outcome areas are substantively studied and no effect sizes are reported.

paper_profiles.title: A systematic review of research on large language models for computer programming education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews empirical research on large language models (LLMs) in computer programming education, addressing how these tools are being used, what benefits and concerns have been reported, and what future research and practice directions are suggested. The review was motivated by the rapid rise of ChatGPT and related tools and the lack of a consolidated synthesis of their role in programming education, especially in higher education.

The authors reviewed 42 empirical studies published from 2023 to March 2024, drawn from major databases and three ACM computing education conference proceedings. They used bibliometric analysis, thematic analysis, and structural topic modeling to synthesize the literature. The review shows that most studies involved undergraduate learners and focused on ChatGPT, with common uses including code generation, debugging, explanation, project support, and feedback. Across the literature, LLMs were often reported to improve learning experiences, self-efficacy, motivation, efficiency, and support for instructors, but some studies found no significant learning gains and many raised concerns about inaccuracy, academic dishonesty, bias, and possible harms to higher-order thinking and equitable access.

The paper concludes that the field is still early-stage, with limited experimental and longitudinal evidence, and it recommends broader research methods, larger samples, stronger attention to assessment design, and more interdisciplinary collaboration. It also proposes a conceptual framework for integrating LLMs into programming education that emphasizes stakeholder goals, pedagogy, AI literacy, and clear usage guidelines.

finding.finding_summary: The review found consistent evidence that LLMs can save instructors time and reduce workload by helping with lesson planning, assignment and exam generation, feedback, and administrative support. Reported benefits were based on qualitative interviews and case studies; for example, instructors (n=12 in Husain, 2024; n=20 in Lau & Guo, 2023) described improved efficiency, and virtual TA systems were reported to outperform human TAs in clarity and engagement in one study.
finding.measure: Instructor workload, time savings, feedback efficiency, and instructional support

finding.finding_summary: Several studies reported that LLM use improved students’ motivation, self-efficacy, self-confidence, and perceptions of support and learning experience. For example, Yilmaz & Yilmaz (2023a, 2023b) reported gains in computational thinking, programming self-efficacy, and learning motivation, while other studies found students perceived ChatGPT or similar tools as helpful, effective, and reliable.
finding.measure: Motivation, self-efficacy, confidence, enjoyment, perceived support, and learning experience

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests LLMs may support durable skills such as computational thinking, metacognition, and problem decomposition, but evidence is mixed because some studies also raised concerns that over-reliance could weaken critical thinking and problem-solving. For instance, Prather et al. (2023) reported benefits for cognitive coding and metacognition, while other studies noted possible setbacks to critical thinking and problem-solving abilities.
finding.measure: Computational thinking, metacognition, critical thinking, problem-solving, and related higher-order skills

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesized multiple studies on programming-learning outcomes, showing positive effects in some cases but also several null findings. Positive reports included improved coding, debugging, and project completion, but Kosar et al. (2024) and Sun et al. (2024) found no significant differences in learning outcomes between ChatGPT and comparison groups, although students often perceived ChatGPT-based learning more favorably.
finding.measure: Programming learning outcomes, coding performance, debugging performance, and project/task completion
finding.study_size: varied across studies; review reports studies with n=6 to n=1,211

finding.finding_summary: The review found that LLMs may influence assessment practices, academic integrity policies, and course design at the institutional level, but the evidence is largely conceptual or practice-oriented rather than outcome-based. Studies discussed cheating detection, new assessment formats, guidelines for acceptable use, and the need to rethink foundational programming courses in light of AI tools, but the review did not report direct institutional effect sizes.
finding.measure: Assessment practices, academic integrity strategies, and course/institutional policy implications

paper_profiles.title: Non-invasive Techniques for Flow Rate Measurement in Water Pipes: Protocol for a Systematic Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a protocol for a systematic literature review on non-invasive techniques for measuring water flow rate in pipes. The authors frame the problem around the need for accurate, low-cost, and non-invasive monitoring methods to support water resource management, leak detection, and residential consumption tracking without altering existing infrastructure.

The paper does not report results from an empirical evaluation of an intervention. Instead, it details a Kitchenham-based review protocol: research questions, search strategy, study selection criteria, quality assessment, data extraction forms, and synthesis methods. The planned review will compare sensor types (e.g., ultrasonic, accelerometer-based, optical), application environments, signal processing methods, and machine learning approaches, with attention to accuracy, precision, energy consumption, and implementation context.

The intended population/context is water-flow monitoring in domestic, distribution-network, and industrial settings rather than a human learner population. The authors conclude that the protocol should yield a comprehensive evidence map, identify research gaps, and support future development and deployment of non-invasive water monitoring technologies. Because this is a protocol paper, it provides no empirical findings about effectiveness beyond describing the planned review scope and methods.

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of Peer Assessment on Academic Performance: A Meta-analysis of Control Group Studies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This meta-analysis examines whether peer assessment improves academic performance, addressing the gap left by prior narrative reviews and correlational work. The authors focus on experimental and quasi-experimental control-group studies to estimate the causal effect of peer assessment on subsequent academic outcomes, rather than on perceptions or score agreement with teachers.

The review synthesizes 54 studies (55 articles; k = 141 effect sizes) across primary, secondary, and tertiary education and across multiple subjects. Peer assessment showed a small-to-moderate overall positive effect on academic performance (g = 0.31, 95% CI [0.18, 0.44]), with benefits versus no assessment (g = 0.31) and teacher assessment (g = 0.28), and no significant difference versus self-assessment (g = 0.23, ns). Moderator analyses suggested the effect was broadly robust across online/offline delivery, anonymity, frequency, transfer, and most subject areas, but grading appeared to matter more in tertiary settings than in primary or secondary settings.

finding.finding_summary: Peer assessment improved literacy-related academic performance, especially in writing-focused studies, with effects similar to the overall meta-analytic result. In the writing subgroup, the effect was g = 0.30 (p = .001), and the broader literacy-related pool also showed positive effects across studies.
finding.measure: Academic performance in writing and reading-related tasks (e.g., writing quality, essays, reading outcomes)

finding.finding_summary: Across all academic subjects combined, peer assessment had a significant positive effect on academic performance compared with control conditions. The overall meta-analytic effect was g = 0.31, 95% CI [0.18, 0.44], based on 54 studies (k = 141 effect sizes), with no meaningful moderation by subject area when writing was compared with other subjects.
finding.measure: Standardized academic performance outcomes across subjects (e.g., tests, essays, course grades, practical tasks)

finding.finding_summary: Studies in statistics showed positive effects of peer assessment on mathematical/numeracy-related outcomes, contributing to the overall beneficial effect of the intervention. The paper reports a positive subgroup effect for statistics studies, though it does not provide a separate pooled effect size specific to numeracy beyond the overall analysis.
finding.measure: Statistics performance / quantitative academic performance

finding.finding_summary: Science studies also showed positive effects of peer assessment on academic performance, consistent with the overall meta-analytic finding. The paper indicates that peer assessment was effective across science tasks, but it does not report a separate pooled science-specific effect size in the text provided.
finding.measure: Science academic performance and related task outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses motivation, perceptions, and self-efficacy as plausible mechanisms, but these were not the primary outcomes of the meta-analysis and were not directly synthesized as empirical endpoints. As a result, evidence here is indirect and primarily theoretical rather than outcome-based.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The intervention likely supports durable skills such as critical thinking and metacognitive comparison of work, but the paper’s direct quantitative outcome is academic performance rather than a standalone durable-skill measure. The authors frame peer assessment as helping students identify gaps and errors in their own knowledge, yet they do not report a pooled durable-skills effect size.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: A Systematic Review of Peer Assessment Design Elements
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a basic but important question in peer assessment research: how diverse are peer assessment designs in the literature, and which design elements most commonly co-occur? The authors argue that prior typologies of peer assessment have become difficult to use consistently, and they aim to provide a clearer empirical picture of how studies actually implement peer assessment across contexts, purposes, objects, outcomes, and moderators/mediators.

To answer this, they conducted a systematic review of 449 studies published in peer-reviewed English-language journals, spanning primary through postgraduate education. They coded each study on a large set of context and instructional-design features, plus outcome variables and moderators/mediators, and then used latent class analysis to identify recurring design patterns. The review shows that peer assessment is used most often in arts and humanities and in higher education, with formative purposes more common than summative ones. Written assignments were the most common object of assessment, and beliefs/perceptions were the most frequently studied outcomes.

The latent class analysis identified five prototypical peer assessment design patterns, largely distinguished by instructional design features such as formative vs. summative purpose, group constellation, revision, contact mode, privacy, matching, and scope of involvement. The paper concludes that peer assessment designs in research are less diverse than they could be, and that a relatively small set of design elements explains much of the observed variation. It does not test the effects of peer assessment on learner outcomes; rather, it maps the design space and highlights which features are most characteristic of different peer assessment configurations.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic review does not evaluate student achievement or implementation effects; instead, it synthesizes how peer assessment is designed and reported across 449 studies. The main finding for the field is descriptive: peer assessment research clusters into five recurring design patterns, with instructional-design elements such as purpose, revision, privacy, matching, contact, and scope of involvement discriminating most strongly between patterns (e.g., revision R2=.476; purpose R2=.370; contact R2=.315).
finding.measure: Latent class analysis of peer assessment design elements across studies; model fit and effect sizes (R2) for design elements

paper_profiles.title: The Effect of Formative Assessment Practices on Student Learning: A Meta-Analysis Study
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Assessment Tools in Education
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Undergraduate/Pre-service Teacher, Adult
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This meta-analysis examines whether formative assessment practices improve student learning in Turkey, and whether effects differ by feedback source, education level, and publication type. The review included 32 experimental or quasi-experimental studies yielding 47 effect sizes drawn from journal articles, master’s theses, and doctoral dissertations, across primary, secondary, and tertiary settings. The studies covered multiple subject areas (e.g., language, science, mathematics, foreign language, social sciences) but were synthesized around student learning outcomes rather than subject-specific achievement domains.

The paper reports a positive overall effect of formative assessment on learning in the random-effects model (g=.72, SE=.07, 95% CI [.59, .85], p<.05), indicating a moderate-to-large benefit. Subgroup analyses found that the type of formative feedback mattered: student-initiated feedback showed the largest effect (d=1.16), followed by mixed feedback (d=.83), adult/teacher-initiated feedback (d=.69), and computer-initiated feedback (d=.42). Education level and publication type did not significantly moderate the effects, suggesting that formative assessment was beneficial across primary, secondary, and tertiary levels and across published and unpublished studies.

finding.finding_summary: Across 32 studies and 47 effect sizes, formative assessment interventions produced a significant positive effect on student learning. The random-effects mean effect size was g=.72 (SE=.07, 95% CI [.59, .85], p<.05), indicating a moderate-to-large benefit on academic achievement/learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Student learning / academic achievement outcomes
finding.study_size: 32 studies; 47 effect sizes; total N=3253 participants

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that student-initiated formative feedback had the largest effect (d=1.16) and mixed feedback also showed a large effect (d=.83), implying that learner involvement in assessment processes was strongly associated with improved outcomes.
