Although the primary measured outcome was academic learning, the authors explicitly discuss learner engagement and active participation as important mechanisms in formative assessment.
finding.measure: Formative assessment intervention type involving student-initiated feedback, mixed feedback
finding.study_size: 20 studies (adult initiated), 10 studies (student initiated), 12 studies (computer initiated), 5 studies (mixed)

paper_profiles.title: In-training assessment using direct observation of single-patient encounters: a literature review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This literature review addresses the use of workplace-based assessment instruments for directly observed single-patient clinical encounters, including the mini-CEX and related tools. The authors were interested in how these instruments differ in content and format, and what is known about their feasibility, reliability, validity, and educational effects. The review is situated in undergraduate and postgraduate medical education, especially residency and clerkship settings, where authentic assessment of clinical competence is challenging.

The authors systematically searched PubMed and identified 39 articles covering 18 assessment instruments. They found that the instruments are generally intended for formative use, are usually feasible to implement, and can reach acceptable reliability with about 10 encounters. Validity evidence is strongest for the mini-CEX and clinical encounter card, but the literature on educational effects is thin and mostly limited to learner or assessor satisfaction rather than measured improvement in skills or patient care.

Overall, the review concludes that these assessment tools are promising but under-studied, with especially sparse evidence on learner training, assessor training, and downstream educational impact. The paper emphasizes that the instruments should be evaluated and implemented within the broader curriculum and assessment program rather than in isolation.

paper_profiles.title: A new criterion for assessing discriminant validity in variance-based structural equation modeling
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This methodological paper addresses a measurement-model problem in variance-based structural equation modeling (SEM): how to assess discriminant validity reliably. The authors argue that two widely used approaches in PLS and related SEM methods—the Fornell-Larcker criterion and cross-loadings—often fail to detect a lack of discriminant validity, especially in common applied-research settings.

To evaluate this claim, the paper proposes the heterotrait-monotrait ratio of correlations (HTMT) as an alternative criterion and statistical test. The authors support the proposal with Monte Carlo simulation studies that vary loading patterns, sample sizes, and inter-construct correlations, plus an empirical illustration using the American Customer Satisfaction Index (ACSI) model. Across simulations, HTMT-based procedures show much higher sensitivity than the traditional criteria, while the Fornell-Larcker criterion and cross-loadings perform poorly.

The paper’s main conclusion is that HTMT is a better standard for discriminant validity assessment in variance-based SEM, with the choice among HTMT.85, HTMT.90, and HTMTinference depending on how conservative the analyst wants to be. It also provides practical guidance for diagnosing and addressing discriminant validity problems by refining, splitting, or merging constructs when theory supports such changes.

finding.finding_summary: This is a methodological SEM paper about discriminant validity assessment, not an educational intervention or learner outcome study. It reports simulation evidence that the traditional Fornell-Larcker criterion detects discriminant validity problems poorly (e.g., 14.59% sensitivity in one initial simulation; 20.82% average sensitivity across extended conditions), while HTMT performs much better (99.90% average sensitivity for HTMT.85; 99.45% for HTMT.90; 97.01% for HTMTinference).
finding.measure: Sensitivity and specificity of discriminant validity criteria in simulation studies; empirical HTMT values in an ACSI example
finding.study_size: 816000 simulation runs; N=10,417 in empirical illustration

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and postsecondary educators/students (broader education contexts; examples span high school and undergraduate)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative/practical review of how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback. The authors organize the discussion around a classic formative assessment framework: clarifying where learners are going, understanding where learners are, and helping learners move forward. They argue that current LLM applications in education are often evaluated with technical metrics that do not adequately capture formative assessment quality, such as whether feedback is task-, process-, or self-regulation-oriented.

The paper does not test a single intervention experimentally. Instead, it synthesizes prior work and provides concrete prompting examples and classroom-use cases, including rewriting formal learning objectives into student-friendly language, co-constructing success criteria with students, generating sample work of varying quality, and producing feedback or questions for short-cycle formative checks. The examples span multiple contexts, including high school biology and undergraduate fMRI instruction, but the central audience is educators who may use accessible LLMs in classroom assessment practices.

The main conclusion is that LLMs can augment formative assessment by reducing teacher workload and making feedback and goal-setting more scalable, but they should not replace pedagogical expertise. The authors emphasize that educators must check accuracy, adapt outputs to local context, and design AI-aware assessments that foster deep learning, critical thinking, and self-regulation rather than overreliance on AI-generated answers. They also call for better evaluation metrics and more collaboration between educators and computer scientists.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce educator workload by automating or speeding up formative-assessment tasks such as rewriting objectives, generating questions, creating exemplar work, and drafting feedback. No original empirical study is reported, so no effect size or sample size is available; the paper is a narrative review with illustrative examples rather than a measured intervention.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review claims LLM-supported formative assessment can foster critical thinking, metacognition, and self-regulation when used to prompt reflection, co-construct goals, and critique AI-generated exemplars. These claims are conceptual and supported by cited prior literature and examples, but the paper reports no direct empirical outcome data (no n, effect size, or confidence interval).
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on using LLMs to support subject-specific academic tasks such as generating student-friendly learning objectives, sample work, and feedback in biology and functional MRI coursework. It presents examples showing how LLM outputs can be adapted for different disciplines, but it does not evaluate student achievement outcomes empirically.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Electrotactile feedback applications for hand and arm interactions: A systematic review, meta-analysis, and future directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews and quantitatively synthesizes research on electrotactile feedback for hand and arm interactions. The central problem is that conventional haptic devices can be costly, bulky, and hard to wear or port, which limits adoption in human-computer interaction, teleoperation, prosthetics, and related settings. Electrotactile interfaces are presented as a potentially more portable and lower-cost alternative because they use electrical stimulation rather than mechanical actuation.

The authors systematically reviewed studies from 2010–2021 and conducted a meta-analytic-style aggregation of findings across application areas including portable devices, augmented haptics, guidance and notification, biomedical assistive devices, prostheses, and teleoperation/VR. The review emphasizes how stimulation location, electrode design, pulse parameters, and calibration affect perceptual outcomes such as touch, texture, motion, force, and spatial discrimination. Across studies, electrotactile feedback was generally successful in rendering tactile sensations and improving task performance, but many studies used small samples and varied methods, limiting generalizability.

The main conclusions are that electrotactile feedback is promising for improving portability/wearability while still supporting useful haptic perception and performance benefits. However, the paper highlights recurring limitations: small sample sizes, calibration challenges, electrode durability, and gaps in understanding embodiment and long-term use. It also notes that many effects were demonstrated in healthy adults rather than target end users such as amputees, so more rigorous and population-relevant studies are needed before broad deployment.

paper_profiles.title: Cloud Failure Prediction with Hierarchical Temporal Memory: An Empirical Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether Hierarchical Temporal Memory (HTM), an unsupervised streaming anomaly-detection approach, can support early failure prediction in cloud systems. The motivation is operational: cloud environments change over time, failures are frequent, and supervised models typically require labeled failure data and repeated retraining, which is costly and often impractical.

The authors implement HTM as the anomaly detector in a KPI-driven failure prediction pipeline and test it on a Clearwater telecom cloud system. They analyze 72 parameter configurations across 12 seeded fault scenarios (CPU hogs, memory leaks, packet loss, and excessive workload under different activation patterns) plus 12 normal runs, using 150 KPIs collected from six virtual machines. Two global prediction strategies are compared: vote-based and single-resource aggregation of local failure predictions.

Results show that HTM can predict failures with useful effectiveness, especially under the vote-based strategy. The best configuration achieved F-measure = 0.76 (precision = 0.65, recall = 0.92), and failures were predicted typically tens of minutes in advance (median 54 minutes for vote-based and 53 minutes for single-resource). Performance varied by fault type, with CPU hogs easier to predict and excessive workload hardest. The paper concludes that HTM is a practical unsupervised alternative for cloud failure prediction, though effectiveness is slightly lower than approaches trained with failure samples.

finding.finding_summary: HTM supported practical cloud failure prediction with useful accuracy and lead time. The best vote-based configuration achieved F-measure = 0.76 with precision = 0.65 and recall = 0.92, and predicted failures a median of 54 minutes before occurrence; the best single-resource configurations reached F-measure = 0.73 and median prediction time of 53 minutes.
finding.measure: Failure prediction performance (precision, recall, F-measure) and prediction timeliness (minutes before failure) in a KPI-driven cloud monitoring pipeline
finding.study_size: n=24 evaluated executions (12 fault scenarios + 12 normal executions), across 72 HTM configurations

paper_profiles.title: Assessment of Personalized Learning in Immersive and Intelligent Virtual Classroom on Student Engagement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether immersive, intelligent virtual classrooms can be used to assess personalized learning and student engagement using eye-tracking. The authors motivate the work by arguing that conventional engagement measures in virtual learning are too coarse, and that gaze-based indicators could provide a more objective, fine-grained view of student attention and interaction.

The study combines a literature review, a VR application prototype, and a small case study with eight participants. The application, built in Unity for a PICO VR 4 PRO headset, captures 2D and 3D gaze behavior, saccadic reaction time, gaze offsets, and related metrics while students complete virtual classroom tasks. Participants also completed an 11-item Likert questionnaire covering cognitive, behavioral, and affective engagement.

The authors report that personalized learning in the VR environment was associated with generally high self-reported engagement, and that eye-tracking metrics such as gaze patterns, fixation duration, and especially saccadic reaction time may be useful for assessing engagement. However, the paper is exploratory, based on a very small case study, and does not provide inferential statistics or a causal estimate of personalized learning effects. The main contribution is methodological: demonstrating a prototype for engagement assessment in immersive virtual classrooms and suggesting eye-movement measures as promising indicators for future research.

finding.finding_summary: In a case study with eight participants (n=8), the authors report that personalized learning in the VR classroom was associated with higher self-reported engagement across cognitive, behavioral, and affective dimensions. Mean engagement scores in Table 1 were generally high, and the paper highlights Participant 2 as showing consistently high scores (5.00 across all three dimensions), though no inferential statistics or effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: 11-item Likert questionnaire assessing cognitive, behavioral, and affective engagement; eye-tracking indicators of engagement

paper_profiles.title: Machine Learning Applications to Diffuse Reflectance Spectroscopy in Optical Diagnosis; A Systematic Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews machine learning applications to diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (DRS) for optical diagnosis in medical settings. The authors ask how DRS data have been processed with ML, which clinical applications have been studied, what methodological gaps remain, and what should be prioritized in future research.

The review follows PRISMA guidelines and synthesizes 77 studies retrieved from multiple databases plus additional studies from SPIE and domain knowledge. It focuses on how ML models such as SVM, LDA, neural networks, KNN, CART, and related methods are used to classify or regress on DRS signals for disease diagnosis, especially cancer-related applications. The studies are predominantly on human tissue, often ex-vivo, and cover colorectal, breast, skin, oral, brain, cervical, liver, and lung cancers.

The main conclusion is that DRS combined with ML shows strong potential for tissue differentiation and clinical diagnosis, often with high classification accuracies. However, the review emphasizes substantial limitations in the evidence base, including small samples, limited in-vivo validation, heterogeneity in preprocessing and instrumentation, and especially weak patient-wise data stratification, which raises concerns about leakage and generalizability. The authors recommend more rigorous stratification, diverse datasets, improved reporting, and explainable models before broader clinical deployment.

paper_profiles.title: Learning Outcomes, Assessment, and Evaluation in Educational Recommender Systems: A Systematic Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how educational recommender systems (ERS) measure and optimize learning, with a particular emphasis on whether they use learning outcomes and outcome-based assessment rather than proxy metrics such as user ratings or relevance. The authors frame the issue as a mismatch between standard recommender-system evaluation and educational goals: in education, the recommended item is not the end goal, so the system should be judged by whether it helps learners achieve intended learning outcomes.

The study is a systematic literature review of 28 ERS papers selected from 1,395 candidate publications drawn from IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and SpringerLink. Across the reviewed papers, the most common contexts were formal education, especially higher education, with learners as the main end users; the dominant recommendation methods were knowledge-based, collaborative filtering, and machine-learning approaches. The review also catalogues target metrics, evaluation methods, and whether studies included or assessed learning outcomes.

The main conclusion is that ERS research still relies heavily on user-rating/relevance proxies, while only 12 of 28 papers optimized learning-centered metrics and only about one-third used outcome-based assessment. When learning outcomes were assessed, it was usually in formal courses or training settings using formal assessment, whereas informal-learning settings lacked robust outcome-based evaluation. The paper argues for broader evaluation criteria that prioritize learning outcomes while still accounting for user-centric and system-level metrics, and it highlights the need for more efficient and scalable ways to implement outcome-based assessment.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds a substantial gap in how educational recommender systems are evaluated: only 28 papers met inclusion criteria, and only about one-third used outcome-based assessment to measure pedagogical effect. The authors conclude that ERS research is still dominated by proxy metrics such as user ratings and relevance, and that outcome-based evaluation is used mostly in formal university courses rather than at scale or in informal learning settings.
finding.measure: Systematic review of target metrics, evaluation methods, and outcome-based assessment practices across 28 ERS papers

paper_profiles.title: Toward cross-subject and cross-session generalization in EEG-based emotion recognition: Systematic review, taxonomy, and methods
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how machine-learning methods can improve generalization in EEG-based emotion recognition across subjects and recording sessions. The central technical problem is dataset shift caused by the non-stationarity of EEG signals, which makes emotion classifiers trained on one subject or session perform poorly on others.

The authors conducted a systematic review of EEG emotion-recognition studies published from January 2010 to March 2022, retrieving 418 papers and retaining 75 eligible studies after PRISMA-based screening. They organize the literature into classical machine learning, transductive learning, and transfer learning, with transfer learning further divided into source selection, shallow domain adaptation, and deep domain adaptation/generation approaches.

The review concludes that transfer learning methods generally outperform classical approaches for cross-subject and cross-session EEG emotion recognition. It also highlights that performance is influenced by the choice of emotion model and by psychological screening of participants, suggesting that experimental design and subject characteristics can materially affect classifier generalization. Because this is a review rather than a primary intervention study, it does not report a single pooled effect size but instead synthesizes patterns across the reviewed studies.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed EEG emotion-recognition literature, transfer learning methods generally improved cross-subject and cross-session emotion classification relative to classical machine-learning baselines. The review synthesizes 75 eligible studies and concludes that these methods better handle EEG non-stationarity and dataset shift, which are central barriers to robust emotion recognition.
finding.measure: Emotion classification accuracy and related generalization performance across subjects/sessions

paper_profiles.title: Meta-analysis of Life Cycle Assessments for Li-Ion Batteries Production Emissions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the manufacturing-related greenhouse gas emissions of lithium-ion batteries, focusing on how emissions vary across published life cycle assessment (LCA) studies and how they are affected by electricity mix and production scale. The authors conduct a meta-analysis of two decades of battery LCA studies, standardizing results by functional unit, chemistry, system boundaries, and regional electricity mix, and then compare those findings with a cradle-to-gate LCA of an NMC 811 battery with a silicon-coated graphite anode.

The approach combines literature synthesis with a case-study LCA for China, South Korea, and Sweden, using GREET inventory data, Ecoinvent emission factors, Activity Browser, and ReCiPe midpoint methods. The paper also develops regression models linking annual battery production and the carbon intensity of China’s electricity mix to specific emissions, finding that a multivariate linear model explains the averaged data with moderate accuracy (R2 = 0.6034).

The main conclusion is that battery manufacturing emissions are strongly shaped by upstream energy-intensive processes, especially cell and cathode production, and that relocating final assembly alone yields only limited reductions if the supply chain remains carbon-intensive. The results suggest that decarbonizing the full supply chain and accounting for learning effects from scale-up are important for realistic emissions forecasting. The statistical evidence for learning effects is suggestive but based on a small number of observations, so the authors caution that the regression findings should be interpreted carefully.

paper_profiles.title: ANALYSIS OF OPINIONATED TEXT FOR OPINION MINING
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how different kinds of linguistic meta-information can improve sentiment analysis of opinionated text. The authors ask whether features beyond surface words—such as inter-sentence coherence, emotion categories, WordNet syntactic domains, word senses, sentiment lexicons, and meta-characters like punctuation and rating patterns—can help classify review polarity more accurately.

The study uses a dataset of 294 consumer reviews sampled from books, DVDs, music, electronics, and videogames. The work is not an intervention study in education; rather, it is a technical analysis of text classification features for opinion mining. The authors apply word sense disambiguation, WordNet-based similarity, and lexicon cross-checking to explore how these features relate to positive, negative, and neutral sentiment at the sentence and document level.

Their main conclusion is that meta-information and linguistic features beyond word tokens can materially improve sentiment classification performance. They report that combining emotion distributions yielded 60% accuracy at the sentence level and 75% at the document level, and they argue that inter-sentence polarity, syntactic domains, word senses, lexicons, and meta-characters all provide useful signals for sentiment prediction.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring critical components of an integrated STEM curriculum: an application of the innovation implementation framework
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a common problem in K-12 STEM reform research: although curriculum innovations are often evaluated for outcomes, the field has comparatively few detailed studies of how those innovations are actually implemented in classrooms. The authors argue that fidelity of implementation is especially important for understanding why a curriculum succeeds or fails, but that existing FOI work often lacks clear frameworks and systematic methods.

To address this, the paper applies the innovation implementation framework to a newly developed integrated STEM curriculum, STEM-ID, used in sixth-, seventh-, and eighth-grade engineering classes. The curriculum is organized around contextualized, problem-based design challenges and emphasizes the engineering design process, math/science integration, advanced manufacturing technology, and collaborative group work. The study used classroom observations, teacher interviews, and student interviews across a 2-year implementation period in four middle schools in an urban fringe district serving a predominantly low-income student population.

The paper’s main contribution is methodological rather than outcome-oriented. It shows how identifying critical components helped the team specify what counted as intended implementation, design observation and interview protocols, and detect different enactment patterns across classrooms and grade levels. The authors conclude that the innovation implementation framework is useful for studying curriculum use during design and development, especially when researchers want to understand not just whether a curriculum was delivered, but how key components were enacted and adapted in practice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that using the innovation implementation framework improved the research team’s ability to specify critical curriculum components, align observation and interview protocols, and document implementation patterns in a 2-year study. The approach also helped researchers target data collection more efficiently to sessions where critical components were likely to occur, although no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Research process efficiency and utility of implementation protocols for curriculum monitoring

finding.finding_summary: The study substantively examines collaboration as one of the STEM-ID critical components and documents variation in how students engaged in group work across classrooms and activities. Teachers did not always identify collaboration as central, and observations/interviews showed both positive and negative collaboration experiences, indicating mixed enactment rather than a single uniform pattern.
finding.measure: Classroom observations and teacher/student interview evidence on collaborative group work

finding.finding_summary: The curriculum and the implementation analysis heavily focus on the engineering design process, including identifying problems, understanding requirements, ideating, evaluating, prototyping/testing, and communicating solutions. The paper reports that these components were observable in classrooms, but implementation varied by grade level and by teacher, with some activities enacted more fully than others.
finding.measure: Engagement in the engineering design process during STEM design challenges
finding.study_size: n=92 students; 6 teachers; classroom observations across 2 implementation years

finding.finding_summary: Math integration is one of the explicit critical components of STEM-ID, and the study documents that students applied math concepts such as measurement, data analysis, probability, modeling, and profit calculations during design challenges. The paper is descriptive and does not test a causal effect, but it indicates that math/science integration was enacted in ways aligned with the curriculum’s goals.
finding.measure: Observed and reported math integration in STEM-ID challenges

paper_profiles.title: How Educators Perceive the Process and Implementation of a Multi-Tiered System of Supports (MTSS): A Case Study
paper_profiles.venue: Northeastern University Doctor of Education dissertation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines how educators in one Massachusetts elementary school perceive the process, structures, fidelity of implementation, and impact of an RTI/MTSS model. The study is motivated by the concern that simply adopting MTSS is not enough; schools also need to know whether the framework is being implemented as intended and what supports or barriers shape implementation fidelity.

Using a qualitative case study design, the researcher collected student assessment data, individual interviews, self-report surveys, a focus group, and document review from three grade-two teachers, a special educator, a psychologist, a literacy coach, and the building administrator. The study focuses on how staff understand key MTSS features such as multiple tiers of support, assessment, data-informed decision making, collaboration, shared accountability, and procedural fidelity.

Findings suggest that educators viewed RTI/MTSS positively as a general education initiative that can personalize instruction and reduce special education referrals. The main facilitators of implementation were assessment, data use, collaboration, and shared responsibility, while barriers included limited resources, insufficient planning time, unscheduled extra tiers of instruction, and inadequate training. The dissertation concludes that districts need systems for measuring fidelity and supporting staff if they want MTSS to improve student outcomes and sustain implementation.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that educators perceived RTI/MTSS as a general education initiative that supports personalization of instruction and may reduce special education referrals, but implementation was constrained by limited resources, inadequate planning time, unscheduled additional tiers, and insufficient training. The evidence is based on a qualitative case study of one Massachusetts elementary school involving three grade-two teachers, a special educator, a psychologist, a literacy coach, and the building administrator (n=7).
finding.measure: Educator interviews, self-report surveys, focus group discussion, document review, and student assessment data related to MTSS implementation fidelity and perceived impact

finding.finding_summary: Educators identified lack of resources, inadequate planning time, unscheduled additional tiers of instruction, and insufficient training as barriers to implementing RTI/MTSS with fidelity. These findings indicate implementation strain and reduced operational efficiency in the school’s MTSS process, although no quantitative workload metric or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived implementation barriers and supports for RTI/MTSS delivery

paper_profiles.title: Guided inquiry in school science: a mini review of orchestration, assessment, and AI
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Undergraduate
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mini review asks how guided inquiry in school science should be orchestrated so that it produces durable understanding, participation, and inclusion, rather than treating inquiry as either inherently superior or inferior to direct instruction. The paper synthesizes 26 peer-reviewed studies published from 2017 to 2025, spanning classroom interventions, systematic video studies, large-scale secondary analyses, discipline-specific and teacher-education reviews, technology-mediated inquiry, flipped classrooms, and AI-supported inquiry.

The review codes studies by inquiry phases, forms and timing of guidance, assessment practices, and outcomes. Across the corpus, the paper argues that guided, discourse-rich inquiry is more dependable than minimally guided or high-autonomy inquiry for conceptual understanding, higher-order thinking, and motivation, while simple counts of inquiry activities are a weak proxy for quality. It highlights two recurring bottlenecks: weak enactment of preparation and consolidation phases, and limited assessment literacy for scientific practices such as modeling, data analysis, and argumentation.

The review also examines technology and AI as formative infrastructure rather than as answer engines. It concludes that flipped structures and AI copilots can be productive when they scaffold prediction-evidence-explanation sequences, preserve learner agency, and generate actionable process evidence for teachers. The overall recommendation is to prioritize phase-specific orchestration, practice-focused assessment, and equitable supports that widen participation in core scientific practices.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, guided inquiry that foregrounded evidence use, modeling, and argumentation was associated with stronger conceptual understanding and higher-order scientific thinking than minimally guided or purely high-autonomy inquiry. The review does not report a single pooled effect size because it is a mini review, but it consistently concludes that phase-specific guidance and discourse-rich consolidation improve scientific reasoning outcomes.
finding.measure: Conceptual understanding, evidence use, modeling, argumentation, scientific literacy, and higher-order thinking outcomes across multiple studies

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that guided inquiry was linked to stronger motivation, enjoyment, and engagement, especially when tasks were well scaffolded and teacher support was visible. It also notes that perceived teacher support predicted inquiry engagement via hardiness in technology-embedded settings, and that inquiry designs could improve intrinsic motivation in secondary science.
finding.measure: Motivation, enjoyment, engagement, hardiness, and intended STEM choice across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper consistently emphasizes gains in higher-order thinking, reasoning, planning, and creative idea generation when inquiry was structured to require prediction, evidence, and explanation. It also reports that unstructured autonomy was less reliable, indicating that durable skills were strengthened more by guided orchestration than by raw inquiry frequency.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking, reasoning, planning, creative ideation, and science process skills

finding.finding_summary: The review includes evidence that guided inquiry improved scientific literacy and science process skills in biology and other science contexts. It also notes that inquiry-based laboratory redevelopment increased relevance and engagement, but these findings are discussed as part of science learning rather than literacy in reading/writing or language.
finding.measure: Scientific literacy and science process skills

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests that technology, flipped structures, and AI can improve the efficiency and usefulness of inquiry lessons when they organize data capture, structure reflection, and free class time for investigation and sense-making. However, the paper frames these as conditional supports rather than measured productivity gains, and it does not report pooled quantitative effects on workload or time use.
finding.measure: Class time allocation, process scaffolding, and the practical organization of inquiry and consolidation routines

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that system-level implementation should shift from raw inquiry frequency to phase-sensitive quality indicators, assessment literacy, and teacher capacity building. It also notes that beliefs, resources, and implementation support shape uptake and fidelity, but these are synthesized recommendations rather than direct institutional outcome estimates.
finding.measure: Implementation fidelity, assessment systems, and teacher capacity for inquiry orchestration

paper_profiles.title: Implementation Fidelity of Universal Design for Learning and Effects on Student Achievement Engagement and Belonging
paper_profiles.population: K–12 and postsecondary (community college and teacher education programs)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study investigates how faithfully Universal Design for Learning (UDL) was implemented across a large set of educational institutions and whether stronger implementation was associated with better student outcomes. The authors focus on a multi-level implementation problem: not just whether UDL was adopted, but how structural supports, instructional processes, and perceived outcomes varied across settings and over time.

Using a convergent mixed-methods longitudinal design, the study followed 2,473 students and 342 teachers across 87 institutions over 24 months. Quantitatively, the authors measured implementation fidelity through classroom observations, educator self-reports, artifact review, and student experience surveys, while also tracking student achievement, engagement, and social belonging. Qualitatively, interviews, focus groups, observations, and document analysis were used to explain implementation patterns and identify facilitators such as administrative support, professional development, technology infrastructure, collaborative pedagogy, and flexible data use.

The main conclusion is that higher-fidelity UDL implementation was associated with better student outcomes, especially in institutions that fully enacted all three UDL principles: engagement, representation, and action/expression. The paper reports substantial gains in overall learner performance and even larger gains for disengaged learners, alongside positive relationships with engagement and belonging. The authors argue that durable UDL impact depends on coordinated system-level support rather than isolated classroom adoption, and that implementation fidelity is a critical mediator between UDL principles and student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Institutions that fully implemented all three UDL principles showed a 37.4% increase in overall learner performance and a 42.8% increase in performance for disengaged learners. The study reports a significant association between UDL implementation fidelity and student achievement outcomes across 2,473 learners in 87 institutions over 24 months, with p < 0.001.
finding.measure: Standardized assessments, course-specific performance indicators, and authentic assessment portfolios
finding.effect_size: 37.4% increase overall; 42.8% increase for disengaged learners

finding.finding_summary: UDL implementation fidelity was positively associated with student engagement and social belonging. The paper states that the relationship was significant (p < 0.001) and that effects were more pronounced for engaged learners than for disengaged learners, though exact coefficients are not reported.
finding.measure: Student Engagement Scale, behavioral observation protocols, learning analytics, and modified Psychological Sense of School Membership scale

finding.finding_summary: Higher UDL fidelity was associated with stronger institutional conditions for inclusion, including administrative support, professional development, technology availability, collaborative pedagogy, and data use. The study concludes that coordinated multi-level support is a key mechanism for sustained UDL implementation across 87 institutions.
finding.measure: Organizational surveys, implementation fidelity framework scores, interviews, policy/document analysis

paper_profiles.title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable / theory paper with classroom K-12 examples
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a theoretical framework for formative assessment, aiming to clarify what counts as formative practice and how such practices relate to broader theories of learning and pedagogy. Black and Wiliam argue that formative assessment should be understood as the elicitation, interpretation, and use of evidence about student achievement to make better-founded decisions about next steps in instruction.

The paper synthesizes prior work on formative assessment, self-regulated learning, cognitive acceleration, dynamic assessment, and classroom discourse. It proposes five key strategies of formative assessment: clarifying learning intentions and success criteria, engineering discussions/tasks that elicit evidence, providing feedback that moves learners forward, activating peers as instructional resources, and activating learners as owners of their own learning.

Rather than reporting a new empirical study, the article is a conceptual analysis grounded in existing research and illustrative classroom examples across K-12 contexts, including mathematics and science. Its main conclusion is that formative assessment is most effective when teachers interpret student responses contingently, align feedback with learning goals, and use classroom interactions to regulate learning processes. The paper also emphasizes that superficial adoption of techniques without an underlying theory risks weakening implementation fidelity and impact.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment supports metacognition, self-assessment, and learner autonomy by activating students as owners of their own learning. This is a theoretical synthesis rather than a direct empirical test, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-assessment, learner autonomy, and ownership of learning as discussed in the literature

finding.finding_summary: The authors contend that formative assessment can support motivation, persistence, and well-being by helping learners stay on a growth track rather than shifting to avoidance or defensive responses. These claims are based on conceptual integration with self-regulated learning literature, not original outcome data.
finding.measure: Motivation, persistence, well-being, and emotional regulation as described in self-regulated learning theory

finding.finding_summary: The paper uses mathematics classroom examples extensively, including discussions of equivalent fractions, square roots, and structured problem solving, to show how formative assessment strategies can improve mathematical reasoning and lesson design. No direct quantitative evidence is presented in this paper.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning and reasoning in classroom examples

finding.finding_summary: The authors discuss science examples, such as plant growth and photosynthesis, and link formative assessment to improved scientific explanation and reasoning through contingent feedback. The paper provides illustrative argumentation rather than direct empirical results.
finding.measure: Scientific explanation and reasoning in classroom examples

paper_profiles.title: Turkish Teachers’ Practices of Assessment for Learning in the English as a Foreign Language Classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Language Teaching and Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Turkish EFL teachers understand and enact assessment for learning (AFL) in their classrooms, with particular attention to two AFL dimensions: monitoring learners’ progress and scaffolding learning. The study responds to a perceived gap in the Turkish EFL literature, where assessment has traditionally emphasized summative, exam-oriented practices rather than formative approaches that support ongoing learning.

Using an online self-report questionnaire (TAFL-Q) administered to 120 EFL teachers in public and private institutions, the author measured teachers’ preferred assessment methods and their reported AFL practices. The paper found that teachers relied more heavily on conventional tests (e.g., fill-in-the-blank, multiple choice, true-false) than on formative techniques such as self-, peer-, rubric-, portfolio-, or observation-based assessment. At the same time, teachers reported high levels of perceived monitoring and scaffolding overall, with mean scores above 4 on a 5-point scale, though items involving student agency and decision-making were comparatively weaker.

Inferential analyses suggested that years of teaching experience were associated with differences in monitoring practices, and that private-school teachers reported higher monitoring than public-school teachers. Gender did not show a main effect, but gender-by-sector interactions were significant for monitoring. The study concludes that Turkish EFL teachers generally value AFL, especially scaffolding, but still tend to practice conventional assessment more than formative assessment, and it recommends greater support, training, and observational follow-up to better understand and strengthen AFL enactment.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported substantial use of conventional assessment methods rather than formative practices, suggesting limited enactment of AFL even though they endorsed monitoring and scaffolding conceptually. The paper does not estimate workload or efficiency effects directly, but it indicates a practice gap between intended and enacted formative assessment, with self-reported monitoring and scaffolding means of 4.20 and 4.33 on a 5-point scale.
finding.measure: Self-reported assessment method preferences and AFL practice ratings (TAFL-Q)

finding.finding_summary: The study found that Turkish EFL assessment practices are shaped by institutional context, especially years of teaching experience and school sector. Years of teaching experience had a significant main effect on assessment practices (Wilks' Lambda=.648, F(6,66)=2.664, p=.022), and private-school teachers reported significantly higher monitoring than public-school teachers (t(118)=2.253, p=.026).
finding.measure: Questionnaire-based comparison of monitoring/scaffolding practices across teacher and school variables
finding.effect_size: partial η2=0.195; partial η2=0.270; partial η2=0.27; partial η2=0.26

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported high levels of practices associated with learner reflection, guidance, and support, which are intended to strengthen student monitoring of learning. In particular, perceived monitoring averaged above 4 on all but a few items, with 82.86% agreement overall; the highest-rated item was giving students guidance and assistance (M=4.58, SD=.71), and scaffolding was similarly high at 86.94% agreement overall.
finding.measure: Self-reported perceived monitoring and scaffolding practices on TAFL-Q
finding.std_deviation: SD=.71 (item 11); overall subscale SDs not reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies monitoring and scaffolding as formative assessment practices that support learner reflection, self-regulation, and participation. Teachers reported high agreement with items such as encouraging reflection on learning (M=4.34), discussing progress (M=4.29), and giving students opportunities to ask questions (M=4.65), indicating strong perceived support for metacognitive and collaborative classroom practices.
finding.measure: TAFL-Q perceived monitoring/scaffolding items related to reflection, decision-making, questioning, and collaboration
finding.std_deviation: SDs for key items ranged from .65 to .92, including item 25 SD=.65

finding.finding_summary: Although the study is not an intervention on student fluency, it focuses on teacher practices intended to support English language learning in EFL classrooms, including feedback, discussion of progress, and scaffolding during oral and written classroom work. Teachers reported high frequencies for monitoring and scaffolding behaviors that would support speaking, listening, and classroom interaction, but no direct learner outcome data were collected.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported AFL practices in English as a foreign language classrooms

paper_profiles.title: Reviewing the Challenges of Implementing Formative Assessment in Asia: The Need for a Professional Development Program
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews research on the challenges of implementing formative assessment in Asian classrooms, with a particular emphasis on barriers to effective enactment and the need for teacher professional development. Using multiple electronic databases, the authors identified 21 studies conducted in Asian countries and categorized the reported challenges using Kozma’s micro-, meso-, and macro-level contextual framework.

The review finds that the most common obstacles are at the micro and macro levels, especially inadequate teacher knowledge of formative assessment, teacher beliefs shaped by traditional assessment cultures, student discomfort with self- and peer-assessment, and large class sizes. It also highlights two inherent disadvantages of formative assessment practice—its time-consuming nature and heavy workload for teachers. The paper concludes that improving formative assessment in Asia requires sustained professional development, school support, and assessment activities that fit local cultural and institutional conditions.

finding.finding_summary: Across the 21 studies reviewed, the dominant practical barriers to formative assessment were that it is time-consuming and adds heavy workload for teachers. The review reports that 33.3% of studies (7/21) noted time consumption and 28.5% (6/21) noted heavy workload, indicating these are persistent implementation costs rather than isolated issues.
finding.measure: Reported challenge frequencies across reviewed studies (time-consuming, heavy workload)

finding.finding_summary: The review shows that implementation of formative assessment in Asia is strongly shaped by school and policy context, especially examination-oriented culture, limited school autonomy, and weak institutional support. Macro-level barriers were common; 28.5% of studies (6/21) reported examination-oriented culture as a challenge, and the authors argue that school authorities and national testing pressures often constrain formative assessment enactment.
finding.measure: Reported contextual barriers at school and policy levels across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The review indicates that formative assessment practices such as self-assessment and peer-assessment are difficult to enact in Asian classrooms because students are often unfamiliar with these approaches and reluctant to challenge teacher authority. The authors describe barriers to student self-assessment, peer-assessment, and student engagement, but also note that when guided carefully these practices can support learning.
finding.measure: Reported challenges to self-assessment, peer-assessment, and student engagement in reviewed studies

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing teaching and learning in higher education through formative assessment: Teachers’ Perceptions
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Assessment Tools in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how teachers in Bangladeshi higher education perceive formative assessment and how it is currently used to support teaching and learning. The authors frame the problem as a gap between the widespread theoretical support for formative assessment and the continued dominance of summative, end-of-term examinations in Bangladeshi colleges.

Using a mixed-method design, the researchers surveyed 100 teachers and interviewed 6 teachers from a government college (RJ College) in Bangladesh. The quantitative strand used a 12-item Likert questionnaire, and the qualitative strand used semi-structured interviews analyzed through content analysis. The paper focuses on teachers’ understanding of formative assessment, current classroom practices, attitudes toward it, and barriers to implementation.

Findings suggest generally positive teacher perceptions: respondents associated formative assessment with greater student attentiveness, engagement, in-depth learning, reduced absenteeism, and better tracking of learning progress. However, the study also shows that formative assessment is often used mainly for grading rather than feedback, which limits its formative value. Major obstacles included large classes, teacher workload, inadequate infrastructure, power outages, resource scarcity, and political or administrative pressure that can distort grading practices. The authors conclude that formative assessment could improve higher education in Bangladesh if these implementation barriers are addressed and if feedback-oriented practices are strengthened.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that formative assessment increased students’ engagement, attentiveness, interest in study, and reduced absenteeism. In the survey, the highest-rated items included that class-performance-based formative assessment makes students more attentive (mean=4.25, SD=0.81, n=100) and helps engage students with their study (mean=4.24, SD=0.74, n=100).
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of student engagement, attentiveness, interest, and absenteeism

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that formative assessment supports in-depth knowledge, problem-solving, and confidence, which the authors and participants treat as durable learning capacities. Survey items on allowing students to acquire in-depth knowledge were rated highly (mean=4.15, SD=0.95, n=100), and interviewees explicitly linked formative assessment to problem-solving skill development and coping with the competitive real world.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of students’ problem-solving, confidence, and depth of understanding

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed formative assessment improved students’ learning outcomes in higher education generally, especially by helping them understand course content more deeply and prepare for final examinations with less pressure. Survey results were positive for allowing teachers to assess gradual development of learning outcomes (mean=4.24, SD=0.62, n=100), while interviews described improved standard of education and better final-exam results.
finding.measure: Perceived learning outcomes, course understanding, and exam preparation

finding.finding_summary: The study found that formative assessment is present in the institution but is constrained by structural and governance problems. Teachers reported challenges including large classes, shortage of teachers, resource scarcity, infrastructure problems, insufficient power supply, workload, and political/administrative pressure that can affect grading and create bias; these conditions limit effective implementation despite positive attitudes.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported institutional barriers to implementing formative assessment

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified formative assessment as adding workload and becoming difficult to implement in large classes or under time pressure, suggesting reduced operational efficiency. Interviewees specifically cited heavy workload, shortage of teachers, and limited time for classroom activities as barriers to carrying out formative assessment effectively, although no quantitative productivity metric was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload and feasibility of implementing formative assessment

paper_profiles.title: Effects of computer-based feedback and formative assessment on learning outcomes
paper_profiles.venue: Can Tho University Journal of Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether integrating a student response system (SRS) into computer-based feedback and formative assessment improves learning outcomes in a postsecondary physics course. The research is motivated by the growing use of technology for real-time assessment and by the need for formative assessment practices that support students’ progress toward intended learning outcomes.

The study was conducted during COVID-19 in an online course with first-year electrical and electronics students at Cao Thang Technical College in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Using a pretest-posttest non-randomized control group quasi-experimental design, two classes were assigned to experimental and control groups (total n=148; experimental n=75, control n=73). Both groups studied the same energy topic in physics; the experimental group received computer-based feedback and formative assessment through SRS/Google Forms, while the control group received instruction without SRS-supported formative assessment.

The main finding was that the experimental group outperformed the control group on the posttest. Pretest scores did not differ significantly between groups, suggesting baseline equivalence, but posttest scores were significantly higher for the experimental group (M=6.68, SD=1.67) than for the control group (M=6.00, SD=1.68; t(146)=2.46, p=0.015). The author concludes that SRS-supported formative assessment can improve learning outcomes and classroom engagement in online higher education contexts, although the study does not report an effect size.

finding.finding_summary: The experimental group that received computer-based feedback and formative assessment via a student response system scored significantly higher on the posttest than the control group. Posttest performance on a 20-item physics test was M=6.68 (SD=1.67) for the experimental group versus M=6.00 (SD=1.68) for the control group, with t(146)=2.46, p=0.015.
finding.measure: 20-item multiple-choice physics achievement test on the energy topic

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that student response systems and real-time formative feedback helped students stay engaged, attentive, and participatory during learning, but these outcomes were discussed qualitatively rather than tested with a dedicated engagement instrument. The empirical evidence reported is primarily academic achievement, so the social-emotional impact is inferred from the study narrative rather than directly measured.
finding.measure: Engagement/participation described in discussion and conclusion; no direct scale reported

paper_profiles.title: Comparative Study of Game-Based Epedagogies in an Online Undergraduate Course
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether two game-based formative assessment approaches produce different learning outcomes in an online undergraduate course: Socrative, a game-based student response system, and an interactive PowerPoint game. The study is motivated by a gap in the literature on whether digital game-based learning tools improve learning in distance education, especially at the postsecondary level and in formative assessment contexts.

Using a quasi-experimental, posttest-only between-groups design, the author compared two intact course-section groups in an online undergraduate philosophy course at a four-year university in the southwestern United States. Students in both groups received the same content and instruction, but one group completed a Socrative-based formative assessment and the other used an interactive PowerPoint game; the outcome was performance on a 10-item summative quiz on logical fallacies. The interactive PowerPoint game group scored significantly higher than the Socrative group, with a statistically significant difference (t(216) = -3.33, p = .001) and a medium effect size (r = .24), leading the author to conclude that the interactive PowerPoint game was more effective for improving posttest performance in this context. The findings are limited to one institution and one course, but they suggest interactive PowerPoint games may be a promising formative assessment tool for online undergraduate instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Students who received the interactive PowerPoint game as a formative assessment scored significantly higher on the Topic 4 Fallacies Quiz than students who received Socrative. The mean difference was -4.144 points, 95% CI [-6.552, -1.737], with t(216) = -3.33, p = .001 and a medium effect size (r = .24).
finding.measure: Summative assessment score on the Topic 4 Fallacies Quiz (10 multiple-choice items on logical fallacies)

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames the interventions as supporting active learning and knowledge retention, but the empirical test outcome is achievement on a content quiz rather than a direct durable-skills measure. Evidence for durable skills is therefore indirect, based on the claim that the game-based pedagogy improved learning and retention of course concepts.
finding.measure: Posttest quiz performance used as a proxy for learning/retention

paper_profiles.title: Mapping research in student engagement and educational technology in higher education: a systematic evidence map
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate and postgraduate higher education students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a systematic evidence map of research on student engagement and educational technology in higher education. The authors ask how studies define and theorize engagement, what engagement and disengagement indicators are reported, and what learning scenarios, delivery modes, and technology tools are used across the literature.

The review searched four databases and screened a large corpus of higher-education studies published between 2007 and 2016, ultimately coding 243 studies. The mapped corpus was dominated by quantitative and mixed-methods research, with undergraduate students, universities, blended learning, and text-based or learning-management-system tools most common. Most studies did not define student engagement or use an explicit theoretical framework, highlighting substantial conceptual fuzziness in the field.

Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the paper synthesizes patterns across studies of educational technology use and student engagement. It concludes that behavioral engagement is the most frequently documented dimension, while disengagement is reported far less often; it also identifies gaps by geography, methodology, and study level, especially the relative underrepresentation of graduate students and non-English-speaking regions. The paper’s main contribution is descriptive and agenda-setting, offering a map of where the field has concentrated and where future research is needed.

finding.finding_summary: Across 243 higher-education studies, educational technology was associated with frequent reporting of engagement indicators such as participation/interaction/involvement (118 studies), achievement (106), positive interaction with teachers and peers (100), enjoyment (55), learning from peers (54), and self-regulation (39). However, the review also found that disengagement indicators like frustration (33), opposition/rejection (20), and boredom (10) were reported in a substantial subset of studies, indicating that technology use did not uniformly produce positive engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Student engagement and disengagement indicators coded from study reports

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies durable-skill indicators including deep learning (45 studies), critical thinking (25), learning from peers (54), and positive self-perception (26) as recurring outcomes in the literature on educational technology and engagement. Because the paper maps reported indicators rather than estimating causal effects, it shows that these skills are commonly targeted and observed, but does not provide pooled effect sizes or a directional causal estimate.
finding.measure: Coded durable-skill engagement indicators in the included studies

finding.finding_summary: The map reports that 'achievement' was one of the most frequently identified engagement indicators (106 studies), and that educational technology was commonly used in blended learning, distance education, and face-to-face higher-education contexts. However, the study does not evaluate direct academic achievement gains from a specific intervention; it only documents how often achievement-related outcomes appeared in the literature.
finding.measure: Achievement-related indicators reported in studies using educational technology

paper_profiles.title: Online eLearning for undergraduates in health professions: A systematic review of the impact on knowledge, skills, attitudes and satisfaction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether online eLearning is effective for undergraduate health-professions education, with particular attention to knowledge, skills, attitudes, and student satisfaction. The motivation is the global shortage of health professionals and the increasing use of internet-based training as a potentially scalable alternative to classroom instruction.

The authors conducted a systematic review of randomized and cluster-randomized trials published from 2000 to 2013, including 59 articles (60 trials) and 6,750 students in medicine, dentistry, nursing, physical therapy, and pharmacy. Interventions included full online eLearning, blended learning, spaced education, videoconferencing, and other web-based formats, compared mainly with traditional face-to-face learning or with other eLearning formats.

Across studies, online eLearning was generally equivalent to traditional learning and sometimes superior, especially for knowledge and skills. Twelve studies reported significantly higher knowledge gains, six reported significantly higher skill gains, and student attitudes were usually similar across conditions; satisfaction was somewhat more often neutral than positive. However, the review emphasizes substantial heterogeneity and a generally high or unclear risk of bias, so the authors conclude that the evidence is promising but not definitive, and that better-designed studies are needed.

finding.finding_summary: In 60 randomized trials (n=6750), online eLearning was generally equivalent to traditional learning and sometimes superior for knowledge outcomes. Among studies comparing online eLearning with traditional learning, 12 studies reported significantly higher knowledge gains for the online condition, while 24 found no significant difference, 3 found mixed results, and 3 favored traditional learning.
finding.measure: Knowledge tests, including multiple-choice questions, written case analyses, test questions, exams, and other knowledge assessments
finding.study_size: n=6750 across 60 trials; knowledge assessed in 53 studies

finding.finding_summary: Online eLearning showed somewhat better skill outcomes than traditional instruction in several trials. Of the studies measuring skills, 6 found significantly greater skill acquisition for online eLearning, 3 found no difference, 1 found mixed results, and 1 favored traditional learning; reported sample sizes in the positive studies ranged from 44 to 303.
finding.measure: Clinical skills assessments, OSCE-style rating scales/checklists, search skills tests, written case analyses, self-assessment, and time to complete tasks
finding.study_size: Skills assessed in 16 studies; 15 studies compared online eLearning with traditional learning

finding.finding_summary: Attitudes toward eLearning were usually similar across conditions, and student satisfaction was more often unchanged than improved. For attitudes, 8 of 12 studies found no difference or mixed results, and none favored online eLearning; for satisfaction, 4 of 29 studies favored online eLearning, 20 found no difference, 4 did not test significance, and 1 favored traditional learning.
finding.measure: Attitude and satisfaction questionnaires/surveys
finding.study_size: Attitudes assessed in 14 studies; satisfaction assessed in 33 studies

finding.finding_summary: The review did not include any formal cost-effectiveness analysis, but several studies discussed resource implications of online delivery. Reported examples suggested possible efficiency gains, such as lower production costs for video cases (US$2200 vs about US$5400 for an in-person exam) and comparable setup costs for videoconferencing after an initial hardware investment of less than US$10,000, but these were narrative observations rather than pooled estimates.
finding.measure: Narrative reports of costs, resource use, and delivery efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that online eLearning could support broader adoption in health-professions education and help institutions and policymakers scale training capacity, especially in settings facing health-worker shortages. These conclusions are based on the synthesis of trial evidence and narrative discussion, not on direct measurement of institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of implications for policy and institutions

paper_profiles.title: Reading as A Pre-Writing Activity and the Writing Skills among ESL Students
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Social Science Humanity & Management Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This quasi-experimental study examines whether reading used strictly as a pre-writing activity improves the essay writing skills of fourth-year college ESL students in the Philippines. The authors were interested in writing proficiency across three dimensions: content, conventions, and structure, and whether repeated formative assessments mediated any change over time.

The intervention consisted of five writing tasks across five weeks: a pre-test essay, three formative writing activities, and a post-test essay. Before each formative writing task, students read a related passage; the post-test also required reading, and all writing was scored with a researcher-made analytic rubric. The sample included 34 fourth-year college students from several departments at Manuel S. Enverga University Foundation enrolled in English for Occupational Purposes.

Results showed no significant improvement from pre-test to formative assessment and no significant difference between pre-test and post-test in content, conventions, or structure. Formative performance was relatively stable in content and somewhat better in conventions, but structure remained weak; the only significant comparison was a negative decline from formative to post-test in content. The authors conclude that reading alone, especially with limited teacher guidance and without explicit instruction or feedback, did not meaningfully improve students' writing proficiency, and they recommend closer monitoring, clearer rubrics, more feedback, and stronger instructional support.

finding.finding_summary: The study found no significant difference between pre-test and post-test writing performance overall (content, conventions, and structure all p>0.05), suggesting that reading as a pre-writing activity did not reliably improve ESL students' writing. The only significant comparison was a negative change from formative test to post-test in content (t=3.230, df=33, p=0.003), indicating a decline after the formative phase.
finding.measure: Essay writing scores/rubric ratings for content, conventions, and structure across pre-test, formative assessments, and post-test
finding.std_deviation: Pre-test/post-test means and SDs reported: content 2.12 (SD=0.946) to 2.09 (SD=0.965); conventions 2.94 (SD=1.594) to 2.62 (SD=0.954); structure 2.79 (SD=1.591) to 2.41 (SD=1.104)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that students' ability to integrate multiple reading sources, follow rubrics, and organize ideas did not improve meaningfully through the intervention alone. No significant pre-test to formative differences were found for content, conventions, or structure, and the discussion emphasizes weak source use, limited organization, and overreliance on provided materials.
finding.measure: Performance on rubric-based essay tasks requiring source integration and organization

paper_profiles.title: Robust Estimating Method for Propensity Score Models and its Application to Some Causal Estimands: A review and proposal
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a methodological problem in causal inference: how to estimate propensity scores robustly when the propensity score model may be misspecified. The author reviews several existing approaches, including covariate balancing propensity scores, boosted CART, and a sufficient-dimension-reduction approach, and then proposes a new two-step integrated strategy that combines multiple parametric propensity score models rather than selecting a single one.

The paper is not an education intervention study; it is a statistics / causal inference methods paper. The population is a generic observational-study target population rather than a specific student or school sample, and the examples are simulation-based. The proposed integrated method is motivated and evaluated through simulated data for average treatment effects (ATE) and average treatment effects for the overlap population (ATO), with additional discussion of how the approach could be used in applied settings via standard GLM software.

The main conclusions are that boosted CART and CBPS with higher-order balancing conditions perform well for ATE estimation, while boosted CART with IPW and CBPS with AIPW or BR-type estimators perform well for ATO estimation in the simulations. The proposed integrated method can be consistent when the true model is among the candidates and can improve Kullback-Leibler divergence even when it is not, but in the simulations it often produced unstable inverse-probability weights and large variance. Overall, the paper concludes that propensity score model specification remains important and that robust estimation may be improved by combining multiple candidate models.

paper_profiles.title: Bayesian-based Propensity Score Subclassification Estimator
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a statistical problem in observational causal inference: how to estimate treatment effects with propensity score subclassification while properly accounting for uncertainty in both the estimated propensity score and the number of strata used to form subclasses. The authors argue that standard subclassification methods usually fix the number of strata arbitrarily, which can understate uncertainty and distort variance estimates.

They propose a Bayesian-based subclassification estimator that combines general Bayesian updating with reversible jump MCMC (RJMCMC). The approach treats the number of strata as uncertain rather than selecting a single “best” value, and uses a loss-function-based Bayesian framework instead of a full likelihood for the outcome model. The method is evaluated in simulation studies modeled on a poor-overlap treatment assignment scenario inspired by Kang and Schafer.

The simulations compare the proposed Bayesian procedure against frequentist IPW, fixed-strata subclassification, frequentist strata selection, and a loss-likelihood bootstrap approach. Results suggest the proposed Bayesian method gives improved or comparable performance, especially in terms of coverage probability and uncertainty quantification, though intervals can be conservative. The paper concludes that the Bayesian framework can better propagate design-stage uncertainty into the analysis stage and may be extended to other causal settings, including ATT and sequential treatments.

paper_profiles.title: Manipulation-Robust Regression Discontinuity Designs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a theoretical framework for regression discontinuity (RD) designs when the running variable may be manipulated. The authors argue that standard RD identification arguments are often too high-level because they do not explicitly define manipulation, and they propose a potential-outcomes framework that separates manipulated and non-manipulated versions of the running variable.

The paper’s main contribution is methodological: it states low-level conditions under which RD identification holds despite manipulation, and it derives auxiliary assumptions under which the density test and balance/placebo tests are valid diagnostics for manipulation. In particular, the authors show that identification depends on both the distribution of the manipulated running variable and on whether manipulation is one-sided around the cutoff. They also discuss how these results clarify or revise interpretation of existing empirical RD studies, but the paper does not estimate any intervention effects or analyze an education program directly.

Because the paper is a theoretical econometrics article rather than an empirical education study, its relevance to education is indirect. The examples and discussion include educational contexts such as test-score cutoffs, examination retakes, and class-size rules, but these are illustrative rather than the object of new data analysis. The central conclusion is that researchers should interpret RD designs more carefully when manipulation is possible, and that a continuous density at the cutoff can be informative about identification only under additional assumptions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is methodological and theoretical, focusing on how manipulation of the running variable affects RD identification, diagnostic testing, and partial identification. It does not report an empirical effect size; instead, it derives conditions under which existing RD estimates and density tests are valid or invalid, implying that institutional research designs can be either credible or compromised depending on manipulation assumptions.
finding.measure: Validity of RD identification and diagnostic tests under manipulation; conditions for continuous density at the cutoff

paper_profiles.title: Embedded Formative Assessment in the Undergraduate Engineering Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the pedagogical role of embedded formative assessment in undergraduate engineering classrooms and argues that it can improve learning by making student thinking visible to instructors. The authors frame formative assessment as an ongoing in-class process where instructors collect student responses, interpret them, and use that feedback to adjust instruction in real time.

The paper focuses on technology-facilitated approaches, including clickers, mobile-response systems, and open-format tools such as InkSurvey, to reduce the clerical burden of collecting student responses and to make formative assessment more feasible in large undergraduate engineering courses. Rather than reporting a new experimental study, the paper synthesizes theory, prior engineering-education reports, and illustrative classroom examples from an undergraduate electromagnetics course to show how open-format questions can reveal misconceptions, support metacognition, and prompt instructional adjustment.

The main conclusion is that embedded formative assessment has strong potential in undergraduate engineering education, especially when paired with responsive teaching and questions that elicit student reasoning rather than only right answers. The authors emphasize that technology helps scale this practice, but its effectiveness depends on instructor follow-through and on designing prompts that expose thinking, not just attendance or short factual responses.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that embedded formative assessment can improve metacognition and critical thinking by prompting students to make their reasoning visible and reflect on what they do and do not understand. In the illustrative undergraduate electromagnetics examples, open-format responses revealed gaps in calculus fluency, symmetry reasoning, and transfer of prior work to a follow-up graphing task, but no formal effect size or controlled comparison is reported.
finding.measure: Student written/open-format responses in class; qualitative evidence of reasoning, metacognition, and problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that technology-facilitated formative assessment reduces the clerical burden on instructors by enabling immediate collection and inspection of student responses. The authors describe clickers, mobile devices, and InkSurvey as streamlining real-time feedback and making formative assessment more feasible in large undergraduate engineering classes, but they do not report a quantitative productivity outcome.
