finding.measure: Instructor burden / ease of collecting and reviewing student responses

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the value and feasibility of formative assessment in a university setting, with a particular focus on implementing frequent low-stakes assessments through Blackboard’s online test tool. The authors argue that formative assessment can improve learning by providing timely feedback, breaking content into smaller topic-based assessments, and helping students stay engaged throughout the semester.

The paper combines a conceptual discussion of formative assessment with a student survey conducted at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus). The proposed implementation involved weekly or fortnightly online tests on Blackboard, including immediate score reporting and detailed feedback. Survey responses suggest that students generally supported continuous assessment and especially valued immediate teacher feedback, flexibility, and the ability to study in smaller chunks.

The study is not an experiment and does not measure actual changes in achievement from the Blackboard intervention; instead, it reports perceptions and attitudes toward formative assessment and online testing. Students from different streams differed somewhat in their ratings, but the overall conclusion is that students viewed formative assessment and the Blackboard implementation positively and believed it could support both ongoing learning and later summative performance.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent online formative assessments were helpful because they provided immediate feedback, reduced uncertainty, and helped them keep in touch with the subject throughout the semester. Open-ended responses also suggested that the approach could support motivation by making progress visible, although some students worried that too many tests could create stress and pressure.
finding.measure: Student survey perceptions of continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and Blackboard online test implementation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment can support metacognition and self-monitoring by helping students identify strengths and weaknesses and check whether they are on track. Students also endorsed the idea that splitting content into small topic assessments made studying more manageable and encouraged progressive learning across the semester.
finding.measure: Student survey perceptions of self-monitoring, understanding strengths/weaknesses, and progressive learning

finding.finding_summary: Students expressed support for the proposed formative assessment model and believed that frequent Blackboard-based tests could improve learning of course content and help them prepare for semester examinations. The paper does not report achievement outcomes, but it does report strong perceived usefulness of the assessment approach for course learning.
finding.measure: Student survey perceptions of learning from continuous assessment and Blackboard tests

paper_profiles.title: Experimental momentum spectra of identified hadrons at e+e− colliders compared to QCD calculations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether the momentum spectra of identified hadrons produced in electron-positron collisions are consistent with predictions from perturbative QCD, specifically the Modified Leading Log Approximation (MLLA) combined with the Local Parton Hadron Duality (LPHD) hypothesis. The central observable is be*_p, the position of the maximum in the hadron momentum distribution, extracted from published spectra across many collider experiments and center-of-mass energies.

The analysis is not an intervention study; it is a secondary analysis of experimental particle-physics data from LEP and earlier e+e− colliders (e.g., ARGUS, CLEO, TASSO, JADE, TOPAZ, DELPHI, OPAL, L3). The author compares observed scaling of be*_p with theoretical formulas, fits effective QCD parameters such as 9b_eff and hadron-dependent constants, and studies how be*_p varies with hadron mass and flavor. The main conclusion is that the broad energy dependence is reasonably described by LPHD+MLLA, but there are significant hadron-dependent deviations that suggest limitations or partial breakdown of LPHD at the level of precision studied. A value of b1_s is extracted that is broadly consistent with other determinations, but the paper emphasizes that this method is not a precise way to measure b1_s because systematic uncertainties are difficult to control.

paper_profiles.title: Predicting Community College Astronomy Performance through Logistic Regression
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks which demographic and academic factors predict success in introductory community college astronomy courses. The motivating problem is that astronomy is often a gateway science for non-majors, yet little is known about what helps or hinders performance in this postsecondary context.

The authors analyzed institutional transcript data from 1,909 students who took astronomy at a large suburban community college in New York State between 2015 and 2019. Using Spearman correlations followed by logistic regression, they examined demographic variables (gender, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, age) and academic variables (cumulative GPA, mathematics performance, developmental math enrollment, repeated mathematics, major, and number of astronomy/science courses taken) as predictors of earning a C or better in astronomy.

The main finding was that mathematics-related preparation and performance were the strongest predictors of astronomy success. Students who had better mathematics grades and those who had taken more astronomy courses were more likely to pass, while students who had enrolled in developmental mathematics or repeated mathematics were less likely to pass. Demographic variables were not significant predictors in the multivariable model. The authors conclude that astronomy may function as an access point for STEM in community colleges, but that student outcomes are closely tied to prior mathematics pathways rather than demographic characteristics.

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics preparation and performance were the clearest predictors of astronomy success in this correlational study of n=1,909 community college students. In logistic regression, each 1-point increase in mathematics GPA was associated with higher odds of passing astronomy (OR=1.54, 95% CI [1.349, 1.759]), while enrollment in developmental mathematics (OR=0.568, 95% CI [0.456, 0.709]) and repeated mathematics courses (OR=0.671, 95% CI [0.513, 0.877]) were associated with lower odds of passing.
finding.measure: Astronomy course performance (pass C or better vs. DFW) predicted by mathematics GPA, developmental mathematics enrollment, and repeated mathematics courses

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines performance in introductory astronomy, a science course requiring application of basic quantitative scientific concepts and reasoning. Students who took more astronomy courses were more likely to pass astronomy (OR=1.705, 95% CI [1.150, 2.530]), and the overall model significantly predicted whether students earned a C or better (Nagelkerke R2=0.104; correctly classified 71.2% of cases; n=1,909).
finding.measure: Introductory astronomy performance (ABC vs. DFW)

finding.finding_summary: The authors interpret taking multiple astronomy courses as a possible marker of student interest and persistence in the subject. In the logistic model, each additional astronomy course taken increased the odds of passing astronomy (OR=1.705, 95% CI [1.150, 2.530]), though the paper notes that causality is ambiguous because interest and prior success may both drive re-enrollment.
finding.measure: Number of astronomy courses taken; subsequent astronomy course performance

paper_profiles.title: Access to undergraduate research experiences at a large research university
paper_profiles.venue: Physical Review Special Topics - Physics Education Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines access to undergraduate research experiences (UREs) in the University of Colorado Boulder Physics Department and asks how a large research university can improve awareness of and pathways into research for physics and engineering physics majors. The authors define access broadly as both awareness of URE opportunities and the ability to select among on- and off-campus research options.

To study the issue, the authors used interviews and two department-wide surveys, one for students and one for faculty. The interview data informed survey development, while the surveys measured student familiarity with research-related programs, sources of information about UREs, perceptions of what undergraduate research entails, and faculty mentoring capacity and expectations. The student sample included 76 of 493 majors, and the faculty sample included 47 of 50 faculty members.

The study found that only about 20% of majors were engaged in UREs in Fall 2014, and student awareness of research opportunities and research practices varied substantially by prior research experience. Students with research experience were more familiar with research programs, research groups, and local labs, and were more likely to identify authentic research activities such as reading scientific papers and writing a thesis. The authors used these findings, along with faculty constraints on mentoring capacity, to propose five departmental recommendations: a website FAQ, annual symposium, poster session, sophomore research methods course, and partnerships with local national labs. The paper concludes that departmental change efforts should combine centralized communication, student learning about research practices, and preservation of faculty mentoring autonomy.

finding.finding_summary: The study identified multiple institutional barriers to undergraduate research access at a large research university and used survey results to generate five department-level recommendations. After faculty review, the recommendations received departmental support and a Committee on Undergraduate Research was created to oversee implementation.
finding.measure: Student and faculty surveys on research access, mentoring capacity, awareness of UREs, and departmental recommendations

paper_profiles.title: A difference-in-differences estimator by covariate balancing propensity score
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a new econometric estimator for treatment effects in a two-period difference-in-differences (DID) design: a covariate balancing propensity score (CBPS) estimator for the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT). The core problem the authors address is that standard DID estimators can perform poorly when the propensity score model and/or outcome regression model are misspecified, especially when both are only approximately correct.

The proposed method adapts CBPS to DID settings with panel data and is shown theoretically to have several desirable properties. Under correct specification, it is locally semiparametrically efficient; when either the outcome model or the propensity score model is correct, it is doubly robust for consistency; and unlike standard AIPW DID estimators, its influence-function-based inference remains valid when one working model is misspecified. The authors also show that under local misspecification of both models, the CBPS DID estimator can converge faster than AIPW DID. Simulation evidence supports these theoretical claims.

The empirical illustration reanalyzes the LaLonde job training benchmark using CPS and DW comparison groups, with real earnings as the outcome. In those adult labor-market data, CBPS DID generally performs competitively and often yields smaller bias or shorter confidence intervals than AIPW and OR estimators, while IPW is typically the least stable. The paper is methodological rather than educational, and it does not study a formative assessment intervention or a K-12/ postsecondary learning outcome directly.

paper_profiles.title: Investigating Awareness and Usage of Electronic Resources by the Library Users of Selected Colleges of Solapur University
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines awareness, access, and usage patterns of electronic resources among library users in selected colleges affiliated with Solapur University in Maharashtra, India. The authors focus on how often users visit the library, how long they stay, what they use the library for, what devices they use to access electronic resources, how they learn about IT services, whether they receive training, and how frequently they use various web technologies.

The study uses a survey design with a structured questionnaire administered to 1,022 randomly selected library users across 26 colleges. The sample includes users from aided, self-financing, engineering, education, and pharmacy colleges. The analysis is descriptive with chi-square tests for associations across college categories; there is no intervention, randomized assignment, or quasi-experimental comparison.

Findings suggest that electronic-resource awareness and use are common, but uneven. Users primarily visit libraries for issue/return of books and data collection, while mobile phones and library computers are important access devices. Most users reported learning about services from friends, teachers, or staff rather than websites, and the majority reported no IT training. The authors conclude that greater publicity, orientation, and ongoing information-literacy training are needed to improve effective use of electronic resources and related web technologies.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports substantial use of digital tools for accessing library resources, but also identifies low training and uneven adoption that limit efficient use. Among 1,022 respondents, mobile phones were the second-most preferred device for accessing e-resources (33.9%), while 86.8% reported no IT-based training, suggesting a gap between available tools and efficient use.
finding.measure: Device usage for accessing e-resources; self-reported IT training participation

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that institutional supports for e-resource use are uneven across colleges. Users mostly learned about library IT services through friends (31.3%), teachers (22.3%), and staff (20.8%), while only 14.9% learned through websites; 86.8% reported no IT training, and the authors argue that libraries need better publicity, orientation, and training infrastructure.
finding.measure: Sources of awareness about IT services; reported access to training; use of library websites and orientation programs

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats e-resource searching, web technologies, and information literacy as user skills that support effective academic work. Although usage is fairly common for some tools (e.g., internet surfing 37.2% daily; search engines 36.8% daily), many advanced tools are rarely used, and the authors attribute this to lack of awareness and training rather than lack of need.
finding.measure: Frequency of use of web technologies and e-resource search tools; reported training/awareness

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that users rely on electronic resources for academic information gathering and research-related tasks. In the purpose-of-visit rankings, electronic sources were used for data collection and information retrieval, and the conclusion states that use of electronic resources improved research output, though no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Purpose of library visit; reported use of e-resources for research and data collection

paper_profiles.title: College Spread of COVID-19 in Ohio
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether Ohio counties with NCAA-affiliated colleges experienced different COVID-19 spread patterns than counties without such colleges during the pandemic. The authors motivate the study by noting that colleges reopened in varied ways and that campuses were widely suspected to contribute to community transmission, especially among college-age populations.

Using county-level COVID-19 case data from the Ohio Department of Health, county population data from the Census Bureau, college-enrollment/location data from IPEDS, and metro/non-metro classifications from NCHS, the authors constructed monthly county-level indicators including median percent change in cases, average percent change in cases, and cases per 100,000 residents. They tested normality and then used non-parametric analyses (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and a Kruskal-Wallis test) to compare counties with and without NCAA colleges, and to further compare metro/non-metro subgroups.

The analysis found mixed evidence. Counties with colleges had significantly higher median percent change in cases and higher average cases per 100,000 than counties without colleges, but the average percent change comparison was not statistically significant. When counties were divided into four groups by metro/non-metro status and college presence, the Kruskal-Wallis test found no significant differences in cases per 100,000 across groups. The paper concludes that college counties showed some higher spread indicators overall, but that metro/non-metro context did not materially change the average case rate comparison.

finding.finding_summary: The paper compares county-level COVID-19 spread in Ohio counties with NCAA colleges versus those without colleges, using cumulative case data and non-parametric tests. Results were mixed: counties with colleges had significantly higher median percent change in cases (Wilcoxon p=0.02) and higher average cases per 100,000 (Wilcoxon p=0.00), but the average percent change comparison was not significant (p=0.25); a four-group metro/non-metro Kruskal-Wallis test was also not significant (p=0.80).
finding.measure: County-level COVID-19 cases per 100,000 residents; monthly median percent change; monthly average percent change

paper_profiles.title: Promoting Saving for College Through Data Science
paper_profiles.venue: Bloomberg Data for Good Exchange Conference
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how the Illinois State Treasurer and Civis Analytics used data science to increase enrollment in Illinois 529 college savings plans. The core question is not about student learning directly, but about whether predictive modeling and targeted digital outreach can identify likely savers and increase college-savings account openings among Illinois residents.

The intervention/approach combined record linkage, lookalike modeling, and digitally delivered advertisements. First, accountholder records were matched to a consumer file to build a richer demographic profile of current 529 account holders. Then the authors trained sparse logistic classifiers to identify likely signups among Illinois residents, with separate models by race/ethnicity to avoid reinforcing demographic imbalances in the existing account-holder base. Top-ranked targets were served digital ads encouraging college savings, and account openings among targets were tracked.

The population was adult Illinois residents, particularly those likely to be parents or household decision-makers for college savings. The setting is a state-administered public savings program, not a school-based instructional context. The paper reports that targets were 4.4 times more likely to open an account than non-targets, and that total signups and direct-plan signups were higher than the prior year during the campaign period. The authors conclude that person-level modeling and targeted outreach can improve efficiency and increase participation in public benefit programs such as 529 plans, though the design is not randomized and the evidence is primarily programmatic/observational.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that data-driven targeting and digital outreach increased participation in the Illinois 529 college savings program. During the campaign period, targets were 4.4 times more likely to open an account than non-targets, and first-quarter 2017 signups were 23% higher than the previous year (26% higher for the direct 529 plan).
finding.measure: College savings account openings / signup rates for the Illinois 529 plans
finding.effect_size: 4.4x likelihood of opening an account for targets vs non-targets; 23% higher total signups year-over-year; 26% higher direct-plan signups year-over-year

paper_profiles.title: Making Science Personal: Inclusivity-Driven Design for General-Education Courses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether an inclusivity-driven redesign of a general-education college astronomy course can help students connect science content with their personal identities and lived experiences. The authors argue that many introductory science courses isolate content from students’ ‘life files,’ which can limit relevance, belonging, and meaningful learning, especially in courses that may be students’ last formal science experience.

The intervention was a Spring 2019 University of Arizona undergraduate astronomy course (ASTR 201: Cosmology) redesigned around three guiding principles: continually integrating science content with the human story of science, explicitly valuing diverse perspectives, and creating frequent opportunities for students to connect course ideas to personal experiences. Implementation included classroom norms affirming diverse voices, a guest lecture from a Tohono O’odham community member, inclusive think-pair-share activities, and regular reflective writing prompts and homework/quiz items that linked astronomy concepts to students’ own lives.

The study used multiple forms of evidence: student reflections, course evaluation comments, course grades, and a pre/post survey of views about science (TSSI subset). The authors report generally positive student reactions, no detectable grade differences by gender or culture/ethnicity, and a small positive shift on the survey overall (Δ=0.07, p=0.170; n=13 matched respondents). The paper concludes that the course design created a positive and inclusive learning environment and suggests the framework may be useful for other instructors, while noting that more rigorous future evaluation would be beneficial.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that the course was engaging, respectful, and comfortable for expressing honest opinions, and final-exam/TCE comments were consistently positive about classroom norms and opportunities for self-expression. The authors interpret these reflections as evidence that the inclusivity-driven design improved students’ sense of belonging, comfort, and relevance of course material to their lives.
finding.measure: Final exam reflection question; anonymous Teacher-Course Evaluations (TCE); student comments
finding.study_size: n=34 enrolled; n=20 demographics responses; qualitative comments from final exam/TCE not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The course emphasized critical thinking, perspective-taking, and connecting ideas across contexts through writing prompts and think-pair-share activities. Student comments explicitly described improved critical/scientific thinking and the ability to consider multiple viewpoints, but the evidence is mainly qualitative rather than from a controlled skill measure.
finding.measure: Student reflection responses on final exam and TCE comments related to critical thinking and perspective-taking

finding.finding_summary: The pre/post TSSI results showed a small positive change in overall views of science after the course (overall average 0.63 to 0.70; Δ=0.07, p=0.170; n=13 matched respondents). Several individual items moved in a more inclusive direction, though changes were small and often driven by only one or two students.
finding.measure: Pre- and post-course Thinking About Science Survey Instrument (TSSI) subset

finding.finding_summary: Course scores did not differ detectably across demographic groups, with similar average cumulative scores for male vs. female students (84.3% vs. 85.7%, p=0.877) and non-URM vs. URM students (84.8% vs. 85.8%, p=0.915). The authors present this as evidence that the inclusive redesign did not disadvantage students academically.
finding.measure: Average cumulative course score by self-reported gender and culture/ethnicity

paper_profiles.title: Peer Instruction: Comparing Clickers to Flashcards
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether wireless clickers add learning value to Peer Instruction (PI) beyond a lower-cost flashcard method. The broader instructional approach, PI, uses conceptual multiple-choice questions (ConcepTests), peer discussion, and instructor follow-up to promote conceptual change and problem solving in science courses.

The study was conducted in a first-semester algebra-based mechanics course at a two-year Canadian public community college. Students were randomly assigned by the registrar to one of two course sections taught by the same instructor: PI with clickers (n=41 initial; n=35 analyzed in the table) or PI with flashcards (n=42 initial; n=34 analyzed). Both sections used the same course structure, content, and lab component. Conceptual understanding was measured with pre/post Force Concept Inventory scores and normalized gains, and traditional problem solving was measured with the final exam.

The results showed no statistically significant differences between clickers and flashcards on any measured learning outcome. Pretest and posttest conceptual scores were similar, and the reported normalized gain and exam performance also did not differ significantly between groups. The author concludes that the pedagogical benefits come from Peer Instruction itself rather than from the clicker technology, although clickers may still have practical advantages such as data archiving and supporting classroom implementation of PI.

finding.finding_summary: Clickers did not improve conceptual learning relative to flashcards in a Peer Instruction physics course. The study reported no significant differences on the Force Concept Inventory pretest (clickers M=11.9/30 vs flashcards M=13.6/30, p=0.209), posttest (19.9 vs 21.3, p=0.351), or normalized gain (0.486 vs 0.520, p=0.745).
finding.measure: Force Concept Inventory (pretest, posttest, normalized gain)
finding.study_size: n=35 clickers, n=34 flashcards (randomly assigned sections; initial n=41 and n=42)

finding.finding_summary: Clickers did not improve traditional problem-solving performance compared with flashcards. Final exam scores were very similar across conditions (69.8% for clickers vs 71.6% for flashcards), and the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.630).
finding.measure: College comprehensive final examination in algebra-based mechanics

paper_profiles.title: Predicting Community College Astronomy Performance through Logistic Regression
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks which academic and demographic factors predict whether community college students pass introductory astronomy courses. The authors motivate the work by arguing that astronomy is a common gateway science for nonmajors and that understanding predictors of success could help identify interventions to improve STEM access and persistence.

Using institutional transcript data from a large public community college in New York State, the study analyzes 1,909 students who took astronomy between 2015 and 2019. The authors examined demographic variables (gender, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, age) and academic variables (cumulative GPA, mathematics performance, developmental mathematics enrollment, repeated mathematics, science coursetaking, STEM major status, and number of astronomy courses taken) and modeled the binary outcome of earning a C or better in astronomy.

The main findings were that demographic variables were not significant predictors of astronomy performance in the multivariable model. In contrast, mathematics-related preparation mattered: stronger mathematics performance and taking more astronomy courses were associated with higher odds of passing, while enrolling in developmental mathematics and repeating mathematics were associated with lower odds of success. The authors conclude that astronomy performance appears to be driven more by academic preparation, especially mathematics, than by demographic characteristics, and they suggest that math remediation and advising may improve community college STEM outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics performance was a significant positive predictor of astronomy success in the logistic regression. Each one-point increase in mathematics GPA was associated with 54% higher odds of passing astronomy (odds ratio 1.540, 95% CI [1.349, 1.759], p<0.001) in a sample of n=1,909 community college students.
finding.measure: Mathematics course GPA predicting passing astronomy courses with a grade of C or better

finding.finding_summary: Astronomy coursetaking itself was associated with better performance. Students with more astronomy courses had higher odds of passing: each additional astronomy course was associated with 70.5% higher odds of passing astronomy (odds ratio 1.705, 95% CI [1.150, 2.530], p=0.008).
finding.measure: Number of astronomy courses taken predicting passing astronomy courses with a grade of C or better

finding.finding_summary: Institutional developmental mathematics placement was associated with lower astronomy success. Students enrolled in developmental mathematics were 43% less likely to pass astronomy (odds ratio 0.568, 95% CI [0.456, 0.709], p<0.001), and students who repeated mathematics were also less likely to pass (odds ratio 0.671, 95% CI [0.513, 0.877], p=0.004).
finding.measure: Developmental mathematics enrollment and repeated mathematics predicting passing astronomy courses with a grade of C or better

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats enrollment in multiple astronomy courses as a proxy for astronomy interest, but this is inferred rather than directly measured. Students taking more astronomy courses were more likely to pass astronomy, yet the direction of causality is ambiguous because higher interest may both result from and contribute to better performance.
finding.measure: Number of astronomy courses taken as a proxy for astronomy interest

paper_profiles.title: Access to undergraduate research experiences at a large research university
paper_profiles.venue: Physical Review Special Topics - Physics Education Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the state of access to undergraduate research experiences (UREs) in the University of Colorado Boulder Physics Department and asks how the department can improve access for all majors. The authors define access broadly as both awareness of UREs and the ability to select from available on- and off-campus opportunities.

To study this, they conducted interviews and then administered separate surveys to 47/50 faculty members and 76/493 majors in fall 2014. The student survey probed awareness of research opportunities, perceptions of UREs, and experiences in research; the faculty survey focused on mentoring capacity and expectations. The analysis primarily compared students with research experience to those without, using chi-squared tests for some item-level differences.

The results suggest that students already involved in research are more familiar with research-related programs, research groups, local labs, and the practices of research, while students without experience report less awareness and fewer informational pathways. Faculty capacity and preferences also constrain the number and structure of UREs the department can offer. Based on these findings, the authors propose five department-level recommendations, including creating a URE FAQ webpage, hosting annual symposium and poster sessions, developing a Research Methods course, and expanding partnerships with local national labs. The paper is best understood as an institutional needs assessment and change-oriented study rather than an evaluation of a specific instructional intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The study found substantial institutional constraints on access to undergraduate research at CU Boulder: only about 20% of majors were actively engaged in UREs in Fall 2014, and faculty mentoring capacity was limited, with about half mentoring only 1–2 students per year. The resulting department-level recommendations were supported by the department, and a Committee on Undergraduate Research was created to oversee implementation.
finding.measure: Department-wide survey data on faculty mentoring capacity, student participation in UREs, and departmental response to recommendations
finding.study_size: students n=76; faculty n=47; department population of majors n=493

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in Higher Education: Evidence from an Elite College
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate students at a highly selective U.S. liberal arts college adopted and used generative AI soon after the release of ChatGPT. The authors ask how widespread academic AI use is, which students are most likely to adopt it, how students use AI across academic tasks, and how institutional policies and beliefs shape adoption. The paper is motivated by concerns that generative AI may either support learning or undermine academic development, and by the lack of systematic evidence on student behavior in higher education.

The study uses novel survey data collected from Middlebury College students between December 2024 and February 2025. The final analytic sample includes 634 students, with poststratification weights used to better match the college population on field of study. The survey measures AI adoption, task-level use (e.g., explaining concepts, summarizing texts, writing essays, coding help), perceived educational benefits, peer-use beliefs, and responses to different institutional policy environments including prohibition and citation requirements. The paper is descriptive and correlational rather than experimental.

The main findings are that generative AI adoption is extremely high: 82.5% of students report academic use, with rapid growth from under 10% before Spring 2023 to over 80% by Fall 2024. Adoption is uneven across demographics and disciplines, with higher use among males, Black and Asian students, lower-achieving students, and students in natural sciences. Students use AI more often for augmentation than automation, though both are common. Explicit prohibition is associated with a large self-reported drop in intended use, but policy effects differ across student groups and many students lack clear knowledge of institutional rules or available AI resources. Overall, students generally believe AI helps learning more than grades, and those beliefs are strongly associated with adoption; students also substantially underestimate peer AI use.

finding.finding_summary: Students report using generative AI to save time and improve workflow across academic tasks. Among AI users, 61.2% use AI for augmentation tasks and 41.9% for automation tasks; 59.4% believe AI improves their ability to complete assignments on time. Open-ended responses frequently describe AI as an "on-demand tutor" or a tool for efficiency when workload is heavy.
finding.measure: Self-reported AI use for augmentation/automation tasks; perceived impact on assignment completion time

finding.finding_summary: AI is widely used for writing-related academic tasks, but more often for support than for full content generation. Among AI users, 54.1% use AI for proofreading, 47.3% for editing essay drafts, and 23.5% for writing essays. The paper interprets this as evidence that students use AI for literacy support and partial automation rather than uniformly substituting AI for their own writing.
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency of AI use for proofreading, editing essays, and writing essays

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI affects students' learning processes, metacognitive support, and problem-solving, with more use for augmentation than automation. Students frequently use AI to explain concepts (80.3% of users), summarize materials (74.0%), and generate ideas (61.9%), suggesting support for understanding and task management; however, automation use is also substantial, raising concerns about reduced cognitive engagement on some tasks.
finding.measure: Self-reported AI use for explaining concepts, summarizing materials, generating ideas, and related augmentation/automation task categories

finding.finding_summary: Students report that AI helps them manage workload and deadlines, indicating perceived benefits for self-regulation and persistence under time pressure. Specifically, 59.4% believe AI improves timely assignment completion, and open-ended responses emphasize using AI when overloaded or facing looming deadlines.
finding.measure: Perceived impact of AI on time management / timely assignment completion

finding.finding_summary: Institutional policy meaningfully shapes intended AI use, but effects vary across student groups and are moderated by information gaps. Explicit prohibition is associated with a 39 percentage-point drop in intended use overall, with a 37.8 pp decline in reported use under a ban and larger reductions for females (49.6 pp) than males (40.1 pp). The paper also documents substantial confusion about rules, citation practices, and access to college-provided AI resources, implying that policy design and communication affect adoption and equity.
finding.measure: Self-reported likelihood of AI use under different policy scenarios; awareness of policy rules and college-provided AI resources
finding.effect_size: 39 pp intended-use decline under prohibition; 37.8 pp usage decline under ban

finding.finding_summary: Students use generative AI extensively for non-writing academic support tasks such as explaining concepts, summarizing texts, finding information, and coding assistance. The most common task is explaining concepts (80.3% of AI users), followed by summarizing texts (74.0%), finding information (63.1%), and coding help (34.4%), showing broad integration into general coursework across disciplines.
finding.measure: Self-reported AI use across academic tasks outside literacy-specific writing

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes limited evidence on language-related support, primarily through proofreading and student comments about non-native English use. Non-native English speakers mention using AI for proofreading to overcome language barriers, but the paper does not provide a dedicated language-fluency outcome or direct performance measure.
finding.measure: Self-reported use of AI for proofreading and qualitative mentions of language-barrier support

paper_profiles.title: Everyone’s Universe: Teaching Astronomy in Community Colleges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter-length paper argues for the importance of introductory astronomy teaching in community colleges and synthesizes evidence about who takes Astro 101, who teaches it, and what conditions shape teaching and learning in this setting. The central problem is not a single intervention but the broader question of how community college astronomy differs from four-year contexts and what that means for student success and faculty preparation.

The paper draws on prior studies, national statistics, and author experience rather than reporting a new empirical study. It describes Astro 101 enrollments, student demographics, academic preparedness, and the prevalence of part-time faculty, then discusses constraints such as limited budgets, heavy workloads, lack of support staff, and uneven access to professional development. It also highlights learner-centered teaching and institutional supports as practical responses, but does not test a specific treatment or formative assessment intervention.

Overall, the chapter concludes that community college students are highly diverse, often underprepared for college-level work in general, and frequently balancing work and family responsibilities. The author argues that introductory astronomy can still support strong learning gains across institution types when interactive methods are used, and that instructor preparation, discipline-specific expertise, and institutional support matter for both student outcomes and faculty effectiveness. However, the piece is primarily a narrative synthesis and professional commentary rather than a randomized or quasi-experimental study.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter cites prior research showing that students in Astro 101 can achieve similar learning gains across institution types, class sizes, and backgrounds when learner-centered teaching is used. It also argues that introductory astronomy is a science-literacy course that can shape students’ scientific understanding and attitudes, but it does not present a new causal estimate or a specific effect size.
finding.measure: Astro 101 learning gains / science literacy outcomes from prior studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that interactive learning and well-designed Astro 101 courses can help students succeed regardless of preparedness, and it discusses student persistence and engagement as important concerns in the community college context. It cites prior evidence that positive course experiences can influence whether students continue in STEM, but no new empirical estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Student persistence/engagement in introductory STEM and Astro 101

finding.finding_summary: The chapter discusses students’ need to learn time management, scheduling, task organization, and help-seeking in the community college environment, framing these as prerequisites for academic success. It also notes that high-impact practices and support structures can help students develop these durable skills, but the paper does not report new measured effects.
finding.measure: Student self-management, time management, and study habits

finding.finding_summary: The paper portrays community college astronomy teaching as operationally constrained by very small program budgets, limited instructional support, heavy grading loads, and substantial service and administrative burdens. It reports descriptive figures such as average astronomy program budgets of about $940 (or $1127 including all surveyed institutions) and typical full-time teaching loads equivalent to five three-credit courses per semester, but these are descriptive rather than experimental estimates.
finding.measure: Program budgets, teaching load, support staffing, and faculty workload

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that community college structures—open enrollment, part-time staffing, shared governance, and limited resources—strongly shape both instruction and student access. It presents descriptive institutional statistics such as 58% of community college courses being taught by part-time faculty and discusses how policy and staffing patterns affect student persistence, but it does not test an intervention or provide a causal institutional effect size.
finding.measure: Institutional staffing patterns, governance structures, and student access/persistence

paper_profiles.title: EXPTRIALMNG: A Universal Experiment Trial Manager for AR/VR/MR Experiments Based on Unity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents ExpTrialMng, a Unity library designed to reduce the programming burden involved in building psychological and human-computer interaction experiments in VR/AR/MR environments. The authors motivate the tool by noting that existing Unity-based frameworks can be difficult for non-expert programmers to use, may include unnecessary functionality, and often lack robust support for restarting experiments after unexpected hardware or tracking failures.

The proposed library separates trial randomization from experiment execution by using a pre-generated CSV file, automatically saves trial results to CSV after each trial, and supports resuming an experiment from a specified trial number. The paper describes the system’s workflow, implementation details, and intended use in a broad range of Unity-based experimental studies. It does not report an empirical evaluation with participants; rather, it argues that the tool can improve usability, reduce data loss, and help researchers focus on experiment and stimulus design.

The paper’s context is research tool development for cognitive psychology, HCI, and design experiments, primarily for researchers using Unity. Its contribution is methodological and infrastructural, not an educational intervention or learner-outcome study.

paper_profiles.title: Covariate adjustment in subgroup analyses of randomized clinical trials: A propensity score approach
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops and evaluates methods for covariate adjustment in subgroup analyses of randomized controlled trials. The authors address the problem that subgroup analyses often have smaller sample sizes and therefore greater chance imbalance on prognostic covariates, which can reduce precision and power when estimating subgroup average treatment effects or treatment effect heterogeneity.

The paper proposes propensity score weighting approaches for subgroup analysis, especially inverse probability weighting and overlap weighting, and compares them with an ANCOVA-based subgroup model. The methodological argument is supported by extensive simulations across several scenarios, including correctly specified and misspecified outcome models, single and multiple subgroups, and small versus larger subgroup sample sizes. The authors also illustrate the approach using the HF-ACTION randomized trial in adults with chronic heart failure, estimating the effect of exercise training on 6-minute walk distance at 3 months across prespecified subgroups.

Overall, the paper concludes that adjusted estimators are more efficient than unadjusted subgroup comparisons, and that specifying the propensity score model with subgroup-covariate interactions is crucial. Overlap weighting with a full-interaction propensity model is especially effective in small subgroups and can outperform ANCOVA when the outcome model is misspecified. In the HF-ACTION example, adjusted analyses produced smaller standard errors than unadjusted analyses and, in several subgroups, changed conclusions about statistical significance.

finding.finding_summary: In an adult RCT context, covariate-adjusted subgroup analyses were more efficient than unadjusted subgroup analyses for estimating treatment effects on the 6-minute walk distance. In the HF-ACTION example (N=1724 analyzed; 2331 randomized), adjusted methods reduced standard errors and in several subgroups yielded treatment effects of roughly 22-31 meters that were not detected in the unadjusted analysis.
finding.measure: 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) at 3 months in the HF-ACTION trial

paper_profiles.title: Higher education assessment practice in the era of generative AI tools
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate and postgraduate higher education students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI tools such as ChatGPT-4 and Google Bard (Gemini) perform on higher-education assessment tasks and what that implies for assessment practice in the era of AI. The authors are concerned with whether GenAI can complete authentic disciplinary assessments well enough to affect student learning, academic integrity, and the validity of assessment in higher education.

The study uses three case-study assessment instruments drawn from master’s-level data science, data analytics, and construction management. The authors prompted ChatGPT-4 and Bard to solve the tasks, then graded the outputs using criterion-referenced assessment and a standard letter-grade scale, with moderation by subject-area colleagues. The paper is explicitly an experiment with assessment artifacts, but it is not a student-level randomized or quasi-experimental study; it is a qualitative/analytical evaluation of AI-generated responses.

The main conclusion is that GenAI tools can perform strongly on some assessment types, especially in data science and data analytics, showing subject knowledge, problem-solving, analysis, critical thinking, and presentation skills, which may facilitate unethical student use and hinder learning. Performance was weaker on the construction-management task, suggesting that GenAI capabilities are discipline-dependent and that project-based, contextualized assessments are harder for the tools to complete. The authors recommend redesigning assessments, using authentic and reflective tasks, and combining AI detectors with plagiarism tools and human review in higher education.

finding.finding_summary: Across three master’s-level assessment case studies, ChatGPT-4 and Bard demonstrated durable skills such as subject knowledge, problem-solving, analytical reasoning, critical thinking, and presentation/communication. However, performance varied by discipline, and the tools struggled with more complex, contextualized construction-management problems, indicating that the observed skills were uneven and discipline-dependent.
finding.measure: Criterion-referenced grading of AI-generated solutions to three master’s-level assessment case studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluated GenAI performance on higher-education assessments in data analytics, data science, and construction management. The tools produced coherent, often high-quality solutions for data-oriented tasks, but were less successful on the construction-management assessment, suggesting a mixed overall effect on discipline-specific academic task completion.
finding.measure: Grades/marks awarded to AI-generated responses on three discipline-specific assessment tasks

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that generative AI requires institutional response in higher education, including assessment redesign, contextualized authentic assessments, reflective tasks, and combining AI detectors with plagiarism tools and human review. The paper does not report quantitative institutional outcomes, but it provides concrete policy and governance recommendations based on the observed assessment vulnerabilities.
finding.measure: Policy/recommendation analysis grounded in assessment-case results

paper_profiles.title: The Scalability, Efficiency and Complexity of Universities and Colleges: A New Lens for Assessing the Higher Educational System
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how institutional size relates to the costs, revenues, and educational outcomes of U.S. higher education institutions. The authors frame the problem as one of scalability: whether universities and colleges become more or less efficient, productive, or affordable as enrollment increases, and whether different sectors of higher education follow distinct scaling regimes.

The study uses a large observational dataset covering 5,802 accredited U.S. postsecondary institutions from the 2013 Delta Cost Project/IPEDS system, supplemented with College Scorecard/Mobility Report Card earnings data. Institutions are grouped into seven sectors (e.g., public research universities, private research universities, state colleges, community colleges, nonprofit private colleges, professional schools, and for-profit colleges). The authors examine how total revenue, total expenditure, instruction spending, maintenance, faculty size, tuition, completion rates, and mid-career earnings scale with enrollment.

The main conclusion is that higher education is not uniform: different sectors exhibit distinct scaling patterns. Research universities tend to show superlinear scaling in revenue, expenditure, research activity, and student outcomes, but with higher tuition and greater selectivity. State and community colleges show strong economies of scale, with sublinear spending and generally stable or improving completion outcomes, suggesting increasing affordability at larger sizes. Nonprofit private colleges and professional schools diversify into student services and often rely more on tuition, while for-profit colleges reduce costs aggressively and widen profit margins with size. The paper is descriptive and comparative rather than causal, and it argues that sector-specific scaling tradeoffs are central to understanding institutional roles in the higher education system.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds strong sector-specific economies of scale in higher education operations, especially in instruction, maintenance, and administration. For example, state colleges, community colleges, and for-profit colleges show sublinear expenditure scaling, while public/private research universities show superlinear scaling in several cost categories; the study is descriptive and reports scaling exponents rather than causal effects.
finding.measure: Total expenditure, instruction expenditure, maintenance costs, faculty counts, faculty pay, student services, and revenue components as functions of enrollment

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is a taxonomy of institutional scaling regimes across the U.S. higher education system. It shows that sectors differ systematically in affordability, research intensity, selectivity, revenue structure, and completion outcomes, implying that public research universities, state colleges, community colleges, nonprofit private colleges, professional schools, and for-profit colleges play different system-level roles.
finding.measure: Sector-level scaling relationships for revenue, expenditure, tuition, completion rates, and earnings

paper_profiles.title: Experimental momentum spectra of identified hadrons at e+e− colliders compared to QCD calculations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a high-energy physics analysis, not an education study. It examines experimental momentum spectra of identified hadrons produced in e+e− collisions and compares the observed distribution maxima to predictions from perturbative QCD in the Modified Leading Log Approximation (MLLA) under the Local Parton Hadron Duality (LPHD) hypothesis.

The author compiles published measurements of the variable ξ*_{p} for several hadron species (pions, kaons, protons, Λ, etc.) across a range of center-of-mass energies from lower-energy colliders through LEP. The main approach is to fit the energy dependence of ξ*_{p} and infer effective parameters such as Q0 and eff, then compare how well these fits agree with the theoretical scaling laws.

The conclusion is that the overall energy dependence of ξ*_{p} is broadly described by LPHD+MLLA, and a consistent value of s can be extracted. However, the paper also finds notable hadron-species dependence and tensions in the fits, suggesting that LPHD begins to break down at the level of precision considered. Because this is a particle-physics paper, it contains no postsecondary education intervention, no formative assessment, and no educational outcome data.

paper_profiles.title: Propensity score weighting for covariate adjustment in randomized clinical trials
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of covariate adjustment in randomized clinical trials, focusing on how to improve precision and balance when baseline characteristics are imbalanced by chance. The authors compare traditional regression adjustment (ANCOVA), inverse probability weighting (IPW), and a newer propensity-score-based approach called overlap weighting (OW), which is framed as a balancing-weight method.

The main methodological contribution is theoretical and simulation-based: the paper shows that OW can exactly balance covariates included in a logistic propensity model, and that it is asymptotically equivalent to efficient ANCOVA/IPW estimators for continuous outcomes. The authors also derive variance estimators for continuous and binary outcomes and evaluate finite-sample performance through simulations under balanced and unbalanced randomization, treatment-effect heterogeneity, and model misspecification.

An applied example using the BestAIR randomized trial illustrates the method on adult patients with obstructive sleep apnea and cardiovascular risk, comparing treatment effects on blood pressure and daytime sleepiness. Across simulations and the case study, OW is generally more efficient and more robust than IPW, and often competitive with or better than regression adjustment in small samples or under model misspecification. The paper is about general clinical trial analysis rather than education, and does not study educational outcomes directly.
